en: Preface:
The Buddha spoke of the simultaneous urgency of the Vehicle (the Mahāyāna path) and the Precepts; this is precisely what the Patriarchs meant by the correspondence of understanding and practice.

From the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs until now, they have never depicted Chan and the Precepts as two separate dharmas. Yet, as the distance from the Sage has grown long and the various Dharma-gates have come to favor contention, those who practice Chan disparage the *vinaya* (mokṣa).
Like chaff and husks, they indulge in unrestrained license; those bound by the rules regard investigation as being like water and fire, clinging to appearances until the end of their lives.
Within the Great Sameness of the Dharma, [the tradition] has been almost entirely torn asunder; only the Elder of Tian-shan follows the bequeathed instructions of the former Buddhas.

He demonstrated Chan to nurture the life-force of the Buddha and propagated the Vinaya to discern the capacities of practitioners. His dual eyes were perfectly clear and bright, as luminous as the sun and moon.

My elder brother, Master Shishu, was erudite and widely learned; possessing a deep awareness of the Dharma, he harbored a sense of awe. He concealed his traces among ten thousand peaks and collated the *Biyánjí* (Blue Cliff Record), which has already been published.
Furthermore, lamenting that the study of the Vinaya had fallen into desolation and was gradually becoming superficial and vulgar, he first took up the *Sā*... [text continues]
This *Essential Compendium of the Vinaya for Daily Use* gathers and classifies related meanings and collates them with commentaries and exegeses.

From the oceanic treasuries of the jeweled cases to the secular classics and histories, as well as all internal and external texts, nothing has been left unsearched. Furthermore, beneath each sentence of every matter, it weaves together the *Lamp of Chan* and cites public cases (*gongan*).
Thus, not only will beginners and the ignorant find clarity upon opening the volume, but they shall also come to understand both Chan and the Vinaya.
Those of the same lineage—namely, those who have long been practitioners—desiring profound and subtle conduct, must also secretly investigate within this.
The First Patriarch said, "Skin, flesh, and bone and marrow are all penetrated by one thread. In the past, Master Yunqi (Lianchi) composed commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Some remarked that because the sūtra itself is already clear and manifest, these works instead made it obscure; they did not realize the nature of the Buddha-dharma.
Fundamentally, there is no distinction between the shallow and the deep; whether coarse words or refined speech, all are the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

When the true eye is obscured by delusion, even the "thorny plums" and the "golden circle" are merely the gateways and doorways of common parlance. When wisdom shines forth with penetrating clarity, even the colloquialisms of the marketplace and street talk become golden chapters and jade verses.

Why then should one seek to simplify daily life? It is not that these things cannot be made divine and luminous through spiritual realization. I pray that those who read this collection [will understand this].
I have cleared away all barriers; do not give rise to views based on distinctions such as "great" or "small," or "refined" or "coarse.

May you strive so that both precepts and wisdom are urgent, and practice and understanding correspond, thereby becoming a great banner of light for the Dharma in the age of the Final Dharma. This serves as the preface.
Inscribed and written by his own hand as a preface by his younger dharma-brother Jie Xian of Huishan at Lingyin Monastery:
"At that time, I was at Ciguang Temple on Mount Huang, perusing the Dragon Canon (Tripitaka). When I reached the volumes of the *Śrāmaṇera-sūtras*, each case was as follows..."
The sun and moon shine brilliantly in the sky; without even realizing it, he joined his palms in praise and said: "This sutra is the very crux of all Buddhas and patriarchs.

Just as the sixteen princes in the *Lotus Sutra* requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma while simultaneously being śrāmaṇeras—their words and teachings still remain—so too did Zhaozhou and Yangshan of the Five Lamps simultaneously become śrāmaṇeras, and their public cases (gong'an) persist to this day. I have heard that since ancient times, as soon as one emerged from the mother’s womb, the transmission of the lamp was continued.

Having subsequently compared various editions of the world’s texts, I find that only the *Essentials* (Yao lue) by the Yunqi novice is widely circulated. Those who harbor doubts claim that even the Buddhist scriptures do not equal these Essentials;
others say that the phrases of the Buddhist scriptures are archaic and profound, difficult to recite, and that we must rely on our Master Yunqi Lianchi, who is a second coming of a Western Sage.

He descended to the city of Wulin and frequented the schools before becoming a śramaṇa. His speech and pronunciation accorded with those of this region, making it convenient for students to recite his works.
Thus, one may observe that his exposition of the *Daśa-śīla-vinirdeśa* resembles the *Chunqiu*, while his exposition of the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* resembles the *Liji*.
However, just as those who read the *Chunqiu* cannot understand the *Chunqiu* without a meticulous study of its four commentaries, so too [is it with his own works].
Regarding the origins and sources: one who reads the *Liji* (Book of Rites) cannot grasp its fundamental principles without thoroughly investigating the various histories.
How much more so for one reading the various sutras of the śrāmaṇera—how could they attain the essential tenets without delving deeply into the scriptural treasury?

Now, this *Yao lue* (Essential Abridgment), which concurrently masters both internal Buddhist scriptures and external secular histories, ought to flourish widely in the world. However, there are certain points within it that remain difficult to understand. Śā...

Throughout the various sutras, there were originally no verses or mantras. [The author] took the essential verses and mantras from other scriptures and compiled them into the section on *vinaya* (ritual conduct).
This was something that no one else dared to do, yet he did it alone; thus, one can see that his discernment and capacity far surpassed those of others.
When this *Yāolüè* (Essential Compendium) first circulated in the region of Wumen, the Vinaya Master Baoguo Maofa saw it and was immediately filled with admiration. Thereupon—
It is said: "This is the banner of light within the Dharma-ending age. Alas, it was regrettable that the verses and dhāraṇīs were incomplete;

I have supplemented them by carving the *Vinaya Daily Practice* (*Pini Riyong*) for subsequent printing. To this day, the precept-recitation ceremonies in all quarters follow these two texts as their standard.
Since I received the transmission from the Venerable Master Sheng'en, I have also been charged with the protocols of the ordination platform, and likewise employ these two texts."
He lectured and debated for the sake of various students, once saying: "The phenomena of heaven and earth consist merely of the odd and the even.

The human body stands upon the earth with its head reaching toward heaven; it, too, consists merely of the odd and the even. For instance, the head is the most honored part of the body and cannot be even;
if it were even, it could not be called 'honored,' and thus it is made odd. The hands and feet serve as the instruments of the body and cannot be odd."
If it were merely eccentric, it could not accomplish its purpose; therefore, it has been paired with the essential points of daily practice.
The whole is the Prātimokṣa; thus, one should treasure it as one’s own head, hands, and feet, never parting from it for even a moment.
Why not compile it into a single collection so that students may carry it upon their heads? Nevertheless, who am I to do so?
I venture to formulate this discourse because the aspirations of Yunqi [Zhuhong] to serve the state remained unfulfilled;
I have therefore recompiled and arranged them to ensure their completeness, rather than adding anything extraneous.

Nevertheless, fearing that students might not understand Yunqi’s method of excerpting passages, I have provided citations from the classics and histories beneath each section and compiled these annotations, so that they may immediately recognize the sources of the classics and histories.

I have been thorough; it shall not be obscure. Furthermore, fearing that students might encounter obstacles at every turn and become stuck on words, failing to recognize the mechanism beyond the conventional, I have again selected passages from the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of various masters in the Five Lamps (*Wudeng*).

This is to dissolve their habitual attachment to literary expression, so that they may directly expose their own inner realization without needing to borrow from others. Thus, I have combined these elements for investigation without confusing them, and investigated them through combination without categorizing them.
Equanimity. For example, regarding the myriad dharmas before one's eyes, there are none that do not reside within this Great Circle (Dharma-realm).
When they are unified, the myriad dharmas are entirely gathered back; when they are differentiated, the myriad dharmas are entirely released.

Through this differentiation and unification, manifesting them with spiritual brilliance, one need not hesitate to briefly extract a single word from within this sutra. By means of this, one can verify all quarters: whether they are ordinary or holy, correct or deviant, and so forth.
This is Tathāgata-dhyāna; this is Patriarchal Zen. Who is able to pass through this single-character barrier? Therefore, I say:

this sutra is the pivotal crux of all Buddhas and all patriarchs. For those who investigate it together, is this not the turning of the pivot of the Tathāgatagarbha and the opening of the key to the Patriarch’s barrier? One who attains its method does so without expending even the slightest effort. No...

A padlock must be used; it opens of its own accord when one attains sudden enlightenment. Without this method, even if one possesses the strength to lift a cauldron or pull up a mountain, it will be difficult to open that which is firmly closed.
Now, however, both the lock and the method for the key are fully present, awaiting those who pass through the barrier to verify them for themselves at once.
Preface to the General Rules,
written by the Daoist Shishu at Wumen on a boat during the spring of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era.
This is for combined consultation. It is only for śrāmaṇeras and bodhisattvas of the highest faculties that this may be consulted;

it is not taught for those of small roots or small capacities. Therefore, when practicing *cánchán* (Chan meditation), one must not look at the *yùlù* (recorded sayings) before attaining "entry into the head" (*rùtóu*).
One who has not received the precepts must not first read the *lǜzàng* (Vinaya Pitaka). This is why, when initiating the seven-day *cánchán* retreat:

All the scriptures are placed upon high shelves. When reciting the precepts or performing the formal confession of the precepts (*poṣadha*), those who have not yet received the precepts are strictly examined and must first be sent away.
This shows that the ancient methods for entering the gates of meditation and discipline still persist.

Now, if you desire to study these together, you must resolve to receive the precepts before you may peruse them; even then, it would not be too late. Should you violate this, you will incur [transgression].
One would be guilty before the former sages and bring calamity upon oneself.

What is most valued in the fundamental principle is that meditation (*dhyāna*) is identical to precepts (*śīla*), and precepts are identical to meditation; meditation and precepts proceed together without contradiction.
Therefore, when practicing Chan, one reaches a state where "contact" and "aversion" cannot be grasped; one dwells in right view where neither "observance" nor "violation" can be found.
The points where upholding and transgressing cannot be found; the points where right view encounters and turns away from them cannot be found.
Where the four paths of encountering, turning away, upholding, and transgressing intersect, how can one avoid them? All who read this must keep their eyes wide open.

The origins of the Sūtras and Vinaya are direct and straightforward, yet their principles are inherently profound and subtle. They encompass not only the texts of the Great Canon but also penetrate the essential tenets of the separate transmissions (*biezhuan*).

Therefore, all that is annotated here consists of the scriptures and histories of the sages and worthies; every citation and proof is none other than the pivotal机缘 (*jīyuán*) of the patriarchal masters.
I laugh at myself for having been dull-witted since ancient times, remaining ignorant while shut away in my room. Now, I seek only to inspire the heroic spirits of future generations.
There is benefit in opening this scroll. One may suddenly perceive the thousand ages before one’s eyes and awaken to the eternal truth beneath a single word.
Thus, disregarding my advanced years and the decline of my writing strength, I have dedicated myself solely to its circulation, composing this work in a hurried and rough manner.

I only fear that there may be errors in the phrasing or confusion in the strokes and characters; rather than incur the offense of the ancient sages, I would prefer to leave behind these potential mistakes.
To my future descendants: I look up to your lofty character and your tireless instruction of others. May you take pity on my earnest efforts and grant me your guidance;
this would be a second lifetime’s debt of gratitude to my teacher, for which I shall feel profound appreciation beyond measure.
Master Mugong compiled the *Ten Precepts Treatise* (*Shijie lun*), which was completed only after he had meticulously searched through and scrutinized every word of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
He further cited the Sūtras and Vinaya as annotations beneath the treatise. Readers claim that one should not use the Sūtras and Vinaya as annotations for a treatise;

yet they fail to realize that it is the treatise that annotates the Sūtras and Vinaya. Will those who read this not be struck with awe and vigilance, and from now on seek to cultivate goodness and abandon evil?
It is therefore appended here in sequence following the section on the Ten Precepts.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One shall not study external books, histories, or secular treatises. The *Bhikṣu-kuśala-śīla-sūtra* states:
"If for the purpose of debate to refute false views, or if one uses two parts of the Sūtras and one part of external books, there is no offense. It is because of this [that it is permitted].
One should examine them and distinguish whether those texts are heterodox or orthodox, acceptable or unacceptable; it is not that one speaks at random of being unpracticed in this regard.

For a beginner on the first stage (*ādikarmika*), there is no leisure for such study. However, if one is engaged in debate to refute heterodox views, one should employ the orthodox classics of the world to provide guidance;

these are identical to the True Dharma (*saddharma*) spoken by the Tathāgata. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says regarding the governance of the world: [the Buddha] taught... [treatises on] worldly governance.
Speech regarding livelihood, sustenance, and so forth—all such matters accord with the True Dharma; how could they be false?
Now, this compilation not only habitually employs the language of the Six Classics, but even down to poetry, prose, and folk proverbs, there is nothing that has not been gathered and selected;
all serve as auxiliary wings to the Buddha-Dharma, enabling later students to gain clear self-understanding. As for those words that are absurd, heterodox, or deviant, [they have been excluded].
I have strictly prohibited this.

Although the scriptures and their volumes are identical, the matters and principles differ from one another in sequence; therefore, I shall no longer provide separate titles for them, but instead distinguish them with this symbol (◎).
Do not allow the internal structure to become disordered, and the distinction between the "Jing" and the "Wei" will naturally be discerned.
Wherever there are no titles for the scriptures above the commentary, or where a space of one character is left blank, these represent my own limited perspective on the general meaning;
they are intended to provide an introduction for beginners and are not intended to defile the ears and eyes of the venerable masters.
Regarding the "Five Non-Translations" among the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanation of Terms in Translation), concerning the "non-translation of the secret," the ancient masters said:

"The *dhāraṇī* collections are all unintelligible. I say: Among the secret dharmas taught by the Buddhas and the Grand Masters, there is nothing that cannot be translated, nor anything that cannot be understood.
As for the function of mantras, they eliminate all leakage [of energy] and, directly, cause...

It is simply that each person must understand and awaken for themselves. I have often observed those who were illiterate—unable even to recognize the character "ding"—yet who possessed profound faith in the recitation of mantras.

Undaunted by cold or heat, they practiced with such diligence that they forgot their fatigue. Suddenly, one day, there was a sudden breakthrough; the texts of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings became transparent to them, penetrating without obstruction.

Is this not precisely the case where understanding arises from within that which is not understood? Therefore, regarding the various dhāraṇīs in the sutras below, we follow the bequeathed instructions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs:
they are neither translated nor explained, for it depends solely upon the individual’s own awakening.
The words and phrases of the sūtras and verses of this division may be recorded by hand; however, their meanings are inexhaustible.

Even if one possessed the wisdom of Śāriputra or the eloquence of Mañjuśrī, they could not fully praise them, let alone someone like me with the limited vision of a tube-gaze attempting to extol even a ten-thousandth part of them. Should one happen to encounter those of vast learning and wide experience...
Scholars, regarding those places where cited proofs do not reach their full conclusion, may nonetheless extract and briefly indicate them;

these should then be appended to the end of this volume for the benefit of those with the aspiration to study them in conjunction. To supplement [the work] once more, how could the merit of such a gift of Dharma ever be measured?

According to the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya Sūtra*, the Buddha commanded Ānanda to shave Rāhula’s head, and further ordered that fifty princes of noble lineage all be ordained as renunciants.
[Note]: *Abhūta-dharma* in Sanskrit; in the language of China, it means "unprecedented" or "rare. It is recorded in detail throughout the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
*Ānanda* in Sanskrit; here it is translated as "Joyous Celebration" (*Qingxi*). He is foremost among those of extensive learning (*bahu-śruta*). *Rāhula*:
in the language of Qin, this means "obscuration," referring to that which obscures the sun and moon. When the *asura* eclipses the sun or moon, he is named Rāhula. Regarding his causes from the past:
In a previous life, he blocked a rat's burrow for six days; consequently, he was caused to dwell in the womb for six years.
Because he was obstructed by the Buddha [in that past life], this became his name. Among the śrāvakas, he was foremost in secret practice. Regarding the account of Rāhula’s birth:

on the day the Bodhisattva renounced the world, the physiognomists said, "If he does not renounce the world tonight, tomorrow the seven treasures will come of their own accord, and he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). The King...
Throughout the four continents, that very night, musical performances were increased even further to delight his mind.
Thereupon, a desire arose within the Bodhisattva, and Rāhula was immediately conceived in the womb; Yaśodharā became pregnant that night.
At this, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens lamented together: "The Bodhisattva is entangled by desire; how pitiable are sentient beings! Who indeed..."

The Deliverer immediately transformed all the female entertainers so that they appeared exactly like dead people, most terrifying to behold, causing the Bodhisattva’s heart to give rise to weary detachment.
He then exhorted him to leave the household life. Chandaka led the horse, and the Four Heavenly Kings supported his feet as he passed over the city wall and went forth.
He went beneath the Bodhi tree and reflected. After six years of ascetic practice, he attained Buddhahood at the end of the first watch of the night;
at that time, Rāhula was born. Once born, he was returned to the Buddha’s wet nurse, who then said, "Siddhārtha has been away from home for six years;
from where have you now come into being? To carry a child for six years is something unheard of in the world. When the Śākyas heard this, they deliberated together, saying, "This is most..."
The details were unknown. [The King] thought, "She has brought disgrace upon the Śākya lineage; she must have stolen it secretly. I shall put her to death by the Dharma.
Yaśodharā said, "I wish to see the Great King before I undergo death. The King then sent word through a curtain, questioning her about the circumstances. Yaśodharā related the truth:
that this was the offspring of the Prince, and that ever since the Prince left home, she had been consumed by grief and distress, sleeping only on cold ground.
Therefore, the appearance of this child was no different from that of the prince. The king then wept and said, "He is truly my grandson.
At that time, the Buddha, wishing to provide witness, manifested as a brahmin and entered the royal palace. The child then asked him, "What is your name? He replied:
His name was Rāhula. A brahmin praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! By virtue of the causes and conditions of your karma, your fame accords with your reality.
This was the prediction regarding the circumstances of Rāhula’s renunciation.
At that time, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "Go now to the city of Kapilavastu to visit my father, King Śuddhodana, as well as my maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī."

Third, having introduced his father, King Droṇodana, and the others, he further consoled Yaśodharā, Rāhula’s mother, urging her to sever her affection and release Rāhula so that he might practice the Noble Path. Maudgalyāyana received these instructions and reported them in due order.
When Yaśodharā heard that the Buddha had sent a messenger to take Rāhula away, she was overcome with grief and distress, and she issued a strict command.
The supervising officials closed the palace galleries and placed everyone under strict guard. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived at the palace gate but was unable to enter;
he then used his supernatural powers to fly up onto a high tower. When Yaśodharā saw Maudgalyāyana approaching, she immediately rose to pay her respects.

The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to take his seat. He inquired after the World-Honored One’s health, asking whether he was free from illness and affliction, and whether his teaching and transformation of sentient beings were proceeding without weariness.

"I have now sent this superior man here; for what purpose has he come? Maudgalyāyana replied, "Prince Rāhula is already nine years old and should be permitted to leave the household life to cultivate and study the Noble Path.
All affection and attachment will before long change and perish; such is the nature of karmic retribution."
When the time arrived, suffering and happiness were in different places; though mother and child were close, neither could substitute for the other.

"If you would study the Way, you should return to deliver your mother. Thus Maudgalyāyana exhorted her with various arguments, but Yaśodharā remained sorrowful and resentful, stubbornly refusing to be converted.
Maudgalyāyana took his leave and informed the King. The King summoned Mahāprajāpatī and exhorted her repeatedly, yet she remained firm and did not comply. At that time—
The World-Honored One immediately dispatched a manifested person who spoke from mid-air, saying: "Yaśodharā, do you perhaps remember the vow you made in the distant past?

At that time, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I purchased five stalks of lotuses from you for five hundred gold coins and offered them to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, you requested of me that we be together in every life where we were born."
“Husband and wife—I do not wish to accept [this]. I have already told you: ‘I am a bodhisattva who has practiced vows for many kalpas;
in all acts of giving, I do not oppose the wishes of others. If you can do the same, I will allow you to be my wife. You then made this vow:

‘In every lifetime in which we are born, my kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and even my own body shall follow your commands in being given away; I swear never to have a heart of regret. Now, why [do you act otherwise]?”

She cherished Rāhula and would not allow him to leave the household life to study the Noble Path. Upon hearing this, Yaśodharā suddenly and clearly understood the causal conditions of her past karma as if she had seen them only yesterday.
Her maternal affection for her beloved son naturally subsided; she then invited Maudgalyāyana to perform a rite of repentance on her behalf and offered her apologies.
She took Rāhula by the hand and entrusted him to Maudgalyāyana. At that moment, mother and son parted, weeping bitterly.
Weeping with grief, Rāhula knelt long and addressed his mother, saying, "Do not grieve; I shall go to attend upon the World-Honored One and will soon return to see you.
At that time, King Śuddhodana summoned the prominent clansmen of the kingdom and addressed them, saying, "The Prince of the Golden Wheel..."
"I shall now go to the kingdom of Śvetī to renounce the world under the Buddha. You all should each send one son to serve as my companions.
At that time, the various ministers, obeying the command, escorted fifty princes to follow Rāhula to the place where the Buddha was.
They prostrated before the Buddha and renounced the world.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra to serve as his preceptor (upādhyāya) and commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana to serve as his teacher (ācārya).
At that time, Śāriputra, having received the command, administered the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts to Rāhula and ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.

[Commentary: *Śāri* in Sanskrit; this is translated here as "Śāri" (Sparrow). *Śāri* is the name of the mother. *Putra* means "son. The two are joined to form the name [Śāriputra]. Śāriputra’s maternal uncle was Kauṣṭhila.
When he debated with his sister Śāri, he was defeated. Kauṣṭhila reflected and thought: "This is not due to my sister's own power.
It must be that a person of wisdom is dwelling within her, using her mouth as a vessel for their words. Even before birth, she is already like this. And...
As he grew up, what was to become of him? Therefore, he left the household life to become a brahmacārin and entered South India, where he vowed never to clip his nails.
He studied eighteen kinds of sūtras; thus, Śāriputra is called foremost in wisdom. Mahāmaudgalyāyana—here translated as "Great Maudgalya"—is foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
To this day, the ritual procedures for the precept-teacher (śīla-ācārya) during the recitation of the precepts are performed in accordance with the honored Buddha’s injunctions.
Question: Why is it that while the Buddha is able to preach the Dharma for all sentient beings, he alone did not recite the precepts for Rāhula?
Answer: The Buddha commanded Śāriputra to recite the precepts for Rāhula for three reasons: first, because it was easier to teach him as if he were his own son;
second, to sever Rāhula’s feelings of attachment and longing; and third, because Śāriputra...
Because Rāhula’s spiritual capacity was in perfect accord with the occasion, at that time Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic radiance, expounded this dharma of precepts;
although the World-Honored One did not move his tongue, he had already expounded it profoundly.

In the *Sūtra on the Fields of Merit for All Virtuous Ones*, a śrāmaṇera should know five virtues. First, he resolves his mind to leave the secular world, cherishing and wearing the Way within his breast.
[Commentary:

This means generating a courageous and resolute mind to liberate oneself from the mundane world and practicing the Bodhi of the Buddha, cherishing and wearing the subtlety of the Way within his breast.
Second, one destroys one's physical beauty because one should wear the Dharma robes. [Commentary:
This means shaving off the beard and hair, destroying the marks of worldly appearance, discarding secular clothing, and donning the Dharma robes;
thus possessing the majestic deportment of a Buddha and remaining in accord with the Way.
Third: They have forever severed affectionate ties because they harbor neither partiality nor aversion. [Commentary]:

This means they have cut off emotional attachments so as not to be bound by longing; they possess no heart of partiality that seeks refuge with those of a different surname, yet they possess no heart of aversion toward living together in harmonious union.
Fourth: To cast away one’s body and life in order to revere and honor the Way. [Commentary]:
This means being able to cast away one’s body and life without any regard or attachment, striving solely with a single mind to seek realization of the Buddha-way.
Fifth: He aspires to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering sentient beings.

[Commentary: This means that he constantly harbors the intention to rescue all things and devotes himself single-mindedly and diligently to seeking the Dharma of the Mahāyāna in order to deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
These are called the five virtues. [Commentary:

Indeed, when one who has left the household life possesses these five pure virtues, they become a field of merit for the world. In the *Jizhong Jingxun* (Admonitions for the Monastic Community), these five virtues are considered the great essentials of leaving the household life.
All five groups of practitioners should uphold them together; it is not merely for those of lesser standing. They should be practiced throughout one's entire life.
Regarding the initial reception [of the precepts],
according to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, one should explain the ten items to a śrāmaṇera. The first is that all sentient beings exist by means of food and drink.

[Commentary]: In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is said that such worlds and the twelve classes of sentient beings cannot sustain themselves independently; they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), namely:
edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*), volition-nutriment (*manasikāra-āhāra*), and consciousness-nutriment (*vijñāna-āhāra*).

Therefore, the Buddha stated: "All sentient beings abide because of nutriment. [Ju-li] explains: "Edible food" refers to physical morsels, which have the three sense objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as their substance. Upon entering...
The stomach undergoes transformation and decay. Because it provides nourishment to the sense faculties, there is the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*). This refers to the encounter;

it takes up that which is associated with the six consciousnesses, and because it encounters external objects, joy and pleasure arise. The food of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*) refers to mental volition;

it takes up that which is associated with the sixth consciousness, and because volition directs itself toward desirable objects, aspiration arises. The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) refers to the eighth consciousness, which maintains and sustains [the body].

First, by means of the first three nutriments, it is sustained by their functional influence (*śakti-bhāga*), causing this consciousness to increase and become predominant, thereby enabling it to maintain the six types of sense faculties (*indriya*).
Second, the two truths (*satya-dvaya*).
[Commentary] Translation of Names and Meanings: First, "True Reality" (*satyārtha*) reveals the principle of the fundamental reality of the single nature.

This is what is called the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), wherein not even a single speck of dust can be received; both affirmation and negation are extinguished, and subject and object alike vanish. Thus, the myriad phenomena are pointed out as *tathatā* (Suchness).

This brings together the three vehicles to return to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Second is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which reveals the phenomena of the single-nature dependent origination.
That is to say, within the gate of the Buddha’s work, not a single dharma is abandoned: subjects are exhorted to loyalty, children to filial piety;
good is encouraged by showing the bliss of heaven, and evil is restrained by manifesting the suffering of hell.
Third, the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
[Note]: According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, "sensation" means receiving or experiencing. This refers to the consciousnesses of the six sense organs receiving the objects of the six sense fields.

First is painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*), which refers to the suffering of oppression arising from objects among the six sense fields that are contrary to one's feelings. Second is pleasant sensation (*sukhā vedanā*).
This refers to the experience of pleasant satisfaction regarding objects of the six sense-fields that are agreeable to one's inclinations.

Third is the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, which refers to the experience of neither pain nor pleasure regarding objects of the six sense-fields that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable.
Fourth, the Four Noble Truths. [Commentary:

According to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Graded Sequence of the Dharma Realm), "truth" (*satya*) takes "thorough investigation and reality" as its meaning. Understanding arises from hearing; this must rely upon the teachings.

Since the articulation of principle is not false, it is called "thorough investigation and reality. First, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Suffering" takes "afflictions" as its meaning. All conditioned phenomena...

Mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence; therefore, they are called "affliction" (*upāyāsa*). Second, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*):
"Origination" has the meaning of gathering and accumulating. If the mind is associated with fetters and karma, it will certainly gather and accumulate the suffering of birth and death in the future;

therefore, it is called "origination. Third, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): "Cessation" has the meaning of extinguishing and non-existence. Once the fetters and karma are exhausted, then...

Because there is no longer the affliction of birth and death, it is called "extinction" (nirodha). Four: The Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). "Path" takes the sense of being able to lead through as its definition.

There are two kinds of paths: First, the Right Path (*samyak-mārga*). This refers to the actual contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).

Wisdom that takes principle as its object and proceeds as practice is called the Right Path. Second, the Aids to the Path (*mārga-sahāya*). These are the various methods of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) within the contemplation of understanding, as well as...
All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are aids to the Path (*mārga*). These two support one another and can lead to Nirvāṇa; therefore, they are called the "Path.
Fifth are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

[Commentary]: In the Mahāyāna-Vistara-skandha-śāstra, "skandha" (aggregate) means that which covers or obscures; it is also called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*). "Skandha" also means accumulation. 1. The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*):

Form refers to that which possesses resistance and obstruction; this refers to the various faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. 2. The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*): Sensation refers to the act of experiencing or receiving.
This refers to the six consciousnesses corresponding with the six objects, whereby there arise six feelings (vedanā). Third is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);

"perception" means conceptualization, referring to the mental consciousness corresponding with the six objects to form the six perceptions. Fourth is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha); "formations" refers to the process of shifting, flowing, and volitional construction.

This refers to the fact that based on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one conceives of various objects and performs wholesome or unwholesome volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). As for the fifth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), "consciousness" itself is not differentiated;
it refers to the six types of consciousness—those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which illuminate and discern their respective objective spheres.
These five [aggregates] all combine and accumulate together, obscuring the original nature; therefore, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
Sixth: The Six Entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*). [Commentary:

According to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), "entrance" (*āyatana*) means "to enter and proceed. This refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) serving as the bases for the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*), which are able to engage with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Therefore, they are called the six.
Seventh are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

[Commentary: According to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), "enlightenment" (*jue*) means awakening and comprehension; that is, awakening to and comprehending whether the dharmas one cultivates are authentic or spurious.
"Part" (*aṅga*) refers to a branch or constituent member. This means that these seven types of dharmas each have their own distinct branches and boundaries without being confused with one another;

therefore, they are called the "seven factors of enlightenment" (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and also the "seven limbs of enlightenment. Among them, the three factors of investigation-of-dharmas, energy, and joy belong to wisdom (*prajñā*);

the three factors of tranquility, equanimity, and concentration belong to meditative absorption (*samādhi*); and the factor of mindfulness belongs to both concentration and wisdom. Thus, in the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one cultivates these...

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are precisely what constitutes entry into the Path. 1. The factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

This refers to when one employs wisdom to observe all phenomena, being well able to distinguish between the true and the false, and thus not mistakenly grasping at deceptive dharmas. 2. The factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
This refers to when one cultivates the various path-dharmas, being well able to discern and understand them, such that one does not engage in fruitless ascetic practices, and...

3. The awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): When one realizes the true Dharma within the authentic Dharma and attains joy, one is well able to discern that this joy does not arise from perverted dharmas, but abides in the joy of the true Dharma.
4. The awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): This refers to being well able to [apply oneself] when severing the various afflictions upon their appearance.
5. The awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): This refers to relinquishing the objects of attachment perceived through views;
being well able to awaken to their falsity and unreality, one never again recollects them. 6.

The factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): This refers to when one arouses meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), being skillfully able to discern all dhyānas so that afflictions and deluded thoughts do not arise.

Seven: The factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): This refers to when one cultivates the various factors of the path, being skillfully able to discern them and constantly reflecting on the balance between concentration and wisdom.
When the mind becomes dull or sluggish, one should apply the three factors of awakening—discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*)—and perform observation.

Regarding all phenomena, one should prevent mental dullness. When the mind becomes agitated, one should apply the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to eliminate it, and rectify the faults of body and speech.

One does not employ the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to abandon the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), but rather employs the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) to enter right meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
To gather the distracted mind and prevent it from wavering.
Eighth: the Eightfold Noble Path. [Commentary]:

According to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), this refers to the Eightfold Right Path. It means that these eight dharmas are practiced without relying on partiality or deviation.
It is called "Right" (*samyak*). Furthermore, because it can lead one to cessation and nirvana, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*). 1. Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*):

This refers to cultivating the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) so as to clearly perceive the Four Noble Truths, thereby destroying the various false views of non-Buddhists, such as those concerning existence and non-existence. 2. Right Resolve (*samyak-saṃkalpa*):

This refers to, at the time of perceiving the Four Noble Truths, engaging in right mindfulness and reflection, observing and deliberating so as to cause the contemplation to increase. 3. [Right Speech]... [Right Action]... [Right Livelihood]... [Right Effort]... [Right Mindfulness]... [Right Concentration]... (The text continues with the remaining factors of the Eightfold Path).

4. Right Speech (*samyag-vāc*): This means that by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one constantly restrains the activity of speech and remains far removed from all false and unreal words.
5. Right Action (*samyag-karmānta*): This means that by means of untainted wisdom, one cultivates and restrains the mind, abiding in pure right action and severing all perverse and deluded conduct.
6. Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*): This means remaining free from the five kinds of wrong livelihood.
Sixth, regarding gain and offerings: one should always subsist on alms. Seventh, right effort:
this refers to diligently cultivating the path of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), maintaining single-minded focus without interruption. Eighth, right mindfulness:

this refers to being mindful of the correct path of morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the methods for aiding the path through the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*), thereby enabling progress toward *nirvāṇa*. Ninth, right concentration: this refers to gathering together all forms of distraction.
Body and mind are tranquil; one abides correctly in the principle of true emptiness, remaining resolutely immovable.
Ninth: the nine abodes of sentient beings. [Commentary:
According to the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, this is because within the desire realm there is the oppression of suffering from the four miserable destinies, and within the form realm there are five...

The Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) devas, because they quickly delight in *nirvāṇa*, [are excluded]. Among the four *dhyānas*, the two heavens of Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born), and Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) are also not fixed;

for some seek the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), some seek the Pure Abodes, and some seek the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*). Therefore, sentient beings do not all take pleasure in dwelling there.

Only those who take rebirth in the auspicious destinies of gods and humans within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are counted as one. Furthermore, regarding the first *dhyāna* of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)... [the second...]

The first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna—along with the Heaven of Non-conception within the fourth dhyāna, as well as the four heavens of the formless realm—are all places where sentient beings delight in dwelling;
these constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Tenth: The ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (bases of totality). [Commentary:

Also known as the ten *vyāpy-āyatana-samādhis* (concentrations of pervasive spheres). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) serve as the initial gateway; the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*) serve as the intermediate practice;
and the pervasion of all spheres serves as the final accomplishment. This refers to the complete fulfillment of the three types of contemplation, whereby the essence of dhyāna is first attained.
Regarding these concentrations, they are called "pervading all places" because they are so named from the fact that the objects of observation pervade everywhere.
They are: (1) the concentration on blue pervading all places; (2) yellow; (3) red; (4) white; (5) earth; (6) water; (7) fire; (8) wind; (9) space;

and (10) the concentration on consciousness pervading all places. The first four refer to taking up the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) within the state of concentration. The [remaining] eight...
Regarding the blue color seen within the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), one causes it to pervade all places so that everything becomes blue;
the same applies to the other three concentrations. As for the latter six, this refers to taking up the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) once again within concentration.

Regarding the earth-color seen within the eight spheres of mastery, one causes it to pervade all places without exception; the same applies to the other five concentrations. As for the eight liberations: first, possessing the perception of internal forms...

1. One perceives external forms. 2. Having no perception of internal form, one perceives external forms. 3. The liberation of the beautiful, which is personally realized by the body. 4. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space. 5.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness. 6. The liberation of the sphere of nothingness. 7. The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
8. The liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception. As for the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): 1. Having the perception of internal form...

1. Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many. 2. Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many. 3. Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few.

4. Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many. 5. The sphere of mastery over blue. 6. The sphere of mastery over yellow. 7. The sphere of mastery over red. 8. The sphere of mastery over white.
These are extracted from the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
These are called the ten numbers.
[Note: These ten numbers are derived from the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya*. The listings in other schools differ slightly from these.
In the Sanskrit language, a *śrāmaṇera* is...
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Fan-yu" (Sanskrit): From the Han through the Sui dynasties, all referred to the Western Regions as the "Hu" (barbarian) kingdoms.

The Dharma Master Yancong of the Tang dynasty stated: "To the west of the Pamir Mountains, all belong to the Fan lineage; to the left of the Iron Gate, all are called Hu lands. "Fan-yu" refers to the Sanskrit language itself.
At the beginning of the kalpa, when all was vast emptiness, the celestial deity Guangyin descended as the progenitor of humanity and propagated the flow of the Sanskrit sound. There...
The term for *śrāmaṇera* consists of forty-seven syllables. Its original name is *śrī-māṇavaka*. Once the ten precepts have been conferred, he is named *śrāmaṇera*.
The two characters "sha-mi" (沙彌) are an ancient abbreviation. As this usage has been transmitted for a long time, it is not easily corrected;
while the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* simply calls him a *praśnaka*, other schools all use the term *śrāmaṇera*. For now, I shall follow the common usage.

Furthermore, the old designation remains in use. Moreover, there are three names for a śrāmaṇera: first, the "Crow-Driven" (Kākavācana), referring to one who is too young to perform tasks and is made to drive away crows;

second, the "Conforming to the Dharma" (Anuloma), referring to one who, though having shaved his head, has not yet become a renunciant, but after receiving the ten precepts, becomes a renunciant and is able to practice the dharma of a śrāmaṇera;
those from fourteen to nineteen years of age are all termed "Conforming to the Dharma. Third...
"Identical in form" means that once the teacher has performed the tonsure, one is said to be identical in form. Being identical in form is synonymous with having a [monastic] name;
that is, those śrāmaṇeras who have not yet received the ten precepts are all termed "identical in form."
This is called *sikṣācārya*.
[Commentary: "This is called" refers to translation; it explains the terminology of the Western Heaven (India) using the sounds of the Eastern Land (China).
The following clarifies the meaning of *sikṣācārya*.
This means to cease evil conduct through compassion and to extinguish worldly defilements while compassionately saving sentient beings.

[Commentary] In the *Nanshan bie xing pian* (The Separate Practice of Nanshan), it is said: "To cease the emotions of worldly defilement and to save the multitude of living beings through compassion. The preceding text derives from this.
When first entering the Buddha-dharma, one often retains secular sentiments; therefore, it is necessary to cease coarse and evil natures, and furthermore, to practice compassion.
It is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*). According to the *Shishi yaolan* (Essentials for Buddhists), "Xici" (息慈) means the place where one rests in and practices compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).

**Exegesis:** All Buddhas take the salvation through compassion as their fundamental principle. Now, regarding the term "Xici," does it not mean to save others through compassion? **Instruction:** To speak of "resting" (*xi*) means that there is nothing that does not rest;
to speak of "compassion" (*ci*) means that there is nothing that is not compassionate. One should know that the place of resting is itself compassion, and compassion is itself the place of resting.

When one abides thus, [the mind] comes to rest. Above, there are no Buddhas to be realized; below, there are no sentient beings to be saved. This is called "resting in kindness" (śikṣamāṇā), also known as "diligent exhortation" (śrāmaṇerī). [Commentary:

This means that one is free from the four natural transgressions and the six prohibited offenses, diligently exerting oneself through self-exhortation. Furthermore, it refers to the diligent cultivation of all manner of wholesome deeds.
It means to spur on the mental activities. "Spur" (*ce*) refers to the act of whipping; it denotes exerting effort to urge forward one's practice.
It is like a wild ox having a whip, a fine horse having a spur, or a student having a teacher. Yongjia said:
"Day and night, I am diligent and earnest, fearing that conditions may pass me by. When one’s practice reaches this point, one will naturally arrive home.
They are also called *śrāmaṇera* (novices).

[Commentary: According to the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*, "ji" (寂) refers to *nirvāṇa*. This is because it is said that a person leaves the house of afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to seek and proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.
However, if one seeks it, it is not quiescent. If it is already quiescent, what use is there for seeking? It is said that those who first study the Way must necessarily seek it;

by seeking it without ceasing, quiescence arrives of its own accord. Once the state of quiescence has arrived, seeking is forgotten. When both seeking and quiescence are entirely forgotten, this is called true quiescence.
(From the *Lüyi Lu*). Now, I shall explain it solely according to the three meanings of the translated term. First, regarding "stopping and compassion" (*sixin*): stopping...
The śrāmaṇera of the Tripitaka (Āgama) Teaching ceases the afflictions of views and thoughts and cultivates the compassion based on sentient beings.

The śrāmaṇera of the Shared (Pāramitā) Teaching successively ceases the three delusions and cultivates the three types of compassion. The śrāmaṇera of the Distinct Teaching, with a single mind, perfectly ceases the three delusions and perfectly cultivates the three types of compassion.
Next, regarding the *pravrajita* (renunciant): through diligent and energetic exertion, they transcend the realm of分段 (*bheda-bhava*, the mundane world of birth and death).

Regarding birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*): the *śrāmaṇeras* of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings strive with diligent exertion to transcend the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*).

The *śrāmaṇeras* of the Distinct and Complete Teachings [strive for] the three types of seekers of tranquility (*śamaṇera*): those who seek partial, true *nirvāṇa*; those who seek the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings;

and those who seek [the Great Parinirvāṇa] of the Distinct and Complete Teachings. Furthermore, Vairocana is translated as "Pure and Full. It is "pure" because evil does not fail to cease; it is "full" because compassion does not fail to be practiced.
These are the śrāmaṇera precepts; they are the true cause of Vairocana. Furthermore, Nirvāṇa takes non-negligence as its sustenance, and diligent exertion is the very meaning of non-negligence.
These are the śrāmaṇera precepts; they are the Dharma-food of the Great Nirvāṇa. Moreover, they are tranquility.

This is the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). Seeking [this] is the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). The unification of the initial and the original is called ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-awakening*).
These are the śrāmaṇera precepts; they are the main thoroughfare to ultimate enlightenment. Furthermore, the nature of evil is empty by essence, while the nature of compassion is inherently complete.

The nature of the mind is fundamentally free from indolence or neglect; its original nature is empty and quiescent. The *śrāmaṇera* who accords with principle is one who attains the precepts through realization of this principle. The *śrāmaṇera* of name is so called by designation.
The *śrāmaṇera* of contemplative practice is one who has perfectly subdued the five stages of delusion (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*). The *śrāmaṇera* of semblance is one whose six sense faculties are purified.

The *śrāmaṇera* of partial realization is one for whom delusions are shattered and principle is manifested. Vairocana is named "Pure and Full. In Great Parinirvāṇa, one is forever free from negligence.
Initial awakening and original awakening merge in profound non-duality. The ultimate śrāmaṇera is like the sixteen princes during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;

this is the true standard for a śrāmaṇera. According to the *Fahua he lun* (Treatise on the Combined [Meanings of] the Lotus Sutra), when the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had not yet left the household life, there were eight princes who followed their father into renunciation. Through the instruction of the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, they all attained realization.

The Buddha. Yet, there are those whose attainment of Buddhahood is swift and those whose is slow, demonstrating how the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are transformed into the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
If one observes this through the power of knowledge and vision, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are those that attain Buddhahood swiftly within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

As for the fifth and eighth consciousnesses, they are necessarily those that attain Buddhahood slowly after being transformed within the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*). However, as the meaning is not yet fully exhausted, it is now said to be "Great Pervasion" (*mahā-abhisambodhi*).
When the Buddha Jñānavijaya had not yet left the household life, there were sixteen princes who, because their father attained the Way, followed him to make offerings.
They subsequently also left the household life. Their mothers wept as they saw them off, and their grandfather and various kinsmen went together to approach and draw near to them.

Upon seeing that they had attained the Way, [the Buddha] revealed the names and characteristics of the eight consciousnesses as sixteen kinds, in order to accord with and approach [the needs of those princes].

Through the employment of unconditioned great kindness (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*), great compassion of identical essence (*sārabhāva-mahākaruṇā*), and all wondrous merits, they are nurtured and brought to fulfillment;

therefore, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood by the sixteen princes, no priority or sequence is mentioned. As for the fact that among the eight princes who attained Buddhahood under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, only Miaoguang, Mañjuśrī, Ranthadīpa, and Maitreya are specifically named, this is because one perceives only the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the reward body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
Regarding this meaning, the intention behind the transformation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) has not yet been seen.

Therefore, it is now shown that as the sixteen princes shall attain the Buddha-way, they will receive names according to their respective directions; this demonstrates that the vessel-world also undergoes transformation, and Buddhas are realized according to each direction.
In the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, King Aśoka saw a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera, led him to a secluded place, and paid him homage, saying:
The śrāmaṇera said, "Do not tell anyone that I have paid homage to you. At that time, there was a water-pot before the śrāmaṇera;

the śrāmaṇera immediately entered into it and then emerged from the water-pot once again. He spoke to the king, saying, "Be careful not to tell anyone that the śrāmaṇera entered the water-pot and then emerged from it again. The king then said to the śrāmaṇera, "I shall demonstrate this right now..."
People say that [the truth] can no longer be concealed; therefore, various sutras state: "Though a śrāmaṇera be small, he must not be treated lightly;
though a prince be small, he must not be treated lightly; though a dragon prince be small, he must not be treated lightly.

Though a śrāmaṇera be small, he can deliver sentient beings; though a prince be small, he can kill people; though a dragon prince be small, he can raise clouds, bring rain, and produce thunder and lightning."
The *Pilik* (thunderclap) [text] says: "One should be moved by its smallness and not treat it lightly. In the *Five Lamps*: When Zhaozhou was a śrāmaṇera, he visited Nanquan.
While Nanquan was lying down, seeing the Master come to pay his respects, he asked: "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied: "Ruixiang. Nanquan asked:
"Did you see Ruixiang? The Master said: "I did not see Ruixiang; I only saw the Reclining Tathāgata. Nanquan...
He rose from his seat and asked, "Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master? The Master replied, "I am a novice with a master. Xuan said, "Who is your master?
The Master stepped forward and said, "It is bitterly cold in the middle winter; we humbly wish that the Venerable Master is enjoying ten thousand blessings in your daily life.
Xuan held him in high regard and permitted him to enter the inner quarters. Yangshan Huiji went to visit Guishan. Guishan—
Question: "Are you a *śrāmaṇera* with a master, or one without a master? The Master said, "With a master. [The questioner] asked, "Where is the master?
The Master walked from west to east and stood there. Muzhou was struck by this. The Master then asked, "What is the dwelling place of the True Buddha?

Muzhou said, "By means of the wondrousness of 'thinking without thinking,' reflect upon the inexhaustibility of the spiritual flame. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source; this is the nature and its characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*)."
"Permanently abiding; phenomenon and principle are non-dual; the true Buddha is suchness. Upon these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
From then on, he held fast to this realization, remaining there for fifteen years. ○ Gao Shami of Lizhou first visited Yaoshan. Yaoshan asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master said, "I have come from Nanyue. Yaoshan said, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going to Jiangling to receive the precepts. Yaoshan—

Sanshan said, "This novice still has them hanging from his lips and teeth. The Master bowed and withdrew. Daowu came forward to stand in attendance. Sanshan—
[Zhaozhou] said, "Just now there was a lame śrāmaṇera who seemed to have some measure of spiritual breath;

I said that one must not yet place full trust in him, but he must be tested further before it is acceptable. That evening, as the Master ascended the hall, he called out, "Where was that śrāmaṇera from this morning?
The Master stepped forward from the assembly and stood there. The Master asked, "I hear that Chang'an is very bustling; do you know of it? The Master replied:
"Our country is at peace. Mount said, "Did you obtain this from reading the scriptures? Or did you obtain it from seeking instruction?
The Master replied, "I obtained it neither from reading the scriptures nor from seeking instruction. Mount said, "There are many who do not read the scriptures and do not seek instruction;
why is it that they do not obtain it? The Master said, "I do not say that they cannot obtain it; it is simply that they are unwilling to take responsibility for it. Mount then looked toward Daowu.

Yunyan said, "I do not believe the Way. When Shishan Shandao was a śrāmaṇera, Changzi sent him to receive the precepts, saying to him, "On your return day, you must go to the place of Master Shitou to pay your respects. After the Master had received the precepts...
He then went to visit Shitou. One day, while following Shitou on a mountain excursion, Shitou said, "You, chop down that tree in front of me so it does not obstruct me.
The Master said, "Why do you not bring me an axe? Shitou then drew his blade and held it out upside down to him. The Master said:
"Why do you not come over to that side? The Head replied, "What would you do with that side? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He then returned to Changzi. Changzi asked, "Did you go to Shitou? The Master said, "I did indeed go, but I simply could not get through."
Ziz asked, "From whom did you receive the precepts? The Master said, "I do not rely on another. Ziz said, "If it is so in that place, how is it here with me?
The Master said, "It does not contradict it. Ziz said, "You are being quite talkative! The Master said, "Your tongue has never even touched upon it.
Ziz shouted, "Get out! The Master then went out. Ziz said, "How could he have failed to meet [the truth]?"
"Person. Regarding 'restraint' (*vinaya*): it refers to the ten precepts and various codes of dignified conduct. [Commentary:

There are three grades of restraint. First is *vinaya*, which in the language of China means "skillful governance" (*shan-zhi*) or "subduing" (*tiaofu*). Second is *śīla* (Sanskrit), which in the language of China...
"Stopping and attaining" (*zhìdé*) means to cease evil and practice good; it is also called "precept" (*jiè*). The meaning of "precept" is to prevent and restrain.
The three *pratimokṣa*—*pratimokṣa* being translated in Chinese as "liberation"—mean to distance oneself from the fetters of delusion and karma to attain sovereignty.

The Threefold Pure Precepts (*tripuṇyaśīla*) are: first, the precept of restraining discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*). This involves severing every evil and initiating the practice of the Right Path; it is the cause for the quality of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

One cultivates and perfects the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Second is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): there is no good that is not accumulated, giving rise to practices that assist the Path;

this is the cause for the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), through which one cultivates and perfects the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Third is the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): there is no being not delivered, giving rise to the non-abiding path;

this is the cause for the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), through which one cultivates and perfects the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). However, within the single phrase "restraint" (*saṃvara*), both essence and function are fully manifested. As for what is called "essence" and what is called "function," it is said: [text continues].

What is this single phrase? If the essence is one, then function becomes two. If function becomes two, then the essence also becomes two essences. Two twos are not two; both essence and function are negated.
Even the negation itself is negated, so that even "one" cannot be established. At such a time, the benevolent wind blows harmoniously and the moon of compassion is cool and clear.
Nature and characteristics have not yet taken form; sin and merit have no fixed place. It is precisely without grasping—precisely.
Precisely there is no transgression; precisely there is the true locus of the *vinaya* discipline. Nevertheless, one must fix one's gaze upon even a single hair’s breadth.
Otherwise, if one is not bound by the *vinaya*, one will instead flow through the cycles of good and evil.

For example, on this side is a pit of fire and hell, while on that side is a pool of blue lotuses. If one gives rise to even a single thought of gradual defilement, then it is as if one were [caught between them].
Corresponding to the Dharmas of Liberation.
The Section on Precepts and Vinaya [Note]: The *Śrāmaṇera Sūtra* contains texts concerning precepts and dignified deportment; therefore, Yunqi also divided it into two parts, upper and lower.

Section: On the Distinction between Precepts and Dignified Deportment. If one does not understand that dignified deportment is not the precepts themselves, one will have no means of perceiving the essence of the precepts.

If one does not understand that the precepts are not merely dignified deportment, one will have no means of fulfilling the function of dignified deportment. Although there are two categories, they ultimately converge into one.
To state it briefly: the precepts take the restraint of the mind as their foundation, while dignified deportment takes the adornment of the body as its primary concern.

The Buddha established the precepts for those who have left the household life. [Commentary] This text is recorded in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. The Buddha’s establishment of the rules for those who have left the household life is like the system of a sage-king.

It means that those remaining at home are immersed in the dust and toil of worldly affairs, like galloping horses without bridles. Even if they should harbor thoughts of transcending the mundane and advancing toward the Way, how could such a state be possible?
Is this so? Therefore, the dharma of leaving home was established so that one may focus single-mindedly on entering the Way.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Chapter on the Wise and Virtuous," states in verse: "The household is a place of bondage through craving and attachment;

desiring to cause all sentient beings to be entirely free from it, I thus demonstrate that by leaving home one attains liberation and remains unaffected by any sensual pleasures. Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Merit* says: "If one can release others to leave home..."

The merit of receiving the precepts is boundless. For example, even if one were to provide a hundred thousand offerings to as many Arhats as would fill the four continents, it would not equal the merit of someone who, for the sake of Nirvana, leaves the household life and receives the precepts for even a single day and night. (From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*).
When ordaining someone, one should first ask: "For what purpose have you gone forth? If they say it is for the sake of food and drink, they should not be ordained.
If they say it is to seek the wholesome Dharma and to weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, [they may be ordained].
This is from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*: "Whenever one wishes to grant another the going forth, one must first provide them with the six necessary requisites:

the three robes, a sitting mat, an alms bowl, and a water filter. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, it would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings; one must never harbor or support a corrupt and wicked disciple."
They cannot be subdued. Why is this? Because such evil discipline brings calamity only upon oneself;

yet by harboring wicked disciples whom one cannot instruct, one causes immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil, leads them to slander immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas, and destroys the harmony of the Saṃgha, causing many sentient beings to incur uninterrupted karma of sin. Therefore, it is more grievous than mere evil discipline.
[This is] a transgression of the ritual rules. The verse by the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa states: "The teacher and the disciple must examine each other’s capacities.
If one does not first observe [this], both shall incur the offense of violating the Dharma. The *Denglu* records that Lord Cui Zhao asked Jingshan, "May I, your disciple, leave the household life?
The Master replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish."

At this, the Duke attained a realization. Regarding the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source): if one does not understand that the Three Jewels are of one essence and eternally abiding, one does not permit [others] to leave the household life.
If one does not comprehend this, the precepts are not fully possessed. If we speak in terms of contemplating the mind, a single moment of arising is called a "name."

What is called "one sentient being" arises and ceases in an instant; this is termed "one period. Within every thought-moment, the three poisons constantly arise—this corresponds to the three calamities at the end of a kalpa.
Of the three poisons, greed is primary; of the three calamities, fire is foremost. By means of inconceivable *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one contemplates these three poisons:
in a single thought-moment of greed, there is no place from which it arises; this is precisely [the state of] oneness.

It is extinguished by spitting upon the kalpa-fire; when mindfulness is fully realized, it becomes wisdom. Thus, with a single breath, the world is formed, and so forth, even unto all inconceivable and rare phenomena.
Simply by penetrating the single thought of the ignorant mind, one accomplishes the wisdom of all Buddhas.

There is no one who does not thoroughly understand this. If one does not comprehend it, not only will they not be permitted to leave the household life, but none of the myriad virtues will be accomplished, because they do not know the root of the Buddha-dharma.
Before five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*), one should focus exclusively on the Vinaya; only after five summer retreats may one listen to the teachings and engage in Chan meditation.

It is said: "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it dives into the water. Judging from this, the essential principles of the Five Houses can be differentiated, yet they can also not be differentiated.
Ultimately, is it the differentiated that is correct, or the undifferentiated? Only those with the true eye can discern this.
In the *Lamp Records*, it is related that when Yunmen arrived in Jiangzhou, Chancellor Chen invited him for a meal. As soon as he saw him, the Chancellor asked about the Confucian classics.
[The monk] did not ask about the Three Vehicles or the twelve divisions of the teachings, as there were already masters for those.

"What, then, is the matter of a patch-robed monk’s traveling on pilgrimage? The Master said, "I have asked several people about this before. [The monk] said, "I am asking you, Venerable Sir, right now.
The Master said, "Set that aside for a moment; what is the meaning of the teachings? [The monk] said, "Yellow scrolls and red volumes. The Master said, "That is merely the text."
[The student] asked: "Regarding words and language, what is the meaning of the teaching? [Deshan] said: "When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail;
when the mind wishes to contemplate, thoughts vanish. The master [Baizhang] said: "'When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail'—this is in response to the existence of speech.

'When the mind wishes to contemplate, thoughts vanish'—this is in response to deluded thought. What, then, is the meaning of the teaching? [The student] wrote nothing. The master said: "I see you have spoken."

The Minister of State asked whether he had read the *Lotus Sūtra*. He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "The sūtra states that all livelihoods and productive enterprises are entirely non-contradictory to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Now tell me, how many people have fallen from their stations in the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought?
The Minister was speechless. The Master said, "Minister, do not be so hasty. As for the Three Sutras and Five Treatises, they are merely for monks."
"Cast it aside! [The Master said. "Even after ten or twenty years in the monastic community, one still cannot manage it; how much less can you, Official, hope to do so?
The Official bowed and said, "I am guilty of transgression."
Therefore, when a śrāmaṇera undergoes tonsure, he first receives the ten precepts.

[Commentary: According to the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*, the system for renunciation in the Western Regions possesses sacred regulations. Initially, one receives the five precepts and is named an upāsaka;
this is the foundation for first entering the Buddha-dharma and is included among the seven classes of followers. The teacher next prepares a simple robe (*śāṭī*) for him.
The *śikṣāpada* (precepts) include the *saṃkakṣikā*, the lower robe (*antarvāsaka*), the water filter, the bowl, and so forth.

Only when these are conferred is one named a *śrāmaṇera*, at which point one is properly established within the Dharma, subsumed among the five assemblies, and becomes worthy of receiving offerings and benefits. Otherwise, one falsely bears the name of a *śrāmaṇera*;
since one is not fit to consume the constant offerings of the faithful, there is no doubt that one incurs debt. One should therefore act according to the teachings for one's own relief.

*The Scripture on the Conversion of Laymen by the Monk Du*. For those wishing to leave the household life: they shall wear their original secular garments and bid farewell to their sovereign and parents.

A verse says: "Transmigrating within the three realms, One cannot escape the bonds of affection. To abandon the mundane and enter the unconditioned— This is the true way to repay one's debt of gratitude."
Next, one ascends the platform to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
[Commentary: As for "receiving full ordination," this refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣus* and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
With the three masters and seven witnesses, every requirement is seen to be present and fully complete; hence it is called "receiving full ordination."
Now they are called śrāmaṇeras; yet regarding the precepts originally received, the foolish are bewildered and do not know them, while the mad neglect them and do not study them. [Commentary:
"Called by name" refers to those such as the bhikṣus of names mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*. It means that once one has become a śrāmaṇera, one should achieve [the goal].
One who is a vessel for the Dharma, yet possesses only its name without actual practice, is either mad or foolish.
The fool is dull-witted by nature and unable to study the precepts; thus he becomes increasingly estranged from the Dharma and willingly remains base and inferior.

The madman, though possessing some small measure of intelligence, neglects to study out of negligence; his delusion is even greater than that of the fool. Should one urge him to study the Vinaya, he will say:
This is merely taught for the sake of beginners. Why must the Chan school necessarily be like this? One simply fails to realize what Chan and Vinaya truly are.
After the Sixth Patriarch attained enlightenment, he further received the precepts from Zhiguang.
How could the "wild Chan" of today ever surpass that of the Sixth Patriarch? I have often said: within the house of the Chan masters, there remains but one word—Chan.
If there is a "Zen" character obstructing one's chest, it will surely suffocate and kill you. Yet, if there is no such "Zen" character in one's chest, it will likewise suffocate and kill you.
Only by means of this very discipline can one distinguish between the deluded and the foolish; there is not one who is not suffocated by it.
