Stone honey is produced there, and it is prized in China. In the *Hanwu neizhuan*, the Queen Mother of the West said to the Emperor:
"Among the medicines of the Most High are the purple honey of Zhonghua, the vermilion honey of Yunshan, and the stone honey of the kingdom of India. This is also recorded in the *Bencao jing*.
Cui Mi ate it and was not hungry; his vision became clear and his lifespan extended. According to the *Xianjing* (Scripture on the Immortals), honey is the "Mouth-Immortal" (*kouchi*).
However, within the Vinaya, eating after noon is prohibited. As for opening stone honey (*shimì*), it is because its decoction leaves no residue and serves as a medicinal stone.
Furthermore, in the *Zazang jing* (Scripture of Miscellaneous Treasuries), another ghost asked Maudgalyāyana: "Since the beginning of my life, I have constantly swallowed glowing iron balls."
"By what offense was this caused? Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being, you were a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
You took pure water to make a syrup of rock sugar (*śarkarā-maṇḍa*). Because the rock sugar was hard and large, you gave rise to a thieving mind and struck off a small portion.

Before the assembly had even drunk, you stole one mouthful. By these causes and conditions, you have incurred this retribution. This is the 'flower-retribution' (*puṣpa-vipāka*); [the 'fruit-retribution']..."
They are in hell; they fall together into hell. Thus the Sūtra (namely, this very sūtra) says: "It would be better to have one's hand cut off than to take what is not rightfully one's own. Alas!
How can one not be cautious?

[Commentary: "Non-material wealth" refers to wealth acquired through unrighteous means. According to the worldly laws, one who takes wealth through unrighteous means will suffer extraordinary calamities;
according to the Buddhist scriptures, one who consumes what should not be shared will incur the retribution of the Avīci Hell.

It is better to undergo the amputation of one's hand than to take such wealth, for the agony of hell is far more severe than the severing of a hand. Such accounts strike terror into the heart; therefore, this exhortation is made with the utmost urgency.
This is for the purpose of admonishing them.
The Discourse states: The Tathāgata traveled afar through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, steadfastly cultivating the myriad practices and undergoing the utmost hardships until he finally attained Bodhi.
Now, these sons of the Śākya do not weave their own clothes nor till the soil for their food; yet they say, "It is our own virtue that has brought this about. How could this be so?

All that is brought about by the conditions of one's own past actions: every thread and filament of clothing worn upon the body, and every grain or drop tasted by the mouth, were all obtained through the Tathāgata’s accumulation of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and diligence.
They were all acquired by means of the Tathāgata’s exchange of kingdoms, cities, wives, children, head, eyes, marrow, and brain. If one fails to reflect upon this thoughtlessly—

It is then splendid and sweet, more than sufficient to indulge one’s will. Should I fail to repay this even slightly, it would be as if swallowing copper or ingesting thorns—there could be no moment of peace.

Even were I to grind my bones to powder and burn my body to ashes, my gratitude would remain unexpressed; even were I to have my heart carved out and my belly slit open, my shame would be difficult to articulate.
Therefore, I shall not allow myself to rest by day nor permit myself to cease by night; I shall exert every ounce of strength until my very body is exhausted.
Within, there was no heart that wandered toward external things; with utmost sincerity and diligent effort, he sought but a small measure of recompense to fulfill his obligations.

Why, then, would one not give, yet instead seek to obtain what is improper through reckless hunting for non-material gain? Clutching at fraud to pursue one's ends, one lays waste to the property of others to provide for the assembly, only to divert it for private use;
one recruits others to preach for their own causes—how could such a purpose be appropriate? Such contradictions and errors are difficult to enumerate. Intending...
On what can one rely so as not to fear? Observing a grain of millet tasted by chance, I am moved by the thought of the ruminating of many lifetimes.
[Commentary: According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, because of his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he was later born as a human being with the hooves of an ox.
He was fed grass; the Buddha took pity on him, ordained him, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship. According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, Gavāmpati, in a past life, acted as...

Monks, once a bhikkhu plucked a single stalk of grain from the edge of another’s millet field to examine whether it was ripe or unripe; several grains fell to the ground, and for five hundred lifetimes he had to be reborn as an ox to repay that debt.
Having briefly smelled the fragrance of the lotus, he was rebuked by the spirit of the pond.
[Commentary: According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, there was a bhikṣu suffering from eye disease who went to the side of a pond of *padma* flowers and sat there facing a fragrant breeze.
The spirit of the pond accused the bhikṣu of being a thief of fragrance. The bhikṣu replied, "I have neither destroyed nor taken anything."
"What do you call a thief? the spirit asked. "To take what is not given without being asked—how can that not be called theft?
At that time, a man took some lotus roots and departed with them on his back. The bhikṣu said, "Why did you not stop him? Why do you call me a thief?
The spirit replied, "The dark robe of the *kāṣāya* is like ink; it does not reveal itself. How is one fit to speak with such a wicked person?"
A speck of filth defiles white silk; though small, every ink mark on jade or shell is clearly visible.
Only when a wise person has a fault as minute as a hair can others see it as large as Mount Tai. Therefore, one should always seek purity from them.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu sat in meditative concentration with single-minded diligence; he severed all afflictions and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Before the paper had even been paid for, it was suddenly transformed into bolts of silk.
[Commentary]: According to the *Huhai jiwen* (Record of Wonders from Lakes and Seas), there was once a Zen master who was about to pass away.

The temple guardian deity informed him, saying, "Master, you owe the monastery one bolt of silk; pay it back before you depart. The master replied, "I myself never used any silk; how could I be in debt?
The deity said, "At such-and-such a time, you used a single sheet of paper. Calculating the interest on that now, you ought to repay one bolt of silk. The master [realized his error].
[The Master] said, "Nowadays, there are not a few who misappropriate the property of the monastery, yet I have never heard of anyone being made to pay restitution. Why do you alone demand it?

The deity replied, "Those who wander through the six realms of rebirth can repay their debts on their own; there is no need for you to go and seek them out. You, Great Master, have already transcended the three realms;
if you do not take this now, there will be no way to find them later. The Master then entrusted his robes and bowl to the temple administrator.
[End. A minor error in the Sangha Hall results in being suddenly burdened by the fire-torture.
[Commentary: Baodian records that Shouyong of Mount Yungai used the funds for the monks' vegetarian feast to construct the Sangha Hall. After his death, a new...
While Abbot Zhi was sitting in meditation at night, he suddenly smelled the scent of burning wood and saw Xingyong with a flaming cangue around his neck.
Xingyong related his previous history in detail, pleading bitterly that he could only be released from his suffering if the abbot sold the monks' hall to provide a vegetarian feast for the assembly.
Zhi followed these words and held a feast; that very night, he saw Xingyong come to express his gratitude.
Changqiu used a detached force to capture seven fruits (the śrāmaṇera stole seven fruits; details provided in the preceding note).
He sent monastic property to laypeople, causing the "flesh-tree" to wail in grief.
[Commentary]: In the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, it is told that the bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana was constantly tormented by young bhikṣus.
Maudgalyāyana observed this and, using his supernormal powers, caused him to experience terror.
He then led him along until they saw a tree of flesh, which was swarming with many insects devouring its body, leaving no empty space. It wailed and wept with a sound like that of the hells.
A disciple asked his teacher, "What tree is this? Maudgalyāyana replied, "This is the monk Srestha, the administrator of affairs.

Because he acted with self-will, he squandered the property of the Sangha—flowers, fruits, and food—and sent them to laypeople. It is because of these causes and conditions [that he has been reborn as this tree]."

Having received this karmic reward in the present, they will later fall into hell. When those insects that devour trees think of the person who obtained the object at that time, would their gall not fail them?
To all who hold him in high esteem, there is none who does not pass on his precious longevity like ginger.

[Commentary]: Baoshou Zhao served as the steward for the Fifth Patriarch Jie. Once, when the Patriarch was slightly ill and required fresh ginger, an attendant went to the storehouse to fetch some, but Baoshou rebuked him.
The Patriarch, becoming aware of this, instructed the attendant to return with money to purchase it himself before finally granting permission.

Later, when the seat at Dongshan became vacant, the Prefect sent a letter requesting the Fifth Patriarch to recommend someone he knew. The Patriarch said, "The man who sold the ginger will do. He subsequently departed.
Chushi [Dongshan] was renowned for his lamps at Yangqi. [Commentary:
Yangqi Fanghui served as the storekeeper; he would always set out two oil lamps, which he would extinguish whenever he attended to his own personal affairs.

One should maintain a perpetual lamp, using offerings to purchase oil and lighting it separately to illuminate [the scriptures]. In the *Hanshu*, there is an account of an official who extinguished the lamp to read his private books.

One should not merely recite these inherited customs with one's mouth; rather, one ought to vow to put them into practice so that they may match the fragrant tracks of the sages—this is the most excellent course.
Or, having gone astray through error and then feeling remorse, one contemplates recompense for six steps.
[Commentary: In the *Pañcaśata-praśna-sūtra*, there was a bhikṣu who used the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. This bhikṣu was extremely intelligent;
he preached the Dharma and was able to lead others to attain the fruits of the four paths. Yet, because his transgression was so grave, he wished to make amends for it immediately. Thus...
He went to the kingdom of Śākya to beg for alms and obtained a great quantity of money and goods. Upon his return, he wished to repay his debt.

While on the road in the mountains, he was bitten by a seven-step snake. Knowing that he would die within seven steps, he sent his disciple back to his home country after six steps, saying, "Once you have repaid the debt, return;
I shall remain here waiting for you. When the disciple had finished repaying the goods, he returned to report this news.
Immediately upon rising seven paces, he died and fell into the Avīci Hell. At first, he entered a state of warmth before reaching the great heat;
thinking it was a warm bathhouse, he raised a loud voice, chanting sutras and reciting prayers. Those in the hell who heard this chanting of sutras—
Thousands of people attained liberation. The wardens of hell became greatly enraged and struck them with iron clubs. They immediately ended their lives and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Based on this evidence, one must not fail to repay debts owed to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; even though they suffered punishment, they were nonetheless able to escape [the lower realms].

This is surely the next best thing. Otherwise, when a bit of soil is lifted by a fingernail, its ascent is difficult to predict; yet when dust settles upon the ground, its depth can be foretold. [Commentary:

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that performing good deeds leads to pure ascent, which is likened to the soil on a fingernail; performing evil deeds leads to sinking and stagnation, which is illustrated by the dust settling upon the earth.
Dust. In the *Āgama* Sūtras, the World-Honored One took up some dust with his fingernail and addressed his disciples:
"Is the dust on my nail more, or is the dust of the great earth more? The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One, the dust on your nail is very little;
the dust of the great earth is exceedingly vast, such that it cannot even be compared by calculation. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If all sentient beings..."

It cannot be compared by means of calculation. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If among all sentient beings those who obtain a human rebirth were like the dust on a fingernail, those who fall into non-human states would be like the dust of the great earth."

The gravity and lightness of offenses are weighed against one another; yet when merit does not outweigh transgression, the cycle of cause and effect passes from parent to child, and how could retribution ever be exhausted?
One laments the lingering agony of the iron bed and copper pillar; one suffers the slow, piercing bitterness of rebirth in the womb of a horse or the belly of an ox.
[Commentary] *Zhuangchun lu*: To steal even one coin from the permanent property of the Sangha causes an increase of three *fen* and one *li* per day and night.
On the second day and night, interest accrues upon the interest. In a future life, one must repay this as an ox or a horse.
An ox repays eight coins per day; a horse repays seven coins per day.
Rather than devising plans with no means of success and vainly attempting to pull back what has already sunk into the deep abyss,
why not act while there is still time and prepare for the storm before the rain falls?
The third is non-lustfulness.
[Commentary]: According to the *Avataṃsaka*, his nature is not that of one who commits sexual misconduct. A bodhisattva is content with his own wife and does not seek the wives of others.

Regarding the wives and concubines of others, daughters protected by their kin, women betrothed through family mediation, and those protected by the Dharma, he does not even give rise to [lustful thoughts].
Regarding the mind stained by desire, how much more so when engaging in unwholesome paths?
Their minds are intoxicated and dyed by various female forms, like infants who do not perceive their own true nature. They are like plain white cloth, easily dyed by color;
they are submerged by desire and cannot emerge from it, like worms in filth that delight in dwelling among excrement, or like filthy swine.
Adorning the body with impurities—O *Laṅkāvatāra*, if the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths, becoming either a high-ranking Mara-king or a mid-level Mara-subject.

The Inferior Class of Māra-Daughters. ◎ If one who cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) does not sever sexual desire, it is like steaming sand and stones in the hope of producing rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will merely be called "hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not the source of rice; it is composed of sand and stone.
According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva should give rise to a heart of filial piety and compassion to rescue and deliver all sentient beings. This is the pure Dharma.
To engage in sexual intercourse with others, and furthermore to arouse lust in all people— without distinguishing between animals and even one's mother, daughter, or sister—
and to commit incest with one's six close relatives while lacking a heart of compassion, constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva. According to the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections*,
a renunciant śramaṇa severs desire and abandons attachment, recognizes the source of his own mind, and penetrates the profound principle of the Buddha.
Awakening to the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there is nothing attained within and nothing sought without. The mind is not bound to the Path, nor does it form karma.
Without thought and without action, neither practicing nor realizing, one does not pass through the various stages yet is spontaneously most exalted;
this is called the Way. As a verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Just as adding dry wood to a fire increases its blazing intensity, so too is craving..."
Regarding "pleasure": the fire of craving increases ever further. Although the fire of wood, when blazing fiercely, all people are able to abandon;

yet the fire of craving burns the world, so pervasive that it cannot be cast off. In the *Dhyāna-rahasya-sūtra*, when the Elder Maudgalyāyana attained the Way, his former wife followed him, adorned with magnificent finery, intending to corrupt him. At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses for her: [The verses follow.]
Your body’s bones stand joined together, wrapped and bound by skin and flesh; it is filled within with impurities, not a single part of which is a fine thing.
A bellows-bag containing excrement and urine, with nine orifices constantly discharging filth, you are like a ghost with nothing desirable—how could you be worthy of self-pride?
Your body is like a walking latrine, covered only by a thin skin; it is something the wise abandon from afar, like a person [discarding]...
Leave the latrine and depart. If people knew your body as I loathe and detest it, they would all avoid it, just as one avoids a pit of excrement.
Yet you adorn your body with flowers, perfumes, and necklaces—things for which ordinary fools harbor craving and love.
The wise are not deluded by this. Your body is a collection of impurities, an accumulation of various foul and evil things, like a decorated latrine;
yet fools consider it beautiful. Your ribs are fixed against your spine, like rafters resting upon beams and ridgepoles.
The five viscera are within your belly, as impure as a chest of excrement. Your body is like a house of filth, a treasure coveted by fools, adorned with—

This is non-false speech. False speech is that which is deceptive, hollow, and unreal.
To feign ignorance while actually knowing—claiming to be ordinary when one is holy—causes beginners to wander in confusion, lose their resolve, and falter in their progress.

This is precisely what is meant by deceiving the ordinary and deluding the holy, confusing the minds of people, offending the Buddhas above and misleading sentient beings below. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "A Bodhisattva always..."

Right speech and right view give rise to all sentient beings; yet right speech and right view, conversely, further give rise to the wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions of all sentient beings.
This is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva. As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech leads one to ascend to heaven. Truthful speech makes the small as great; through false speech, one enters [hell]."
Hell. Verses on the Primary Retribution: Deceitful in speech and clever at tricking others, one receives punishment in hell with clumsy skill.
Flames and saws dismember the body; red-hot iron plows the tongue; molten copper is poured over it; it is ground by hard steel. The pain shatters the marrow of the bones;

one groans and wails in constant sobbing. Verses on the Habitual Retribution: Through false speech one enters the three miserable realms; once the retribution for sins in the three realms is exhausted—
[The verse] concludes: "Remaining karma leads to birth in the human realm; one is constantly plagued by the anxiety of being slandered and is again deceived by others.
The fire of resentment burns like heat. The wise do not blame others; they must extinguish the causes to verify the fruits. From the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* verse:
"Harsh speech that touches upon afflictions, delighting in exposing the private secrets of others, and being stubborn and difficult to subdue—such lead to birth as a *jvalamukha* hungry ghost."
The Mirror of the School: Regarding the fourth precept, non-lying. There are dharma-gates wherein one has not attained [realization] yet claims to have attained it.

Foolish ordinary beings, amidst the suffering of the lower realms, perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure; they erect the banner of *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am") and beat the drum of self-aggrandizement.

Clinging to existence while disputing with non-existence, and clinging to non-existence while disputing with existence, they give rise to the sixty-two views, destroy the eye of wisdom, and fail to perceive the ultimate reality.
One is fully prepared for the four verbal transgressions. Those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three regard the yellow leaves of birth and death as true gold;
those in the Realm of Neither Perception nor Non-perception mistakenly reckon their own and others' states to be *nirvāṇa*. This is not false speech—what, then, is false speech?

The followers of the Two Vehicles compete to grasp at shards and pebbles with joy, carrying them out and conceiving the thought that they have attained extinction. Yet birth is not yet exhausted; how could they have attained extinction? How could they have attained peace?
They harbor the notion that they have attained what they have not yet accomplished; how can they find peace? In truth, they have not attained complete liberation.
To claim what has not been attained as attained—is this not falsehood? The Buddha, for the sake of those to be taught through the four gates, explained the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Yet, by clinging to "existence" alone, one obstructs the other three gates; even clinging to "neither existence nor non-existence" fails to harmonize existence and non-existence. Indeed...
The true mark (dharmatā) is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. How can one use words? Words are [merely] applied to the wordless.

How can one use numbers? Numbers are [merely] applied to the numberless. Is this not, then, false speech? One who has attained perfect realization (yuanren) observes reality as it is, without conceptual observation.
To speak according to reality means that one who contemplates according to reality does not contemplate internally, nor even externally or both internally and externally;
yet, this wisdom is not attained through non-contemplation. To speak according to reality means that all is real—contemplating reality as neither unreal and so forth.
Thus, all these are called the *Dharmatā-sūtra*. It says: "All Buddhas speak only the truth. This is...
For this reason, the sound of the Buddha-way is made heard by all. Even a person of perfect realization may speak falsely;
for instance, within the Dharma-gate, there is no chariot, yet one speaks of a chariot to entice a young child. There is no pleasure, yet one speaks of pleasure to stop a crying infant.
If there are sentient beings who obtain benefit through false speech, the Buddha also speaks falsely. Furthermore, he says, "I am the Śrī of desire."
"Such as: 'I am a deva,' or 'I am a human. In truth, I am neither a deva nor a human; yet by employing the false to bring forth the false, I cause [others] to attain what is not false.
The commentary states: There are four kinds of false speech. First is lying, which means taking what is right to be wrong, and taking what is wrong to be right.
To say one has seen what was not seen, or to say one has not seen what was seen—such things are false and unreal.
[Commentary: Speech is the sound of the mind. When the mind is upright, speech is upright; when the mind is deviant, speech is deviant.

*Shu* (commentary) refers to speaking directly; it is speech produced from one's own intention. *Yu* (discourse) refers to proclaiming and recounting; it is discourse based upon what has been seen or heard.
It is speech. Therefore, the speech of the Tathāgata is nothing other than that which benefits sentient beings; thus, there are words of truth, words of reality, and words of rectitude.
The speech of sentient beings is nothing other than that which harms sentient beings; thus, there are words of falsehood, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.
Within false speech there are small and great degrees, and in the punishment for it there are light and heavy measures. (From the *Fendeng Lu*, Fanchang).
Yun said: "At the assembly on Vulture Peak, have you ever seen a Buddha who lacks karmic practice?
Or a patriarch who utters falsehoods? It is very much like comparing cow urine to sandalwood; what connection could there possibly be?"
Second, frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) refers to ornate, empty, and insubstantial talk.

[Commentary: Frivolous speech consists of flowery and beautiful words that lack substance; it is speech that glosses over faults and embellishes errors. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that one’s speech must always be beneficial;
the karmic retribution for frivolous speech is such that even if one’s words are true, speaking them at an improper time constitutes frivolous speech as well. (From the *Śata-śāstra*).
The Master said: "To speak at an inappropriate time is also called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). The *Lunyu* states: 'In speech, let it suffice to convey the meaning.
Since this shows that one takes conveying the meaning as the goal rather than regarding richness and elegance as skillful, we see that even Confucius cautioned against frivolous speech."
"Sensual Songs and Erotic Verses" (Yanqu qingci): "They lead to desire, increase sorrow, and distract the human will. [Commentary]:
Regarding the compositions of the ancient Yuefu, none match the Han and Wei dynasties in their correct and elegant prosody. Subsequent imitations gradually became more ornate and beautiful.
This reached its peak when Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty was so infatuated with *faqu* (court music) that he selected three hundred courtesans to train at the Li [Theater].
The Imperial Garden (Liyuan). Those who sing songs today claim that the Liyuan originated from this. The *Zuanyao* states: "Singing in unison is called *ou*;

the songs of Wu are called *yu*; the songs of Chu are called *yan*; and licentious songs are called *wa*. As for the emotional lyrics and melodic rhythms, they are winding and intricate, exhausting the thoughts of the mind.

Regarding the lyrics and the melodies, there is no lack of shifting scales and changing modes; they differ slightly according to the times. Generally speaking, [this applies to] the Han and Tang periods."
The Imperial Music Bureau (Shàng Lèfǔ) was esteemed during the Song and Yuan dynasties; these were all the works of poets and literary travelers, not fields for scholars to trespass upon.
It is said that the passionate lyrics of such songs and verses are the fetters that bind one to delusion and attachment, and the primary culprits that lead toward desire and increase sorrow.
Regarding *Bǐcān*: Lǐ Bóshí was skilled at painting horses. Xiù [criticized] Tiěmiàn’s scolding.

He said, "You are a scholar-official renowned for your painting, and yet you have painted horses; you expected one person to marvel at your skill, but to have your excellence enter into the belly of a horse is enough to cause dread.
Thereupon, Bo Suì set aside his brush. The Master urged him to paint an image of Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgression.
Huang鲁直 (Huang Lüzhi) was skilled in erotic verse, and the Master likewise rebuked and censured him. Huang laughed and said, "In that case, you shall place me in the belly of a horse as well!"

"Yes," he replied. The Master said, "Sensual words stir the lustful hearts of all people under heaven; they do not stop at the bellies of horses, but I fear they will lead one instead to birth in the *niraya* hells.
Huang was struck with awe and repented, apologizing for his error, and thereafter he exerted himself with diligent vigor.
Third is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), which refers to using coarse and abusive language toward others and so forth.
[Commentary: As for "coarse and abusive language," its sound is worse than that of an owl; therefore, it is something virtuous people cannot bear to hear.
How could one ever bear to utter such words? One should know that by maintaining silence, one preserves oneself; the sounds of slander and poison will then cease of their own accord.
Vimalakīrti always used gentle speech because he did not engage in harsh talk. In the *Zhulin*, it is said:
"Anger is the root of losing all wholesome dharmas, the cause and condition for falling into the evil realms, the enemy of the joy of the Dharma, and the great thief of the virtuous mind. It is evil.
The mouth is the axe and hatchet for the merit, wisdom, and internal organs. For ordinary beings, poison is fierce and the fire of anger burns constantly;

encountering conditions, they give rise to obstacles, and touching objects, they produce hatred. Thus, when a single word of rage issues forth, it strikes the mouth and burns the heart, harming the person before them with a pain sharper than being cut by a blade.
This violates the virtuous mind of a Bodhisattva and contravenes the compassionate instructions of the Tathāgata.

The fourth is double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*). This refers to speaking about one person to another, and speaking about that person to this one, thereby creating estrangement between those who share bonds of affection and righteousness, inciting strife, and so forth.

[Commentary] According to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*: "To ensure that one's kin and followers do not become divided, and to skillfully reconcile disputes and litigation, one does not repay others with double-tongued speech. As for double-tongued speech:"
Because they spread rumors back and forth without truthful words, they incite strife between the two parties;
thus, the bond between teacher and disciple is lost and the righteousness between friends is severed, leading even to the calamities of ruining states and destroying families.
...up to praising in front and slandering behind, or being agreeable to one's face while contradicting one's back.
[Commentary: "Praising" (yù) is the pivot for extolling the good; "slandering" (huǐ) is the mechanism for proclaiming evil. In the "Yuanjian" chapter of the *Fangzi*, it says:
"False praise is a thief of benevolence (*rén*); false slander is a thief of righteousness (*yì*). A thief of benevolence is akin to the "village original" (*xiāngyuán*). Thief...

The *Yìjìnxiāngshàn* (Satires on Intimate Matters) and the *Yìlín* (Forest of Meanings) cite the *Wángsūnzǐ*, which says: "Those who wag their lips and ply their tongues to arbitrarily create right and wrong are the same as those who praise others to one's face and yet disparage them behind one's back."
To testify to another's transgressions and to proclaim another's shortcomings.
[Commentary]: To hear of another’s faults is like hearing one’s father’s name; it may only be heard by the ear, but must not be uttered by the mouth.
All of these belong to the category of false speech.

[Commentary: According to the *Vinayaviniścaya*, a disciple of the Buddha should always speak the truth and ought not to take oaths, because doing so would serve only to clear one's own name while expressing a lack of trust in others.
Even if one is falsely accused or slandered, one should still not make a vow. This is as stated in the *Caryā-melāyana-sūtra*.
Their speech is gentle, yet their hearts harbor malice; they look upon others with great joy and associate with them as if they were kin.
Their words are soft, but within their hearts they contain poison—like a tree whose flowers are brilliant in color, yet whose fruit is bitter as venom.

If an ordinary person claims for themselves that they have realized the state of a sage—[Commentary: To claim for oneself that one has realized the state of a sage is like an ordinary person falsely styling himself a sovereign;
he brings about his own execution and destruction. *Ārya* is translated as "sage" (*sheng*) and is also said to mean "to transcend suffering. How easy is it to claim such realization? In the past...
The Grand Chancellor of Shang asked Confucius, "Are you, Master, a sage? He replied, "I, Qiu, am merely widely learned and possess a strong memory;
I am not a sage. [The Chancellor] asked, "Were the Three Sovereigns sages? He replied, "The Three Sovereigns were adept at employing wisdom and valor;

whether they were sages is beyond what I know. [The Chancellor] asked, "Were the Five Emperors sages? He replied, "The Five Emperors were adept at employing benevolence and righteousness; whether they were sages is beyond what I know."
The Grand Chancellor was startled and asked, "In that case, who is the sage? Confucius paused for a moment, then, with a change in his expression, replied, "To the west there is a sage.
He inspires confidence without speaking; he brings order without governing; he effects transformation without acting.
How vast and boundless he is! No one is able to give him a name."
As it is said, "one has already attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.

[Commentary]: This is translated as "Stream-enterer" (preliu). In this stage, one eliminates the eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).

Because one perceives the True Truths, it is called the Path of Insight (*darśana-mārga*), and it is also termed the Stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya-avasthā*). One enters the stream of the Dharma of the Noble Path; as the *Vajra* states, "one enters."

Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Alternatively, it is translated as "one who flows against the current," because they flow against the stream of birth and death and do not incur the karmic debts of the three miserable realms.
Once-returner fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
[Commentary]: This is translated as "one who returns once. In this stage, one severs the first six of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm.
Exhausted. Because the final three grades [of defilements] still remain, one returns once more.
This is the fruit of Anāgāmin.
[Commentary]: This is translated as "Non-returner. It means that at this stage, having exhausted the final three grades of afflictions of the desire realm, one does not return again.
Because of taking birth in the desire realm, [one attains] the fruit of Arhatship. [Note:

This is translated as "One Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa). This means that at this stage, the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) pertaining to the form realm and the formless realm have been completely severed; [this is characterized by] the four knowledges (*jñāna*).
"I have already perfected [the path]. I have already transcended the three realms. I have already realized *nirvāṇa*.
Because there is no further Dharma to learn, I am called one who speaks great falsehoods. This sin is extremely grave. [Commentary:
To falsely claim to have realized the four fruits when one has not; to falsely claim to have attained the four dhyānas when one has not; to have failed to awaken...

Regarding the Way: to falsely claim to have realized the Way, or to falsely claim that devas, dragons, ghosts, or spirits have come, and so forth—these are empty and unreal, deceiving and deluding the people of the world;
this is called "great false speech. If one’s practice has gained some efficacy, yet one does not understand the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), [one may fall into such errors].
This refers to what is called *adhimāna* (conceit), such as regarding one's own [attainments] as the true fruit. Since there is originally no intent to deceive, one does not lose the precepts.
However, one must inquire of a wise teacher or a senior practitioner to correctly resolve what is right and wrong.

One must earnestly repent, relinquish all attachment to the mind, and seek the essential truth with diligence; only then will one avoid falling into ruin. This applies whether one originally intended to speak falsely or...
If one does not clearly understand or has not yet received [the teaching], or if one desists and does not speak, these constitute offenses of preparatory transgression that are subject to confession.
Regarding other instances of false speech, there is no offense if it is employed as a skillful means out of compassion to rescue another from urgent distress or to provide beneficial aid.

[Commentary]: Once there was a hunter pursuing a rabbit. The rabbit fled and took refuge beneath the Buddha’s seat. A short while later, the hunter arrived at the Buddha’s location and asked, "Did you see the rabbit?
The Buddha replied, "I did not see it. The hunter then departed. Later, a disciple asked why the Buddha, when the rabbit was clearly beneath his seat, had said he did not see it.
The Buddha replied, "It was for the sake of saving the rabbit. The words of the World-Honored One are indirect [for the purpose of compassion]."
Within this there is rectitude. Therefore, although his words were not straightforward, they possessed the merit of benefiting all things.

In the *Analects*, regarding the case where a father stole a sheep and the son testified against him, Confucius said: "The father conceals for the son; the son conceals for the father. Rectitude is found therein.
Although the son’s testimony that his father had stolen the sheep was straightforward, it was straightforward without propriety (*li*); therefore, he incurred [punishment].

Regarding the sin of filial impiety, the ancients said it is the essential requirement for conducting oneself, beginning with the refraining from false speech; how much more so for one who studies the Way that transcends the world.
[Commentary] Lord Liu Zhongding asked Lord Sima Wen Gong: "The essential requirement for exerting one's mind and conducting oneself throughout one's entire life..."
"Can I hear how one who practices this does so? Wen replied, "It lies in sincerity. He asked again, "What should one take as the beginning when practicing this?
Wen said, "The essential point of self-cultivation begins with not speaking falsely. These two gentlemen were eminent scholars of the Song dynasty.

The *Jintang Fofa* (The Dharma of the Golden Fortification) records this in detail. Those worldly scholars who take the study of the Way as their primary responsibility still deliberate upon words and deeds;
how could the supramundane study allow for such a discrepancy between word and deed?

I have often heard that the virtuous predecessors of old had no words they would not practice throughout their lives, nor any actions they would not speak of. One should reflect upon this three times each day.

How could I not feel ashamed and break into a sweat? From this day forward, I shall take the sincere words of my predecessors as my model, just as an infant learns the words of a compassionate mother, using them to admonish myself.
This is my admonition: Words convey the Way; the vessel of conduct is the foundation of virtue.
If words are lost, the Way is forfeit; if conduct is lost, virtue is diminished. To follow one’s words and practice one’s deeds—the gentleman must contemplate this deeply.
Do not be censured by ghosts and spirits; do not be treated as a mere beast by Heaven and Earth. A single phrase spans from antiquity to the present; a single action becomes a sword’s edge.
Before speech and deed have yet been uttered, one must be most cautious and strictly vigilant. The *Lingyuan Baoxun* says: "In every movement and gesture..."
One must not fail to exercise careful scrutiny. One's words and deeds must not fail to be examined. Those who speak little are not necessarily foolish;
those with eloquent tongues are not necessarily wise. Those who are simple and unrefined are not necessarily perverse; those who are compliant and submissive are not necessarily loyal.

The *Sūtra* (referring to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* and the *Sūtra on Requiting Kindness*) records that a śrāmaṇera once mocked an elderly bhikṣu for reciting the sūtras with a voice like the barking of a dog.
This elderly bhikṣu was, in fact, an arhat. Because he instructed the śrāmaṇera to perform an urgent repentance, the latter narrowly escaped hell;
yet, he still fell into the body of a dog. A single word of evil speech can bring such harm as this.
[Commentary]: According to the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), by uttering a single harsh word, one falls into the body of a dog for five hundred lifetimes.
In his final existence as a merchant’s dog, he was beaten and cast away for stealing meat; wailing in grief with no one to turn to, Śāriputra used his supernatural powers to come to his rescue.
At the end of his life, he was reborn into a brahmin family. At the age of seven, he was ordained as a śrāmaṇera named Kunti.
Having further heard the essential teachings of the Dharma, he attained the realization of arhatship (aśaikṣa). Remembering to repay his teacher’s kindness, he vowed to serve him for all eternity.

As for the one who fell into the body of a dog because of a single word of derisive laughter, it is clear that the fruit does not obscure its cause. It is just like when the śrāmaṇera at that time praised the elderly bhikṣu.
Regarding those who read the scriptures with a voice like that of the Buddha, such śrāmaṇeras will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Thus, the *Dharmapada-gāthā-sūtra* states: "When a man dwells in the world, an axe is held within his mouth; it is by means of this that he cuts himself, for it is through the utterance of evil words. How can one not be cautious?"
[Commentary: *Shuoyuan*, "Tancun": "The mouth is the gate; the tongue is the trigger. If one utters words improperly, even four horses cannot overtake them.
◎ "The mouth is the gate; the tongue is the weapon. If one utters words improperly, they will instead wound oneself."

In the *Fayuan gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Garden of Dharma), it is said: "Weapons are instruments of inauspiciousness; they are employed only when there is no other recourse.
Words are things that do not coexist [with harmony]; they are set forth only when there is no other recourse."
Commentary: Although a lump of glutinous rice may satisfy the palate, one does not on that account discard a treasure worth ten thousand cities.

Though the imperial throne may delight the heart, how could it be for its sake that one undergoes the agony of having one's throat cut? Thus, one merely uses empty words to seek sustenance and profit.

How much gain and honor can there be when the hope for Nirvana has already been severed? This is no different from holding up a handful of millet and a jade disc worth a thousand pieces of gold to show an infant;
the infant takes the millet and casts away the jade (as detailed in the "Chapter on Diverse Treasures" of the *Lüshi Chunqiu*).
To adorn one's speech in order to hunt for fame—though such fame may be attained by chance—it has already opened the gates to the three miserable realms.
This is no different from using the left hand to clutch a map of the world while the right hand severs one's own throat.
For example, in a previous life, Śāntirakṣita and five others spoke to one another with false words;
because of this, they passed through various evil realms and returned as slave-girls, where they were subjected to incessant flogging and whipping.

[Commentary] From the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra*: The Buddha said, "In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, in the kingdom of Pai-shan-sha, there was a woman named Ti-wei who served the five bhikṣus with great devotion.

However, the five bhikṣus, desiring to seek wealth and riches, took turns among themselves to travel through various villages, telling people: 'Those four bhikṣus have realized the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*')."
Upon hearing this, the people made various kinds of offerings. Later, the five bhikṣus fell into hell for eight thousand *koṭis* of kalpas;

they took the form of hungry ghosts for eight thousand kalpas, and took the form of six domestic animals for eight thousand kalpas. Having completed their retribution as animals for eight thousand lifetimes, [they were finally released].
Although they had obtained human bodies, they lacked the sexual organs of either male or female.
For eight thousand lifetimes, they constantly repaid their debts through manual labor. The one named *Tive* was Queen Mallikā;
the five bhikṣus were the four Śaṇḍilas and one who cleaned the latrines in the palace. The Queen said, "From this day forward, you five shall be forever released."
They went freely in all directions, yet the five men wept and did not wish to leave. The Buddha said, "Śāṇḍila and the others have not yet finished repaying their debts;
bound by the constraints of karmic conditions, they cannot depart. Once the repayment of these conditions is complete, they shall naturally attain liberation."
Kiliśa, in a past kalpa, he caused his disciples to speak at length using names and metaphors;
because of that false speech as well, he underwent various bitter sufferings, further falling into blindness and deafness, while being devoured by insects and snakes.
[Commentary]: In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūryagarbha Sūtra*, among the assembly at that time, there was one who was blind and deaf named Phala-kiriśa.
Raising his voice, he wailed aloud, saying: "I pray you, rescue me! Within my body now I undergo great suffering and affliction;
day and night I am constantly being bitten and eaten by various kinds of insects, small snakes, and frogs, dwelling as I do in hot water. There was no [refuge].
"Temporary happiness. The Buddha said, "In a past life, you were once a bhikṣu who violated the prohibitions and precepts.
You outwardly manifested the appearance of virtue while extensively coveting followers; your disciples were numerous.
Those disciples said, 'Our upādhyāya has attained arhatship,' and because of this, you received much offerings, which you enjoyed alone. When you saw those who upheld the precepts..."
On the contrary, he spoke with malice. That person was filled with remorse and thought to himself: "In every life throughout my births, may I wherever I am eat the flesh of your body.
Due to the causes and conditions of that evil karma, after death he fell among the *nāgas* and received this retribution of blindness, dwelling in hot water.
Furthermore, in the past, for immeasurable *kalpas*, he remained in the hell of molten red copper, constantly [suffering] at the hands of all...
Devouring by worms; while deluding and confusing the ignorant laity and pointlessly consuming their offerings—how could one not have anticipated that the calamity would be as fierce as this?
The Vinaya states: "It would be better to eat burning stones and swallow molten copper than to consume the faithful offerings of others through falsehood."
(From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*) Those who heard this were without exception struck with awe in their hearts; they submitted themselves to these brilliant instructions.
Therefore, he did not deceive even the tiger blocking his path, casting his body away to protect the precepts—this principle was indeed as it ought to be.

[Commentary: Once there was a bhikṣu who had violated all four of the [major] precepts. The deities of the twenty minor precepts had all departed, but as for the deity of the precept against lying, she alone refused to leave.
She transformed herself into a tiger and blocked the path in order to cause him to break that precept.
The bhikṣu said to the tiger, "I have a prior engagement; if you devour me, it will cause me to violate my commitment."
"My precepts would then be violated. Release me and let me go; I shall return immediately. Let you devour my body; I speak no falsehood and will certainly not deceive you.
The tiger released him, and upon arriving, he took his leave to return. He went to the place where the tiger was, laid aside his clothes, sat upright, and offered his body as food for the tiger.
Suddenly the tiger vanished, and he saw the Spirit of the Five Precepts, who sighed and said, "Excellent! Well done! and so forth.

Chen explained his true intention, vowing never to be separated from the precepts. The bhikṣu felt remorse and reproached himself, firmly upholding the five precepts. The twenty deities of the precepts returned to protect him.
The bhikṣu practiced the Way with diligence and subsequently attained the stage of fruition.
Regarding the parable of the washing basin and Rāhula’s reprimand:
[Commentary] According to the *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Parables), before Rāhula had attained the Way, he was said to lack sincerity and faith.

The Buddha commanded Rāhula to go and reside at the Kalandaka Vihāra, where he was to guard his speech, restrain his mind, and diligently cultivate the sutras and precepts. Later, the Buddha went to visit him and instructed Rāhula...
[The Buddha] said: "Rāhula, having taken water to wash your feet, the Buddha said to Rāhula: 'This water was originally pure, but now it has received dust and grime;

it can no longer be used for drinking, eating, washing, or rinsing. If you do not contemplate diligence, nor restrain your mind and guard your speech, and the filth of the three poisons fills your breast, you will be like this water—no longer fit for use. Furthermore, although a clean basin is empty..."
It may be used for holding food and drink. Although you are a śramaṇa, your mouth lacks sincerity and truth;
you have borne an evil reputation and are like a wash-basin unfit for holding food. Furthermore, this vessel is of low value, yet you cherish it and do not let go of it.

You fail to restrain your body and mouth, uttering coarse words and evil speech that cause much injury. Unaccepted by the multitude, when the body dies and the spirit departs, you will revolve [in saṃsāra].
On the path of transmigration, one undergoes immeasurable suffering; that which the Buddhas and noble sages do not cherish is just like this bowl.
"That which you do not cherish," the Buddha told Rāhula, "is like the elephant sent by a king to go into battle, which conceals only its trunk."
"Protect it so that you do not fight. Why is this? An elephant's trunk is soft and fragile; if it is struck by an arrow, it dies immediately.
You must protect your mouth, just as an elephant protects its trunk. Rāhula was moved by these words and exerted himself with diligence, thereby attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
Daining’s flattery; Linyuan was rebuked. [Commentary:
According to the *Baotrun*, when Linyuan was attending Huitang at Zhangjiang Temple, he once entered the city and returned late in the evening.
Huitang asked, "Where did you go today? He replied, "I just came from Daining. At that time, Sishin was standing nearby and raised his voice sharply.
Heshan said, "One who studies Chan with the desire to escape birth and death must first ensure their speech is sincere. Elder Qing, how can you speak such falsehoods?
Lingyuan’s face flushed with shame, and he did not dare respond. From that time on, he no longer entered the city or town, nor did he utter a single false word.
All were filled with shame and trepidation, moved to feel inspired and diligent. Indeed, though the eastern horizon has passed, one may still gather the fruit in the shade of the mulberry trees;

if one returns before it is too late, there will ultimately be good fortune. Now that these śrāmaṇeras are said to be in accord with the Dharma, how could they lack the instructions of their teachers and the counsel of their friends?
Be careful not to behave like those who stop up their ears when flattery is addressed to them.
[Commentary: This is a note on the *Shijing*. "Tǒu" (褎) is the appearance of frequent laughter. "Chōng'ěr" (充耳) refers to ear-stoppers. Those with hearing loss often laugh much;
they reject unmerited gifts and distance themselves from excessive praise. Even as one seeks to avoid drowning by heading toward a mountain peak, one still fears being pressed close.
Fleeing from a fire into a well, one still fears its proximity; how could it be that every person does not become a vessel for the Dharma?
Fifth is "not drinking alcohol.
[Commentary]: According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva should engender the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings, yet instead, they further give rise to...
For a bodhisattva, the perverted mind of any sentient being constitutes a *pārājika* offense. As stated in a verse from the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*:
"Drinking alcohol leads to great negligence; in this present life, one is constantly deluded and forgets all matters."
One is constantly rebuked by the wise; in future lives one remains perpetually dull-witted and loses many merits.
Therefore, a person of wisdom avoids the faults of drinking alcohol. Alcohol is the root of heedlessness; by not drinking, one closes off the evil realms.
One would rather sacrifice hundreds of thousands of bodies than violate the teachings of the Dharma; one would rather let the body wither away than ever drink this wine. Even if...
If one were to break the precepts and live out a full hundred years, it would not equal the merit of guarding the prohibitions even for a single moment until the body perishes.
[The medicine] is certain to cure the illness; yet I still do not drink it. How much more so now, when I cannot know for certain whether it will cure me or not?
Having formed this resolute mind, my heart gave rise to great joy, and I immediately attained the vision of the Truths. My ailment was then—
Eliminating [the five transgressions], the *Zongjing* [Lu] states: "The fifth is not drinking alcohol. Regarding the explanation of this Dharma gate:
delusion and inverted views are called "alcohol. Indeed, alcohol is unwholesome and the root of all evils. Drinking alcohol invites madness and [leads to becoming] externalists (*tīrthika*);
this is what is meant by worldly intoxication. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "From time immemorial, we have always been intoxicated by sounds and forms, wandering through birth and death."
The humans and devas of the three realms all share this intoxication. Those of the Two Vehicles have not yet vomited out the wine of ignorance; they are like those suffering from a partial seizure.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* cites the case of the intoxicated man returning home as an analogy. The world lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet [the Two Vehicles] speak of self and purity;

the Tathāgata possesses true permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet speaks of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—just like that intoxicated man who sees the sun and moon revolving. This is the intoxication of the Two Vehicles.

The Bodhisattva has not yet exhausted ignorance; they do not fully understand, yet they perceive with clarity. It is like seeing a painted image at night, or like a drunken man who sees the road in a blur.
Kāśyapa said: "From this point onward, we have all been called people of wrong views. This is the intoxication of the Bodhisattva.
Those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan) practice the conduct of the Tathāgata; though they possess the nature of afflictions, they are able to know the secrets of the Tathāgata.
This is the secret treasury. Although one possesses only the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. That which can be seen by it is such that nothing further remains to be seen;
thus, the five abodes, along with their active and latent tendencies, are simultaneously eliminated without remainder. Once the dharma of wine is removed, what is there to intoxicate?

Even for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanren), there is a Dharma-gate of drinking wine. Aṅgulimāla said: "Carrying the vessel of true emptiness, one fills it with the wine of the true mark (lakṣaṇa).
Transforming throughout the five paths, one proclaims the lion’s roar. When King Prasenajit became intoxicated and acted excessively, Queen Mallikā drank [the wine] as well. The Buddha said:
"One who upholds the precepts may enter a tavern, establishing their own resolve and also establishing the resolve of others. Thus, one attains [liberation].
As for that gate, one must be appropriate whether moving against or with the current; he who loses its handle will cut his hand while wielding the blade.
Thus we know that those who are able to take worldly toil and afflictions as the work of a Buddha have seen that all phenomena are the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Within the true mark of the single mind, seeing no phenomena of worldly faults, calamities, or obstructions—then what [could there be]?
Having relinquished [all things], one does not perceive any supramundane, extraordinary, or sublime dharma; thus, what is there to be grasped?

It is only because they have not yet entered the gate of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that they perceive distinctions such as ordinary beings and sages, and consequently give rise to attachment and aversion.

Therefore, in accordance with their capacities and inclinations, and following their actions, I employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to guide and transform them. All [of this is done for their sake].
It causes one to enter this single limit of equality, free from contention and error, the Dharma-gate of self-realization, which is ultimately eternal bliss.
To reveal it in this way is not to fail the previous capacity [of the listener]. If one understands the method behind the elbow, it is like reaching for a treasure within a bag;
it is truly the foremost teaching. It encompasses the beginning and the end, opening the gate of great giving. Who could surpass this?
Afterwards, one attains the marrow of one's own *dharmakāya* and reaches the source of the ocean of the single mind-intelligence. From the initial letter *A* onward, it encompasses the infinite;
beyond the letter *Ta*, there are no further words to be spoken.
The commentary states: "Drinking alcohol" refers to consuming any kind of intoxicating liquor.
[Note: Since there are many varieties of alcohol, it is termed "all. The following text provides a formal explanation of this "all. This means that alcohol can cloud the divine intellect;
therefore, those of clear understanding regard alcohol as a fountain of calamity and resolutely sever their ties to it. Now, for the sake of uprooting [this habit]...
Regarding birth and death and false views, how could one drink from this fountain of calamity?
In the Western Regions, there are many kinds of wine; whether made from sugarcane, grapes, or various flowers, all may be used to produce wine.

[Commentary]: The *Shenxian Fushijing* (Scripture on the Elixirs of the Immortals) states that one gathers the *nanzhu* herb and boils its juice to make wine, which possesses the spiritual power of reflecting five colors like emerald.
The *Fusangji* records that in the kingdom of Donxun there is a tree resembling the *anju* pomegranate;
by taking the juice of its flowers and storing it in a basin, fine wine is produced within several days. The *Dongmingji* states that Yaokun is ninety thousand *li* from the Jade Gate (*Yumen*).

There is a green herb; when it is cut and used to brew wine, drinking one *hé* (a measure) causes one not to sober up for three days. Drinking water from Sweet Spring (*Gān-xī*) restores consciousness.
According to the *Nánshǐ*, the kingdom of Kulu has a "Nymph of the Water" tree (*shuǐxiān shù*), within whose trunk there is water called "Immortal Elixir" (*xiānjiāng*).

Those who drink it remain intoxicated for seven days. According to the *Gōngjīn zhù*, the kingdom of Wusun has "Green Field Nuts" (*qīngtián hé*). When they encounter water, they take on the flavor of wine.
It is pure and clear; when one drinks it all, one is reborn. It is called "Qingtian Wine" (Green Field Wine), as recorded in the *Fuyi Wuzhi* (Record of Strange Things from Fuyi).
Its flavor is exceptionally fine and fragrant; though people purchase it with gold, they do not consider it precious.
In this region, there are only those made from rice; both are undrinkable. [Commentary:

The preceding passage mentions various types from the Western Regions, while the following refers to those made from rice in this region. The single character "ju" (all/both) serves to subsume them all.
Regarding the fifth precept on drinking alcohol in the *Zhulin*: the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "If one says, 'I am..."
A disciple of the Buddha must not drink alcohol; they must not drink even a single drop from the tip of a blade of grass.
There are two kinds of alcohol: grain-based and wood-based. Grain-based alcohol is that made from various five-grains mixed with rice.
Wood-based alcohol is made using roots, stalks, leaves, or fruits, or by mixing various seeds, fruits, and herbs.
That which possesses the color, fragrance, and flavor of alcohol, and which can intoxicate a person when drunk, is called "alcohol.
If one tastes it or swallows it, it is likewise called "drinking. If one drinks grain-based liquor, one commits an offense with every swallow.
If one drinks sour wine, sweet wine, or consumes yeast that can intoxicate; or if one consumes dregs, or drinks the sediment of wine, or drinks... [the same applies].
If something resembles the color of wine, resembles the fragrance of wine, or resembles the taste of wine, and is capable of intoxicating a person, it constitutes an offense with every swallow.
However, if it merely has the color of wine but lacks its fragrance and taste, and is incapable of intoxicating a person or other drinkers, [it does not constitute an offense].
In all such cases, there is no offense. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if a sick bhikṣu or others cannot be cured by other medicines and uses alcohol as medicine, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is insane, mentally deranged, afflicted by illness, or unconscious.

Except in cases of serious illness, or when there is no other remedy than alcohol, one must inform the assembly before consuming it. Without such cause, not even a single drop may touch the lips. [Commentary:
When a dike is on the verge of collapsing, one must regard even a tiny trickle with great care. Thus it is said: "If not removed drop by drop, it will eventually become a river."

These words begin with a mere drop of moisture and end with a great goblet that never ceases; they illustrate the strictness of the prohibitions against alcohol, and thus it is regulated for all seven classes of practitioners.
Yet, for those with serious illnesses, an exception is made as a matter of expedient means.

This refers to cases where a disease cannot be cured except by wine, and when wine must be used urgently, one takes the wine as medicine; in such a case, it is medicine, not wine. There are also [cases where...]
There are two kinds of alcohol that can intoxicate a person: first, the alcohol of ignorance (*avidyā*), meaning that ignorance obscures the mind so that one’s speech is like that of a drunkard;

second, the alcohol of *prajñā* (wisdom), meaning that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision stagnate and fail to transform, such that even the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the Buddha-dharma are like being intoxicated.
The *Zhulin* states that the Buddha said: "Alcohol has many faults; it opens the gateway to heedlessness."

One should drink [the medicine] like *jiṅli* seeds. Although the accumulated offenses have already been committed, if they can eliminate the suffering of illness, they are not what was previously severed.
In the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*, the Venerable Mahīśāsaka said: "The bhikṣu Sāti had nurtured his life since childhood by means of alcohol.
After he left the household life, because he could not obtain alcohol, the four great elements became unbalanced. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "For the sick, it is permitted to smell [the wine] from atop a jar. If they recover, smelling it is not permitted.
If they do not recover, it is permitted to wash the body with wine. If they still do not recover, it is permitted to mix wine with flour to make cakes and eat them.
If they still do not recover, it is permitted for them to soak themselves in the wine."
One must not even smell alcohol, nor stay in a tavern, nor give alcohol to others to drink. [Commentary]:
Regarding smelling alcohol or staying in a tavern, although one does not drink, there are two great dangers: first, it causes others to harbor suspicions and slander one.
Second, habituation forms one's character; this is also a method for preventing small faults from developing into great ones.

The Brahmajāla Sūtra states that one who gives alcohol to others shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes. The precept against alcohol is extremely strict because while violating the precept oneself results in no more than sin affecting a single body, giving it to others causes harm that does not stop there.
Yi Di created wine. When Yu drank it, he was so distressed that he cut off [the supply]. [Commentary:
According to the *Renwu Kao* (Investigation of Persons and Things), Yi Di was the younger brother of Yu’s consort. He was skilled at making wine.

After Yu drank it and found it sweet, he said, "In future generations, there will surely be those who cause their states to perish because of wine. He consequently distanced himself from Yi Di and forbade fine wine. (From the *Zhongjing* of the Jin Dynasty)
*Book of Jin*: Emperor Yuan was by nature fond of wine. Wang Dao deeply cautioned him against this; when his attendants brought him a cup, he overturned it. *Book of Jin*:
Commoners were not permitted to privately brew or sell liquor. Exceptions were granted for those with marriages or illnesses.
For other offenses, the penalty is a fine of eight *liang*. Mei Cheng’s *Qifā* states: "Wine is a medicine that rots the intestines.
Since antiquity, sagacious rulers and worthy ministers have feared it would burden the people; therefore, they prohibited it.
Zhou constructed a wine pond, and his state perished thereby.
[Commentary: Biographical Examination of Persons. Zhou’s name was Xin. He was the youngest son of Emperor Yi. There were three brothers: the eldest was Wei Zi Qi; the next was Zhong Yan;
both were born of concubines. The youngest was Xin, the legitimate heir, who was Zhou himself. He possessed quick wit and eloquence.
He was violent; his strength was sufficient to grapple with fierce beasts, and his wisdom was enough to reject remonstrance. His words were sufficient to gloss over his errors.
He made meat his forest and wine his pond, causing men and women to run naked among them. At a single drum-roll, three thousand men drank like oxen.
According to the *Han Shu*, Emperor Cheng sat behind a screen, upon which was painted Zhou (King Zhou) drunk and squatting over Jieyi during the "Long Night" banquet.
[King] Yue was so addicted to wine that his gray-haired elders remonstrated with him. It was for this reason that the Duke of Wei (Wei Zi) announced his departure;
it was because of such wailing and lamentation that the *Daya* (Greater Odes) express their lingering sorrow. The prohibitions against debauchery in the *Shi* and *Shu* all originate from wine.
For a monk to drink alcohol is even more shameful. [Commentary:
A monk possesses virtue and reputation, dignity and solemnity; his words and deeds are upright and discreet. He serves as a banner for later students and a pillar and beam for the Dharma-gate.
If he drinks alcohol, his speech will mostly lack foundation and his transgressions will be immeasurable, behaving like one who is insane.
Like an elephant without a hook, resembling a playful monkey in a tree, they remain unaware that their banner has been snapped and their beams and rafters have collapsed;
thus, the Dharma-gate shall fall into peril from this point forward.
In the past, there was an upāsaka who, because he violated the precept against intoxicants, subsequently broke all his other precepts as well. [Commentary:
According to the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), there was once a five-precept upāsaka tilling a field. Being thirsty, he mistakenly drank alcohol and became intoxicated.

Suddenly, a hen from a neighboring house came to him; he immediately killed and ate it. When the neighbor's daughter went to demand her property, he further forcibly committed sexual misconduct with her.

To litigate such matters in an official court and yet persist in false speech without remorse—because of this single drink, all five precepts are lost and the thirty-six transgressions are fully present; the fault is no small matter.

[Commentary]: According to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, those who are unfilial toward their parents, who treat their teachers and friends with contempt and show no reverence for the Triple Gem, will have their ill repute spread abroad;
they shall perish from the heat in the summer months or freeze to death in the cold season.
Those who greedily indulge in drinking will, upon death, fall into the Hell of Boiling Excrement; in every life they shall be born ignorant and dull-witted, losing the seed of wisdom.
This delusive drug that maddens the soul is more virulent than arsenic or lethal poison.
[Commentary: It is said that the poison of arsenic and *dhen* (fatal draught) merely destroys the physical body one was born with; it cannot destroy the seeds of wisdom on the Path.
As for the poison of drinking alcohol, it is not merely called a medicine that rots the intestines, yet it [can destroy] the seeds of wisdom on the Path.
It is extinguished without remainder. According to the *Book of Jin*, Sun Jishu was once drinking with Shi Chong and behaved with excessive arrogance.
Shi Chong intended to report him to the authorities. Pei Kai said, "To give others the intoxicating drug of wine and then demand of them formal propriety—is this not perverse?"
Therefore, the Sūtra says (the Root Sūtra): "It would be better to drink molten copper than to heedlessly violate the precept against alcohol. Alas! How can one not be cautious?
[Commentary: The various words and metaphors from the above sūtras, śāstras, and historical records all collectively exhort one to abstain.
"Abandoning all faults of alcohol" means that among the poisons in the world, none is more fierce than arsenic, lethal dyes, or molten copper;
yet the toxicity of alcohol is even more violent than these. Therefore, one must issue a fervent and urgent warning against it. Yunju Xian said:

"That drinking wine violates the precepts is known to all people in the world. Recently, however, there has been the habit of smoking wine, which has become a widespread custom. Ultimately, [this leads to...]
O teacher-monks, those who follow the current and swallow [the poison] are the most shameful. Holding pipes and tubes in their hands, they spit forth smoke and flames from their mouths;
having lost all dignified deportment, they also increase the stench of evil. Furthermore, we have personally witnessed them falling prostrate and being scorched and mangled by fire.
Those whose physical forms are thus ruined through excessive drinking suffer even greater loss. Whether they have received the precepts or not, none should ever consume it.
This is a great violation of the Dharma that must be strictly avoided.
The Treatise states: The Buddha said, "Alcohol has many faults; it opens the gate to heedlessness. To drink even as much as a mustard seed is called breaking the precepts."
Thus, the Tang dynasty monk Xuanjian smashed his wine vessels, daring to provoke the wrath of powerful clans. [Commentary:

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the monk Sengjian frequently undertook construction projects involving many craftsmen. Whenever anyone sent him wine, he would invariably say, "This is for my own work;
it must be executed according to the rules. I would rather let the work stop than allow myself to drink. This occurred at Qinghua Temple.

While the Buddha hall was being renovated, Sun Yi, a local magnate of the prefecture, presented two vessels of wine to Huiguan. Guanjian immediately smashed the wine vessels, causing the liquid to overflow onto the ground.
Sun Yi was greatly incensed and intended to inflict harm upon him. That night, he dreamed of someone pointing a knife at him.
Upon awakening, he went in person to offer repentance.
The Jin dynasty was lenient in its legal administration; it pardoned a mad monk who willingly submitted to the humiliation of the *jing-tiao* (thorny rod). [Commentary:
According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang*, Huiyu resided at Changsha Temple in Jiangling. A certain monk drank wine and neglected the evening incense offering.
Huiyu merely punished him and did not expel him. Master Dao’an sent a tube filled with thorns to Huiyu; Huiyu then faced the tube and...
Prostrating respectfully on the ground, he ordered the *karmadāna* to administer the staff; shedding tears, he reproached himself.
Indeed, as a leader for future generations, one who sustains and prolongs the True Dharma cannot help but act in this way. Furthermore, the Buddha said:

"If it serves to alleviate the suffering of illness, that which was previously prohibited is not [a violation]. Thus, regarding this precept, a temporary relaxation has been permitted for those in critical illness. How [could it otherwise be]?
He was a bhikṣu of the Bamboo Grove. When his illness had subsided, he felt deep shame and confessed his transgressions in detail.
[Commentary: In the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, it is said that a certain bhikṣu at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery was gravely ill and near death.
Upāli asked him, "What medicine do you require? He replied, "I need wine. This truly violated the Vinaya; rather than [preserve the rule], he would have preferred to let his life end.
The Buddha commanded: "There must be no indulgence in alcohol. Upāli said, "If it is for the sake of illness, it is permitted by the Tathāgata.

Thereupon, he took wine and his illness was cured. The bhikṣu felt ashamed and still considered himself to have violated the Vinaya; he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and earnestly repented his transgression.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the path of Arhatship.
Master Yuan. Among the various elders, he opposed their earnest entreaties. [Commentary]:

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, when Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu during the Jin Dynasty was gravely ill, the various elders all prostrated themselves and requested that he drink fermented soybean wine (*dǐjiǔ*), but he did not permit it.
They further requested that he drink rice gruel, but he did not permit it. Upon repeated requests, they offered water mixed with honey.
Having drunk, he then commanded the Vinaya Master to open the scroll and search for the text; only after he had dared to drink did he pass away before the scroll was half-finished.
Bai Ma Fen remarked that [the Master’s] end must have been imminent, for how could it have deviated from his original resolve?
[Commentary]: According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the monk Hui-fen of the Qi dynasty initially resided at Changshan Temple in Gu-shu County.

When the Wei dynasty suppressed the Buddhist Dharma, he returned south to the capital and stayed at Baima Temple. When his illness became critical, people urged him to take medicine with wine. Hui-fen said:
Having maintained the precepts for many years, how could one allow them to be compromised at the point of death?
Consequently, they all became increasingly rigorous, even exceeding the original regulations; yet there was never a time when they did not suspect that their own practice had gone too far.
Furthermore, consider the Arhat Śāgata, who was able to cause the wicked dragon to be converted, suddenly causing it to lose its majesty as a subduer of frogs.
[Commentary: According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, in the kingdom of Ceti there was a wicked dragon named Āmrapālī.
It violently harmed humans and birds and devastated the autumn harvests. The Arhat Śāgata went to that place, beneath a tree.
As he spread out his seat, the dragon gave rise to wrath; smoke and fire issued from its body, and it rained down hail and thunderbolts, along with centipedes and millipedes.
Śāgata transformed these into *utpala* and *padma* lotuses, thereby neutralizing all the power possessed by the evil dragon.
All who appeared there were unable to overcome him. Because he had received the Three Refuges, he committed no further evil deeds. There was a poor woman who had faith and reverence for Śāgata;
she prepared a milk-rice porridge with ghee that looked like water-colored wine and brought it to Śāgata.

He drank it without looking at it. Having finished drinking, he departed. At that time, the effects of the wine took hold and he fell unconscious to the ground. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "Śā..."
"Gāthā, can you now subdue this frog? Even a sage who drinks wine may still suffer such a loss; how much more so for an ordinary person?
From this day forward, none of my disciples shall drink alcohol—not even a single drop as small as one on the tip of a blade of grass."
Regarding the late Master Nan of Xinsi Temple: having departed for the realm of the unseen, he was ultimately denied the blessing of ascending to the distant heights.

[Commentary] According to the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Omens), Jiang Xiaode of the Song dynasty died and subsequently revived, saying that he had been released from the underworld and was returning home.
On his way, at a certain location, there was a dilapidated and humble hut; in front of the hut, he encountered the late Master Nan of Xinsi Temple, who said, "I have come out..."
He came home and had never drunk wine before, yet he went to Master Lan. Master Lan earnestly exhorted him, pressing him until he drank about one *sheng*.
Because he was summoned and employed by the King, [he said]: "If it were not for sitting here [drinking], I would have attained rebirth in heaven."

Tracing back the origins of this, one is struck with awe and trembles with fear. How could one afford to be expansive in disposition and lax in discipline, thereby inviting regrets that can never be undone?
The sixth [precept] states: "One shall not wear fragrant flower garlands nor anoint the body with perfumes."
[Commentary: The Tathāgata’s majestic virtue is fully perfected in every respect; his adornments of both the primary body and the environment are objects of aspiration for the world.

He seeks nothing and lacks for nothing; whatever is required arrives at the proper time. Flower garlands, pearl necklaces, and ointments, as well as celestial music from the sky, are bestowed like clouds.
