That the Tathāgata accepts them with compassion is merely an exercise of skillful means (*upāya*). If one were to conceive of receiving them as a source of craving and attachment, it would be a delusion.
The messengers had not yet reached the Snow Mountains when his craving and views were eliminated; he abandoned his wife and children of ten thousand chariots.
At midnight, under the bright star, as he sat alone in contemplation, it was truly marvelous how from that moment on he forgot all nobility.

All people know that the Tathāgata’s adornments of the physical body and the environment are peerless in this world, but they do not know that the Tathāgata’s environment and body were attained through ascetic practices over vast eons.

Furthermore, these are brought about by the severance of craving; yet nowadays, people do not practice asceticism and do not sever their craving, yet they wish to imitate the dependent and primary environments of the Tathāgata.
This is like a poor man wearing the robes of a sovereign: his calamity will arrive swiftly.
The commentary states: Regarding "flower garlands" (*mālā*), people in the Western Regions string flowers together to form garlands to adorn their heads.
In this land [of China], it refers to items such as turbans and crowns fashioned from silk, wool, gold, and precious gems.
[Commentary: A *mālā* (garland) refers to the adornment of the topknot with pearls, flowers, and various jewels. Thus it is said:

"Flower garlands are not found only in the Western Regions; here in this land as well, men adorn their head-wraps and crowns, while women adorn their topknots and hair-bands, thereby distinguishing the nobility and commonality of social rank."
Regarding "applying incense to the body": the nobility of the Western Regions (India) use famous incense as a powder and have their maidservants in green robes (*qingyi*) rub it onto their bodies.

[Commentary: Exotic fragrances are of many varieties only in the Western Regions; therefore, the nobility bathe their bodies with incense and rub them with it, which is equivalent to bathing with scented soap in this land.
The maidservants of the Western Regions all wear green robes, hence they are so named.
It is like the case of Xuanzhenzi, who instructed Qiaoying to brew tea within the bamboo groves;
in this land, it refers to wearing incense, burning incense, and the like, such as cosmetics and fragrant powders.

[Commentary]: *Pei xiang* (scented pendants) refers to either sachets or scented cakes. *Xun xiang* (incense for fumigation) refers to incense used in tubes or censers. According to the *Er yi lu*, *yan zhi* (vermilion rouge) originated with Zhou;
it was made from the juice of red-blue flowers (*hong lan hua*) to serve as a "peach blossom makeup," and it was produced in the state of Yan.
Regarding *yin fen* (silver powder), the *Gu jin zhu* states that during the Three Dynasties, lead was used as face powder.
"How can those who have left the household life appropriately employ such things?

[Commentary: A practitioner of the Way should use the fire of wisdom to incense the fragrance of precept and meditative concentration, thereby adorning the formless body and directly beholding the crown of the formless.
Thus revealing the primordial light alone, how could one rely on external ornamentation? All of the above matters were addressed by the King.
What I have done has not been adopted by the practitioners. If you instead use exotic incense to make offerings to the various Buddhas, you will thereby accomplish merit and wisdom.
The Buddha prescribed the three robes (the three robes refer to those with five strips, seven strips, and twenty-five strips) and mandated that all be made of coarse hemp cloth.
To use animal fur or silk—both of which harm living beings and violate compassion—is improper.
[Commentary] This is the writing of the Holy Master of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan). He states that the robe of compassion—how could it be made from the skin and fur of slaughtered animals?
Furthermore, he says: "Even if one were to obtain such materials, they should be cut up and used as plaster for walls or for whitewashing.

This means that the hair of beasts and the mouths of silkworms are not as secure and stable as hemp cloth. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one claims that a bhikṣu does not wear [silk] from the East..."
As for fine silk, cotton, and woven fabrics, as well as the boots, furs, and woolens of this land—monks such as these are truly liberated from the world;
they have settled their past debts and no longer wander within the three realms. Why is this? Because wearing the products of others' labor constitutes a karmic bond with them.
It is like a person who eats the hundred grains grown in the earth; their feet do not leave the ground. Thus prophesied by the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa.
Ming said: "In a past life, I was the King of Vaiśālī. In that kingdom, there was a class of people who had the bodies of horses but lacked clothing.

The King exercised his supernatural power to divide his body into silkworms so that they might obtain clothes; thus, the silkworms were formed as the horses died, and the horses died to become silkworms."
They belong to the same class. Later, when the King was born again in Central India, his horse-man (Aśvaghoṣa) remained filled with longing and grief, neighing incessantly;
therefore, he was named Aśvaghoṣa, "Horse-Neigh. The Buddha taught that even those who wear silk and fine fabrics must repay their karmic debts;
it would be better to observe the precepts so as to have no regrets hereafter.
Except for those who are seventy years of age or older, whose physical decline is so extreme that they cannot stay warm without cotton, it may be permissible for them to do so.
For all others, it is not permitted.
[Commentary: At seventy, a person’s blood and qi have declined; their strength is insufficient to endure coarse, heavy cloth garments; therefore, [cotton] is not [otherwise required].
If one does not accept this [interpretation], then it is known that prior to his seventieth year, Mencius also wore robes of silk;
perhaps he did so specifically because he was ill, as a skillful means (upāya).
Emperor Yu of Xia wore coarse clothing.
[Commentary]: According to the *Tongjian*: Bo Yu, the Xia Hou, was named Wenming and styled Gaodi. His ancestor was Zhuanxu; his father was Gun.

He was conceived two months after the year [of Gun’s death], on the sixth day of the sixth month in the fifty-eighth year of Yao’s reign (the Wuxu year). He was born from a rock at Shiniu Village in Buda and grew up among the Western Qiang.
He ruled as King by the virtue of Earth (*tude*). He established the calendar with the month of Yin (*zheng jian yin*) as the first, and he reigned for one hundred and six years.
In the year [of his death], he passed away at Kuaiji. One man dressed in coarse clothing composed a eulogy for the virtue of King Yu.

King Yu delighted in plain cloth and did not prize fine silks or cotton; his love for the people and his frugality regarding blessings were such as this. It is only fitting that he possessed such a heart.
The world was governed with great order.
Gongsun Bupi was a noble subject of the King; he ought to have done what he did not do. [Commentary:

According to the Tongjian, during the transition between the Shang and Zhou dynasties, there was as yet no title for "bedding" (bei). Hong was a man of extraordinary character and vast learning. He was constantly...
It was said that the fault of a sovereign is not being magnanimous, while the fault of a minister is not being frugal.
It was commonly remarked that when Minister Gongsun wore a cloth robe, people called it hypocrisy; yet when Minister Sima also wore a cloth robe, people called it frugality.
It is possible. To cause others to practice frugality is called "parsimony"; to do so without resorting to deception is not impossible. *Book of the Later Han*, Biography of Wang Liang:

When Wang Liang served as Grand Minister of Education, he was respectful and frugal in his official duties. His wife did not enter the official residence; they used coarse cloth for bedding and earthenware vessels.
At that time, the minister’s subordinate, Bao Hui, passed by his home and saw the lady dressed in plain clothes, returning from the fields trailing firewood. The official—
In admiration. (From the *Ganying Zhu*: Emperor Wen of Han. The lady he favored wore garments that did not drag on the ground.
Emperor Wen of Tang once took out his sleeve to show his ministers, saying, "This garment has already been washed three times. Duke Wen of Jin wore no more than a single layer of silk.)
Zi Xia wore clothes like those of a hanging wren; Yan Ying’s concubines did not wear silk; Dong Wei tied together scraps of rope for a garment, calling it "the hundred-knot robe";
and Ji Tong never had a spare set of clothing—all these were ways of cherishing one's fortune. Thus, Master Nanchan in the *Lamp Records* often said:
"When Cuiyan Yue and I were at Fuchang, I happened to suffer from a cold and took medicine that caused me to break out in a sweat."
Yue followed his fellow meditators everywhere seeking to borrow bedding, but none could be obtained. When he encountered anyone with a paper quilt, Yue would count it over and over.
He sighed and said, "Master Shan is truly a master craftsman of the original style."

How could it be that those who have attained the Way, on the contrary, covet ornamental finery? To wear robes of "ruined colors" (壞色) and to cover the body with refuse-grass rags is indeed what is fitting for them.
[Commentary: "Ruined colors" refer to blue-black and madder-brown hues; these distinguish the monastic from the lay and manifest the meaning of impermanence as a warning.

This refers to later practitioners. Regarding "rags from a dust heap" (*pāṃśukūla*): these are the garments of those who died in former ages, as well as the clothes of women who gave birth, all of which were discarded in the wilderness or among refuse.
A bhikṣu takes what has been cast away and washes it seven times in mountain streams or ravines until the impurities are gone;
he then sews them together into a patched robe (*kaṣāya*) merely to ward off the cold. This is the practice of *dhūta*. In recent times, [the rags of] those who have died or given birth...
As for this, one does not discard their robes. Thus, those who study the dhūta practices in the present age find them even more arduous than in previous ages.
Regarding the "Rough Draft on Seeking Silk Threads": I left home at the age of seven. My parents loved me and clothed me in light, warm garments;

however, by nature I was fond of the simple and austere, and looking upon beautiful clothes, I could not bear to wear them. I constantly reflected that every single thread and fiber originates from the mouth of a silkworm. From [the time]...
From a foot to a ten-foot length, the span of life cannot be calculated. He took pleasure in wearing coarse cloth for clothing, yet his strength could not sustain it;

thus, he wove together discarded scraps of silk from others to make a patched robe (*kaṣāya*). As he gazed upon the mountains and waters over the long course of days and months, he did not notice its decay and tattered state.
Even if he wished to go into the wilds or among the refuse heaps to gather leftover rags, they would no longer be found there.
In the spring of the Wuzi year, I passed through Guangling and saw the fine garments being fashioned by various gentlemen. The waste silk, damask, and raw silk threads were all discarded;
I begged them for myself and, with meticulous care, stitched them onto the torn patches of my patched robe until it became a seamless whole.
Rain could not wet it, and wind could not penetrate it. When sitting, it served as meditation; when walking, it served as precept-keeping; when staying still, it served as a curtain.
When lying down, it serves as a blanket; when disordered, it serves as the armor of patience; when still, it serves as gathered feathers;
when deployed, it serves as a blade sharper than steel. How joyful! That upon a single strand of hair there is such utility.
It not only extinguishes my own greedy thoughts over many lifetimes, but also preserves for all of you an inexhaustible store of merit.
In antiquity, there was a high monk who wore a single pair of shoes for thirty years. [Commentary:

Huilin notes that his cloth shoes were patched a hundred times and sewn together a thousand times; when he encountered soft ground, he would walk barefoot, fearing he might damage the offerings of the faithful.
"A pair of shoes" (*liang xie*) refers to a set of two boots. According to the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, Chan Master Huitong entered Mount Taibai without carrying provisions.
When hungry, he ate wild fruits; when thirsty, he drank from mountain springs. He rested beneath trees, and after five years, he attained realization.

In his later years, he possessed only a single skirt and a single cloak, wearing hempen sandals for thirty years. His patchwork robe was sewn with layers of cloth, which he never changed throughout both winter and summer.
◎ The Elder Xuantai wore only plain cloth. At Rui Lu Monastery, bedding was originally not provided;
he did not change his silk robes even after an entire day of the morning meal.
How much more so for ordinary people! Alas, should one not be cautious?
The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states that among three types of mind, one must abandon one: namely, the mind that delights in and enjoys adornment.

Now, those who have left the household life wear robes made of cut-off rags or cover their bodies with refuse-rags; how could they again harbor stained emotions for finery or allow their wills to sink into such things?

Their fragrance was pervasive; they surely did not care for their robes, ornaments, or rare treasures. Their radiant appearance moved the multitudes, and wherever they encountered them on the thoroughfares, people gasped in wonder and marveled at their excellence.
Yet those who uphold the Way perceive nothing of this; they only sense that [the worldly] embody defilement and physical impurity.
To the wise, such people are viewed as no different from rats in a latrine or insects in a privy. As for the bhikṣu Udāyin, he delivered his mother and rescued her from peril.
[Commentary]: In the *Uttaramātṛ-sūtra*, it is said that Uttara honored the Buddha and delighted in the Dharma.
He did not let wine pass his lips, did not eat after noon, and never applied perfumes, flowers, or cosmetics to his body.

When his mother became a hungry ghost (*preta*), Uttara filled a jar with water, placed willow twigs within it, and covered the top with his dharma robes. He then provided a meal for the community of bhikṣus, reciting her name and offering prayers of blessing. His mother...
He was spared from grave retribution.
A man of South India heard the Dharma and realized the state of sainthood.
[Commentary: According to the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, there was a man in South India who left the household life within the Buddha-dharma at a young age.
He was content with his desires and took no pleasure in honor or fame. He did not anoint his body with ghee or oil, nor did he bathe in warm water.
He did not consume ghee or oil, nor did he wish for floral ornaments. Constantly fearing birth and death, he went to the kingdom of Mathurā to pay homage to Upagupta.
Upon hearing a single teaching on the Dharma, he applied himself with diligence and contemplation, attaining the fruit of Arhatship.

Comparing what they have attained with these flower garlands and fragrant oils, which is more abundant? Furthermore, there were former virtuous ones of this land who wore but a single robe through both winter and summer. [Commentary:
Xuanlang of the Tang dynasty mended his tattered robes until they were thick enough that he did not change them between winter and summer.
Or one may patch clothing with paper.
[Commentary: During his lifetime, Tang Jinglin’s robes were worn out; he would patch them with paper.
Furthermore, how could there be flower garlands or remnants of clothing that he did not wash?
[Commentary: Liang Hui-kai’s robes were so covered in dust and grime that he never once raised the thought of washing them;
at times, he did not even consider shaving his head.
[Commentary: Yuan Gaofeng’s dwelling was a stone cave where water flowed down from above and the ground below was muddy; he neither bathed his body nor shaved his hair.
Furthermore, what leisure would there be to rub the body? How could it be that glorious fame does not shine for a thousand ages, and fragrant virtue not be inherited across the eight directions?
As for the World-Honored One, he distantly bound himself to former regulations, carefully receiving [offerings] within the pearl casket.

[Commentary]: The *Zhulin* (Forest of Pearls) records that when the Buddha first left the city, a tree deity presented him with a silk *saṃghāṭī* robe left behind by Kāśyapa Buddha, handing it over and saying, "This silk *saṃghāṭī* is not for my use;
I have heard that whenever Buddhas appear in the world, they do not wear clothing made from silkworms.
Upon opening the pearl casket, he saw the inscription of Kāśyapa Buddha which stated: "This *saṃghāṭī* has been transmitted [through successive Buddhas]. This is recorded in the sūtras.
The Great Brahmā Heavenly King produced the warp from the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā; the silk was born through transformation, not from the spinning of cocoons.
The Buddha then accepted it and bestowed it in its entirety upon Du Jian for future generations. Jian declined the gift of the purple robe.
[Commentary]: According to the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song), the monk Quanfu of the Five Dynasties period during the Jin dynasty resided at Qinghua Chan Monastery.
When the Prince Qian Zhongxian dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a purple *kāṣāya*, Quanfu submitted a memorial to decline the honor. When the envoy went again, he declined once more, saying:
"It is not that I am merely feigning modesty; I fear that others might follow my example and indulge their own desires."

The concern for the loss of compassion is not reserved solely for the Benevolent One; conversely, the restraint against the indulgence of desire is exercised with even greater leniency in these final ages.
Moreover, these four elements are distinct and perish in an instant; once entrusted to a single earthenware vessel, they quickly turn into decaying soil.

Walking corpses and running skeletons are needlessly adorned with finery; devoured by ants and fed to crows, all that precious care is rendered empty labor. Thus, one fails to reflect upon the struggle for dominance.

They surpass others, yet feel ashamed that they cannot match the exquisite cultivation of the sages; they merely strive for victory in the depths of worldly existence, competing with one another to flaunt their conduct before the vulgar.

They consider the "horse-teeth" (aging) and "bird-traces" (ancient scripts) to be beyond their lot. Alas! The *śūka* (hemp) plant treats the "beast-hair" and "silkworm-mouth" (the production of silk) as its natural duty, while its fine brocade-like blossoms rot away.
I recall how, in the past, you left your kin and severed your attachments, originally intending to cultivate the sublime path that transcends the world.
This is the cause. It is like the vying for splendor and boasting of beauty seen today; toward what path, then, shall one set foot? How tragic! Seventh:
not performing songs, dances, or theatrical performances, nor going to watch or listen to them.
[Commentary: During the Buddha’s lifetime, great empowered bodhisattvas manifested in the forms of devas and humans, constantly praising him with *brahmaghoṣa* chants and songs.
Regarding the Buddha, he may manifest sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self to cause all sentient beings to attain realization and awakening;
he can even cause waterfowl, birds, trees, and forests to all proclaim the sublime Dharma, which is not like the worldly songs and dances of sensual beauty.
I have often considered that while the ears and eyes regarding sounds and forms most easily cloud the human spirit and intellect, they can also trigger the faculty of awakening.
Therefore, when the Immortal contemplated this, his supernormal powers (ṛddhi) were instantly lost; yet because of it, Louzi’s mind-ground was suddenly opened wide.
If one investigates the source of delusion and wisdom, one finds that they are both driven by the flow of sounds and forms; thus, this is called "flowing with the current" or "the downward flow.
If one investigates the source of awakening and realization, one finds that one is no longer driven by the flow of sounds and forms; thus, this is called "flowing against the current."
It is also called "upward-flowing. Among the ordinary people of this world today, who is not carried away by sounds and forms?

Thus, they drift further and further from the Way day by day. Therefore, those at the beginning stage of practice should avoid sounds and forms as if they were swords and blades; in this way, they will naturally draw near to the Way.
The commentary states: "Singing" refers to the production of songs from the mouth; "dancing" refers to the performance of dramatic movements with the body.

[Annotation]: Regarding singing and dancing, if there is something insufficient in the singing, one uses dancing to complete it; if there is something insufficient in the dancing, one uses singing to complete it.
Then they sing to exhaust its meaning. They sing it and dance it; it is utterly good and utterly beautiful.
"Performers" refers to those who play instruments such as the *qin*, the *se*, the *xiao*, and the *guan*.
[Commentary]: "Singers and performers" is a general term. According to the *Baihutong* (Comprehensive Discussions on the White Tiger): "The *qin* (zither) means 'to restrain.

It is used to prohibit depravity and lust, thereby rectifying the human mind and will. The *se* (psaltery) means 'to be frugal' or 'to be restrained. It is used to punish anger and stifle desire, thereby rectifying the virtue of the person.

According to the *Lüshi Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn of the Lü Clan): "During the era of Lord Zhuxiang, there was much wind throughout the world, and the Yang energy did not accumulate. As a result..."
This is not established as a fact. Thus, Emperor Wen of the Bin state fashioned a five-stringed *se*, while Gu Sou created a fifteen-stringed one;
Shun added eight strings, making it twenty-three strings. During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, singing girls played on twenty-five-stringed instruments, including the *konghou* and the *se*.
In antiquity, there was an official in charge of music, from whom the "Record of Music" (*Yue Ji*) originated. According to the *Shishuo Xinyu*, Dai Andao...
He possessed a rare reputation for excellence. When the Governor of Wuling heard that he was skilled at playing the *qin*, he sent a messenger to summon him.

Dai An arrived before the messenger and broke his *qin*, saying: "Dai Andao cannot serve as a musician for kings or lords. According to the *Fengsu Tong*: Qiu Zhong invented the flute (*di*). "Flute" (*di*) means "to cleanse" (*di*);
it is used to sweep away depravity and filth, leading one toward the refined and upright. According to the *Yue Shu*: [The flute] cuts through the clouds...
The "Dream of the Frosty Bamboo" (Meng zhi shuang jun) contains the extraordinary melodies of Master Fa’s poetry.

The *Tongyi zuan* states that Fuxi fashioned the sixteen-pipe *xiao*, though some say it was created by Nüwa. According to the *Erya*, the large flute is called a *guan* and the small flute is called a *xiao*.
The *Shiming* explains that *xiao* means "solemn" (*su*), for its sound is solemn and clear.
One must not perform it oneself, nor go to watch or listen while others are performing it.

[Commentary] When making offerings to the Buddha, it is appropriate to have others perform the music; it is not appropriate to do so oneself. Question: According to the Ten Major Precepts of the Brahma Net Sūtra, one must not instruct others to perform it.
Now, if one does not perform it oneself but has others perform it, does this not contradict the Brahma Net Sūtra? Answer: It does not.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra does not instruct others to perform acts such as killing or stealing; indeed, killing and stealing are harms that are no small matter.

However, having others create music to make offerings to the Buddha brings immeasurable merit, which is not the same as the ten grave precepts. It is simply because one lacks the leisure to perform music oneself during the practices of the first stage (bhūmi) that one has others do so.
In ancient times, there was an immortal who, upon hearing the subtle and exquisite melody of a woman’s song, suddenly lost his supernormal power of flight. Such is the harm caused by listening;
how much more so for those who commit it themselves!
[Commentary]: In the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*, it is said that King Udayana went to the Udumbara forest and prohibited men from entering.
He indulged himself in the five desires with women alone. Their voices were pure and exquisite, and they burned various famous incenses.
At that time, the palace ladies danced naked; just then, five hundred rishis passed by. They became stained by the sounds, scents, and forms. Thus...
He lost his supernormal power of the bases of psychic potency (*ṛddhipāda*) and fell into that forest. The king asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are sages.

The king said, "Have you attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*)? They replied, "No. He asked, "Have you attained the first dhyāna?
They replied, "We once attained it, but we have now lost it. The king, becoming angry, said, "Men of desire look upon my palace women!"
This was by no means appropriate; he immediately drew a sharp sword and severed the hands and feet of five hundred sages.
It is said that as soon as they conceived a single thought of desire, they lost their five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The foolish people of the present age, because the *Lotus Sūtra* contains phrases regarding the lute, the gong, and the cymbal, indulge themselves in the study of music.
However, the *Lotus Sūtra* is for making offerings to the Buddhas; it is not for one's own amusement.
[Commentary] "Zheng" (Sign): The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma does not involve two kinds of speech.
Although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the Vinaya differ as Sūtra and Vinaya, both are the Buddha’s teaching.

Why then would the *Lotus Sūtra* regard music as a merit while the Vinaya regards singing and performance as an obstacle of transgression? [Explanation]: That which constitutes sin or merit refers to making offerings or indulging in self-pleasure.
It is merely a matter of distinction. If those within the Vinaya discipline take performing as a meritorious act, then the Vinaya is transformed into the Lotus Sutra.
If those within the Lotus Sutra take pleasure in music for their own amusement, then the Lotus Sutra is transformed into the Vinaya.
Although this is so, it is easy for Mount Sumeru to contain a mustard seed, but difficult for a mustard seed to contain Mount Sumeru.
Only those who are not hindered by such considerations of ease or difficulty may perhaps be capable of responding to this.
It may still be permissible to establish a ritual site (*maṇḍala*) for human affairs within the monastery.

[Commentary: The phrase "it may still be permissible" is not a term of urgency; rather, it is essential that one perform repentance and recite sutras according to the Dharma as the primary task, with the playing of music being secondary.
Now, for the sake of birth and death, one has abandoned the secular world to leave home; how could it be appropriate not to cultivate the primary task?

[Commentary: Everyone says they have left home for the sake of birth and death, yet when we examine them in their daily lives, when have they ever treated birth and death as a matter of primary concern?
Tell me, where is birth and death? If you ask lightly about it, out of ten people, not even one will reach the mark.
Come! Yet there are five pairs that grant wide latitude; thus, unaware and unknowing, one flows into the sea of the two deaths, where all is a vast expanse.
Now, before these very eyes, how many heroes have been drowned and destroyed by this "mouth of the sea"?
You must quickly take action and apply yourselves exclusively to the primary task. Only when your hands and feet are truly steady shall you not [fall].
Renounce the world to become a true man of the Way. What is called the "primary task" (zhengwu) is that which cannot be attained through cultivation or realization, nor can it be defiled.
To eliminate all phrases before one’s eyes is not the primary task;
your bringing forth questions is not the primary task, and my offering answers is likewise not the primary task. Ultimately, what is the primary task?
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, no one else can act on one's behalf.
In the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, the Buddha asked the śramaṇas, "In what interval does human life reside? They replied, "For several days. The Buddha said, "You have not yet heard the Way."
He asked another śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "In the interval of a meal. The Buddha said, "Son, you have not yet heard the Way.
He asked another śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "In the interval of a single breath. The Buddha said:
"Excellent! You understand the Way.
Yet you seek out skilled musicians and entertainers, even engaging in such matters as go (圍棋), board games (陸博), dice-throwing (骰擲), and gambling with *chūpú* (樗蒲).

[Commentary] According to the *Bowuzhi* (Records of the Wondrous and Extensive), Yao invented go to instruct Dan Zhu. According to the *Fangyan* (Regional Dialects), in the region east of the Guanzhong pass, it is called...
Regarding *yi*: the commentary to the *Hanshu* states that it is a board game played on a grid (*luobo*), where pieces are moved.
*Baohong’s Bójīng* explains that two sets of pieces, half black and half white, are cast. *Shanhugou Shihua* notes that *chupú* was invented when Laozi entered the Hu lands;
what is called *hulu* today involves winning by drawing a pure color. The *Wudeng Huiyuan* records that Dharma Master Fayuan resided at Fushan, as did the Duke of Wencheng, Ouyang Xiu.
Huiyuan was renowned for his extraordinary brilliance. [Dongshan] went to his quarters, yet he perceived nothing unusual. Huiyuan was playing chess with a guest; Dongshan sat beside them.
Dongshan abruptly gathered up the board and requested that Huiyuan expound the Dharma by means of the game. Huiyuan ordered the drum to be beaten and ascended the seat, saying:
"If one discusses this matter, it is like two parties playing a game of chess. Why is this so? When facing an opponent who understands the art, one must not yield when the moment arrives."

If one merely strings together five [points] and adds three more, only then can one begin to penetrate a single path. There is a certain class of people who only know how to "make a living" by closing their doors;
they cannot "seize the corner" or "break through the pass. Their stubborn resistance is like a tiger's mouth wide open, yet once the game is broken, they are left exposed.
All this is merely exhausting labor. Thus, it is easy to fatten the periphery, yet difficult to slim the belly. When one thinks and acts, one often loses the connection;
when the mind is coarse, one frequently strikes one's head. Cease boasting of being a master of the game, and stop vainly speaking of immortals.
Whether winning the board or losing the counters is of no concern; tell me, rather, before black and white have even been distinguished, where does that first move fall?
After a long silence, he said: "From the beginning, there have been nineteen paths; how many people have been deluded or awakened? Wen Zhong sighed in admiration for a long time.
Fushan used the game of chess to preach the Dharma; his intent lay beyond words, yet he was seen to be so adept at responding to circumstances as the occasion demanded.

Those of later generations who are ignorant, whose great matter remains unclarified, and who have not repaid their deep debt of gratitude, spend their whole days playing chess, neglecting their practice.
At that time, the matter was lost. Thus, comparing the manual discourse of Zhi Daolin with the "Seated Obscurity" of Wang Wenlang is a great error for a lifetime. How tragic!
Both disturb the mind of the Way and increase transgressions and evils. Alas! Can one not be cautious?
[Commentary] Good and evil oppose one another like the points of two arrows meeting. Ultimately, it is easy to do evil, but difficult to do good.
To do evil is like letting loose an unbridled horse; to do good is like rowing a boat against a current.
This is said as an exhortation for those who practice goodness.
Treatise: A Kṣatriya is the noblest in a single kingdom, yet none who receive his rank and mandate fail to be illustrious and honored.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Honored One of the Three Realms; how could those who don his dharma-robes be partial, meager, or base?

Ignorant laypeople, unaware of the sons of Śākya, do nothing but spit upon them and cast aside their sweet delicacies, loathing the splendor of fine mansions. Thus, they maintain their physical forms while subsisting on alms from bowls, dwelling...

To dwell among burial mounds is precisely intended to strip away arrogance and sever the entanglements of confusion; it is truly a matter of exalting one’s own dignity rather than seeking lowly humiliation.
For laypeople to turn their hearts against such practitioners and treat them with contempt is already a grave error.

Yet for those who have become sons of the Śākya to fail to respect themselves—reducing themselves to the level of entertainers blowing conchs and beating gongs—is to bring a stain upon the Dharma-gate; how could this be more extreme?
Now, as for Master Che, who climbed the pine trees and let out a long whistle, even he was obstructed by Donglin; how much more so would this apply to singing? [Commentary:

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the Song dynasty monk Che often went to the Southern Mountains to climb pines and whistle. Thereupon, a pure breeze gathered from afar and flocks of birds sang in harmony.
He was transcendent and possessed a superior spirit. Later, he consulted Donglin, who informed him that the monastic discipline strictly prohibits pipes and strings.

He strictly prohibited singing, dancing, chanting, and whistling. [The Master] asked, "Is it permissible to do so? Lin replied, "When discussing the matter of distraction, all such acts constitute a violation of the Dharma.
Thereupon, [the Master] desisted.
When the Venerable Asaṅga leaped across a body of water, he incurred the censure of those living nearby;
how much more so for one who dances? [Commentary: In the *Pañcaśata-praśna-sūtra*, there was a virtuous upāsaka who invited a bhikṣu, wishing to offer him a fine robe.
The bhikṣu traveled with him, and midway they encountered a water pit. He then leaped across it. The virtuous man thought to himself: "I intended..."

He offered a single fine robe, but because [the monk] was leaping over [the puddles], he reduced it by half. The bhikṣu, possessing the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, understood the noble one's intention.
As he proceeded, he again saw four or five water pits and therefore leaped over them. The noble one thought to himself:
"I shall reduce [my offering] until there is no robe left, and keep only a single meal. The bhikṣu proceeded further; seeing the water pits, he did not leap over them. The noble one asked:
"Why do you not step forward? He replied, "If I were to step further, I fear I might lose my food. The worthy man was struck with amazement;
realizing this was a practitioner of the Way who was repenting his error, he invited him home to provide offerings.
Even as for games of dice and gambling, external texts refer to them as "the pastimes of a swineherd. [Commentary:
According to the *Jin Zhongxing Shu* (Book of the Jin Restoration), when Tao Kan was the Governor of Jingzhou, he saw the implements used by officials for gambling and said:
"Go-boards were devised by Yao and Shun to instruct their ignorant sons; gambling was created by Yin Zhou. You gentlemen are all vessels of state—why do you occupy yourselves with this?"
The Sage treasures every inch of time; the common person treasures every fraction of time.
Whenever the various assistants would neglect their duties for games, he would take the *chupú* dice and cast them into the river, saying: "Chupú is merely the game of a swineherd's servant."
Regarding the practice of divination by observing celestial phenomena and performing calculations, the *Śāstra* refers to this as "living by wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*).

[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Śāriputra said: "For one who has left the household life, compounding medicines, sowing grain, or planting trees constitutes an impure means of livelihood;
this is called 'eating with the mouth downward. Furthermore, observing the stars and constellations, the sun, moon, wind, rain, thunder, hail, and lightning..."

A pure livelihood is called "looking upward for food" (*ūrdhvamukha-bhakṣa*). A corrupt livelihood that involves fawning upon those in power and acting as a messenger to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much gain, is called "looking toward the four directions for food" (*caturmukha-bhakṣa*).
A corrupt livelihood that consists of studying various arts and divining good or bad fortune through calculations is called "looking around for food" (*vidik-mukha-bhakṣa*).
For those who tread the Way, even a minor transgression—even for the duration of a finger-snap—is sufficient to defile their pure virtue.
Consider Master Xuanzang’s youth: when he encountered those engaged in frivolous play, he rebuked them, saying that such behavior squanders a hundred years of life.
[Commentary]: According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty entered the monastic order at the age of eleven.

Observing some śrāmaṇeras engaged in boisterous conversation and playful antics, he said to them: "Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). How could they engage once more in childish play?"
One might say that such people have merely squandered a hundred years of their lives;

yet gambling with dice and board games is even more extreme. Master An once saw, while in meditative concentration, that when those who discuss worldly gain and sustenance walk by, evil spirits sweep away their footprints.
[Commentary]: During the Guangxiao era of the Song dynasty, Anzhu was staying at Qingtai Temple. While in meditative absorption, he saw two monks leaning against a railing and conversing in private.

Initially, celestial deities gathered to protect them, listening for a long time before dispersing. Shortly thereafter, malevolent spirits spat upon them and reviled them, even sweeping away their footprints.
When he later inquired about the reason for this, it turned out that the two monks had first discussed the Buddha-dharma, then recounted their long separation, and finally engaged in [worldly talk].
Regarding sustenance: from this point until the end of his life, he never once spoke of worldly affairs.

Yet, as for divining signs and casting lots—could such things truly be appropriate? You should know that once one has withdrawn the hairpin [from office], it is fitting that the mind should likewise hold the jade scepter.
Be careful not to treat with such casual familiarity a body that is most supreme and most noble.
The eighth is: not sitting on high, wide, or large beds.
[Commentary: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings;

responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet he eternally dwells upon this Bodhi seat. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "By means of my wondrous clarity..."
Extinction does not arise; it is unified with the *tathāgatagarbha*. This *tathāgatagarbha* is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears.
Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it pervades the worlds of the ten directions. The body contains the infinite space of the ten directions. Within this one...
Upon the tip of a hair, he manifests a Jewel-King realm; seated within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
The commentary states: The Buddha prescribed that the height of a corded meditation seat must not exceed eight finger-widths of the Tathāgata; to exceed this constitutes an offense.

[Commentary]: Regarding the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, there are rope beds (*śayanāsana*) and wooden beds. A rope bed is constructed by binding ropes together; it is provided for those who travel on foot (*caryā-vartin*).

A wooden bed is for sitting; it is provided for those practicing meditation (*dhyāna*). According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha’s eight fingers measure approximately one chi and six cun in height, which corresponds to one cubit (*hasta*) for an average person.
When sitting, the feet must not dangle in the air. Any [bed] exceeding this measurement is called "high. However...
That which can accommodate the turning over of the body is called "wide" (*viśāla*). That which is both high and wide is called "great" (*mahat*).

Yunqi [Zhenjie] spoke these words for the sake of beginners on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) to warn them that they must not allow their bodies and minds to become lax, thereby increasing their transgressions and evils.

If one says that the measure of the Tathāgata’s recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*) already exceeds the limit of eight finger-widths, how much more so must this be true for the measure of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*)!
Therefore, the *Two Adornments Sūtra* (*Dvaya-vyūha-sūtra*) is cited first to clarify this point.
Even adding colors, carving, and such, as well as items like silk curtains and padded mattresses, are likewise unsuitable for use.

[Commentary] *Kunxue jiwen* (Notes on Learning Amidst Hardship) states: "When Shun made his eating vessels, he applied lacquer and ink to their surfaces. Those within the state who were not submissive [were thereby distinguished]."
Thirteen men. When Yu fashioned sacrificial vessels, he lacquered their exterior and painted them red within. Those states that remained unsubdued numbered thirty-three.
Shun and Yu were sage rulers; it was not an excess for them to use lacquer for their vessels.
Yet there were virtuous ministers who offered remonstrance, fearing that the officials and common people would be led to wasteful and insubstantial expenditures.
Thus, later generations know only of the sagehood of Shun and Yu, without realizing it was because of their virtuous ministers assisting them that they became sages.

Today, those who have left the household life decorate their private chambers and refine their utensils; their regulations violate the admonitions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and their enjoyments rival those of kings and lords.

As for these offerings: those who offer loyal words that are harsh to the ear and provide direct admonition are considered "old" [in style]; those who hunch their shoulders, flatter with smiles, and serve with crookedness are considered "fashionable.
This is why the monastic communities are daily falling into decay. As recorded in the *Chūgakuki*: "Thatch palaces and reed pillars are truly the pure strategies for the flourishing of a state;
jade mats and pearl robes are the corrupting transformations of a perilous realm."
The ancients used grass as seats.
[Commentary: When the World-Honored One practiced the Way on Mount Himavat, he used grass as his seat.

Later, after bathing in the Nairañjanā River, a celestial being gathered fresh green grass from the riverbank and spread it out as a seat for him. During the time of Fuxi, people dwelt in nests or caves. All...
Using grass as a seat. Verse: Tender grass serves as the spread for sitting; tall pines resound with the sound of the *brahman* voice.

The monk, having practiced meditative concentration, once spread the grass; the heavens, moved by the hearing of the sutra, again rained down flowers. One can thus imagine the refined atmosphere of the ancient practice of using grass seats.
I stayed overnight beneath a tree.
[Commentary: A Verse on the Dhūta Practices. Ancient trees support the heavens; they appear as if from the beginning of the kalpa. Why trouble oneself further with binding tiles?
How joyful it is to have this temporary hut! Deer pass by as moss divides in shades of green; birds pick up fallen flowers and place them upon the hem of my skirt.
Turning my thoughts back to the Yellow-Faced Old One, how could I help but sigh deeply?
Now that I possess these beds and mats, they are indeed superior; why not make them even higher and wider, so that this illusory body may indulge itself in ease?
[Commentary] The origins of objects can be traced back to Shen Nong, who first began making beds and mats. Before the era of Shen Nong, there were no implements for sitting on beds;
that we now possess beds and couches is already superior to the world of Shen Nong. Why must they be high and wide?

Having become high and wide, one further prizes elaborate carvings, yet fails to realize that this body is not of the nature of metal or stone and will ultimately not endure long. This is merely a waste of effort.
What waste! How much better it would be to have a bamboo bed or a wooden pallet, with bedding of straw and reeds—warm in winter and cool in summer, easily adjusted according to the season.
This is how one creates merit. *Wudeng Huiyuan*: Zhaozhou Congshen, when he first resided at Guanyin Monastery, disciplined his body with ascetic austerity.

There was no upper tier in the monks' hall; a corner of his rope bed had broken off, so he tied together some firewood to support it. Several times there were those who wished to provide a new [bed] for the Master.
Those who [sought his favor] were never granted their requests. He served as abbot for forty-five years, never once sending a single letter to a donor.
Venerable Pārśva never let his side touch the mat throughout his entire life.

[Commentary]: According to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), Venerable Pārśva left home at the age of eighty. A youth mocked him, saying, "The practice of leaving home consists of two things:
first, practicing meditation; second, reciting the scriptures. Now that you are so old and decrepit, what progress can you possibly achieve? When the Venerable heard this, [he replied:]...
He made a vow, saying: "If I do not master the Tripiṭaka, sever the five desires, attain the six supernormal powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never let my side touch this mat.
By day he studied the teachings and principles; by night he practiced meditative concentration with a focused mind.
After three years, he fully realized what he had vowed. The people of the time revered him and called him the Venerable Xié (脇尊者).

In the *Wǔdēng Hóngjù* (Five Lamps Record), it is recorded that Bìfēng Jīn went to study under Jìn Yún-hǎi. Yún-hǎi showed him that "the myriad dharmas return to One. Jīn harbored doubts for three years.

Once, while he was picking vegetables, he suddenly became motionless for a long time. Yún-hǎi asked him, "Are you in meditative absorption? He replied, "Absorption and movement do not concern me. Yún-hǎi said, "Absorption and movement..."
"It is not that. "What kind of gold? [Zhaozhou] showed him a basket. Haichang would not accept it. [Zhaozhou] threw the basket to the ground; still he would not accept it.
Thereafter, his practice became even more earnest; his ribs did not touch his mat. He sat for seven days straight. Upon hearing the sound of wood being felled, he attained great enlightenment.
Chan Master Gaofeng Miao observed the "Six Vows for Three Years," never touching a bed or a chair. [Commentary:
The Master’s name was Yuanmiao. He was the son of the Xu family of Wujiang. His mother dreamed of a monk arriving by boat before she conceived him.

Upon reaching the age when he was no longer in swaddling clothes, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture. Whenever he encountered a monk entering the gate, he would immediately wish to follow him.

At fifteen, he left the household life and entered the service of Master He Fazhu. At sixteen, he shaved his head; at seventeen, he studied the teachings of Tiantai; and at twenty, he changed his robes.
He entered Jingci Monastery and established a three-year limit for his death, never letting his side touch the mat and forgetting both mouth and body.
In a stone cave west of Shiziyuan on Mount Tianmu, he constructed a small room shaped like a boat and inscribed it with the name "Gate of Death. He severed all attendance;

as the cave could not be ascended without a ladder, he removed the ladder to cut off all external ties. Although his disciples rarely had the opportunity to see him, he passed away with this verse of enlightenment: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Coming, one does not enter the barrier of death; going, one does not exit the barrier of death. An iron serpent drills into the sea, toppling Mount Sumeru.
Even those who attain enlightenment and receive the seat of fragrant sandalwood still diminish their merit and invite retribution. Alas! How can one not be cautious?
[Commentary: Preface to the Water Repentance Ritual. Dharma Master Zhixuan encountered a monk who was suffering from *kāmalā* disease; he attended to him without weariness.

As they were about to part, the monk said, "In the future, when you encounter difficulty, you should go to Mount Chengtealongs in Pengzhou, Western Sichuan, where two pines shall serve as your marker.
Later, Zhixuan resided at An Guo Temple. Emperor Yizong paid him homage and bestowed upon him a seat of agarwood. Suddenly, [a growth] appeared...

He had a carbuncle on his face; physicians all stood with their hands folded in helplessness. Recalling the words of the monk, he entered the mountains to seek him out. Between two pine trees, the monk came forth to meet him.
Xuan detailed his agonizing suffering, to which the monk replied, "It is no cause for alarm. There is a spring at the foot of the cliff;

if you irrigate it with its water, you will be cured. At dawn, he was led to the spring. Just as he cupped the water in his hands, the carbuncle spoke, saying, "Have you ever read the *Book of Western Han*?"

"No. Gong is Yang, and I am Cuo. For generations we have sought retribution; Gong has been a high monk for ten lifetimes, his observance of the precepts being so pure and strict that our vengeance could not find its mark.
Now, having received this gift of a precious sandalwood throne, the mind of fame and profit has arisen within him, and thus we were able to harm him.
Fortunately, Venerable Kanakavatsa neutralized us with the water of samādhi; now we shall no longer be a source of trouble to you."
He cupped some water and drank it; his pain was severed, and after reviving, he was immediately healed. The two ancient pine trees and the old temple were all hidden from view.
Commentary: As for the sequence of a śramaṇa’s practice, one should naturally rest from all affairs and relinquish all external conditions, so that body and mind become as one.

Movement and stillness are without interval; for supernatural powers are the supreme karmic fruition that do not arise except through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the faculty of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*) does not manifest except through tranquility.
It is only when the water is cold and the waves are clear that the luster of the pearl appears.

[Commentary]: The Ritual for Seated Meditation. To seek the pearl, the waves should be calm; to retrieve it from moving water is difficult. When the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is clear and still, the pearl of the mind manifests of itself.
By locking the mooring rope to the pillar, the leaping of the monkey comes to rest.
[Commentary]: An essential explanation of the Dharma of meditation (*dhyāna*). It is like a monkey tied to a pillar. Throughout the day it runs to and fro, yet the chain always pulls it back;
only when exhausted does it finally rest, its point of reference remaining fixed upon the pillar. In this analogy, mindfulness is like the chain and the mind is like the monkey.
When the practitioner contemplates the mind, it is exactly like this.
The tortoise fears being devoured and hides it with care; thus, the water dog can never find an opportunity against it. [Commentary:
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, there was once a practitioner by a river under a tree who studied the Way for twelve years.
His greedy thoughts were not eliminated; though his body remained still, his mind wandered, finding no rest whatsoever. He was unable to attain the Way. The Buddha then manifested as a sand...
[The Buddha] arrived at that place. A tortoise emerged from the river and came beneath a tree.

There was also a water-dog, wandering about in hunger seeking food, which intended to devour the tortoise. The tortoise drew in its head, tail, and four legs, concealing them within its shell so that the dog could not devour it.
The Buddha said, "I observe that people of this world are not like this tortoise; they indulge their six sense-faculties, allowing external demons [to enter]."

Finding his opportunity, [the demon] destroyed the body and departed with the spirit; birth and death have no beginning, as one revolves through the five realms, suffering hundreds of thousands of afflictions.
Then he spoke this verse: "Hide the six senses like a tortoise; guard the mind like a city wall. With wisdom, wage war against Māra; victory brings no further suffering."
The horse was ashamed of its dullness yet set out first; the divine steed, on the contrary, was far surpassed in its ability. [Commentary:
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is like two people traveling to the same destination: one rides a swift horse, while the other rides a dull horse.
Although he rides the dull horse, because he set out earlier, he arrives first. This refers to those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), who practice with diligent effort.
Advancing, one first reaches nirvana;
how could there be any pursuit of external conditions? One rests peacefully upon the seat. The Buddha ordained that śrāmaṇeras receive [alms] in succession from the great saṃgha.
[Commentary]: In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "How should rooms and bedding be assigned to śrāmaṇeras? The Buddha said:
"They shall be assigned in order, starting from the most senior among the great bhikṣus."
Who would allow them to sit or turn around on a wide seat? Furthermore, it does not yet permit one to lie down upon it at ease.
[Commentary: In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is said that at that time, novice monks soiled their woven cord beds and bedding with excrement, urine, and vomit.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From now on, you must not allow novices to sit or lie down upon woven cord beds."
Regarding beds: if one can protect them from being soiled, sitting upon them is permitted.

However, how could it be appropriate to recline on high beds? Such actions bring calamity that violates [the laws of] ten generations. (The sudden realization of the enmity of Xuanda is as seen previously.)
Had it not been that his life was destined to end within seven days, he would not have been able to overcome the delusion of his handsome appearance.
[Commentary]: According to the *Sutra on Seeking Release from Prison*, King Aśoka had a younger brother named Shanrong (Good Appearance). While out hunting, he encountered several Brahmins.
[The King] practiced naked asceticism. He asked, "What obstacles and failings prevented you from achieving success?
The Brahmin replied, "While sitting, a herd of deer would gather together frequently. When I saw them, my mind was stirred and I could not control myself.

Your Majesty’s younger brother thought to himself, 'If even these Brahmins still possess lustful desires, how could the Śākya śramaṇas—who eat delicious food and sit upon fine couches—possibly be otherwise?'"

When King Anicchaśruta heard that his younger brother had developed wrong views and feared he would be forever lost in delusion, he commanded his court ladies to dress in finery and go to Sumanas’s residence to enjoy themselves together. Before long, the king went in person to speak to his brother:
"Why have you taken my various concubines to indulge yourself as you please? He then ordered his chief ministers to go to the marketplace and execute him. The ministers remonstrated, saying:
The king said, "I am merely this younger brother of yours. I pray that you will grant me seven days. The king consented, and within the inner palace, singing and music were performed.
When the seventh day arrived, the king asked, "Were you happy during these seven days? The brother replied, "I saw nothing and heard nothing; what joy could there have been?
The king said, "The various musicians were amusing themselves; why do you deceive me with your face and say you were not happy? The brother said, "For one who is about to die,"

"And what attachment do you have for the five desires? The King said: "If you now feel anxiety and grief over the cessation of this single body and find no joy in desire, how much more so should a śramaṇa feel anxiety and grief over the death and destruction of one body, only to receive another body for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes?"

The body and mind undergo suffering; because he felt such sorrow in his heart, he left the household life to pursue the Way, seeking the essential method for transcending the world through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Had he not applied himself with diligence, he would have endured suffering for kalpas. Upon hearing the King’s instruction, the younger brother finally attained awakening.
One should contemplate the twelve dhūta practices and dwell among burial mounds.
[Commentary] Verse: Ninth, Dwelling Among Burial Mounds—How desolate are the abandoned tombs! All that is heard therein is mournful. Old mounds are covered with fresh earth;
it is easy to witness the rite of impermanence. In this profound stillness, one gives rise to the nine contemplations, and all craving and desire are left far behind.
Rising from the ground, he turned away from his delusions; through the corpse, he awakened to what he had contemplated. A bhikṣu has four reliances (*niśraya*);
for his dwelling, he contemplates staying under a tree. [Commentary:

*Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemo* (The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya: Miscellaneous Karmavācanās). A bhikṣu receives the four reliances: first, rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*); second, alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*); third, [the remaining two].
Sitting beneath a tree. Four [points]: using decomposed medicine; not letting the side touch the mat;
generating diligence with difficulty; forgetting fatigue. [Commentary]:
The *Lamp Records* state that the Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Śrīparvata, was a native of Central India named Nan-sheng (Difficult-to-Born). The Ninth Patriarch was Bodhidharma.
Guṇamati shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him. He attended to him at his side, never once sleeping;
it was said that his ribs never touched the mat, and thus he was called the Venerable Pārśva.
Dust accumulated on his sitting mat. Huixi disciplined himself with rigorous austerity; like Bakula, he did not lean against the wall for ten days.
[Annotation]: In the Madhyama Āgama, there is a passage concerning a certain heterodox practitioner who was the Venerable Bakula before he left the household life.
His kinsmen and friends went to where Bakula was and inquired about the meaning of this. Bakula explained it for them, saying:
"Since I began training in this true Dharma and Discipline eighty years ago, I have remained in the full lotus posture, never leaning against a wall or a tree."
Master Miaoshan did not touch his bed or chair for three years; how much more so should this person, who has now first resolved to purify their mind and aspire toward the Holy Path?
One should carefully examine the profound meaning of the term *śramaṇa* (the seeker of tranquility) and the significance of the name *pravrajita* (the one who has gone forth).

Even if one stands on tiptoe to sigh in admiration of the virtues of Triśaṅku, one cannot hope to equal the merit of nine kalpas [of practice] (as detailed below in the section on Dignified Conduct). Therefore, by binding one's mindfulness [to the goal], one attains longevity.
Regarding the title of "old": how could it not evoke the shame of being eighty years of age?
[Commentary: In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, at that time the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to the assembly. There was an elderly bhikṣu.

The Buddha was sleeping with his feet extended toward him. A novice monk named Śramaṇera, eight years of age, sat not far from the Buddha in the full lotus posture, fixing his mindfulness before him. The Buddha spoke this verse:
"Those who are called 'elders'—even if they have not yet shaved their hair and beard and are advanced in years—if they do not avoid evil conduct, there are those who are younger..."
The faculties are untainted and unimpaired; this is called the Elder’s discernment of the practice of the True Dharma.
The Buddha said: "For one who has left the household life, mastery is suffering, while lack of mastery is happiness."
[Commentary]: In the *Madhyama Āgama*, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked the Buddha, "What is suffering for one who has gone forth? The Buddha replied, "For one who has gone forth, autonomy is suffering.
This means that by following after desire, hatred, and delusion, and failing to maintain the precepts, one consequently experiences anxiety and confusion;
therefore, autonomy is considered suffering. He asked again, "What is happiness? The Buddha... [text continues]
He said: "The renunciant takes non-autonomy as his joy. This means that in practicing the Way, he does not follow greed, hatred, or delusion;
he follows the precepts and exercises self-restraint. Being free from strife, resentment, and sorrow, and because there is meaningful benefit [in this], he takes non-autonomy as his joy."
At this time, you should repeat these words three times; do not allow even a single kṣaṇa to pass in vain.

Only then will you be able to restrain your foolish thoughts and cast aside arrogance and indolence, so that the seeds of your roots of goodness may once again blossom, and the branches of the Tree of the Path may flourish.

One becomes increasingly emaciated and withered; suddenly, one returns forever to the long night, where provisions for the journey are abruptly exhausted. When interrogated by the authorities of the underworld, what will one have to offer in response?
Thereafter, in a state of frantic panic and distress, one thinks to utter the cry of a ruddy sheldrake, but alas, it is already too late.
[Commentary]: According to the *Pāṇḍubhikṣu-sūtra*, on the day of a festival in foreign lands, all women wear *utpala* flowers as floral ornaments.
There was a wife of a poor man who said to her husband, "If you can obtain these flowers for me, then you are my husband;
otherwise, depart elsewhere. Although her husband was poor, he was skilled at imitating the cry of a ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). He immediately entered [the flower garden].
At King’s Pond, a poor man stole a blue lotus (*utpala*). When the pond-keeper asked, "What sound was that in the pond?
the impoverished man, having lost his composure, said, "I am a ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). He was immediately seized and taken before the king.
On the way, he again cried out with the call of a ruddy sheldrake. The pond-keeper said, "You did not cry out before; what is the use of crying now? So too are the fools of this world.
Thus it is. Having spent one's entire life inflicting harm and committing manifold evil deeds, one fails to practice mental cultivation to bring the mind under control.

Only when facing the end of life does one wish to cultivate goodness; yet the wardens of hell lead one away and deliver one to the abode of Yama. Although one wishes to cultivate goodness at that time—
How could it possibly compare?
Ninth is: not eating at improper times.
[Commentary: "Proper time" refers to from the appearance of the dawn light until midday. "Improper time" refers to from when the sun begins to slant until...

The following day, before the appearance of dawn, eating at an improper time is called a violation of the precepts. One who commits this must immediately perform repentance, except in cases of illness.
If one is hungry, one may take all grains, beans, or wheat and boil them until the husks are not broken;
the strained liquid may be drunk at an improper time. Likewise, the juice of pears, dates, and other fruits, sugarcane juice, or lotus-root juice that is as clear as water may be consumed.

If one has a thirst-related ailment, or is engaged in manual labor, or is being provided for by a donor, one may drink at improper times [liquids] purified with water, such as honey, rock sugar, or molasses syrup.
If one has a feverish ailment, or is traveling a long distance, or is unable to obtain food, [these may be consumed].

If there is little food, or if water is mixed at a place where water is distributed, it may be drunk even at improper times. Water remaining at the bottom of a vessel that has been washed by rain is also considered pure.
This applies equally to clarified butter (*sarpis*) and fresh butter (*navanīta*). However, in this region, cow’s milk is foul-smelling and unfit for consumption;
like *yavaka* (coarse grain) and similar items, it must not be touched or eaten. If it is mixed with other medicinal substances such that its flavor has already changed, [it is permissible].
[One] should wear [it]. If it is not fit to be eaten as food, one may mix it with *kālāhāra* (timely food), such as rice, cakes, or parched grain flour (*maṇḍaka*), but it must not be eaten [alone].
The commentary says: "Non-time" (*akāla*) refers to that which passes midday; it is not the time for the Sangha’s meal. The various devas eat early.
The Buddha eats at midday; animals eat after midday; ghosts eat at night.
[Commentary] From the *Samādhi-vyūha-sūtra*. After midday, even if it is but the passing of a hair’s breadth or a single instant, it is no longer the proper time.
By not eating at improper times, one obtains five kinds of benefit: first, freedom from all greed and desire; second, clarity and vigor of spirit; third, the ability to...
1. It dispels the demon of sleep. 2. The work of the Path is easily accomplished. 3. It increases merit and longevity. As stated in various sutras, the Buddha said:
"There are five blessings in not eating after midday: first, little lust; second, little sleep; third, attainment of one-pointedness of mind; fourth, freedom from flatulence;
fifth, the body attains stability and does not fall ill. *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination): One day and night consists of twelve [periods].
At that time, [the day] was divided into four periods: first, the morning period (*pūrvāhṇa*), namely the hours of *yin*, *chen*, which is the mealtime for the devas;

second, the midday period (*madhyāhna*), namely the hours of *si* and *wu*, which is the mealtime for humans and Buddhas; third, the afternoon period (*sāyāhna*), namely the hours of *shen*, *you*, and *xu*, which is the mealtime for animals;

and fourth, the night period (*rātri*), namely the hours of *hai*, *zi*, and *chou*, which is the mealtime for ghosts and spirits. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty provided a vegetarian feast for the monastic community, sitting together with the assembly upon the ground.
The meal was delayed, and the assembly suspected that it would be past noon before they could eat. The Emperor said, "It is now just midday.
Master Huiyuan (Sheng Gong) said, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; if Heaven says it is midday, how can it not be midday? He then took up his bowl and ate, and the assembly followed his example.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. He inquired about the ritual protocols for the vegetarian offering, noting that according to proper etiquette, the Buddha should come first and the gods second;

yet now, when the various gods eat their morning meal, they place the gods first and the Buddha second. [Wang] Xun replied: "If one calculates this based on the solar calendar of this land using the meridian and hour angles..."
Regarding the notion that heaven comes first and the Buddha later: if one observes the lotus flowers of the Western [Pure Land], heaven does not precede and the Buddha does not follow.
Why is this? It is because in the West, day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of the lotus flowers.
When one contemplates the realms of the ten dharma-worlds where beings make vows according to their karma, one sees them intermingling with the light of the Great Lotus Flower.

At that time, there was not even the slightest error. As for those devas who eat early, it is said that because they were diligent in their causal state through the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, they attained birth in the heavens;

thus, as a retribution, they appear at the moment the lotus is about to open, and they behold the light of the lotus while taking exquisite delicacies and fine foods as their meal. As for the Buddha’s midday meal, it is said that in his causal state...
With all virtues perfected and all practices fully accomplished, his adornments—both the primary body and its environment—are peerless in every respect.
Thus, while the lotus flower is in full bloom, its radiance mingles with the light of the sun, and he takes the joy of dhyāna and the bliss of the Dharma as his sustenance.

As for animals that eat in the afternoon: this refers to those who, during their causal state, lost their original nature, harmed and killed living beings, lacked a sense of shame, and committed unwholesome karma;
therefore, as retribution, they exist at the time when the lotus is about to close and is about to depart from its radiant light, taking water and grass as their food.
As for hungry ghosts that eat at night: this refers to those who, during their causal state, slandered the Three [Jewels]...
O Bhikṣus, those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds shall, as retribution, find themselves within closed lotuses where they cannot see the light of the flowers;
they shall take molten copper and iron balls as their food.
Therefore, monks should emulate the Buddha and not eat past midday.
[Commentary: Monks are born from the mouth of the Buddha, just as a son inherits and carries out his father’s will.

[He] continued the joy of the Dharma. Li Biao, courtesy name Daogu, served during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei. He held successive offices including Censor-in-Chief and Director of the Bureau of Historiography.
Once, he entered Zhongxing Temple to visit the monk Shi Sengzhong. At that time, it was already somewhat late in the day, yet Sengzhong had not yet eaten. Daogu said, "What kind of śrāvaka is this?"
