When hungry ghosts hear the sound of the alms bowl, fire flares up in their throats; therefore, even at midday meals one should maintain silence, let alone after noon."
[Commentary]: In their causal state as hungry ghosts (*preta*), they plundered the food of others to sustain their own lives, causing others to suffer from hunger.

Because they committed these karmic deeds upon bowls and alms-basins, they receive retribution upon bowls and alms-basins. For this reason, when eating, one must not allow the bowls or basins to make noise; this is out of compassion.

In the past, there was a eminent monk who, upon hearing his neighbor in the next room lighting the hearth after midday, could not help but weep, grieving for the decline of the Buddha-dharma. [Commentary:
This eminent monk took the Buddha-dharma as his own responsibility; thus, hearing that the hearth was lit after midday, he knew that the destiny of the Dharma was nearing its end.
In autumn, one weeps and laments with grief.
Nowadays, people are physically weak and prone to many illnesses; those who wish to eat frequently may be unable to maintain this precept.

Thus, the ancients referred to eating late as "medicinal stone," taking it to mean the intent of treating illness. One must certainly recognize that [frequent eating] violates the Buddha’s regulations.

One should feel great shame and remorse, contemplate the suffering of the hungry ghosts, and constantly practice compassionate relief. One should not eat much, nor eat fine food, nor eat with a restless mind;
only then can one hope for success. If it is otherwise, the transgression incurred will be even more grave. Alas! How can one not exercise caution?
[Commentary]: Yunqi [Zhenke], out of compassion for the suffering of the sick and the elderly, and in emulation of the Buddha’s kindness, composed this chapter.
At that time, senior scholars held differing opinions, asserting that according to the Vinaya, even medicinal food was not permitted after noon.
How much more so when taking late meals as medicinal food! As for medicinal food, this was already spoken of by the ancients;
what has it to do with Yunqi? Fourth, regarding the separate consumption of communal food: except during the "exceptional times," it is a *pāyattika* offense.

The "exceptional times" are: when one is ill, when making robes, when food is being distributed, when traveling on a journey, when traveling by boat, when a great assembly has gathered, and when śramaṇas are distributing food.

This is the proper time. These Vinaya texts are clear and manifest; the Buddha’s intent is perfectly preserved therein. Thus we know that Yunqi did not intend to mislead others, nor did he mislead himself.
Generally speaking, regarding the prohibitions within the Vinaya, one must be strictly solemn; yet regarding the occasions for permission, one must likewise be precise.

One must employ skillful means. Let not later generations use skillful means as a pretext to regard health as illness, to grow old before their time has come, or to indulge in eating and drinking in defiance of the Buddha's prohibitions.
Treatise: At the beginning of the eon, the sages observed the fast by abstaining from food for one day. The World-Honored One established the practice of eating only one meal at midday.

Because the Buddha severed the causes for rebirth in the six realms and caused his followers to accord with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, he established noon as the proper time for the dharma-meal.
Furthermore, when Nanda’s mother offered gruel to the Buddha, the Buddha accordingly permitted the bhikṣus to eat gruel.
[Commentary] This matter is seen in the "Ten Benefits of Eating Congee.
One takes the appearance of the white light (aruṇa) as the proper time for eating congee.
[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that there are three types of the white light: first, when the sun shines upon the trunk of the Śāmbuka tree, the sky appears black.
Second: When the sun shines upon the leaves of a tree, the sky appears blue; when the sun passes over the tree, the sky appears white.
Among these three colors, one must take the white as correct. Only when one extends the hand and the lines on the palm are clearly visible may one begin to eat the congee.
As one who is a disciple of the Tathāgata and aspires to seek nirvāṇa, how could one descend to share in the realms of evil destinies?
As for the celestial food at dawn, it may be shared in a limited way.
[Commentary]: In the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Huìfǎ: "There are four kinds of eating times: early morning is the time for devas to eat;
midday is the time for the Dharma to eat; evening is the time for animals to eat; and night is the time for ghosts and spirits to eat.
Because the Buddha has severed the causes of the six destinies and causes them to be equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, midday is the time for the Dharma to eat. Beyond this..."
Subsequently, it is the same as the lower realms; since it is not the time for superior food, it is called "non-time.
Therefore, even if a wheel were to tilt in a single instant or the shadow of a sundial were to pass by the width of a hair, all such [meals] are prohibited and severed.
[Commentary]: *Kṣaṇa* (instant) refers to the movement of the eyes. Two *kṣaṇas* are called one *tatkṣaṇa* (finger-snap). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"If even a single *kṣaṇa* has passed since noon, one must not eat. If the sun's shadow has passed the meridian by even as much as a single hair’s breadth, one must not eat."
Now, pungent vegetables, meat, wine, and sweet spirits are listed among the precepts; not eating them at improper times is what is called the method of fasting (*zhāifǎ*).
Yet those today who wear square robes and shaven heads have never observed a single day of fasting. At dusk they eat sumptuously, and in the middle of the night they gorge themselves;

broth and grains are strewn about, and spoons and chopsticks lie scattered in disorder. If they were to discipline themselves according to the Vinaya, it would be difficult to show them leniency. The Buddha said:
Even the various brahmins do not eat at improper times, much less my disciples who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma;
how could they act in such a way? Anyone who does so is not my disciple.
[Commentary]: In the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Śāriputra asked: "There are donors who construct monasteries and provide abundant provisions to support renunciants.
If, at an improper time, those who have come to the steward ask for food, what kind of offense do the one who gives the food and the one who eats it incur?
What kind of merit does the donor obtain? The Buddha said: "One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts."
Such a person is a thief. One who gives at an improper time is likewise a person who has broken the precepts and is also a thief.
They have stolen the property of the donor; since it was not the intention of the donor, the donor gains no merit, just as if they had lost their own goods.

There is only the merit of the initial resolve to establish [the practice]. Śāriputra said: "If one holds and receives food during the proper time, and there is food that remains uneaten, and one eats it again at an improper time, or..."
"Sometimes one receives food until the time for non-meal-time eating (*vikālabhojana*). Would one still obtain merit? The Buddha said: "Those who eat at the proper time are pure;
they are the field of merit, they are the renunciants, they are the Saṃgha, they are the good friends of devas and humans, and they are the guides of devas and humans.
Those who are impure are as those who have broken the precepts; they are a den of sin for hungry ghosts who steal through the eons."
At that time, one who seeks [alms] but gives them at an improper time is called a Māra who retreats from the Path;

he is called a person of an evil path, a broken vessel, and a leper, because he destroys the fruits of goodness. For all Brahmins and non-Buddhist ascetics (brahmacārins) do not eat at improper times.
They do not even consume food improperly; how much less so my disciples. You should know that one who practices according to the Dharma must understand the law:
if one steals or causes another to receive even a single morsel, a single handful, a fragment of salt, or a drop of vinegar, they shall all die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines.
The clear instructions are manifest, yet none take the trouble to reflect upon them. This is truly a matter of the heart. It is like attempting to carry a raw clay vessel;

while many may be broken, few remain intact. To mold frost into a vessel, it is easy to destroy but difficult to maintain. One does not consider that the faithful offerings are difficult to digest, nor does one acknowledge that the field of merit is becoming increasingly meager.
Consider the account recorded in the Vinaya of a bhikṣu who fell ill; the Buddha instructed him with various methods of treatment.
The Dharma is still not equal to eating and drinking. [Commentary:
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who had taken emetic medicine; as it was not yet time for his meal, his stomach felt empty and distressed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Anoint the body with ghee. Still, he did not recover.
The Buddha said, "Anoint the body with ghee mixed with parched rice flour. Still, he did not recover. The Buddha said, "Bathe and sprinkle him with warm water.
Still, he did not recover. The Buddha said, "Give him warm water to drink; it will sustain him until dawn. No one is permitted to eat past the proper time."
If this were so, even those who are ill would not recover, let alone those who are healthy. Furthermore, external records state that the monk Zhideng revived after death;
it is said that he took medicine after noon, though this was added by later generations and is not the Buddha’s original intent.
[Commentary]: According to the *Youyang zazu*, during the Zhenyuan era, the monk Zhideng of Tianchong Temple in Jingzhou habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When he fell ill and died, his disciples found that his hands and feet remained warm; fearing they might be premature, they did not dare to enshroud him.

After seven days, he returned to life and said: "At first, I saw the King of the Netherworld. As I joined my palms and descended the steps, he questioned me, saying: 'By virtue of your merit in reciting the sutra, you shall further...'"

He extended his life for ten years and strove to escape the cycle of birth and death. He further asked about the people of the world who, during the middle and later parts of the day, take medicine as food and eat *yǎngyìrén* (coix lacryma-jobi).
This greatly contravenes the fundamental teachings. Huìdēng said, "The Vinaya contains both allowances and prohibitions.
The King said, "This was added by later generations; it was not the Buddha’s intention. Nowadays, among the monastic community in Jingzhou, there are none who consume medicine after midday."
If one does not even heed medicine, how much less so that which is not medicine? Thus, they indulge their passions in unrighteousness and remain utterly negligent.

When questioned about what constitutes an offense or its violation, they are as bewildered as if in a dream. Yet Lord Yama thoroughly investigates the Buddha’s precepts; he is precisely refined and proficient in them.
How can one continue to accumulate transgressions until the end, gathering sins to face the final reckoning? This is like running while carrying a bundle of firewood.
Amidst fierce flames, one might carry stones and leap across spring ice; yet how could one hope for a fortunate escape?
If there is even a slight transgression during the time of the Rear Hill retreat, one remains empty and desolate throughout the entire day.

[Commentary]: According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), the Qi dynasty monk Shi Senghou returned to the capital from Shu. He established a stone chamber on the Rear Ridge to serve as a place for *an-zen* (dhyāna).
From his initial entry into the religious life (*śrāmaṇera*) until he attained the stage of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*), every day the shadow of his body shifted ever so slightly.
He would often pass by while the temple was empty.
When Master Shun’s illness became critical, he mistakenly swallowed some food; he vomited the grains and passed away.
[Note: According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Shi Zhishun of Yunmen Temple in the western suburbs of Liangshan fell gravely ill and did not eat for many days.
When the single meal was finished, the disciple Tanyue had been abstaining from grain for a long time; he secretly boiled half a measure of rice and offered it to Shun.

This truly enables one to discipline the person and solemnize the mind; how could one then worry about the authorities of the underworld opposing or challenging them?
Tenth: Not grasping or holding living beings, images, gold, silver, or precious objects. [Commentary]:

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that names are established according to the Dharma and designated in accordance with the Dharma. Those dwelling among the sages are called "true" (zhen), while those residing among the ordinary are termed "worldly" (su).
It is like gold fashioned into vessels; each vessel receives its name according to its form. What is on the finger is called a ring, while that which adorns the arm is named a bracelet.

Thus, when the one mind remains unmoving, it grasps distinct appellations and the myriad dharmas appear as differences. Yet the true gold does not shift; yet by recognizing these divergent names, the thousand vessels appear unequal.
If one knows that every dharma is the whole mind acting as a vessel, then when the vessels are exhausted, only gold remains; names and appearances can no longer [obstruct].
Dried up! How could right and wrong delude you? Furthermore, it is like a round vessel and a square vessel; their names differ. Or like raw gold and refined gold; their verbal designations vary.
Yet when one traces back to the origin and investigates the essence, all phenomena are empty. There are only mental expressions (*manojalpa*), with distinctions of name and meaning.

When stirred, they are the eight consciousnesses; when stilled, they become the One Mind. Having attained the ultimate principle, one forgets conditions; wherever one encounters them, [there is liberation].
"Without reliance.
The commentary says: "Birth" refers to gold. "Image" means resemblance. That which resembles gold is silver;
this means that while the nature of gold is inherently yellow, silver can be dyed yellow so as to resemble gold.
[Commentary] Translation: The Sanskrit term *jātarūpa* means "gold and silver" here. It refers to items such as those encased in gold. According to the Vinaya:

"Raw" (*jāta*) refers to precious metals such as gold and silver that have not been fashioned by human labor; "shaped" (*rūpa*) refers to precious objects made from gold and silver that have been formed into vessels by human craftsmanship.
Yunju Xian’s annotation and Yunsqi’s explanation are indeed correct: all items fashioned from gold and silver [are included].
Images, various utensils, head ornaments, and the like are all termed "images made of living beings" (*jōzō*).
These, as well as treasures—namely the category of the seven precious gems (*saptaratna*)—are likewise not to be grasped or held.
[Commentary] Regarding the translation of the "seven precious gems," the accounts found in various sutras differ. There are two types in the older versions; among them, the names are identical.

However, the Chinese and Sanskrit terms do not always correspond. Now, following the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanation of Terms in Translation), I shall provide two types of examples, all using the Sanskrit as the primary name, with the Chinese explanation provided below each.
First: *sūda-ra*, which in the Chinese language means "gold" (*jīn*). [See] the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra).
Gold is found within mountain rocks, sand, and red copper, and it possesses four characteristics:
first, its color does not change; second, its substance is unstained; third, it can be refined without obstruction; and fourth, it makes people wealthy. For these reasons, it is called a "treasure.

Second, *ārupa*—in the language of the Flower [China], this means silver. Silver is produced from scorched stones and is known in the world as white gold. It also possesses four characteristics, which are...
The preceding [category] is the same as gold; therefore, it is called a treasure. Third is *vaidūrya*, which in the language of China means "blue-colored treasure.

According to the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* (*Guanjing shu*), *vaidūrya* in the language of China means "not far away" (*bùyuǎn*). This refers to a mountain in the Western Regions that is not far from the city of Vārāṇasī.
The mountain produces this gem; therefore, it is named after it. This gem is blue in color, and none of all other gems can destroy it.
Its substance is firm and lustrous, rare in the world, and thus it is called a "gem" (*ratna*). Fourth is *vaidūrya*, also called *sphaṭika*;
in the language of China, it means "water-jade," which refers to azure jade. It is also called "crystal. Its substance and color are clear and glossy.
It is rare in the world; therefore, it is called a "jewel" (ratna). Five: Mūṣalagarbha. In the language of China, this means the "azure-white jewel," which is carnelian (*śaṅkhaśilā*).
Its shape is like the *gū* (the channel) of a chariot, or the *ya* (the spokes) and *wang* (the rim) of a chariot wheel;
it is named for these reasons. Because its substance is hard and its color is luminous, and because it is rare in the world, it is called a "jewel. Six: Ma...

it is named for this reason. Because it can be carved into vessels and is rare in the world, it is called a "jewel. 7. *Padmarāga*.
In the language of China, it is called "red pearl. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is produced by red insects.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this jewel emerges from the bellies of fish and the heads of snakes; its color is brilliant and translucent, making it the most excellent, and for this reason it is named a "jewel."
All of these increase greed and obstruct or cause the abandonment of the path of practice.

[Commentary: The word "all" clarifies that [objects such as] living beings and images are extremely easy to cloud the human spirit and wisdom. For example, an ancient mirror is originally bright and pure;
it cannot tolerate even a speck of dust. If even a single speck of light lands upon it, it immediately becomes an obstruction.
Obstruction. Now, as for the Way, not even a single speck of greed may be attached to it. If even a single speck is attached, the Ultimate Way becomes discordant and perverse.

This single greed immediately shuts down immeasurable Dharma-gates; from this point on, one has missed the mark.

It is like bees making honey: others obtain it while the bees themselves do not. Wealth and treasures are likewise thus.

Therefore, when the Buddha was in the world, the *saṃgha* all relied on alms; they did not maintain hearths for cooking, nor did they possess clothing or dwellings, leaving these entirely to external conditions.

Amidst the sounds [of the teachings], he attained realization and composed verses, claiming with full confidence that he had reached a definitive conclusion.

Little did he expect that his elder brother, Master Yangshan, would strike him once, thereby changing his very vision until he was so impoverished that he had no place even for a needle; Yangshan then struck him yet again.
The Way was not yet fully realized. It was only upon reaching the third verse that he finally granted him an understanding of the Patriarchal Chan.
Had it not been for those two blows from Yangshan at that time, how nearly would he have had a beginning but no end?

Why did Yangshan let him off so lightly? Let us set aside the matter of letting him off for a moment; tell me, was there any difference or similarity in the mental conduct of this father and son? Speak quickly!
The Way.

Nowadays, people are unable to practice alms-gathering together. Whether they enter monasteries, stay in hermitages, or travel to distant regions, they still cannot avoid the expenditure of gold and silver.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "unable to beg for food": foreseeing the decline of the Dharma, how could one not feel a sense of lamentation?
From this point down to the mention of "the expense of gold and silver," Yunqi was compelled to "enter the water to save those drowning. This was out of compassion.

Some have claimed that because there is no textual provision for a temporary relaxation of the rules within the Vinaya, Yunqi’s approach is a fabrication; yet these critics fail to realize that the Buddha himself [resided in such flexibility].

In the time of the True Dharma, what use was there for gold and silver? Therefore, they were not handled or possessed. Now, during this period when the Semblance Dharma abides in the world, transactions cannot be conducted without money.
Fearing that this might block the path of those seeking to study the Way, I have realized the Buddha’s intent and composed this treatise in accordance with the times.
Thus, in the following text, I shall alternate between permitting and prohibiting, so as not to allow later students to amass wealth and thereby increase their greed.
Do not seek after gain; do not hoard; do not engage in trade; do not adorn clothing, vessels, or other items with the seven treasures.
Only by doing so may you hope for success. If it is otherwise, the transgression will be all the more grave. Alas! How can one not be cautious?

[Commentary: Having just ascended to the First Stage (Prathamabhūmi), one focuses exclusively on the cultivation of the Way. Fearing that they might indulge and allow greed to grow, even gold and silver must not pass through their hands, let alone be accumulated.
It is observed today that those in charge of managing money and grain within the monastic communities treat these duties with utter negligence.

Can you remain untainted by greed? Xun, you are currently in charge of managing money and grain; all of these are the property of the Buddha, the property of the Dharma, and the property of the Sangha.
What do they have to do with you personally? If you allow even a hair’s breadth of defilement to enter this matter, it will be like the cauldrons and burning coals of hell.
If, within this, the Jing and Wei rivers are clearly distinguished, this is the "Treasury of the Blue Lotus. Regarding the "Precious Instructions," Sishi said:
"Those who seek profit cannot be given the Way; those who seek the Way cannot be given profit. It is not that the ancients were unable to practice both simultaneously;
it was simply that their circumstances made it impossible. If profit and the Way were practiced together, then merchants, butchers, and commoners—"

Even those who are lowly merchants like Yan Fu can seek it; why must one follow the ancients by renouncing wealth and honor, forgetting fame and achievement, extinguishing the heart's fire and dissolving one’s will amidst empty mountains and vast marshes, drinking from mountain streams and eating from trees for the rest of one’s life?
One must simply act so that profit and the Way proceed without mutual conflict or obstruction—just as if one were holding a leaking cup...
If one pours [liquid] into a cauldron that is already burning, not a drop can fall in.
Treatise: Among the ten non-virtuous actions, those of mental karma are supreme; among the three poisons, greed occupies the foremost place. Regarding wealth and profit for people...
It is the most severe form of calamity; yet among śramaṇas, there are those who are even worse than this.
The Vinaya states that there are four afflictions of a śrāmaṇera, and handling gold and silver is listed alongside drinking alcohol, sexual misconduct, and living by wrong livelihood.
[Commentary]: According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya may not grasp, hold, or possess gold, silver, or money.
The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya renounce precious treasures, pearls, and necklaces, and do not wear ornaments for adornment.

If one were to grasp gold, silver, or money while not relinquishing pearls, necklaces, and precious treasures, then one would be subject to the five desires. If one is subject to the five desires, one is not a śramaṇa son of the Śākya.
Dharma. The sun and moon have four afflictions. What are these four? Asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist—these are the great afflictions of the sun and moon.
When they encounter these afflictions, they are neither bright nor pure; they cannot illuminate anything, nor do they possess majestic power.
Śramaṇas also have four afflictions. What are these four? If a śramaṇa does not renounce the drinking of alcohol... [text continues]
Abandoning sensual desire; not abandoning the holding of gold and silver; and not abandoning wrong livelihood for one’s own sustenance—these are called the four great afflictions of a śramaṇa.
They cause a śramaṇa to be neither clear nor pure, unable to illuminate anything, and lacking in majestic power.
If one were to hold it in hand, one would privately hoard it; by privately hoarding it, greed and attachment arise.
Consequently, the wealth of the Dharma is lost and the life of wisdom is destroyed. A foul reputation spreads, and one is held in contempt and shame by the world.
Therefore, money was tied to the collar of the robe, and non-humans cast dirt upon it.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu who took a śrāmaṇera with him to visit his relatives. On the way, they passed through a vast wilderness where a non-human being manifested as a nāga.
This being circumambulated the śrāmaṇera clockwise, scattered flowers over him, and praised him, saying, "Excellent!
You have gained great merit by leaving the household life to go forth and refraining from handling gold, silver, or coins. The bhikṣu then arrived at the home of his relatives.
Having exchanged greetings, he wished to return. At that time, a female relative said to the śrāmaṇera, "As you are returning now, you may take some money with you to purchase what you require.
The śrāmaṇera accepted it and tied it to the collar of his robe. On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera carrying the money walking behind the bhikṣu;
he then transformed himself into a dragon, circled the śrāmaṇera to the left, and threw dirt upon him.
The Elder then said, "You have lost a great benefit. Having left the household life to practice the Way, you carry money while walking.
The śrāmaṇera then wept. The bhikṣu looked back at the śrāmaṇera and asked, "Why are you crying? The śrāmaṇera weeping replied, "I did not intend to commit a transgression;

I was distressed for no reason. The teacher asked, "What is it that you are holding? He answered, "I brought this money. The teacher said, "Discard it. Once discarded, it is no longer [a transgression].
The people again made offerings as before;
however, because the golden sand was applied to Śrīghana’s head, he found it difficult to fly through the air.
[Commentary: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, after the meal, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana and the novice Śrīghana went to Jambudvīpa.
While practicing meditation on the shore of Lake Anavatapta, the novice monk Cūḍapanthaka saw golden sand along the edge of the lake.

A greedy attachment arose in his mind, and he took some of the sand and placed it inside the Venerable One’s water pitcher. When Maudgalyāyana rose from his meditative absorption, he immediately returned through the air by means of his supernormal power.
At that time, the novice was possessed by a non-human spirit and was unable to fly through the sky. Maudgalyāyana called out to him: "Mī! (Cūḍapanthaka).
They went together. Mi said, "I cannot go. Lian asked, "Do you have anything with you? Mi replied, "I am carrying this gold sand.
Lian said, "You should discard it. Once it was discarded, he immediately ascended into the air and departed.
Is it not evident that the harm of grasping and holding things is like this? Thus we know that Tang Zhituo possessed nothing besides his spoon and alms bowl;
the multitude called him mad, to which he replied: "Those who call me mad are themselves the ones who are mad."

[Commentary]: According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Zhi Ze of the Tang dynasty possessed nothing beyond his earthenware bowl and a wooden spoon. He lived in a single room with his door left unbarred;
the public called him a madman. Having left secular life for the monastic path, his mind remained preoccupied with food and clothing, and he sought to shield himself during all his movements.
"Bian Shu sealed his chest; he neglected his time and disrupted his work, wandering about in restless anxiety, yet this was not madness—and there has never been one more mad than he.
How profound these words! Never in the world have we heard of a śramaṇa practicing the Way who died of hunger."

Seeing that there were sons of the Śākya who, despite maintaining their precepts, were killed by cold, one should simply remain constant and firm in one’s conduct, forever exerting oneself with the original resolve.
Acting spontaneously and proceeding with a straightforward mind, one will naturally not fall into want; if one were to worry about such scarcity, [the goal would be lost].
Consequently, almsgiving is obstructed; fearing its exhaustion, begging for food begins to become difficult. Why is this so?
A mind anxious about scarcity is far removed from the Way, and the concern over depletion is increasingly at odds with the Dharma.
Therefore, although they are disciples of the Tathāgata, neither dragons nor devas will escort or protect them, nor will benevolent deities grant them guardianship, leading to such karmic conditions.

To be cut off by such circumstances and driven to the brink of starvation is not at all surprising; yet, instead of examining oneself, one claims that the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy, hoarding wealth for personal gain and seeking profit through the five kinds of improper conduct.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five kinds of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): first, feigning extraordinary physical characteristics; second, boasting of one's own spiritual powers; third, practicing divination of omens and portents;
fourth, raising one's voice to manifest an air of authority; and fifth, proclaiming the gains one has obtained to stir the hearts of others.
The eight impure requisites for livelihood.

second, planting roots and sprouts; third, hoarding grain and millet; fourth, keeping male and female slaves; fifth, raising herds of livestock; sixth... [text continues].
7. Hoarding gold, silver, coins, and treasures; 8. Hoarding ivory and objects such as carved carvings; 9.
Hoarding copper and iron cauldrons and pots for one’s own cooking and heating.

[Commentary] *Udānavarga*: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "Do not covet the offerings of Devadatta. Devadatta has brought ruin upon himself and will likewise bring ruin upon others.
Long ago, there was a flock of vultures, each brooding over its young. A vulture said to its chicks:"
"If you learn to fly, you must remain suspended in the void so that the earth appears like a shallow bowl;
do not soar too high, for there is the Sūciloma wind which will injure you, scattering your head, brain, and limbs to different places.
At that time, the fledgling did not follow his parents' instruction and flew beyond the proper limit; blown by the wind, he lost his life in another place.
This is the constant practice regarding fodder and water. Suddenly, [the horse] was offered butter and parched grain, yet its body was set ablaze. [Commentary:
According to the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), in the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi, it was the common custom to feed pigs with parched grain fried in butter.
At that time, a state horse colt said to its mother: "We exert ourselves for the King, regardless of distance or nearness, always responding to his commands. However..."
They were fed with grass and fodder and given rainwater to drink. Their mother said, "Be careful not to harbor such thoughts as to envy the roasted barley mixed with butter.
Before long, you shall see proof for yourselves. As the festival season drew near and the New Year was about to arrive, every household tied up pigs and cast them into boiling cauldrons;
they wailed and cried out at the top of their lungs. "O horses, sons of the auspicious mother! Do you remember?"
"Was the barley fried in ghee? If you wish to know the proof, you may go and observe it for yourself.
When the young colts see that this is indeed the case, they will realize their former transgression; even if they encounter barley while grazing, they will never dare to eat it."
An ancient worthy said: "Do not fear spears and halberds falling from the sky; a single thread through a lotus root can entangle one to death.
Is this not what a śrāmaṇera should contemplate deeply?
[Commentary]: *Avataṃsaka*. O Son of the Buddha: It is as when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven engage in battle with the asuras.

When the gods achieve victory and the asuras are defeated and retreat, the King of the Asuras—his body being seven hundred yojanas tall and surrounded by fourfold armies numbering in the tens of millions—by the power of his illusory arts, leads his host of troops simultaneously.
They enter into the pores of a lotus fiber. In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has likewise already well accomplished the stage of wisdom regarding all illusory dharmas.
Illusory wisdom is itself the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva is himself illusory wisdom.

He is able to enter meditative absorption within non-differentiated dharmas and emerge from it within differentiated dharmas; he enters meditative absorption within differentiated dharmas and [emerges from it within non-differentiated dharmas].
*Record of Faching*: While the Master was eating lotus roots with the assembly of monks, he said:
"In the past, the Asuras once engaged in battle with Śakra. When the Asuras were defeated, they retreated and entered into the pores of the lotus fibers.
You all eat lotus roots; have any of you ever bitten into one of those Asuras? At that time, there was...
A monk made a gesture of vomiting. The Master said, "The assembly is eating lotus roots; why do you make such a gesture?
The monk said, "If I did not act this way, I fear I would be ridiculed by others. The Master said, "Even if you were to act this way, you would still be ridiculed by others.
The monk asked, "How about you, Master? The Master said, "Just eat the lotus root; what else is there to do?"

Poem on Lotus Fibers In the north of the Lotus Garden, a beautiful woman from the West washes lotus roots. In her hand she holds a golden knife, as if cutting jade. Who within the jade can recognize the hidden ice-silk?
Stroke after stroke, the jade is severed, yet the fibers continue. Moved by this, I have spontaneously composed a song;
Within its lines, the musical notes of *gong* and *shang* require careful refinement. The icy sound upon my teeth and gums forgets the heat of the sixth month; The low humming fills [the air].
Mouthfuls of frost and snow, chewing and singing, the threads multiply. Though the Weaver Girl is skilled, she grieves at the autumn waves.
Thank heaven my tongue reaches the springs and valleys; fragrant eddies wind through the belly of the lotus. Earth’s warp and Heaven’s woof are chanted by gods and ghosts;
thread after thread, brilliant and shimmering, illuminates the mountains and rivers. Do not let the root and stem be startled and consumed; leave behind but a single strand.
