There is nothing inferior. Today, as the mountain monk walks along and casually swings my arm, I shall explain it through for all of you:

the phrase "passing over water" leaves one not even wet; within the storehouse, pearls are piled high. The phrase "passing over water" leaves one not even dry; though one lacks a single needle, how can one speak of poverty?
Neither the path of dryness nor the path of moisture is traversed; let the green waters and blue mountains be as they are. ◎ Magu Baoche.
While traveling with Mazu, the Master asked, "What is Great Nirvana? Mazu replied, "Hurry. The Master said, "Hurry for what? Mazu said, "Look at the water.
The Master, together with Nanquan and Guizong, went to visit Jingshan. On the road, they encountered an old woman.
He asked her, "Which way does the path to Jingshan go? The woman said, "Go straight ahead. The Master said, "But the water ahead is deep."
“Is it possible? Venerable Pāṭali said, “The feet do not get wet.
Details regarding carrying the water jar, the mendicant’s staff, and so forth are as described in the Vinaya; they are omitted here for fear of excessive length.
If one must travel separately, one should agree to meet at a certain place and must not arrive late.
[Commentary]: "Corner" refers to going there briefly on some business. "Appointment" refers to fixing a time. "Later time" means missing the appointed time.
When receiving the *śīla* (precepts), one should stand in attendance. Once the bestowal of the *śīla* is completed, one again stands in attendance to receive the *dakṣiṇā* (offering).
[Commentary]: Receiving offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) is entirely the duty of the attendant. However, the attendants of today are not the attendants of former times.

There are those who mistakenly use the teacher’s offerings for themselves; failing to honor their own spiritual nature, they ruin their human character for a lifetime with a few coins—this is truly lamentable.
Regarding the seventy-two rules of decorum: when arriving at a donor’s house, one must request pure water to wash the bowl. The teacher sits and holds [the bowl].

One should hand the hand-towel and bowl to the teacher and then return to one's own seat. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, when sitting in a row for a meal, one must not eat before the teacher.
Once the teacher has finished eating, one should rise and take up the bowl. When sitting separately near the teacher, one should remain standing by the teacher’s side.
When the teacher instructs one to eat, one should sit down to receive the food. When taking a separate seat for the meal, there are four matters to observe:

first, one should stand beside the teacher; second, one should only depart when the teacher instructs one to do so; third, one should prostrate with the head to the ground in salutation; fourth, while eating, one must not sit haughtily or play about.
After the meal is finished, one should go and stand beside the teacher; only when the teacher instructs one to return to one's seat should one sit.
This is the rule for taking separate meals. [Section] Fourth:
Entering the Assembly.
[Annotation]: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, because the noble disciples of the Buddha abide in harmony, there are two kinds of dharmas: first, those of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Speech. Second, the noble silence. Relying upon the furnace for refinement, one must certainly provide service; being smelted by the bellows and forge, it is appropriate to first enter the assembly.
When the function of conforming to the dust is uniform, the merit of saving sentient beings will naturally be universal.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, whenever one wishes to enter the assembly, one should possess five qualities: first, one should act with a mind of loving-kindness; second, one should humble oneself, like wiping away dust.
The *Jin* (Towel). The *Nanshan Chao* states: "Shift what is straight onto others and draw what is crooked toward oneself;
constantly examine one's own faults and do not litigate the shortcomings of others. The *Record* says: "The *jin* is able to take filth upon itself, causing other things to become clean;
thus one should know the three methods for rising and sitting. If you see a senior (*upādhyāya*), you should not remain seated; if you see a junior, you should not rise. This is for...
A bhikṣu shall speak. If a śrāmaṇera sees anyone who has received full ordination, he must always rise to stand.
When among the saṃgha, he must not engage in miscellaneous talk or discuss worldly matters, whether speaking on his own behalf or requesting another to speak.

Fifth, if one perceives something improper within the Sangha and feels mental unease or intolerance, one should remain silent. Regarding this, Xuedang quoted the "Precious Instructions" (Baohuan), which states:
"When eminent monks preside over an assembly, they must say: 'Within this assembly, you must recognize those who possess true understanding.
I asked him the reason for this, and the Hermitage Master said: 'Have you not seen how Guishan taught: 'In your conduct, look to the superior; do not follow the mediocre with arrogance.'"
I am base. Throughout my life among the masses, I have never sunk to the bottom. Fools all give this same excuse.
Among the dense throngs and vast multitudes, the base are many while the wise are few; the base are easy to associate with, while the wise are difficult to approach.
If one can truly exert oneself among them, it is like a single man facing ten thousand enemies; the power of vulgar habits will be exhausted, and one will emerge truly upright.
Truly, he was a man of immeasurable capacity. Throughout my life, I have practiced his words, and only then was I able to remain true to my original vow to leave the household life.
Verse for Entering the Assembly: If you see a gathering of the assembly, you should wish that all sentient beings may preach the most profound Dharma and that all may be in harmony.

[Commentary]: *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra*. Second, the vow upon beholding the objective realm. First, beholding the assembly: because the gathered multitude was discussing many meaningless things, he vowed to preach the profound Dharma;
because the minds of the assembly were prone to discord, he vowed to bring them into harmony. This most profound Dharma cannot be expressed by worldly words and letters.
If it could be expressed by worldly words and letters, there would be no way to perceive this Dharma.
In the profound depths—where even words cannot reach—one perceives the depth of this Dharma.

Thus, if even worldly characters cannot fully express this most profound Dharma, how could it be spoken by the mouth? Therefore, that which is spoken is non-speaking, and that which is heard is non-hearing.
When there is neither speaking nor hearing, all things are in harmony; when all are in harmony, [the Dharma is realized].
[This is] appropriate. This is called the profoundly deep Dharma.
One must not contend for a seat. [Commentary]:
To sit without propriety results in the offense of pride (*māna*). To sit while contending shows a lack of magnanimity toward others. Furthermore...
This violates the dignity of a great man. However, regarding seating arrangements in monastic communities, there are already the *Baizhang Qinggui* (Pure Rules of Baizhang);
one should not strive for a seat through ill will. Alas! I have never seen anyone who strove for morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness.

Morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are attained through non-contention; a seat is occupied through non-contention. Formerly, Yan Luyou had the "Seating Arrangements Letter" (*Zengzuowei Tie*); because of this, I...
There is the "Clerk's Letter on Contending for Seats in the Meditation Hall," which censures petty men who despise the worthy and envy the capable,
while extolling scholars who value humility, reverence, and deference.
One must not call out to, speak with, or laugh with others from a distance while seated in the hall.
[Commentary: "Calling out and laughing from afar" refers to those who, while sitting at a great distance from others, shout and laugh wildly as if no one else were present;

such people are like those who see boiling water and would not dare to approach it. In the *Lamp Records*, when Chan Master Hongzhi was serving as the attendant to Chan Master Chun, he was engaged in a debate with a monk in the quarters and suddenly burst into loud laughter. Chan Master Chun happened to pass by and heard it.
When night fell, he questioned him about this. Zhì said, "I was merely engaged in a debate with a monk; my coarse nature could not contain myself, and I laughed.

Chún said, "Indeed, by that single laugh of yours, you have lost how much of the good fortune! Have you not heard it said: 'To be absent for even a moment is as if one were dead'? Zhì bowed in submission.
Thereafter, although he was in the dark, he never again dared to be negligent in his practice.
If there are those among the assembly who lose their dignified decorum, one should conceal their faults and proclaim their virtues.
[Commentary: Regarding "losing decorum," this refers to matters such as calling out to one another from afar and laughing aloud. One ought to conceal the faults of others and promote their virtues.
*Baohun* (Precious Teachings) records that the Patriarch Yan said: "The ancients delighted in hearing of their own transgressions and took joy in performing good deeds. Long...
In embracing the unruly, he was generous in concealing their faults; he was humble in befriending others and diligent in aiding the multitude. He did not allow his mind to be divided by gain or loss;
thus, his brilliance and magnificence shine forth, illuminating both the present and the past. When Lingyuan heard that Juefan had been exiled to the South of the Ridges, he sighed and said:
"An orchid planted on a roadside path will surely lose its verdancy before long; but a cassia tree growing in a secluded ravine will ultimately [endure]..."

I harbor a sincere aspiration that has persisted for many years. Throughout antiquity and the present, those who have lost their lives through their talent and wisdom, or who have met with calamity due to slander and calumny, are numerous;
yet those who were able to remain submerged deep within themselves while floating along with the world are few. Therefore, the Sage said:

"Those of this age who are clever and profoundly observant, yet come close to death, are those who love to criticize others. Those who are erudite, eloquent, and magnanimous, yet endanger their own persons, are those who love to expose [the faults of others]."
The faults of men exist even in Juefan.
He must not boast of his toil to manifest his own achievements. [Commentary:
"Boast" (fá) means to exaggerate; it refers to the act of over-exaggerating one's own abilities. However, even if one possesses great merit, why should one boast of it?

There were those who, precisely because they did not boast, saw their merits become even more manifest. Zhongfeng Ben, who resided at the two monasteries of Dajue and Shizi, was able to achieve his success only through the Master’s guidance;

yet when he was commissioned by imperial decree to compose an inscription for a stele, he refused to claim even a fraction of the credit for himself, nor would he allow even a single name to be included.
Chengfan and his colleagues were harmonious and benevolent toward one another, and they shared in mutual benefit.
There are those who substitute for one another. *The Classic of the Way and Its Power*: "He who is self-satisfied does not manifest his excellence; he who boasts of himself has no merit;

he who is self-conceited does not flourish. *The Book of Changes*: "The humble and humble gentleman finds good fortune in the end. The *Hexagram Commentary* says: "In humility, the honorable becomes lowly and takes precedence. *The Analects*:
Yan Hui said, "I wish that I might not boast of my goodness, nor display my hardships. ◎ Xie Zi parted from Yichuan for a year, when suddenly they met again...
Yunmen saw him and said, "It has been a year since we parted; what progress have you made? Xie replied, "I have only managed to eliminate one thing:
the character for 'self-conceit' (jīng). Yunmen asked, "How so? Xie said, "Upon careful examination, I found that my illness lay entirely here.
Only when this fault is rectified will there be a place for further advancement. Yunmen nodded and said, "The predecessors had no room for self-conceit or boastfulness."
This is not merely a matter for public officials;
it applies to everyone everywhere. When sleeping, do not be in front of others; when rising, do not be behind others. [Commentary:

If one studies the Way with diligent effort, the demon of sleep will naturally depart. When alertness and stillness mutually illuminate one another, then in every matter one will always be ahead of others.
In every action, do not fall behind others; what cause for concern is there that the Way will not be realized? According to the Pure Rules (*qinggui*):
when the five-watch bell is about to toll, rise quietly and sit upright. Do not fan the wind or cause others to become distracted in thought.
The Verse on Hearing the Bell.
[Commentary] According to the *Tongzai zhuan* (Comprehensive Record of the Transmission): During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, in the Sūtra Hall of Gandhāra, he fashioned a bell of blue stone.
At the time of sunrise, various transformation Buddhas emerged together with the sun and secretly expounded and clearly proclaimed the twelve divisions of the sūtras. Upon hearing this—

The number of those who realized the Dharma and attained sainthood is beyond counting. According to the *Zhouli Kaoshi*, the artisan Fu fashioned the bells. The *Wujing Tongyi* states that the bell is the sound of the autumnal equinox;
when all things reach autumn, they come to fruition, and by winter, they are stored away. Thus, metal is used for the bell so that its resonance continues without interruption.
The *Xijing Ji* records: "The whale is struck, and the magnificent bell rings. Xue Zong’s commentary notes that this refers to a great fish of the sea.

It is called a whale. On the islands of the sea there is a beast named Púláo (Pu-lao), which fears the strike of the whale; whenever the whale strikes Púláo, the latter immediately lets out a great roar.

Whenever one wishes for the sound of a bell to be magnificent, one fashions it in the likeness of Púláo so that the striker may produce the "whale-sound. There is an inscription in seal script [on this image].
Whenever one hears the sound of a bell, one should silently recite this gāthā. "Silent recitation" refers to the voice of the mind; the mind possesses a voice.
Is it that the mind has no sound? This soundless sound can only be heard by oneself; it cannot be heard by others. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says, "Reverse the hearing to hear one's own nature.
Why not simply hear this by hearing for oneself? This is what is meant by the "sound of the mind."
Upon hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light.
[Commentary: "Afflictions" refers here to the root and derivative afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the method of calming and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*):
afflictions disturb and disorder the mind, causing it vexation and distress. If one hears the sound of the bell even once, even the most heavy of afflictions will be transformed.
It is a light and pure sound.
Wisdom grows long; Bodhi arises. [Commentary: Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*):

"intelligent discernment" is called *jñāna* (knowledge), and "discriminative analysis" is called *prajñā* (wisdom). These correspond to the latter two types of knowledge among the faculties. Regarding Bodhi: it is wisdom.
This is the fruition. If one hears the sound of the bell but once, the flower of the wisdom-mind will suddenly blossom, and the fruit of the path to Bodhi will be swiftly realized.
One will leave the hells and emerge from the fiery pit.

[Commentary]: Regarding the Fourfold Teaching Ritual (*Sijiaoyi*), the hells: the Sanskrit term is *naraka*, also called *niraya*. This is translated as "instruments of suffering" (*kugu*) or "vessels of suffering" (*kqi*).
They are called "hells" because they lie beneath the earth. These refer to the eight cold and eight hot hells, among others.

Each major hell has its own retinue, numbering in the infinite. Those who undergo suffering therein receive their retribution according to their specific karma, each in varying degrees of lightness or severity.
It is heavy. For kalpas equal in number to [the aforementioned], in its most severe regions, one undergoes eighty-four thousand births and deaths within a single day for immeasurable kalpas.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil deeds of the highest grade experience rebirth in this realm.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, this hell lies five hundred *yojana* beneath Jambudvīpa. Furthermore, these hells vary in size; among them, the largest—
8. The "Small" [Hell] consists of sixteen [subdivisions]. *Huo-keng* (Fire Pit) is one of the names for various hells.
"I vow to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings. Oṃ karateye svāhā. [Note]:
Regarding the vow to attain Buddhahood, there has never been anyone who did not first resolve to deliver sentient beings; nor has there ever been anyone who... [text continues]
The Buddha is one who delivers sentient beings. If sentient beings do not deliver themselves, yet first vow to deliver others, this mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
One should know that this mind and this vow both arise from the moment the sound of the bell is heard.
At that instant, boundless afflictions are severed; the Avīci Hell is shattered from this point; and inexhaustible Dharma-gates [unfold] from this.
One enters and realizes the unsurpassed Buddha-way; from this it is accomplished. Verse: The whale strikes, the *pulao* bell roars;
evening after evening, morning after morning, three times and two times nine. The Universal Gate suddenly appears, and both ears go deaf. Within the eyes, the lion opens its mouth wide.
Opening its mouth wide—Pāpīyān turns his back on Mount Sumeru and flees! *Tu!* According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, when the bell is struck, one should make a vow: [...one] vow.

All the sufferings of the various evil realms shall be brought to a complete halt. If one hears the sound of the bell while simultaneously reciting verses of praise, one shall be freed from the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over five hundred billion kalpas.
◎ It subdues demons, ghosts, and enemies; it eradicates all fetters without remainder. When the *gandi* is struck upon the open ground, the bhikṣus shall assemble.
Those who wish to hear the Dharma and cross the flood of the ocean of birth and death—upon hearing this, [they shall attain liberation].

O you of wondrous resonance, may you well assemble here in the future. According to a verse from another sutra: "If one hears the bell and does not rise from bed, the protective deity of the couch will be incensed.

Because the conditions for merit in the present life are meager, the retribution in the future will be to receive the body of a snake. Wherever the sound of the bell is heard, those who lie down must surely rise;
joining their palms and generating a virtuous mind, all the worthy sages will rejoice. The great bell vibrates with sound, awakening the multitude of the deluded.
The sound pervades the immeasurable lands of the ten directions; all sentient beings hear and know it. It uproots the suffering of living beings throughout the long night.

The six consciousnesses are perpetually clouded by the suffering of the endless night; when covered by ignorance, consciousness becomes deluded. Hearing the bell at a tranquil night, one awakens to enlightenment;
with a serene spirit, one attains supernatural powers within the pure land. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu fǎ zàng jīng), because the king committed acts of killing, he died.
He entered among a thousand-headed fish, where sword-wheels revolved around his body; as he was cut, he was reborn.
An Arhat served as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the Saṃgha and struck the bell at the appointed times. Whenever he heard the sound of the bell, the sword-wheels remained suspended in the air.

For this reason, he sent a messenger to inform the magistrate to strike the bell, saying, "Let me cease from my suffering. After seven days had passed, his suffering ceased. This is recorded in the *Fozu Tongji*, Volume 1.
In Yuanyuan County, there was a man who died suddenly and entered the underworld, where he saw those bound with wooden stocks and shackles. They told him, "We were the former rulers of Southern Tang.
We were mistakenly attacked by the armies of Song and Qi; we killed over a thousand surrendered soldiers from Hezhou, and because of this grievance, we have been imprisoned here."

"Entrust this message to you to deliver to the successor on the throne: whenever bells are struck in temples or monasteries, one should prolong their resonance. When I undergo suffering, hearing the sound of a bell alone allows me to find temporary relief;

it would be even better if a single bell were specially cast for this purpose. He further said, "During my reign, the Kingdom of Khotan presented me with a jade statue of the Heavenly King (Devadatta).
It is hidden within the left knee of the Buddha at Waguan Temple, and no one knows of its existence. You [should retrieve it]."

This was the proof; he then revived. He reported this to the Ruler of Tang, and it indeed came to pass as he had said. The Ruler wept with emotion and commissioned a bell for Qingliang Temple, inscribing upon it:
"To dedicate to the late Emperor Gao, my ancestor, so that he may be delivered from the darkness and emerge from calamity.
Furthermore, he erected a pagoda for the jade image and interred it at Jiangshan.
Washing the face with water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings attain the gateway to the pure Dharma, forever free from defilement. Oṃ raṃ svāhā. [Commentary:
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, "To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the resolve of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, when the practitioner washes [their face],...

"Face" refers to having previously made this vow. "Pure Dharma-gates" refers to the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*) being transformed into eighty-four thousand gates of pure Dharma.
"Forever free from defilement" means that after one has attained this for oneself.
Until one attains Buddhahood, there is ultimately no defilement; therefore, it is said that there is "eternal non-existence. When the ancients washed their faces, they would touch their own nostrils.
It is also said that the "True Person of No Rank" enters and exits through the gate of the face. Every morning you wash your faces—have you ever touched your nostrils?
Have you dreamed of this True Person? Tell me, what kind of nostrils are these? What kind of True Person is this? Speak quickly!
The Way:
When washing one's face, one must not use excessive water.
[Commentary] Proverb: One must not burn too much firewood on the mountain; one must not use too much water near the river. This is for the sake of cherishing one’s merit.
Although these are but colloquial words, they should be inscribed upon one’s sash. In the *Lamp Records*, it is said that during his lifetime, Master Zhantang Zun disciplined himself with austerity;

even while leading a community and propagating the Dharma, he did not differ from when he was among the ranks of ordinary monks. After rising at dawn, he would go to the rear hall and take only a small ladle of hot water to wash his face.
Having then washed his feet, he would receive water to irrigate his vegetables and fruits, never letting them go to waste. I have often used [this method] myself.
This is the origin of washing the face with a basin.
When brushing one's teeth and spitting out water, one must lower the head to lead the water downward; one must not spray or splash water upon others.
[Commentary: To spray or splash water upon others causes them to give rise to anger; even if one has rinsed the teeth clean, one cannot thereby cleanse their mouths.
Because this constitutes karma, one should act with meticulous care.
One must not blow one's nose or spit loudly. One must not discharge nasal mucus or saliva within a temple, a stupa, a pure chamber, a pure ground, or into pure water;
these should instead be done in a secluded place.
[Commentary] Vomiting is unavoidable; however, one must not do so loudly. Temples and pagodas are places where Buddha images and śarīra relics are enshrined.
Pure water and other offerings are intended for use by the Buddha and the assembly. To defile these with mucus or saliva is no small offense; therefore, one should choose a secluded spot.
Formerly, there was a monk who sat in a Buddha hall at night and happened to vomit. Under the light of the lamp, he saw the Dharma-protecting deity.
He extended his golden hand to receive [the bowl], whereupon the monk was struck with awe and remained restrained for the rest of his life.
When drinking tea or soup, one must not greet others with only one hand. [Annotation]:

According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to place the hand upon the chest is called *yi* (greeting). It also means "to advance" or "to yield. Pronounced *jiari* (cut by *jia* and *ru*), its sound is *ri*. It signifies a gathering or assembly.
As for bowing with one hand, there are two meanings. First, when drinking tea or soup with one hand, one simultaneously uses that same hand to offer the drink to another person.
Second, when drinking tea or soup with one hand, one simultaneously uses that same hand to perform a bow toward another person.
In ritual propriety, one shows respect with both hands; to use only a single hand constitutes an offense.
One must not rinse one's teeth facing a stupa, nor facing a preceptor (upādhyāya) or an ācārya.
[Commentary]: There is foul breath between the mouth and teeth. One must not face ordinary people with it, much less face a Buddha stupa, or one's *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*.

Regarding the rinsing of the teeth, the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Sea) states that the rules for rinsing the mouth are extremely strict; one must be careful.

According to the *Sānqiān wēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Dignified Conduct), one must not face the Buddha, nor turn one’s back to him. One must not face one’s *upādhyāya*, *ācārya*, or other teachers, nor turn one’s back to them.
Turn your back [to others]. Do not laugh excessively. If you laugh loudly or yawn, you should cover the opening of your sleeve with your robe. [Commentary]:
To laugh excessively or to laugh loudly is either the mark of a fool or a madman. A yawn is the dispersal of the spirit and vital energy; it is called "sinking" (mò).

The underlying meaning is as follows. "Covering the mouth" means to withdraw and collect one's spirit so as not to become dissolute; it signifies being upright and self-respectful. Regarding Wudeng Fanyun:
in his daily conduct and movements, he gazed straight ahead without blinking. For thirty years while presiding over a community, he never once allowed himself to laugh lightly.
In whatever place he resided, upon seeing an image of a sage or a Buddha, he would immediately rise and not sit. ◎ Yuantong Ne was simple and austere, and did not engage in idle speech.

He smiled. He constantly practiced meditative concentration. At first he joined his palms; by midnight, they had gradually risen to his chest. His attendant would watch them every time to await the crowing of the cock, for he was not permitted to move quickly.

[Commentary]: To walk hurriedly is to lack a proper gait; one’s dignified deportment is entirely disregarded. When those who possess discernment observe this from the side, they feel terror on their behalf.
Should one happen to stumble, the body would be mangled and the skin torn, leading to lifelong regret. As the consequences are so grave, one ought to walk slowly.
One must not fail to respond when called. Whenever one is summoned, it is appropriate to respond by reciting the Buddha’s name. [Commentary:

To hear a call and not respond is because that person is possessed of jealousy, anger, and resentment, which obscure and obstruct the mind. The mental capacity of a practitioner of the Way is like an empty valley;
it responds immediately whenever struck. How could one allow jealousy to fester within the breast? To respond by reciting the Buddha’s name—

Because Yunqi exclusively expounded the Dharma-gate of the Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) method, if one is a person of keen spirit, upon merely hearing their own name called out, they will suddenly realize that "the mind is Buddha" and "neither mind nor Buddha," and even penetrate all thousands and hundreds of koans at once. To show later students how to awaken toward the point where the name is called, I shall briefly cite several instances of the karmic conditions of ancient worthies. Hearing the Call and Awakening: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have the Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "Mu (No). A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the Way? Xuefeng said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. A monk asked Dongshan, "How does one enter the gate of the Buddhas? Dongshan said, "Not by means of the three vehicles. The monk asked, "Then how does one enter the gate of the patriarchs? Dongshan said, "Not by means of the five vehicles. A monk asked Linji, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Linji gave him three blows with his staff and drove him out. A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Yunmen said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. A monk asked Fayan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Fayan said, "The sky is blue, the mountain is green. A monk asked Caoshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Caoshan said, "The wind is blowing, the grasses are swaying. A monk asked Touzi, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Touzi said, "The snow on the mountain peak. A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Baizhang said, "The morning star is shining brightly in the east. A monk asked Nanquan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Nanquan said, "The ox is eating grass in the field. A monk asked Shishuang, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Shishuang said, "The water flows to the west. A monk asked Yangshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Yangshan said, "The moon reflects in the water. A monk asked Jiaofan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Jiaofan said, "The stone woman gives birth to a child. A monk asked Xuedou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Xuedou said, "The white clouds are locked within the deep valley. A monk asked Yunju, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Yunju said, "The golden cock crows at midnight. A monk asked Wuzu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Wuzu said, "The iron ox has no horns. A monk asked Fenyang, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Fenyang said, "The red flag flies over the city. A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Dongshan said, "The bright moon shines in the clear sky. A monk asked Guishan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? Guishan said, "The spring water flows to the east. therefore, it is ordained that whenever ascending the hall, one must fasten one's trousers and socks, and must not act according to one's own whims or convenience.
[Commentary: The Great Hall is the place where all the sages assemble; one should ascend it with solemn purity. Regarding the binding [of the lower garment]:
this is for fear that impurities from the lower body might be left upon the Buddha-ground. In the Western Regions (India), there are skirts but no trousers.

"Skirt" (*chun*) is translated as "inner garment. This specific rule is not part of the Buddha's regulations. Yunqi followed local custom to avoid it, as recorded in the *Lamp Records*. Yungju Ying ordered...
The attendant delivered a pair of trousers to a practitioner staying in a hermitage. The practitioner said, "I already have the trousers I was born with," and would not accept them.
The Master again ordered the attendant to ask, "Before you were born from your mother, what were you wearing? The practitioner was speechless. Later, when he passed away, there were śarīra relics.
The Master said, "Even if one were to obtain eight bushels and four pecks of such relics, it would not be as good as having delivered a single turning word at that time."
"Very well.
You must not wander about idly.
[Commentary: The study of the sages and worthies is inexhaustible; there is never a moment of leisure. Even if one attains greatness...

"Xian (leisure/quietude) is Xian. Yet there is still wisdom (*prajñā*) present. The *Yi* says: "To fence off depravity and preserve one's sincerity. This is not merely a matter of fencing off; there is still sincerity (*śraddhā*) present.
We who are currently at the stage of learning must, throughout our lives, employ this word "xian" to remain in a state of quietude.
We must be diligent, taking Chan and the Vinaya as our core concern, so that we do not fail the kindness of our parents and teachers. As the ancient masters said: "When at leisure..."
Reaching the point of falling into emptiness; when busy, one does not fail to pursue objects, yet one does not fall into emptiness nor pursue objects.
Tell me, whose realm is this?
Do not speak too much.
[Commentary] *Baohun* (Precious Instructions). Xuedang said: "When a student does not know where the Way is directed, they seek out teachers and friends to investigate it with them.

Xuedang was compassionate, loyal, and magnanimous; he honored the worthy and respected the capable. Jokes and vulgar speech rarely issued from his mouth. The *Daodejing* states: 'Excessive words lead to exhaustion;
it is better to maintain the center. The *Yijing* states: 'The words of a person of auspicious character are few; the words of a restless person are many.'"
Much. One must not sit idly by while the assembly performs labor, avoiding work out of laziness and seeking only personal ease.

[Commentary] Since what is eaten is shared equally, what is undertaken in service must also be shared equally; in this way, one may hope not to bring shame upon Baizhang. "If for one day one does not work, for one day one shall not eat."
He did not eat. Wudeng huiyuan records that Yangqi said, "Seeking comfort for oneself above and below is a great affliction for the Dharma-gate.

◎ Yuanzhao Ben was naturally gifted with a pure and beautiful character, free from artificial adornment. He followed Tianyi Hui, wearing tattered clothes and personally attending to the well and the mortar while assisting with the cooking.
By day he busied himself with monastic affairs; by night he sat in meditation. He was diligent and rigorous, never for a moment slackening.
Someone said, "The Dhūta practitioner bears the burden of the assembly; this is truly laborious. Dōben replied, "If one abandons even a single dharma, one cannot be called fulfilled in Bodhi.
Desiring to realize this within this very body, how could I dare say it is laborious?"
One must not privately take the bamboo, wood, flowers, fruits, or vegetables belonging to the *caitya*; nor any food or drink, nor any utensils or implements.

[Commentary: *Caitya* refers to things belonging to the four quarters, that is, the property of the permanent endowment (*saṃghika*). "All" means more than one kind. To speak of "one bamboo" is merely an illustration.
A single piece of wood, a single flower, or a single fruit—all these belong to the assembly; to take them for oneself is theft.
One must not speak of the imperial court or government offices, nor discuss the merits or failures of state affairs, nor the strengths, weaknesses, virtues, or vices of lay householders.
[Commentary] Admonitions. Whether traveling through mountains or by the water’s edge, one must exercise caution and restraint in conversation.

To open one's mouth like a bow and let words fly like arrows, to judge worldly affairs with the ease of applying yellow orver-paint, to rate others’ merits, to discuss food while mentioning money, or to scold at the wind and revile the rain—these are all heard by walls; laws have no partiality.

When one suddenly suffers injury from the tiger’s maw, it is only then that one sees how exposed the blade’s tip was. To engage in private discussions regarding the administration of the court [is likewise perilous].

Matters: While residing in the guest quarters of the Gongfu (Ministry of Works) during my private time, I discussed the abundance or scarcity of the realm’s lands, debated the excellence or depravity of its customs, and even engaged in trivialities concerning commerce and industry, idle chatter of the marketplace, military conflicts on the frontiers, banditry in the Central Plains, literary arts, and matters of food, clothing, and wealth.
Since these activities were contrary to meritorious karma and offered no benefit to the path of the mind, such idle discourse all harms one's true substance.
Virtuous One. Sitting here consuming the offerings of the faithful, I look upward with shame before the dragons and devas.
Whenever you address yourself, you should state your two-character Dharma name; you must not say "I" or "this humble monk."
[Commentary]: When responding to others, to say "I" is perhaps too arrogant; to address one as "little monk" (shōsō) is perhaps too condescending.

It is better to use his two-character dharma name, so that he may maintain humility and propriety. Whenever there is one who leaves the household life, the preceptor should observe the excellence or deficiency of their faculties and then establish a name for them.
A single character or a pair of characters is the very first word of instruction used to guide them, intended to cause them to...

A lifetime [of practice]. As the name suggests, those who bestow names today do not understand the proper manner of expounding the Dharma, and those who receive names likewise do not understand the utility of attaining the Dharma;

thus, they have distanced themselves from antiquity. In the *Lamp Records*, regarding Yuanjue of Mount Xiang’er, when the Prefectural Governor filled out the official document, he mistakenly wrote "Yuan" (袁) instead of "Xiang" (象).
Because the Master’s secular surname was Yuan, the Governor jokingly remarked, "This is a single-character name."

"Very well," said the Master. "Even one character is too many. Shou was struck by this remark. Yunju Xian’s commentary states: Whenever one refers to oneself, one must use one's Dharma name (*hōmyō*).
When the character "Somethingsomeone" (甲) appears in written texts, it is because the author did not know the person's actual name and thus left two characters blank as a placeholder.
Nowadays, people who already possess a Dharma name nevertheless refer to themselves as "Somethingsomeone" whenever they meet others; this is a great breach of propriety. — Zhengfeng.
Record: At that time, there was an attendant who had followed him for several years, yet An still did not give him a name.

Whenever he was given a task, he would simply look at him with his eyebrows and eyes; the attendant would then carry out the matter accordingly. A monk asked the Master, "What is this attendant’s name?"
The Master said, "I do not dare defile him. What name would you give him? The monk was speechless.

One must not engage in disputes over trivial matters. Even when faced with major issues that are difficult to endure, one must remain even-minded and composed, resolving them through reasoned argument.
If this is impossible, one should take one's leave; to lose one's temper and act crudely is not the mark of a good monk.
[Commentary: Having spent a long time among the multitude, engaging in the exchange of words and conversation, how could there not be occasions of error?

If others should respond with harsh or offensive speech, one need only rely on the single character "patience" (*kṣānti*). By remaining tranquil and self-governing, one may prevail. Yet, while this single character "patience" is easy to speak of, it is truly difficult to practice.
One must possess great strength of will to be able to subdue the mind. If one's strength is slightly deficient, one will unconsciously...
Driven by the winds of karma, one falls into the realm of the rākṣasa demons. *Baokun* (Precious Admonitions) records that Xuedang said:

"If a student’s temperament (*qi*) overcomes their resolve (*zhi*), they become a petty person; if their resolve overcomes their temperament, they become an upright person; when temperament and resolve are equal, one becomes a sage who has attained the Way.
There are those who are stubborn and fierce, refusing to accept counsel and admonition; this is caused by their temperament. Even if an upright gentleman is made to... [perform such acts].
"It is not good. It would be better to die than to do this; it is one's resolve that makes it so. ◎ Linyuan said to Master Changling Zhuo:
"The propagation of the Way surely has its own time. In the past, Ciming let his mind roam freely among the Jing and Chu regions, enduring shame and bearing insults."
Those who saw him treated it with indifference; Ciming merely smiled. When asked the reason for this, Ciming said, "A city of ten thousand *li* collides with a mere clod of earth;
I knew from the start that it could not prevail. Only after he beheld the Divine Tripod did his fame spread through the monastic communities (*saṅghārāma*), reviving the Way of Linji.
Alas! The Way and the times—how can they be forced? Vajra, I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention.
Among humans, the foremost is the one who practices patience. Among the myriad practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), patience is the foremost.
The *Daodejing* states: "The highest goodness is like water. Water is good at benefiting all things without contending. The Way of Heaven does not contend, yet it excels in victory.
In the *Bishan*, there is an account of a man who was so enraged by a dispute with another that he rushed to appeal to Master Wang Yangming. Wang said, "Go for now."
"I shall speak these good words to you once your mind is calm and your breath is harmonious. The man departed immediately.

After several days of cultivation, he returned and knocked again, saying, "My mind is calm and my breath is harmonious; I wish to hear the good words. The King said, "A calm mind and harmonious breath—this itself is the good word.
The man thanked him and departed.
Entering the Meditation Hall with the Assembly, Part Five (This chapter was originally in the tenth fascicle; it is now placed here).
[Commentary] Chan Master Tianru Ze’s Universal Discourse: At birth, one does not know where one comes from—this is called the "greatness of birth.
At death, one does not know where one goes—this is called the "greatness of death. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives, one is left with nothing but frantic hands.
The feet are already stumbling; how much more so on the vast and boundless path ahead? To follow karma and receive its retribution is precisely the most urgent matter.

This is the realm of the retribution of birth and death. If one speaks of the root of the karma of birth and death, it is this very present moment—a single thought that follows sounds and pursues forms, causing one to fall into the seven topsy-turvy and eight upside-down states. For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs exercise great compassion and may teach...

You practice Chan, or you are instructed to recite the Buddha’s name, so that you may sweep away deluded thoughts and recognize your original face, becoming a free and easy man of great liberation. If you do not obtain spiritual efficacy now, there are three kinds of illnesses:
first, not encountering a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to provide guidance; second, being unable to apply oneself with intense resolve...
Taking the great matter of birth and death as one's primary concern, one may remain drifting aimlessly and indifferently, unwittingly falling into the "armor of non-action.

Third, regarding worldly fame and fleeting profit, one fails to see through them and cannot let them go; delusive conditions and evil habits persist even while sitting in meditation and cannot be cast off.
When stirred by the winds of external circumstances, one unconsciously rolls along with the body into the ocean of karma.
In the midst [of it], drifting eastward and bobbing westward—how could a true practitioner of the Way act in such a manner? You should believe the words of the Patriarch:
when miscellaneous thoughts fly about in confusion, how can you apply yourself? A single *huatou* (critical phrase) is like an iron broom;

the more you sweep, the more there is to sweep; the more there is to sweep, the more you sweep. Suddenly, having swept through the vast void, the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences are all traversed as one path.
Virtuous practitioners of dhyāna, exert yourselves now to bring this life to completion; do not allow yourselves to suffer further calamities for eternal kalpas.
Early Awakening Verse and Dharani (to be silently recited upon waking from sleep): Upon first awakening from sleep, I vow that all sentient beings may attain the awakening of all-encompassing wisdom.
He gazes all around the ten directions. Oṃ Āḥ Hrīḥ.

[Commentary] The Sub-commentary cites: "The Omniscient Awakened One not only possesses simultaneous clarity regarding the three periods of time, but also possesses thorough understanding throughout the ten directions."
If it is thus from the beginning to the end of a single day, all other instances are likewise so. Generally, what one thinks of during the day becomes a dream due to those thoughts at night.
At the very moment when one is about to wake but not yet awake—before being deluded by forms and before falling into the discrimination of consciousness—it is called the "first awakening.
It is the moment when the dream suddenly shatters; one opens the eyes to receive forms, and once again falls back into [the habitual state].
When the consciousness discriminates, it is called "opening one's eyes while dreaming.
Only the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom-awakening shines its light universally even where the sun and moon do not reach; it is the same whether waking or sleeping even where dreams cannot conceive.

Therefore, it is not the case that while sleep has its degrees of magnitude, awakening does not; even down to the scale of years, months, days, and hours, there are likewise extensions and contractions.
It is said in the world that Chen Tuan slept for three thousand years as if it were a single day and night; this was but a minor sleep.
For the Tathāgata, one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa constitutes a single day and night; this is his "great sleep.
As for the people of the world, their sleep does not constitute true sleep, and their waking does not constitute true waking; they do not even know the reason for sleeping or waking.
Waking is like the first rising of the sun; sleeping is like the first appearance of the moon. The spiritual root of humanity is born within heaven and earth and is received from Heaven.
The Way is thus: when the celestial eye sleeps, the human eye also sleeps; when the celestial eye opens, the human eye also opens.

One day and one night, one movement and one stillness, all follow the operation of the celestial Way. If one goes against the celestial Way, then even under the clear blue sky and bright sun, it is as dark as the long night;
therefore, sleep and awakening are not achieved. Only our Greatly Awakened World-Honored One...
He constantly performs the work of a Buddha here, whether sleeping or awake. Therefore, when we are wide awake, we should practice this contemplation and make this vow.
The one of wise vision takes pity on sentient beings who dwell in ignorance and are shrouded by darkness;
thus, with the sun of great wisdom, he awakens and illuminates them. He gazes upon them all.
Its source points back to where [the Buddha] pointed at heaven and earth. This means that those of the Two Vehicles see only a single corner and have not yet seen the whole elephant;
only the Bodhisattvas, having opened their wisdom and awakened their correct eye, are able to survey all around.

They do not merely awaken to and illuminate a single corner of themselves, but are able to awaken to and illuminate unspeakably many sentient beings and unspeakably many worlds—suddenly like clouds parting to reveal the sun.

Manifesting this clear vision is the light of the Great Perfect Circle (Mahāmaṇḍala). It is like when the World-Honored One, immediately upon emerging from his mother’s womb, pointed to heaven and pointed to earth;
this was the realm of the World-Honored One’s minor awakening. Why is this? It is solely because he proclaimed, "I alone am the Honored One.
Furthermore, it is like when the World-Honored One was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat; on the evening of the seventh day of the second month, he entered right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
In samādhi, when the morning star appeared on the eighth day, he attained great enlightenment and sighed, saying: "How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it.
This is the realm of the World-Honored One’s Great Awakening. Why is this? It is simply because it is said that all sentient beings possess [it]."
Therefore, although this is so, let us set that aside for now, World-Honored One. Within the very midst of everyone here at this moment, tell me quickly:
is this a dream, or is it awakening? Speak!
On one's own bedding, one may shake the robes to make a sound that fans the wind, causing those on neighboring beds to become mindful [of their own conduct].
Verse for Putting on Robes: When putting on the upper robe, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma.
[Commentary]: In antiquity, people wore skins; it was the Yellow Emperor who first fashioned garments. According to popular tradition, the "upper garment" (*shàngyī*) refers to the long robe.

It is called a *zhídǔ* (straight-cut robe) or a *hǎiqīng* (sea-blue robe). In a poem by Tàibái (Lǐ Bái), it says: "Fluttering, he dances with wide sleeves, like a bird coming from the East Sea. Another name for it is the "Daoist robe" (*dàofú*).
The Grand Ultimate Perfected One said: "One should cleanse one's garments and prepare the prescribed attire of the headcloth and coarse robe; these are called the 'Attire of Contrary Dharma.
As for the upper garment, it is the most supreme garment of the body; it is said that when wearing this most supreme garment, one should give rise to the most supreme mind."
And they give rise to the most supreme vows. This mind and these vows are themselves the most excellent roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
It is because all sentient beings have lost these roots of goodness and are submerged in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) that they make this vow:

to cause them to possess roots of goodness so that they do not remain submerged, but reach the shore—the ultimate stage. [The stages] of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are all not called "ultimate"; only...
The Buddha’s One Vehicle is called the ultimate shore. Furthermore, the "upper garment" (ūrdhvamśuka), or "upward-turning garment," is also called the "garment of reverence.
It is said that when one wears this garment, one should know there is a matter of upward progression.

Even if one cannot attain sudden enlightenment, one should still gradually cultivate dignified deportment to obtain the most excellent Dharma; thus, with every step, one performs superior and wholesome deeds and ascends to the shore of the Dharma.
This is the ground of goodness.
When putting on the lower garment (*nivāsana*), one should wish that all sentient beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with shame and remorse.

[Commentary: According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), *nivāsana* means "lower garment" in the language of Tang; "garment" (*qun*) refers to a multitude, as it is composed of joined strips of cloth. [Old...]*
It is called *nirvāṇa-saṃgha*; this is a corruption [of the original term]. All roots of goodness are the essence of the pure fundamental source and also the function of the pure *dharmakāya*.
It is said that when one puts on the lower robe (*nivasana*), wholesome dharmas manifest before one. If what is contemplated is not perverse, then one abides in the state of shame and remorse;
this is precisely the locus of the pure source. It is for this reason that people are deluded by the five desires and are unable to achieve purity.
"Purity" arises simply from not knowing shame and remorse. If one is fully possessed of shame and remorse, how could the pure and wholesome dharmas ever be lacking?
Regarding the Five Lamps: A monk asked Huanglong, "The Master’s admonitions and the disciple’s capacity meet with immediate resonance; I beg the Master to convey this message.
Huanglong said, "The skirt-belt burns with incense."
Adjusting one’s robes and fastening the belt, one should wish that all sentient beings restrain their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost.
[Commentary: To fasten the belt means to tie it with cords and pleats; thus, the various schools differ, and the colors vary between yellow and red.

"Adjusting" refers to formal adornment. "Fastening" means to gather and collect. This means that by restraining the various sense faculties, one externally maintains a solemn demeanor while internally gathering [the mind].
Gathering the mind is the very function of the Path.
A single verse follows: From the morning dawn until the evening dusk, may all sentient beings protect themselves.
If one should lose their life beneath my feet, I pray that you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land.

[Commentary]: According to the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), because the Tathāgata’s past mind was pure, free from attachment, and did not afflict sentient beings, his feet remained unstained by dust wherever he traveled, and insects or ants did not harm him.
The Buddha established a precept against causing injury by mistake; because such acts were unintentional, no punishment was incurred, which is consistent with worldly laws.
Nevertheless, even for injuries caused by mistake, there is still the karmic retribution of being injured in turn. See the first section on killing.

Commentary on the Treatise on Precepts. All within the court and the countryside sing its praises: When the five-watch bell ceases and people first awaken, the insects and spirits upon the earth are about to emerge from their burrows.
When the sun approaches the hour of *bū* (the late afternoon) and people wish to sleep, the insects and spirits upon the earth likewise return to their burrows.
Do not mistakenly harm or destroy the lives of these insects; what distinction is there between human nature and insect nature?
Verse on Walking Without Injuring Insects: When lifting the foot, one should wish that all sentient beings emerge from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Oṃ dhiri dhiri svāhā. [Commentary]: "Wholesome dharmas" refers to the practices and vows of a bodhisattva. Among the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, the mark of the feet is foremost.

The mark of virtue (*guṇa-nimitta*). This refers to first fulfilling one’s vows through practice. Thus, whenever a Bodhisattva lifts a foot, they immediately vow that all sentient beings may emerge from the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra-samudra*).
If sentient beings were identical in their practice and vows to those of the Bodhisattva, where could there be birth and death?
It is solely because their practice and vows differ that they falsely cling to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), commit various unwholesome deeds, and drift in the turbulence of suffering.
O Sea, if you can turn back in a single thought and possess all wholesome dharmas, then the other shore is right here;
the current of the sea of suffering will be severed, the name of "sentient being" will be exhausted, and even the Buddha will not exist. This is called ultimate goodness.
One must not speak loudly or raise one's voice.
[Commentary: The meditation hall is the place where the holy and the profane are forged and where dragons and snakes are distinguished; it is also called the "Buddha-Selecting Bodhimanda."
Whenever one enters this hall, one must maintain a disciplined and solemn demeanor, severing all external attachments and refraining from idle chatter.

If even a single person speaks loudly or at a high pitch, and others join in to harmonize with them, the resulting clamor will be unbearable. This obstructs those engaged in authentic practice; no harm could be greater than this.
When lifting the curtain with a light hand, one must keep the trailing hand lowered.

[Commentary] According to the *Jinggui* (Rules of Purity): "The Son of Heaven uses an outer screen; the feudal lords use an inner screen; the Great Officers use a curtain. The *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) states: "Curtain (*lián*) means integrity (*lián*).
It serves as a self-obscuring barrier, representing integrity and shame. In the regions of Song, Wei, Chen, and Chu, it was called a *dí*, or sometimes a *qù*. From... [text continues].
In the region of Zhou, it is called a *bó* (curtain); in Nan Chu, it is called a *péng-bó*. In the *Zhuangzi*, it says: "High gates with hanging curtains.

Regarding those who lift the curtain and then let their hands hang behind them: this refers to pulling the curtain straight down abruptly; the curtain will inevitably be damaged, and furthermore, the coarse and turbid sound will disturb the assembly.
Therefore, one should support it with the hand; only then does one manifest dignified deportment and elegant bearing. As the *Wudeng Huiyuan* records: "Changqing sat until his seat was worn through."
After seven years on the meditation cushion, one day he rolled up the curtain and suddenly attained enlightenment, saying: "How very strange! How very strange!
When the curtain is rolled up, the whole world is revealed. If someone asks me what my school is, I take up my whisk and strike them right across the mouth! He then took up [the whisk].
According to Fachang’s judgment, even if Changqing had such insight, he saw only the world outside the curtain;
he had not yet seen the world inside the curtain. Do you wish to see the world inside the curtain? Fachang has a skillful means:
by sitting and wearing out seven cushions, I can ensure that both the inside and the outside of the curtain are seen at once.
[The Master] said, "I see. Now tell me, is there any distinction of superiority or inferiority between Fachang and Changqing?
If you can speak here, you may roll it up or spread it out as you please. Zhenjing Wen was at Huanglong.

One day, Huanglong happened to order an attendant to roll up the curtain and asked, "When the curtain is rolled up, what is it like? The attendant replied, "It illuminates heaven and earth. [Huanglong] then had him lower the curtain.
[The Master] asked, "What about when it is not leaking through? [Zheng] said, "It is impenetrable. [The Master] asked, "What about when it is neither rolled up nor let out?
[Zheng] was speechless. [The Master] asked, "How about you? Zhen said, "Only if the Abbot takes the attendant's place and goes down to the Nirvana Hall would it be acceptable.
Longhu roared, "A person from Guansi truly has no head! He then looked toward a monk standing nearby. Zhenjing pointed at him and said, "Even this monk is not yet [enough]."

[The Master] said, "I see you in my dream. The dragon laughed loudly. ◎ When Zen Master Wenyi of Qingliang Yuan was receiving a monk for an interview, the Master pointed to the curtain with his finger.
Immediately, two monks went together to roll up the curtain. The Master said, "One gains, one loses.
◎ Xuansha and Quanshou were conversing in the room when a novice monk lifted the curtain to enter, saw them, and then stepped back.
[The monk] went out. The Master said, "That śrāmaṇera deserves twenty blows of the staff. Shou said, "If that is so, then I am at fault.
Tong'an Xian added, "The Patriarch has arrived! The Master said, "The Buddha was not like this."
One must not let sandals make noise. [Commentary:
When walking within the hall, one should maintain dignified deportment; neither too hurried nor too slow—like a white crane in a field of *zhī* grass, or a blue lion moving through a stone cave.
If, during the twelve hours of the day and night, you suddenly step upon your own shadow, you will inevitably see it through.

This is the eye of Caoshan; take it for granted that through this, the task of study will be completed. There is a class of people in the meditation hall who neither practice Chan nor study the teachings.
They habitually drag their sandals back and forth, making a clattering sound like wooden cymbals beneath their feet, which only causes weariness among the assembly.
They waste their time in vain, yet when meeting others, they say, "I have lived under the guidance of such-and-such a master. This is truly lamentable.
How lamentable! In the *Records of Xue’an*, it is said that Master Shantou once remarked that when Master Sheng’en was among the assembly, he exerted himself with diligent self-discipline.
He would investigate his koan until the late hours of the night without going to sleep; fearing that the sound of his footsteps might disturb others, he would remove his shoes and socks.
Walk in meditation barefoot; in winter, simply remove your shoes. Act in this manner at all times;
you are a model for a thousand ages. Do not cough loudly. Do not converse with your neighbors by whispering together about worldly affairs.
[Commentary]: The meditation hall (*zen-dō*) is the great furnace for forging the sons of the Way from all under heaven. Yet nowadays, the prevailing trend declines daily;

those who enter the hall as practitioners do not know what they are doing there. Disregarding their own fundamental duty, they treat the meditation hall as a place for idle chatter about worldly affairs—this is truly lamentable.
As an ancient worthy said: "If the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents."
The Great Matter has already been clarified. It is like mourning for one's parents; how could one allow time to pass in vain or let the daylight go to waste?
Not only would this be a mistake for oneself, but it would also hinder those who are practicing the Way. Therefore, Xueyan Qin established the "Universal Explanation.
At that time, there were seven brothers from the two prefectures of Zhangzhou and Quanzhou who joined me in sitting meditation, remaining at Jingci Monastery for two years. They did not...
He spreads his bedding so that his side does not even touch the mat. Outside [this group] is the Venerable Xiu, also a native of Zhangzhou, who is not included among these numbers;
he simply walks alone and sits alone. Every day upon his meditation cushion, he is like an iron spike.
Morning after morning it is thus; day after day it is thus. Every day I wish to draw near to him and speak with him.
A mere trifle. As soon as he saw me coming from the east, he would go to the west; as soon as he saw me coming from the west, he would go to the east.
For two years in this manner, it was impossible to find an opportunity to draw near him.

If there are fellow practitioners who regard one with affection, one must not converse for long within the hall; rather, one should invite them to the woods or by the water to discuss matters with open hearts.
[Commentary]: One’s natural disposition is most profound; there is none that surpasses that of one's parents. Now that you have taken leave of them, you should take the Way as your parent.
One who inclines their heart toward discourse must be a person of true caliber before one can exhaust the efforts of a lifetime in weighing matters with them.
If we were to discuss worldly truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it would not only defile my lips, but I fear it might also defile the forests and springs. This is merely a "pen-food" (a mere literary snack).
Hongzhi was a native of Xizhou. Among those who were eminent scholars from his own home district while he was still a layman, there was one who had lived in obscurity for over ten years;
his place of birth was not known. Hongzhi, knowing of him, went to visit and said, "This is your fatherland; why do you remain so aloof from the world?

He wished to invite the man into the abbot’s quarters, but the man declined, saying, "I have not yet settled my own affairs; how could I take the trouble to discuss matters of my hometown? He then took up his staff and departed, such that [Hongzhi] could do nothing further.
At dawn, when the second board sounds, you should immediately enter the hall early. [Commentary:

Regarding the bell and the board, these were established by Baizhang. He once carried them on his back along the road, maintaining the rules of conduct without slackening throughout his travels. In the monastic groves...

Master Lin has followed this practice to this day. Regarding the "two boards": this means one board is for pausing, while two boards are not. If the two boards have already sounded, one must enter the hall within the time it takes to drink a single cup of tea.
The third board signals the cessation of activity and the closing of the meditation hall doors; from within, no one is allowed to exit, and from without, no one is allowed to enter.
Therefore, as soon as the two boards sound, one must attend to the call of nature and then proceed to the hall. To delay even slightly is to remain a layman outside the gate. [The lamp].
Recorded: During a formal inquiry in the meditation hall, Master Mingbian asked, "The board sounds; why does the dog bark? Yunfeng secretly offered this verse:
"The Yellow River flows far up among the white clouds; A solitary walled city amidst ten-thousand-fathom peaks. Why need the Qiang flute lament the willows?"
The spring breeze does not pass through the Yumen Pass.
When reading the sutras, one must sit upright, clarify the mind, and contemplate in silence; no sound should be made.
[Commentary: While the assembly remains in stillness to read the sutras, all should understand them silently. If this were expressed through sound, it would result in nothing but confusion.
The meaning of the sutras cannot be grasped through discursive thought; therefore, one must attain realization through clarity, stillness, and silence.
Only then will the meaning of the sutras become clearly understood and wisdom arise therefrom. As for the time of Zen meditation, one must set aside all the scriptures on a high shelf;
each and every truth must flow forth from within one's own breast, so as to encompass both heaven and earth. Only then is it achieved.
Sitting upright with the body straight, one should wish that all sentient beings sit upon the seat of Bodhi, their minds free from attachment.

[Commentary: The *Four Teachings Ritual* (*Sijiaoyi*) and the *Record of the Light* (*Guangming ji*) state that "sitting upright" refers to the physical posture. The methods for sitting are fully set forth in the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra*;
those in need should consult it. Internally, one should employ perfect contemplation; furthermore, engage in recitation, which is like adding oil to a fire to nourish the flame of Bodhi.
The Flower Adornment (Huayan) speaks of the Way. As for the "seat of bodhi," it is the seat of the Dharma King, which is the realization that one's own nature is originally empty.

This seat is inherently possessed by every person; therefore, it is said, "one should aspire [to it]. Because it is like a lotus flower, unstained, it is called "non-attachment. The *Avataṃsaka* states:
"The bodhicitta is like a seed, for it can give rise to all the Buddhas' dharmas. Beneath this, there are one hundred...

Among the eighteen kinds of metaphors, none surpasses this single verse from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "When one sees a painting of [the Buddha] sitting in the full lotus posture, even Māra is struck with awe and fear;
how much more so for those who have entered the Path? With body upright and unmoving, they further practice right contemplation through five kinds of causal conditions."
Therefore, one sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka). First, by sitting thus in quietude, the body and mind are withdrawn and concentrated, whereby pliancy (praśrabdhi) arises swiftly;
this is the most excellent reason. Second, by sitting thus in quietude, one is able to remain for a long duration, as it prevents the body and mind from becoming quickly exhausted. Third.
4. By means of this meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*), it is an unshared quality (*āveṇika-dharma*); for among the paths and doctrines of others, none can equal it. 5.
By means of this meditative seclusion, one’s physical appearance becomes majestic and pure; having seen this, others develop the utmost reverence and faith. 5.
By means of this meditative seclusion, the Buddhas and their disciples alike hear of it with joy, as it is praised by all the worthy and holy ones (*ārya*). The Five Lamps: Muzhou asked Yunyan:
Yan asked, "What does Bodhi take as its seat? Yan replied, "It takes non-action (wuwei) as its seat.
Yan then questioned Guishan, who said, "It takes the emptiness of all dharmas as its seat. He further asked Daowu, "How about you? Daowu said, "If he sits, let him sit."
"If you are lying down, let him lie down. There is one who neither sits nor lies down. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Having said this, he ceased.
Verse on Leaving the Dwelling: When leaving the dwelling, may all beings aspire to enter deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.

[Commentary] A summary of the categories. Regarding the three realms: first is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). There are four types of desire: namely, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), desire for form (*rūpacchanda*), and desire for food (*āhāracchanda*). [Note: *Citta-cchanda* (mental desire) is omitted here as per the provided text.]
It is the realm of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*). Below it extends to the Avīci Hell, and above it reaches as far as the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
Because men and women cohabit there and there is much defiled desire, it is called the Realm of Desire. Second is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). "Form" refers to material substance.
Having already departed from the foul and evil forms of the Realm of Desire, there still remains pure form. It begins from the Brahma Heaven of the First Dhyāna and ends at Akaniṣṭha.
The *Ṭa* Heaven. There are eighteen heavens in total; none possess female forms, nor do they have the defilement of desire. All are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

Because they still possess material form (*rūpa*), they are called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). Third, the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Here there is only mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) and no material form.

Beginning from the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and ending with the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are four heavens in total. They possess only the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*).
The mind has no form or substance; therefore, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

This verse is like beholding a vast scroll of the profound and mysterious Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, while simultaneously encompassing the entire chapter on parables from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Yet, how could the Perfect Mirror of Vairocana have coming or going?
How could the narrow gate of the burning house not be entered or exited? Thus we know that where there is no fire, fire suddenly erupts throughout the triple world.
This refers to the great burning house. Those of small wisdom who are *śrāvakas* have already emerged from this dwelling and enjoy a temporary period of play;

this refers to the small burning house. They do not realize that the fire outside the dwelling is even more severe than they imagine. Unless one deeply penetrates the Buddha-wisdom, [one cannot escape].
How may they be swiftly led out of the burning house and immediately enter the cool and refreshing state?

Appendix: One must not pass straight through the hall; whether moving from an upper bunk to a lower bunk or vice versa, one should always act with care so as not to disturb the thoughts of those in neighboring bunks.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Single" (dān): this has been explained in detail in the preceding section on "Entering the Assembly," so it shall not be elaborated upon here.
Whenever a student first enters a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), the Abbot examines their learning and conduct before they are permitted to enter the ranks of the monks.

At that time, the student's name is written on a "single notice" (*dān-tiē*) and entrusted to the Attendant (*karmadāna*) to deliver to the Meditation Hall (*zhēn-táng*). There, it is posted at the designated spot—what is known as "beneath the three rafters and before the seven-foot mat."

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra Commentary* states: "One who grasps this meaning finds that every step taken and every step set down is the mind of Mañjuśrī; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all the practices of Samantabhadra.
Verse: Single above and single below— The meaning is not of two kinds. Stretching out the legs or drawing them back— What difficulty is there in this?
Neither resenting Shide nor praising Fenggan, Forgetting self and forgetting others, Without obstruction or hindrance. Beside the pillow...
Every night, the red sun is released. The scripture of the wordless casket fills the belly.
One must not write characters upon the single mat. Except when the assembly is viewing the scriptures and teachings, one must not gather together on the single mat to serve tea.
During the night sitting for informal conversation, one must not sew or patch clothing or bedding upon the single mat.
[Commentary]: The meditation mat (*zen-dan*). Because the study of the Way involves diligent toil, this is provided for a brief rest during the middle of the night.

In ancient times, practitioners did not let their ribs touch the mat, exerting themselves in inquiry and investigation. Such effort was undertaken for this very purpose; it is not for trivial or non-urgent matters. This is the admonition of Cishou.
The ancient sages mended their robes to ward off the cold; once the patching was complete, they ceased.
How could they spend morning and evening threading needles and sewing, nor fail to sleep while chatting with those on neighboring mats and causing a disturbance to the assembly?
[Commentary: Heaven and earth are active by day and still by night; men and women work by day and rest by night. Human sentiment thus accords with the principle of Heaven.

The *Analects* states, "When sleeping, one does not speak. This is likely based on this very meaning. As for those who truly practice the Way, how could they merely act like ignorant, dull creatures, seeking only to lie down?
Is it not as if they were undergoing a minor death? One should know that the ultimate Way consists in preserving silence; thus, one is in a state of joyful, dreamlike ease (*xūxū*). Qu...

There is something here that cannot be spoken of to others. For instance, when Wufeng was practicing the state of "no dreams and no thoughts," his meditation pillow suddenly shook with a great roar, and he attained sudden, great enlightenment. This is the very model for those who have slept through the ages.
If one were to sleep while chatting with a neighbor in the same quarters, one would be detested by the community and rebuked by ghosts and spirits.

Section Six: Following the Assembly for Meals [Commentary] An ancient master said: "By following the assembly, one attains liberation. From this statement, it can be understood that if one does not follow the assembly, one will not attain liberation.
Now, I shall briefly discuss following the assembly; there are eight kinds of liberation. First, to go immediately upon hearing the board struck, without indolence.

1. Because of the absence of indolence; 2. because making offerings to those who have manifested [the Buddha-body] saves effort; 3. by practicing the contemplation of equality, there is no notion of self or others; 4.

by ceasing all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) through maintaining right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*); 5. by contemplating and visualizing according to the Dharma, one penetrates deeply into the principle.
Sixth, not eating in private from the assembly, in order to eliminate doubt and slander. Seventh, accepting both sweet and bitter alike, because there is no discrimination.
Eighth, maintaining dignified deportment in all movements, because one is never negligent.
Upon hearing the sound of the *gandi*, one should adjust one’s robes and take up the alms bowl.

[Commentary: As for the *gandi*, it causes things to be proclaimed without the need for speech; thus, as soon as the monastics hear it, they know to cease their activities and attend to matters such as adjusting their robes and taking up their bowls.
In the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), the character for "hammer" (*zhui*) is written with the "earth" radical (*di*), which is an error made by later generations. Up to...

In the text of the *Chao* (Excerpts), the character for *jiānzhui* (gong) was consistently changed to *zhui* (mallet) within the teachings of the founding patriarchs, and it was simply read as "di" (earth).

Upon consulting ancient manuscripts and the Tripitaka’s Vinaya, one realizes this is an error. Regarding the passage in the *Ekottarika Āgama* where Ānanda requests that the gong be struck in the lecture hall, it is said:
"This is the drum of the Tathāgata’s confidence. Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika Vinaya*, there were those who used tiles [in place of the gong].

Objects made of wood, bronze, or iron that produce sound are all termed *gandī* (wooden mallets). According to the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity), upon hearing the sound of the mallet, one recites the following verse of mindfulness:
"The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, Attained enlightenment in Magadha, Preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, And entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.
