Upon hearing the bell struck three times, one must immediately cease all activities; it is first appropriate to enter or exit [the hall]. In the *Denglu* (Lamp Records), when Yaoshan was at his midday meal, he personally beat the drum himself. High...
A śrāmaṇera entered the hall dancing while holding an alms bowl. Baoshan immediately threw down his drumstick and asked, "Which beat is this?
Gao replied, "This is the second beat. Baoshan asked, "What about the first beat? The Master scooped up a ladleful of rice and then went out.
Master Shitai was having his attendant carry his alms bowl to the hall. He called to the attendant, who responded. The Master asked, "Where are you going?
The attendant replied, "I am going to the hall for the midday meal. The Master said, "Do I not know that you are going to the meal?
The attendant asked, "Aside from this, what else would you say? The Master said, "I am asking only about the fundamental matter. The attendant said, "Master..."
Yet, if one were to ask about the fundamental matter, I am actually going to the hall to attend the midday meal. The Master said, "You do not fail in your duty as my attendant.
The Verse on Holding the Alms Bowl: Holding the alms bowl, I vow that all sentient beings shall become accomplished vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans.
Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. [Commentary] The Sanskrit term *pātra* means "receptacle of appropriate measure. This is because its substance is the Dharma, which is primordially accomplished.

The single phrase "accomplishing the dharma-vessel" encompasses emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Furthermore, it includes the rules of regulation, such as the three ladles and the five contemplations.

The essential point is that all things arise from what is appropriate (*yathāpramāṇa*). Thus, there are no dharmas that are not fully present; therefore, one is able to receive the offerings of devas and humans.

If one does not know the dharma of what is appropriate, even a drop of water is difficult to digest, let alone the offerings of devas and humans. *Wudeng Huiyuan*: One day, the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda:
"The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda responded, "As you command. The World-Honored One said:
"Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past. The World-Honored One called for Ānanda, and Ānanda responded, "Yes.
The World-Honored One said, "Go and carry the bowl. Mian Yun said: "How great is the World-Honored One! To be so lightly relied upon by Ānanda—there is no avoiding it;
he has called a bell a jar. Duan’an Yan composed a verse: "The ritual of the seven Buddhas from of old—how could Qingxi (Ānanda)..."
"Never lacking. How laughable is the Yellow-Faced Gautama! He has, for no reason, made a circuit around it. Zhang Wujin’s verse says:

"The sound of bells and drums fades as he returns with his bowl; Yantou’s single squeeze was like thunder. Indeed, he could only live for three years—was this not because he received a prophecy from him?
Tian Shan Lao Ren’s verse says: "Father and son, father and son, in the same pot yet cooking separately."
They were all driven out through the mountain gate together. Only the old fellow Sanfeng remained.
In the *Fǎchāng Lù*, it is said that the calamity of the failure to understand between Deshan and Yantou both originated from Xuefeng’s grasping hold of the wooden mallet.
This caused the old fellow to become entirely out of step with the times; he simply held up his alms bowl right before the sound of the bells and drums. How truly piercing was his vision!

There was no one present. Unexpectedly, from within the shadow of a handkerchief used for wiping the face, a question suddenly emerged, forcing him to swallow his breath and stifle his voice as he retreated to the abbot’s quarters.
Yet Xuefeng continued to speak in riddles, inciting Yantou to scrutinize and judge that even the great Deshan had not yet mastered the "final word.
According to Fachang’s critique, however, that old fellow had not even mastered the "first word."
He spoke the very last word. At that time, had one heard such talk, one should have simply remained securely seated in the abbot’s quarters;
even if Yantou possessed a hundred thousand wiles, there would have been nothing he could do about it.

It was only because [the Master] summoned and questioned Yantou, and even went so far as to secretly reveal his intention to him, that Yantou failed to speak plainly to subdue him—this too shows he was not a master hand. By the next day, the old man...
After Han ascended the seat, he clapped his hands and said, "I am glad that this old fellow has already realized the final word.
He further remarked, "He will live for only three more years. Throughout his life, Deshan’s bearing was like that of a king; he directed strategy from within his tent—how sharp and incisive he was!

Yet how could he have been so outmaneuvered by Yantou, who predicted exactly three years? Indeed, he could not even save himself. Thus, the various quarters of the Chan world have been debating this matter extensively.
[The Master] said: "Furthermore, has there been anyone who could clear the inexplicable calamity for father and son? He spoke a verse: "Before the sound of bells and drums, he carries his alms bowl;
This old man presides over the monastery improperly. Great and small secretly employ their wiles; Their transgressions fill the heavens, defying all regulations.
What need is there to speak of 'three years of life or death'? Fortunately, the alms bowl remains free from ailment. From beginning to end, it is fully upheld; I serve the Most High."
Imperial Decree:

Verse for Spreading the Alms Bowl The Tathāgata’s vessel of appropriate measure, which I now spread out—may it serve all sentient beings, with the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) empty and quiescent. Oṃ smara maṇi svāhā.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha is called "Tathāgata" because, like Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, he practiced the six *pāramitās* and attained the path of Buddhahood;
Śākyamuni Buddha likewise came in this same manner, and is therefore named "Tathāgata. This is like the wisdom of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and the others.
One who knows the characteristics of all phenomena comes from suchness; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Śākyamuni Buddha likewise came in this manner, and is thus called the Tathāgata.
O Vajra, that which comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is therefore called the Tathāgata.
As for the "measuring vessel," it is the dharma-vessel transmitted from one Buddha to another; none of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths know its name.
The reason I am now able to unfold [this teaching] is that I have already received the Buddha’s precepts; thus, I am able to unfold it.
However, unfolding this great meaning is not merely for the sake of one's own benefit regarding speech and body. First, one should make a vow for the sake of the multitude.

Regarding the "emptiness and stillness of the three wheels," this refers to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and its commentaries, which state that at the time of giving, one must realize the emptiness of the giver, the receiver, and the object given.

All are fundamentally empty; thus one can crush and grind away the marks of attachment. This is called the emptiness of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*). First is the emptiness of the giver (*dātṛ-śūnyatā*):

this means that the person who gives realizes that their own body is fundamentally empty. How could there be a "self" acting as the giver? Since one knows there is no self, there is no mind that hopes for a reward of merit.
This is called the emptiness of giving. Second is the emptiness of the recipient (*pratigrāhaka-śūnyatā*): this means that since one has realized...
To realize that there is fundamentally no self who is the giver, and likewise no other person who is the recipient, is called the emptiness of the recipient (3).

Regarding the emptiness of the gift (4): "gift" refers to wealth, treasures, and so forth; it means to thoroughly realize that all things are empty—how could such a thing exist as something to be given? This is called the emptiness of the gift.
The Verse on the Empty Alms Bowl: If one sees an empty alms bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings have minds so pure they are empty of afflictions.
Oṃ bhu liṃ. [Annotation]:
If one sees this bowl, one directly perceives the extent of the *dharmadhātu* and the extent of oneself as equal to true emptiness.
Moreover, there is not even the slightest room for anything; how much less could there be any trace of afflictions, even those that are "pure"? In the *Avataṃsaka*, it says:

"If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, one should exhaust the mind until it is like empty space. Therefore, it is said that "the mind is pure," meaning it has never been associated with defiled dharmas from the outset;
thus, it is said to be "empty and without afflictions."
The Verse on the Full Alms Bowl: Upon seeing a full alms bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings may fully accomplish and perfect all wholesome dharmas.

Oṃ. [Lam]. [Commentary]: Since the rice in the alms bowl is already full before one's eyes, one must not give rise to thoughts of mere greed or gluttony, nor fail to cultivate the pure conduct of *brahmacarya*.
One should contemplate the origin of this food: every grain has come from the offerings of faith. All wholesome dharmas arise from this seed of wisdom;
therefore, the recipient shall be fully endowed with the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and the giver’s fruit of merit shall be brought to fulfillment.
It is like a seed that produces flowers, and the flowers in turn become fruit; this fulfills the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) of a Bodhisattva.
According to the *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions), the Buddha’s almsbowl is in the kingdom of Gandhāra. It is made of green jade and has a capacity of three *dou*.
Although various kingdoms treasure it and offer worship to it throughout the day, even if flowers and incense do not fill it, it becomes full as soon as one speaks of it being full.
The Verse on Holding the Alms Bowl: When holding the alms bowl with food, one should wish that all sentient beings set their minds upon the Great Way and make offerings of the Dharma.

[Commentary: The "Great Way" refers to the means of sustaining the illusory vehicle; it is fundamentally for the sake of practicing the world-transcending path. Therefore, it is said that "the mind is set upon the Great Way.
Among all forms of offering described in the *Chapter on Vows and Practices*, the "offering of the Dharma" is the most supreme, which is to say, an offering made in accordance with the Dharma.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Even if one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in every moment of thought, if one does not know the true Dharma, it cannot be called making an offering.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Food is for the sake of practicing the Path, not for the benefit of the body. When food is obtained, first offer it to the Triple Gem."

Subsequently, the *Sūtra on Sublime Reflection* states that one who does not give rise to non-virtuous karma, nor give rise to meritorious karma, nor give rise to immovable karma, is said to be making an offering to the Buddha.
The *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that if one offers flowers, incense, food, clothing, medicine, and so forth to the Buddhas, it is not called true offering.
[True offering is] the subtle and wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata while seated at the site of enlightenment. If...

Those who are able to practice and learn in this way are said to perform true worship. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadrotsāhana-parivarta* (Siyi jing) asks: "Who is able to make offerings to the Buddha? The Buddha replied:

"One who is able to penetrate the limit of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-koti*). The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-pāramitā-sūtra* records the Buddha asking Mañjuśrī: "How do you make offerings to the Buddha? Mañjuśrī answered:
"If the mental activities of one who is like an illusion are extinguished, then I am making an offering to the Buddha. (Tiantai Teaching)

To make offerings to the Buddha is simply to accord with the Buddha’s words. Now, by following the Buddha’s teachings and cultivating the three contemplations of the mind, one is making an offering to the Buddha.

Because this serves to shatter the five stages of dwelling and attain liberation, it is an offering to the Dharma. Because the principles of the three truths are in harmony, it is an offering to the Sangha.
I pay homage to the Buddha Vairocana, the Pure Dharmakāya.

[Commentary: The Buddha-body is unconditioned; therefore, it is called "pure. "Dharma" means that which is to be followed as a model. By accomplishing this through various teachers, one attains Buddhahood;
because the Dharma constitutes the body, it is named the Dharmakāya. The Sanskrit term *Vairocana* translates into Chinese as "Pervading All."

Regarding the locus: because True Suchness is equal, its nature and characteristics are eternally thus, and there is no obstruction within the body. In the Sanskrit language, *buddha* means "the Awakened One.
As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, the meaning of "awakening" refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body. Thus, by means of non-thought, one is named a Buddha.
The Perfect Reward Body (Saṃbhogakāya) Vairocana Buddha. [Commentary:

It is called "reward" (*pāka*) because it is the result experienced through the cultivation of causes. However, there is a distinction between the "self-reward" and the "other-reward. Self-reward refers to the suchness of wisdom and principle;
other-reward refers to the inexhaustible marks and signs. This is what is termed the Reward Body. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states that awakening possesses...
The meaning [of this] is as follows: First, self-awakening and awakening-knowledge: one’s own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Second, awakening others:
one awakens to all phenomena such that none are otherwise than this. Third, full awakening: these two modes of awakening are perfected in principle; thus it is called "full.

Vairocana is translated here as "Pure Fullness," meaning that all afflictions are purified and exhausted, and all virtues are entirely perfected. It is also said to mean "Universal Radiance," referring to the internal...
The light of wisdom illuminates the true dharma-realm; this is the self-recompense body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). Externally, the light of the physical body illuminates those with great capacities;
this is the other-recompense body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
The thousand, hundred, and ten million transformation bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Commentary: Wisdom and essence are true; they are able to give rise to great function, manifesting universally according to the capacities of beings to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings.

Therefore, they are called "transformation bodies" (*nirmāṇakāya*). Regarding *Śākya*, this is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (*Nengren*); regarding *Muni*, this is translated as "Silent Stillness" (*Jimo*). "Capable Benevolence" refers to the mind.

The nature is boundless and encompasses all things. As for "silent stillness," it refers to the fundamental quiescence of the mind-nature, wherein movement and stillness do not interfere with one another;
therefore, he is named Śākyamuni.
Maitreya Buddha, who will descend to be born in the future. [Annotation]:
Maitreya is called *Cishi* (The Compassionate One) in Chinese; he is the teacher of the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*) assembly in the future. A verse by the Monk with the Cloth Bag states:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya, manifesting hundreds of billions of transformation bodies; at all times he dwells within the world, yet the people of the world do not recognize him."
Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Commentary:
*The Amitābha Sūtra*: At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "To the west of here, beyond a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha titled Amitābha, who is currently present and preaching."

Dharma. Śāriputra, for what reason is that land named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī)? Because the sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore called "Ultimate Bliss.
In the Sanskrit language it is called Amitābha; here it is translated as "Immeasurable Life," and is also named "Immeasurable Light."
All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
[Commentary: The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below are called the "ten directions. The past, present, and future are called the "three periods.

If one speaks of the Buddhas currently existing throughout the oceans of kalpas of antiquity, they are now referred to as "past"; those who are currently present are, in turn, the past [of the future].
That which has not yet come is also the past of the future; thus, within a single *kṣaṇa* of exhalation and inhalation, the three periods of time are established.

As for the Buddhas, this means that throughout the eastern direction, beyond unspeakably unspeakable worlds, unspeakably many Buddhas all appear before me and receive my offerings; it is the same for the other directions as well.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom.

[Commentary: There are six names for Mañjuśrī. First, Wondrous Virtue (Miaode). As stated in the Mahāyāna Sūtras: "To see the Buddha-nature clearly is like [the clarity of] Wondrous Virtue and others."
2. Miaoshou (妙首). *Wuxing jing* (無行經). Manshushri; this is translated as Miaoshou. 3. Name: Pushou (普首).
*Guancha sanmei dajing famen jing* (觀察三昧大淨法門經). 4. Roushou (濡首). Appears in the *Amogha* [sūtra] and the *Puchao jing* (普超經).
5. Jingshou (經首). Appears in the *Wuliangmen weimi jing* (無量門微密經). 6. Miaojixiang (妙吉祥). Sanskrit: Mañjuśrī.
Mahāsattva Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. [Commentary:

To act such that there is nowhere it does not pervade is called "Universal" (Samanta). To protect those above and benefit those below is called "Worthy" (Bhadra). Because he universally protects and benefits all, he is named Samantabhadra.
The Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

[Commentary: Because he perfectly integrates the subjective and the objective, and because both existence and non-existence are fully manifested; because he illuminates and exhausts the true nature and examines its beginning and end, he is called "Avalokiteśvara" (Observer of the Sounds of the World).
This refers to the object of observation: the myriad phenomena are in constant flux, distinct and diverse, with their various sounds resonating differently.

All together receive the blessing of being freed from suffering. Through the great compassion of the Bodhisattva, all are universally rescued and brought to liberation at once; therefore, he is called Avalokiteśvara.
Thus concludes the Mahāprajñāpāramitā of the various Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
[Note]: *Bodhisattva* is fully rendered as *bodhisattva*. In the language of China, it means "enlightened sentient beings," referring to one who awakens all living beings.
Taking the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as their vehicle, they transport all sentient beings out of the triple world (*tridhātu*) and reach the other shore of *nirvāṇa*.
The Sanskrit term *mahā* is translated here as "Great. The Sanskrit term *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom. The Sanskrit term *pāra*...
*Madhu*. This is translated as "reaching the other shore. It refers to the general praise of the merits of all noble ones (*ārya*) and serves as a concluding phrase for the offering.
There are ten benefits to rice porridge that benefit the practitioner; its karmic fruit is boundless, culminating in eternal bliss.
[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, Nanda’s mother prepared food. She first served the bhikṣus and ate later herself.

She then prepared rice in a cauldron and forced the boiled rice upward, drinking the broth herself. She perceived that the internal wind within her body had been eliminated and her indigestion suddenly vanished.
Consequently, she used much water and little rice, boiling them together; she further added black pepper and *pippalī* to season it, and offered it [to the Buddha].
The Buddha, for this reason, permitted the bhikṣus to eat gruel. There are ten kinds of benefits. The Buddha spoke in verse, saying:
"Those who maintain pure precepts are honored by others; If one respectfully offers gruel at the proper time, Ten benefits will enrich the practitioner:

Complexion, strength, longevity, happiness, eloquence, The elimination of undigested food and wind-disorders, and the quelling of hunger and thirst— These are called medicines as taught by the Buddha. [He] desired...

Those born among humans and devas shall constantly experience happiness. One should offer congee to the Sangha for ten benefits: first, it nourishes the physical body, making the countenance full and flourishing;
second, it replenishes those who are weak and emaciated, increasing their vital energy; third, it sustains the fundamental life-force, augmenting the span of one's years;
fourth, it is pure and soft, providing peace and comfort when eaten; fifth, it moistens the throat and palate, so that in discourse there is no...
1. Obstructions are removed. 2. The six sense organs become harmonious and functional. 3. Wind and qi are eliminated. 4. The spleen and stomach are warmed. 5. Stale food is digested. 6.

Qi flows without stagnation or obstruction. 7. Eloquence becomes clear and resonant. 8. The mouth and belly are suitably filled; hunger and emaciation are instantly dispelled. 9. The throat and palate are moistened;
thirst and longing vanish accordingly. *The Book of Zhou* states: "The Yellow Emperor first boiled grain to make porridge. Emperor Wu of Wei suffered from the bitter cold.
Xing said: "The journey has already been long; both man and horse are hungry at the same time. Carrying the bag, he went to gather firewood;
with a cauldron of water, he prepared gruel. *Record of the Lamp*: One day, while Nanquan was serving congee to the assembly of monks, Mazu asked, "What is that in the bucket?
The Master said, "Old man, shut your mouth and stop speaking such words! Mazu then desisted. As for the rest...
His fellow practitioners did not dare to question him. ◎ Zhaozhou asked, "Have you finished eating your gruel? Upon seeing the verse for washing the bowl:
"The three virtues and six flavors / Are offered to the Buddhas and the Sangha / To all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm / May they all equally partake in this offering."
[Commentary] Regarding the three qualities: First is purity, meaning that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must be clean and free from the odor of pungent or impure ingredients.
Second is softness, meaning that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must be tender, sweet, and harmonious, without coarse or astringent flavors.
Third is accordance with the Dharma, meaning that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must be prepared and provided according to the appropriate time and occasion.
It is appropriate. As for the six flavors: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that when various upāsakas prepared various provisions of food to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, they were fully equipped with all kinds of materials, all of which were fuel from candana and agalloch wood and matured by water of eight virtues.
That food was sweet and delicious, possessing excellent qualities. To "make offerings to the Buddha" means to offer to the Three [Jewels].
The "World" refers to all Buddhas. There are two kinds of Sangha: first, the Bodhisattva Sangha; second, the present assembly of the Sangha who offer to the Buddha.
There has never been an offering to the Buddha that did not include an offering to the Sangha; therefore, it says "and.

As for "universally shared," this extends upward to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, sages, and worthies, as well as the devas, nāgas, and Dharma protectors, and downward to all sentient beings; there is none to whom it does not reach. Therefore, it is called "universally shared."
When eating, one should wish that all sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their food and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
[Commentary: According to the *Huayan Shu*, worldly food can only sustain the body within the cycle of birth and death; for those who practice the Way...

Regarding the delicious flavors of the world, the mind does not crave or relish them; rather, by constantly maintaining right mindfulness and taking the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as food, one is able to nurture the roots of goodness and transcend birth and death.
Because they bring about the accomplishment of virtue, there are five kinds of supramundane food.
1. The food of mindfulness (*smṛty-āhāra*): Because those who cultivate the Noble Path constantly maintain right mindfulness. 2. The food of Dharma-delight (*dharma-prīti-āhāra*):

Because one cherishes and delights in the Great Dharma, nourishing the seeds of the Path and giving rise to joy in the mind. 3. The food of meditative rapture (*dhyāna-prīti-āhāra*): Because by attaining the power of concentration, one nourishes the life of wisdom;

as the factors of the Path become perfectly clear and bright, the mind is always joyful and at ease. 4. The food of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-āhāra*): Because one does not abandon the holy life (*brahmacarya*), nurturing [the mind] with singleness of purpose.
It severs all roots of goodness. It is like food in the world, for it nourishes and benefits the faculties of the body. Fifth is the food of liberation (*vimukti-āhāra*);

because it frees one from the bonds of all karma and brings mastery over the Dharma, it nurtures and develops Bodhi. ◎ Not proceeding through a womb and not requiring coarse material food, it consists solely of the food of dhyāna-delight and the food of Dharma-joy.
When eating rice, it shall not exceed seven grains; when eating noodles, not more than one cun; when eating steamed buns, not more than the size of a fingernail.

To exceed these amounts constitutes greed. [Commentary] Yunju Xian’s annotation states: "Greed" here refers to being greedy for merit. To take too much is also contrary to the Dharma; therefore, this regulation was established.
If there is little, one becomes stingy; otherwise, vegetables and tofu are not served. [Commentary:
A stone stands before the dining hall, shaped like a lotus flower. That which faces upward toward heaven and downward toward the earth is called the Platform for Bestowing Life.
Around the perimeter of this platform, the names of the Seven Buddhas are inscribed in seal script, so that all who see it may extinguish their sins and generate merit. As for that lotus flower...
Gazing upward, it is as level as a mirror and as circular as a *maṇḍala*, with Sanskrit script engraved within.
From the seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon which the practitioner focuses, they cause all spirits and deities to partake of this flavor of the Dharma;

because they thereby attain liberation, people today do not know to gaze upon and worship it, but instead treat it with neglect. Consequently, they use it to dry their belongings, even placing shoes, socks, and other filthy garments upon it.
This is the pinnacle of the Buddha-dharma. To fail to perceive or realize this is to incur the grave crime of a great transgression;

seeing such a thing, how could one not feel deep sorrow? Therefore, I point this out so that my mother may not commit it again. As for the evidence: if vegetables do not grow, would one not be stingy? As for the instruction:
seven grains, though possessing all flavors, are able to fill the great trichiliocosm—this is the Dharma. Thus, it is not necessary for vegetables to grow.
Whenever [a being] is born, place it safely within the left palm and perform this visualization.

[Commentary: The practitioner first presses the ring finger and little finger with the thumb of the left hand, extends the index and middle fingers upward, and holds the cooked rice within the ring and middle fingers.
Next, with the right hand, form the mudrā as shown on the left, moving the hands in an interlaced manner while maintaining the visualization.
The seeds of syllables flow forth as inexhaustible Dharma-food, universally saving ghosts and spirits.
The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains pervade the ten directions, universally bestowed throughout the sands of the world-systems.
Oṃ ture svāhā. [Commentary]:

Regarding "obstacles," it refers to the three obstacles of the hungry ghosts (*preta*). First, the external obstacle: this refers to the fact that hungry ghosts constantly suffer from hunger and thirst.
Their skin, flesh, veins, and blood were all withered and parched; their hair was disheveled and matted, their faces were dark and sunken, and their lips and mouths were dry and shriveled.
Constantly licking their mouths and faces with their tongues, they ran about in terror, seeking food everywhere. At whatever springs or ponds they reached, [they found them empty].

Then they see that water turn into pus and blood; these ghosts do not even wish to drink it themselves. Because their food and drink are obstructed by external factors, this is called "external obstruction" (bāhyāvaraṇa).
Second is "internal obstruction" (ādhyātmikāvaraṇa), which refers to the hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles or whose mouths are like torches.
Because their bellies are so vast, even if they obtain food and drink, they are unable to swallow or consume it.
Such hungry ghosts, due to internal obstructions regarding food and drink, are said to have "internal obstructions" (antarāya). Third, those without obstructions:
there are hungry ghosts named "Flaming Garland" (Jvālāmālī) who, although possessing food and drink, have no physical obstructions; however, whatever they consume is immediately set ablaze.
They turn into burning coals. Due to these causes and conditions, there is the great suffering of hunger and thirst; this is called "unobstructed. Regarding the power of the Dharma:
it is the power of mantras, verses, and contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the "inconceivable": it cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can it be expressed in words;
yet through it, one accomplishes inconceivable compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*). Because of this compassion, one attains non-obstruction. Because of this non-obstruction...

Because of this obstruction, he was able to cause seven grains [of sand] to pervade the realms of dust throughout the universe, so that all ghosts and spirits might eliminate their hindrances, partake of the flavor of the Dharma, and attain liberation.
Thus one understands the meaning of the two preceding verses. These two scriptures were originally transmitted from the Nirvāṇa Heaven;

therefore, while the phrasing differs, the meaning is identical. At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] the Mother of Ghost Children and others, who were harassing and harming the people, being fierce and...

Evil is peerless; therefore, one first subdues it with awe and subsequently gathers it in with compassion. By exchanging their physical sustenance for the food of the Dharma, one prevents living beings from entering the gateway of death;

hence, it is called "giving birth" (to life). However, fearing that the transformation through the Dharma might not be constant and that those of a violent and evil nature might still harm living beings, he then commanded his disciples: "In every place where you practice, at the time of eating, you must first offer the Dharma."

"Eating" is for the purpose of fulfilling the Dharma-joy. To investigate: when observing the methods for the distribution of food in the monastic groves (*saṅghārāma*), there are cases where the Abbot and the entire assembly emerge [from their seats] simultaneously;

there are cases where, at the time of eating, a single vessel of rice is first placed before the Mother Hārītī, and at the moment of the *adhivāsana* (invocation of blessings), only the Abbot alone emerges [from his seat]. This concludes the section on the "single-person emergence."
Regarding the birth of many beings, is there any difference? The explanation is that in principle, the one and the many are non-obstructive;

yet in terms of phenomena, the one is ultimately one, and the many are ultimately many. Why is this so? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "For example, if one person eats a meal, will many people be satiated?
Now, the birth of one person is the compassion of that one person; how could it be the same as the compassion of many people?
Therefore, if one person performs good while many people do not, the merit of that one person's goodness is small, whereas the fault of causing many people not to perform goodness is great.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "One who does not give food is not my disciple.
This is because [true disciples] know that when many people are born, each should follow the Buddha’s bequeathed teaching; this is called "each reducing their own portion."
These grains are bestowed according to the Dharma; at once, the light is divided by a thousand fingers. How vast is this compassionate salvation!
As for the number of seven grains—why not six or eight? The explanation is as follows: "Seven grains" signifies the filling of a thousand granaries. It begins from the state of having nothing;
from nothing, two arises, and when two is completed, three appears. Thus, from one comes three; this is the mother.
It is three yet one; it is the child. The child is three and the mother is three, reaching back to the ancestor who is neither one nor many, thereby forming the image of "returning" (laifu).
Its transformations are unfathomable, and thus it can be known that while six and eight exist within the numerical, they do not reside in the numerical.
Therefore, although the measure of seven grains can be counted, the measure of the Buddha-dharma cannot be counted. Formerly, as for the wine of Luan Ba, a minor artifice was able to—
It was transformed into sweet rain. By the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, seven grains sufficed to fill the great trichiliocosm; this is indeed the natural principle.
How could it be that a great vow would fail to surpass a minor artifice?
The Great Golden-Winged Bird (Mahāgaruḍa).
[Commentary: According to the *Lokotpatti-sūtra*, both the dragons and the Garuḍa kings possess the four modes of birth—egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.
The sūtra states: To the north of the great ocean, there is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmalī; it is one hundred [yojanas] in height.
Its branches and foliage cover fifty *yojanas*. This king of birds and the nāgas all dwell upon the four sides of this tree.
On each of its four sides there is a palace, six hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls adorned with the seven precious gems.
First, the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) king of the garuḍas dwells on the eastern side of the tree; when he desires to devour a nāga, [he proceeds as follows].

It flies to the eastern branch and observes the great ocean waters; it then immediately flies down and flaps its wings against the sea, causing the water to part for two hundred *yojanas*, where it seizes and devours the dragons.
This king of birds can only seize dragons born from eggs, but cannot seize those born from wombs, moisture, or transformation.
Second, the king of the womb-born *garuḍa* birds dwells on the southern side of the tree.
When he wished to seize the dragon, the bird king flew to the south of the tree, causing the waters to part spontaneously for four hundred *yojanas*, where he seized and ate the dragon.
This king of birds was able to seize only those dragons born from eggs or wombs, but was unable to seize those born from moisture or by transformation. (3)
The Moisture-born King of the Golden-Winged Birds dwells on the western side of the tree. When he wishes to seize a dragon, he goes to the western ocean of the tree to take it;
the waters part for eight hundred *yojanas*. This bird king can seize dragons born from eggs, wombs, or moisture, but he cannot seize those born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Four. The Transformation-Born King of the Golden-Winged Birds dwells on the northern side of the tree. When he wishes to seize a dragon, he goes toward...
It goes to the Northern Sea to seize them. When the waters part for sixteen hundred *yojanas*, those various *nāgas* are all devoured by this king of birds.
This refers to what is stated in the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra): "The four types of birth *garuḍas* eat the four types of birth *nāgas*."
The host of wilderness spirits and rākṣasīs, including the Mother of Ghosts, are completely filled with nectar. Oṃ mudite svāhā.
[Note:
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, while the Buddha was traveling through a village, there was a spirit beneath a tree named Āṭavaka, who fed exclusively on blood.]
He ate one person every day for his meal. I preached the Dharma to him, yet he was so foolish that he would not accept the path of instruction.
I immediately manifested as a powerful ghost and shook his palace until it could no longer remain stable, causing him to become bewildered and distressed.
Out of compassion, I stroked his body with my hand; he immediately sat up again and gave rise to a virtuous and faithful mind. I returned to my original form and preached the Dharma to him once more.
"Please grant me the precept against killing. The ghost replied, "I and my retinue subsist solely upon flesh and blood.
Now that I have taken this precept, how shall we survive? The Buddha said, "I now command my disciples: wherever they practice and eat, they must first set aside a portion for you.
If they do not set it aside, they are not my disciples. [The Buddha added: "Gulika, the Mother of Demons, is among the rākṣasas."
He was a giant *pō* (demon). He begot a thousand sons; the youngest was named Ainu, whom he cherished most dearly. This demon habitually devoured human children.
The Buddha, seeking to convert him, hid Ainu beneath his almsbowl. The mother searched for him throughout heaven and earth but could not find him.
Once she had submitted to the Buddha, he lifted the bowl and returned [Ainu] to her. His thousand sons all became kings of ghosts (*guǐwáng*), presiding over many...

There was a multitude of ten thousand ghosts; five hundred dwelt in the heavens, constantly harassing the devas, while five hundred remained in the world, constantly harassing the people within the borders of the kingdom.
The Buddha conferred upon them the five precepts and caused them to take refuge in the True Dharma. They attained the stage of Srotāpanna and came to reside in the Buddha’s vihāra.
Those without offspring shall obtain children through their prayers; those with illnesses shall find peace through them. Thus she became the mother of the king of ghosts.
Because she received the Buddha’s precepts, she also summoned her thousand sons to dwell together at the Buddha’s abode, where they no longer troubled devas or humans.
The above describes how the *garuḍa*-demon son was so violent and tyrannical that he could only be subdued by the Buddha’s majestic virtue and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*),
without the Buddha even altering his voice or expression. Nevertheless, because his violent and evil habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were not yet exhausted,
the Buddha first cleansed his heart and mind with the ambrosia (*amṛta*) to tame him, and subsequently filled him with the flavor of the Dharma.
"You hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you. This food is shared universally with all spirits and deities throughout the ten directions.
Oṃ mūliṅ svāhā. [Commentary] As for the words "you," it means that by the power of the Buddha’s mantra, their names are directly invoked to bestow the Dharma-food. This...
Regarding "the food pervades the ten directions": the various spirits and ghosts each disperse throughout the ten directions, yet this consecrated food is able to pervade the ten directions;
this symbolizes the Buddha’s mind of equality, whereby all spirits and ghosts equally obtain the flavor of the Dharma.
When reciting the prayer before eating, one should always be reverent.

[Commentary: There were bhikṣus who accepted invitations for meals from others; they entered in silence and departed in silence. The lay devotees (gṛhapati) rebuked them, saying, "We do not know whether the food is good or not.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, at the time of eating, one should..."
This expresses the intention of the donor.
[Verse for the time of the formal meal.

[Commentary: According to the Vinaya, when about to partake of food, one should silently recite this three times; it is capable of removing [impurities]. *Tripātra-khaṭa* (三鉢羅佉多) is translated here as "the time of the formal arrival."
Because he consumed poison, his name and meaning were [rendered as] *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formerly mistranslated as *Sengba*).
The Buddha established a rule for the bhikṣus:
[Commentary: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Śilakuṭa constantly doubted that the Buddha possessed omniscience; he therefore plotted to place poison in his food at home and [prepared it].

There was a great pit of fire, from which he caused the smoke and flames to vanish and covered it with sand. He spread an unwoven mat upon it and said, "If the Buddha possesses wisdom, he shall not accept this invitation.
Because the Buddha was one who should be delivered, he silently consented. Then he spoke to Ānanda, "Now, let the bhikṣus not go ahead.
Thereupon, leading the bhikṣus, he entered that house; the pit of fire was transformed into lotus flowers. The Buddha and...

The bhikṣus all walked upon the flowers. Their un-woven beds were all transformed into complete and perfect beds. Śrī, moved by this transformation, addressed the Buddha: "This food is mixed and unfit for consumption.
The Buddha said: "Simply offer it. If you eat it, there will be no illness. The Buddha told Ānanda to proclaim: "Until the *dhāraṇī* of aspiration has been recited, none shall eat beforehand.
Once it had been recited, all the food became sweet and delicious. The Buddha returned to his original state [of austerity]. From now on, until...
Recite the prayer for blessings. Do not eat;
when eating, observe the five contemplations.
[Commentary] A detailed explanation is provided below.
Scattered thoughts and idle chatter make it difficult to digest offerings given in faith. When the great assembly hears the sound of the *kṣaṇḍa*, let each maintain right mindfulness.

[Commentary: This is the verse with which the Buddha instructed Ānanda to proclaim to the bhikṣus, warning them that they must constantly cultivate correct contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) before receiving food.
If one does not cultivate contemplation but eats while the mind is scattered and engaged in idle chatter, there is fear that the faithful offering will be difficult to digest.
The ancients said: "A single grain of rice from a donor is as heavy as Mount Sumeru. If one does not realize the Way, it will be difficult to digest;
the two characters 'difficult to digest' are more poisonous than the venom of a *śrīkṛta* snake.
For this reason, the monastic communities have followed the Buddha’s final injunctions to this day; when about to eat, they strike the *qiǎng* and recite verses, causing the bhikṣus to—
Within these sounds, each maintains right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). As for right mindfulness: to mindfully attend in accordance with reality is called right mindfulness.

This mindfulness is itself the wisdom of mindfulness (*smṛti-prajñā*), which refers to being unmoved by states such as laxity (*laya*) or agitation (*auddhatya*), or by existence and non-existence; this is called unmoving right mindfulness. According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
"It would be better to swallow hot iron balls and endure great, raging flames for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever to break the precepts with this mouth."
...the mouth. He partook of the food of a hundred flavors provided by faithful donors; thus did the Venerable Deva receive the five lamps.
After he had attained the Dharma, he went to the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There was an elder named Brahmā Śuddhodana.
One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden, and their flavor was most exquisite. Only the elder and his second son, Rāhula, took them to eat. Having taken them, they ate.
As it grew larger, none of his other relatives could see it. The Patriarch, knowing its past cause, went to the householder’s home.

When the householder asked for the reason, the Patriarch said: "In the past, you once made offerings to a bhikṣu; however, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear, and he thus unworthily partook of your faithful offerings.
Consequently, you have been reborn as a wooden fungus. Only you and your son have diligently provided sustenance, and therefore you alone may enjoy it."

He asked the elder again, "How old are you? The elder replied, "Seventy-nine. The Patriarch spoke a verse, saying: "One who enters the Way without penetrating its principle returns to this body to consume the faithful's offerings.
You shall be eighty-one; this tree will not grow. Later, it was exactly as he had said, for the Buddha indeed bestowed this prediction upon him.
The Three-Spoon Contemplation Method.
[Commentary: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, for one who eats in order to practice the Path, when receiving food, three vows must be made.
First vow: To sever all evil.
[Commentary] When first setting down the spoon, one should make this vow: "May all evil of body, speech, and mind throughout this life be completely severed and exhausted."
2. May I cultivate all wholesome deeds. [Commentary:
Next, when lowering the spoon, one should wish that all wholesome dharmas possessed in this life may be fully perfected.
3. Vow to deliver all sentient beings. [Commentary:
When subsequently lowering the spoon, one should wish that the roots of goodness cultivated in this life be dedicated to sentient beings, so that together they may attain the Buddha-way.
The Five Contemplations on Eating: 1. Calculate the labor expended and measure the source from which it came.

[Commentary] According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this food involves a great deal of effort: plowing, sowing, harvesting, threshing, grinding, winnowing, cooking, and finally preparing it for consumption.

Regarding "measuring the source from which it came," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the donor must diminish their own portion, as well as those of their wife and children, to provide for the request.

For the sake of merit, when giving ordinary food, one should cultivate this contemplation. An ancient poem says: "When the sun is at its zenith, I hoe the rice paddies; sweat drips onto the soil beneath the grain.
Who knows that every grain of food upon the plate is the result of bitter toil? The *Lunheng* states: "The first stage of grain when it has ripened is called *sù* (millet)."
One threshes grain in a mortar, winnows away the chaff and husks, cooks it in a steamer, and heats it with fire until it matures into rice;

only then is it sweet and fit for eating. Yet the flavor of food is produced when the flesh becomes plump. Before the millet has become rice, and before the rice has become cooked grain, there is no flavor.
2. The meat is raw and its "qi" is still pungent; eating it will harm a person.
Furthermore, one should reflect upon one's own virtue and conduct to determine whether one is worthy of receiving offerings.

[Commentary: According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-vinaya*, if one does not practice seated meditation or recite the sūtras, nor attend to the affairs of the Triple Gem, and does not maintain the precepts... [text truncated]

When people offer food out of faith, if one has fallen into the state of being dependent on such offerings, it is not appropriate to accept the meal. If one’s virtuous conduct is complete, then one may rightfully accept the offering and eat.
Whenever accepting food, one should cultivate this contemplation.
3. Guarding the mind to remain free from faults, with the abandonment of greed and other afflictions as its primary aim.
[Commentary: The *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* states that one who has left the household life must first guard against three faults of the mind; namely, giving rise to greed for superior flavors in food.
The inferior flavor of food gives rise to anger; the middling flavor of food gives rise to delusion. Because of this, one lacks shame and remorse and falls into the three evil realms.
Whenever one receives food, one should practice this contemplation.
4. Properly taking good medicine to treat the withered body.
[Commentary: Hunger and thirst are the primary diseases; the four hundred and four diseases are the secondary (guest) diseases. One must take food as medicine to sustain the body.
Whenever receiving food, one should form this contemplation: the four hundred and four diseases refer to the human body, which is a provisional combination of the earth element...

It is composed of the four great elements—water, fire, wind, and earth. If even one of these great elements becomes unbalanced, it gives rise to one hundred and one kinds of diseases; when all four great elements are thus affected, they collectively produce four hundred and four diseases.
5. For the sake of accomplishing the Way, one should accept this food.
[Commentary: If one does not eat, hunger, thirst, and illness will arise; how then can the work of the Way be accomplished? The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Eating too much leads to suffering and affliction; eating too little causes one's strength to decline. One who eats in moderation is like a scale that has neither high nor low. Thus, whenever one receives food...

"One should perform this contemplation while eating. Pen-san cited Huang Shan-gu as saying: "The sequence for eating and drinking taught in the *Li* (Book of Rites) is but the branches of the teaching;
to perform contemplation while eating is the root of the teaching. Today’s scholars and officials merely recite the legal words of the former kings," [yet they do not practice them].
They were originally one person. Their rising, sitting, eating, and drinking were all one and the same; therefore, the establishment of the teachings could not be otherwise.
When a gentleman has reflection, it is lifelong reflection. At the time of eating, he practices the five contemplations; this is reflection during a single meal.
Day by day, acting in this manner, if every thought is imbued with benevolence and wisdom, then those two persons will now become one.
Five Lamps: Huanglong Nan. When the Master of Transformations returned, he ascended the hall and said, "In this world there are five things that are difficult to do:

first, it is difficult for the one who transforms; second, it is difficult for the one who gives; third, it is difficult to transform the raw into the cooked; fourth, it is difficult for the one who sits upright and eats.
What kind of person is there who is yet another thing that is difficult to do? After a long silence, he said, "Huh! and then descended from his seat. At that time, Cui...
Yanjun was the head seat. The Abbot of the Zang asked, "Just now the Master said that the fifth kind is 'not easy.
Who is this person? Yanjun replied, "If you see his cheek behind his head, do not associate with him."
Do not criticize food as being good or bad.
[Commentary: In ancient times, people wore coarse clothing to ward off the cold and ate plain, unrefined food to satisfy hunger for the sake of practicing the Way.

When participating in a communal meal according to the Dharma, to criticize the quality of the food—whether it is delicious or poor—greatly diminishes one's merit. However, if one encounters illness and is unable to eat such coarse and plain food, there is no fault.
Such a person should likewise maintain silence and must not give food from one's own private store.
[Commentary: Giving privately constitutes the karma of theft.
If one were to pluck [a portion] and give it to a dog. [Commentary:
A certain great donor, with sincere reverence, provided exquisite food to the Buddha and the Sangha. At that time, there was a dog with an empty belly wagging its tail, assuming a pitiable posture.
A certain bhikṣu took pity on it and shared some food to feed the dog. The donor was displeased and reported the matter to the Buddha. Thus [it is said].
The Buddha established this rule: When food is brought to be added, one must not say "I do not need more. If one is already full, one should use the hand to signal that one declines further.
[Commentary: The Buddha established the rule that one should eat from the alms bowl until full before setting it aside. If a practitioner comes to add more food...

When eating, he would take his bowl out with both hands. Once satiated, he would place the bowl on a small table. If a practitioner came again to offer more food, he would ward off the offering by gesturing with his hand;
thus, he used his hand to communicate and stop them. In the *Lamp Records*, Yantou said: "To pursue external objects is the mark of the inferior."
"Refusing things is supreme. Now tell me, how does this compare to the refusal [of the food] here? Chan Master Taiyu of Fuyong in Changzhou was serving food when it reached the place of Layman Pang.
As the Layman was about to receive it, the Master withdrew his hand and said, "To receive a gift with a calculating mind was already rebuked by Vimalakīrti.
Depart from this single instance; would you, Layman, accept it? The Layman replied, "At that time, Subhūti..."
"Are you not a master of the house? The Master said, "It is none of your business. The Layman said, "When food reaches the edge of one's mouth, it is snatched away by another.
The Master then set down his food. The Layman said, "Not even a single phrase is necessary. Zhaojue Qin said: "Shanxian was a master; Fuyong was extraordinary.
They were both completely understood at once by Layman Pang. It is just as the Layman said: 'Not even a single phrase is necessary.'"
A single phrase. Now tell me, what is that one phrase? Sitting upright and receiving offerings, may the donor receive peace and happiness.
One must not scratch one's head, lest wind-blown dust fall into the neighboring bowl.
[Commentary: Fragments of food blown by the wind may fall into one's bowl, causing those sitting nearby to feel resentment and leading to a loss of dignified decorum;
therefore, one must not speak while food is still in the mouth.
[Commentary: Wuzu Fayan Yanyi of the Five Lamps school was once traveling with several senior monks through the regions of Xiang and Mian when a monk raised a point regarding the Chan school.
Sheng was quite agile and quick-witted. Once, while having a field meal at a mountain inn, the monks were discussing [the teachings] without ceasing.
The Master said, "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. 'But consciousness, but mind'—what kind of talk is this?
A monk replied, "These are the words of Fayan. The Master asked, "What is their meaning? The monk said, "Because it is but mind, the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another."
"Consciousness-only. Consequently, sounds and forms surged forth. The Master asked, "Is this ancient flavor the sense-faculties and their objects? He replied, "Yes.
The Master placed a vegetable in his mouth with his chopsticks and spoke indistinctly, "What do you mean by 'mutual entry'? Those seated were startled; the monk could not answer.
The Master said, "The joy of the journey is not yet reaching home; insight that penetrates the subtle is not called seeing the Way."
"Study must be genuine study; awakening must be genuine awakening. King Yama does not fear much talk. The monk bowed and withdrew. Regarding speech during mealtime:
it is prohibited not only by Chan and Vinaya, but the Confucian school also constantly cautioned against it.

Exceptions are not considered transgressions when it concerns the karmic conditions of the Buddha-dharma or urgent matters for the sake of the world, such as when Shending Yin gathered for a field meal at a mountain inn.

There are indeed some mad Chan practitioners who, while holding food in their mouths, liken themselves to a divine cauldron; this is much like comparing the scent of asafetida and wormwood to sandalwood.
One must not engage in such frivolous talk.

[Commentary] In the *Miaoxi Jingsai* (Wuwei Shan’s Admonitions), it says: "If one does not understand where things come from and merely claims that 'the Dharma is naturally so,' then after eating, one gathers..."
Do not chatter noisily; speak only of miscellaneous worldly matters.
Do not make noise while chewing food.

[Commentary: Regarding the observance of conduct: when eating, one must not stir the food excessively or make noise while sipping or drinking. Once the meal is finished among the assembly, one must not...
One should eat with a quiet mouth. One does not show reverence by stuffing the mouth, nor by making slurping sounds, nor by returning food to the dish, nor by picking at it.
If one wishes to pick a tooth, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one’s robe.
"Pick" means to scrape. When eating with the assembly, one must not scrape one's teeth. It is appropriate to do so only after finishing the meal, having gone to a secluded place;
even then, if one wishes to scrape one's teeth, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve, for to expose the teeth is to lose one’s dignified demeanor.
If there are insects or ants within the food, one should carefully conceal it so that neighboring monks do not see it and become suspicious.
[Commentary: It is not that practitioners do not wish to offer pure and clean food and drink. Occasionally, insects or ants may inadvertently enter the food.
Upon seeing this, one should hide it discreetly; do not let others suspect that it cannot be eaten. Formerly, there was a monk who saw...
In a bucket were boiled vegetables; a chicken floated on the water, and [the monk] hurriedly took it to eat. Speaking with a slurred tongue, he said, "What a fine head of cooked greens!
Although this monk’s deeds were coarse, they reveal a timely expedient to settle the minds of the assembly.
This monk indeed possessed the power of Fenyang.
One should eat while remaining seated in one sitting. Once the meal is finished, one must not leave the seat and sit again to eat.
[Commentary: When the Buddha taught the practice of eating in one sitting, the bhikṣus praised it and accepted it; they no longer ate further, and their bodies became emaciated.

The Buddha immediately granted permission. After one meal, one may further eat wheat cakes and other foods until fully satiated. "Fully satiated" means that one’s desire is satisfied; it does not refer to a different time.
If it were at a different time, it would constitute eating at an improper time (*vikālabhojana*). In a single day, the alms bowl becomes wet twice:
this refers to eating at the proper times signaled by the bell and the wooden board. One sits once and does not sit again because of the fear of eating at an improper time.
One must not, after finishing a meal, use one's fingers to scrape food from the bowl or alms-basin.

[Commentary: The grains remaining in the center of the bowl should be offered to living beings. If one scrapes them with the fingers to eat, it greatly violates dignified decorum and, moreover, results in the loss of the merit of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the practice of protection: if there is food that has fallen onto the eating cloth, one must not pick it up and eat it.
One should gather [the food] together in one place and place it in the bowl or dish of a *karmadāna*.
When eating, one must not be too fast, nor must one be too slow. [Commentary:
If one is too fast, coarse breath will oppress others; if one is too slow, one will be dilatory and miss the proper timing. Therefore, one must be neither hurried nor sluggish.
Slowly. Eat in proper sequence. Observe the protective conduct (*rakṣā*). When holding the bowl, it must not be held too high, nor too low; it should be kept at the level of the chest.
The bowl and the napkin must always remain separated from the knees. One must not place the hands upon the knees.

According to the Pure Regulations (*qinggui*), one must not bring the mouth to the food, nor bring the food to the mouth. Regarding etiquette: one must not pick up rice from the center of the bowl, nor...
Dainao scraped his alms bowl;
though the food had not yet arrived, he did not give rise to affliction.

[Commentary: During the time of the fast, there is only the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, for there is no affliction. If even one person were to feel affliction, it would affect all four seats.
If one acts with a sense of unease, it will eventually result in affliction; therefore, when performing the *zhāifǎ* (fasting ritual), it is better not to commit an offense.

If there is something required, one should direct others silently. One must not raise one's voice or shout loudly (*zhǐshòu* means to give instructions). One must not allow the bowls or basins to make noise.

[Commentary] Regarding the deportment at the time of eating: the bowls and basins should naturally be without sound. If the bowls and basins make noise, it is because of coarseness and lack of refinement.

If one person is coarse and lacks refinement, it is intolerable for others to hear; if many are likewise so, the regulations of the dining hall will become lax and the rules of the *prātimokṣa* meal will not be observed with reverence.
To whom does the fault belong?
One must not rise before others have finished eating.
[Commentary: In the method of the fast, one must maintain reverence from beginning to end. To depart first after finishing the meal is to have a beginning but no end.

To act with deceit or arrogance toward the assembly is a transgression; however, there is no offense if one has informed the administrators in advance regarding matters pertaining to the permanent endowment or for those traveling on a long journey.
Should one violate the monastic regulations, it constitutes an offense.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "monastic regulations" (*saṃghakāraṇa*): these are the texts expounded within the Vinaya; all such matters constitute monastic regulations.

Should there be a violation, one first strikes the *kīla* (gong) to assemble the community, after which the matter is adjudicated and punishment is heard. In the *Khandhaka*, it is stated that one should not eat with the feet tucked up, as this obstructs the neighboring seat.
Any food that is unfit for consumption should be taken and placed at the side of one's feet; when departing, one should take it away. [This is] the pure rule (*qinggui*). Not...
One may bring the mouth toward the bowl, or bring the bowl toward the mouth; this is the proper etiquette. One must not pick out choice morsels from the center of the bowl.
As stated in the *Weishan Jingce*: "If the bowl or alms-bowl makes noise while eating, and one rises before others have finished, such conduct is discordant and devoid of the character of a monk.

Rising and sitting with agitation disturbs the minds of others; those who prioritize the study of the precepts know this well. A *bhikṣu* wears only the lower robe (*antaravāsaka*) and has no upper garment."
One should not accept food [in such cases]. If one is ill or elderly, one should eat in a secluded place.
Upon hearing the striking of the *paṭaha* drum, one must not resist or refuse to comply.
[Commentary: The striking of the *paṭaha* is the formal decree of the Dharma King and the great function of Mañjuśrī. In all matters today within the monasteries...
Furthermore, the use of the *zhui* (mallet) for the formal announcement (*bai*) does not require words for the assembly to gather; tell me, how is the mallet used for the announcement?

A man of spirit and blood, upon hearing the announcement and the striking of the mallet, realizes it instantly. As for those lacking presence of mind who do not recognize good from evil—according to the *Wudeng Huiyuan*:
when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly had settled, Kāśyapa made the formal announcement, saying: "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma."

"Venerable One," [he said], and immediately descended from his seat. To speak at every moment and in every place without ceasing—once the World-Honored One has ascended the seat, he has already fallen into the second or third category [of conceptualization].

Without cause, the Golden-Colored Dhūta has forcibly applied a "break" to this great, unceasing sutra of the head, such that to this day the reading and interpretation of it by monks throughout the world remains incomplete. Verse: The tongue protrudes from the tip of the staff; The pillar raises its voice.
The sound rises above the sun and descends below the moon; let them proceed together in perfect harmony. ◎ Master Shuangquan:

When Master Kuan first resided at Yunmen, one day he heard the mallet struck to announce, "We request Master Kuan to serve as the head cook (Diansuo). The Master performed a somersault out of the assembly and said, "Yunmen Chan!"
"It belongs to me.
There was grain within the rice; he removed the husks and ate it.

[Commentary: Below the precept against stealing, the *Vinaya* notes that according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one may gather [the grain] in one place and, when departing, take it to give to birds.
The Five Lamps. Shishuang Qing was serving as the rice-mill attendant for Guishan. While he was winnowing the rice, Guishan said, "This is the donor’s rice;
do not scatter it. Qing replied, "I will not. Guishan picked up a single grain from the ground and asked, "What is this?
Qing had no answer. Guishan said, "Do not underestimate this one grain; hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one. Qing asked, "I wonder what this..."
"A single grain. From where does it arise? Guishan laughed heartily. Later that evening, he ascended the hall and said, "The assembly, there are worms in the rice;
everyone, look well! *Zhengfeng Lu*: Shide was a *dhūta* (ascetic) in the kitchen of Guoqing Temple.

After the midday meal, he would collect the leftover broth and cold rice, placing them in a bamboo tube, waiting for Hanshan. When Hanshan saw this, he joyfully carried it down to the base of the cliff.

"Eat quickly and be satisfied. Yunmen Cheng served as the latrine attendant at Yunqi. After clearing away the filth, he would rinse the grains remaining at the bottom of the toilet with clean water and eat them;
these were all instances of "hidden practice and subtle application.
People today certainly cannot act as Hanshan and Yunmen did, yet they may take the leftover broth or stray grains from washing dishes and feed them to dogs and pigs, or provide for fish and shrimp.
To fulfill the virtue of sustaining life is also the way to cherish one’s blessings. Thus, I have composed this "Chapter on Precious Grains" to inform my fellow practitioners:
I observe that countless grains of rice begin from a single seed. There is the grace of Heaven’s rain and dew, and the blood, sweat, and toil of the farmers.
Their intent is to sustain all living beings; their kindness is so great that their labor never ceases. Do not treat even a single grain with levity, for it is as vast as Mount Sumeru.
How can those who claim to be superior men fail to understand the coming of grain? It lies in such disarray that it sprays across the hall; shoes become soaked as they enter the latrines;
last night’s rice is cast away in the kitchen storehouses. While there are those by the roadside dying of hunger, the Celestial Eye sends down thunderbolts. How can you treat things so violently?
For two years in three, there have been famines, and we do not remember eating even chaff and husks. I have composed this "Treatise on Precious Grains" to examine the world from afar.

A gentleman may find a stray grain of rice at the edge of his bowl; upon seeing it, he picks it up immediately. The rice crust at the bottom of the cauldron is fragrant, and when eaten, it is most sweet and delicious.
If there remains a trace of broth on the plate, or the wash-water and oil-sediment from the basin—though he cannot eat these himself, he should feed them to dogs or pigs;
or perhaps pour them into a flowing stream to provide for the bream and carp. Although what is bestowed is minute, one's merit accumulates day by day.
Accumulation [of merit] not only extends the source of blessings, but also serves as the foundation for entering the Way. Regarding the Essentials of Monks:

when Changsha Yi was traveling through Shu, the Regional Inspector Mao Qu provided him with a midday meal. When Yi saw a single grain of rice among the food, he immediately ate it first. Mao Qu secretly respected and marveled at this;
later, he presented Yi with a thousand *hu* of rice, which Yi accepted and distributed as alms.
Appendix: One must not see delicious food and give rise to a greedy mind, eating to one’s heart’s content.

[Commentary]: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one should contemplate this food: from its cultivation, weeding, harvesting, threshing, grinding, pounding, and sifting, until it is cooked and finally prepared.
If one calculates the labor required for even a single bowl of rice—the sweat flowing from the workers—and measures it all together, the food is small while the sweat is vast.

The labor and hardship involved in cultivating and seasoning these fragrant flavors are immense; yet as soon as they are offered upon the three-inch tongue, they become impure. How can one indulge greed without restraint?

One fails to reflect on the triviality of moral virtue; how can such things be digested? I fear that in the future I may fall among the various classes of beings and suffer the bitterness of retribution.
Therefore, give rise earnestly to a sense of shame. As the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra Sūtra* states: "For a person who eats to excess, the body..."
Heavy with excessive indolence, in both the present and future lives, one loses great benefit for the body;
through sleep one suffers for oneself and also troubles others, becoming so bewildered that awakening is difficult. One should therefore measure one’s food according to the proper occasion.
One must not eat apart from the assembly. [Commentary:
"Eating apart from the assembly" means not eating together with the assembly. There are three types of such non-participation:

first, to privately prepare food and drink and eat alone without sharing it with the assembly; this transgression is grave. Second, not to have privately prepared food and drink, yet to sit separately for some reason.
Regarding food: there is no offense in three cases. First, for those who are old or ill and unable to follow the assembly, there is no offense even if they prepare food privately.
*Baohun* (Precious Admonitions) records that Zhu’an said: "When Fojian was residing at Taiping, Gao’an served as the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable of the Hall).

At that time, he was young and haughty, looking down upon those from all quarters, and few could satisfy his mind. One day during the midday meal, when the *ghanṭā* was struck, he saw an attendant setting aside food in a separate vessel."
In front of the mirror, Yun’an left the hall and said in a stern voice, "A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of five hundred monks behaves in such a manner;

how can he serve as a model for future students? Xuedou, as if he had neither heard nor seen this, did not react. When they reached the bottom of the hall, it was discovered that the food was watered-down vegetable soup.

This was because Xuedou had long suffered from spleen ailments and therefore did not eat oil. Yun’an felt ashamed and went to the abbot’s quarters to request his resignation. Xuedou said, "The *weina*..."
What you have said is most appropriate. Because of Huìqín’s illness, he has long heard the words of the Sage, which penetrate all things through principle.
Since his physical condition for consuming food was not superior to that of others, he did not harbor any doubts. The Rector (Weina) possesses a spirit that is clear and far-reaching;
in days to come, he shall serve as a pillar and cornerstone for our school. I hope you will not let this matter become a source of resentment. When Jiàn succeeded to Zhìhǎi, Ān passed by Longmén.
Later, he became the successor of Fuyan (Buddhalocanā).
The ritual method for the fast is as follows: *Namo satvānāṃ samyaksambuddhakoṭīnāṃ tadyathā oṃ jvale jvale*.
Recite "Tāre Tuttāre Ture Svāhā.
As it is said: "Whoever practices generosity will surely obtain its benefit; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely attain peace and joy in the future."
[Commentary: What are called the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth are both derived from giving with joy; therefore, the retribution obtained later is also one of happiness.
When the meal is finished, one should wish that all sentient beings accomplish all that they have to do and be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.

[Commentary] Once the ritual of the one-meal fast (ekāsanika) is completed, if one does not form a vow of aspiration, then the preceding three spoonfuls and five contemplations (pañca-vipaśyanā) will all be redundant words;
there would be a beginning but no end. Therefore, one should vow that all sentient beings shall ultimately accomplish all matters.

To have "all that is to be done accomplished" (*sarva-kṛtya-pariniṣpanna*)—how easy is this to speak of! Briefly stated, having sat upright and received the offerings, the practice of contemplation is complete. [The kitchen...]

The practice of the "Hall of Diligent Cultivation" has been completed. As for entering into profound discourse on the principle: the followers of the Two Vehicles merely sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāva-āsrava*);

Bodhisattvas are about to exhaust ignorance (*avidyā*), yet they are still not called "completely accomplished. Only the Buddha, having thoroughly exhausted the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) and forever forgotten the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*), may be called "completely accomplished."

Verse for Receiving the Offering [Commentary]: In ancient times, when a *dānapati* provided a meal for the *saṃgha*, they would first spread a cloth or woolen mat beneath the seats. After the midday meal was concluded, they would present these mats to be made into robes.
Therefore, [the character] qīn (親) was derived from the character yī (衣). Later, silver coins replaced cloth; thus, qīn was derived from bèi (貝). From the *Jǐgǔlüè* (A Brief Account of Antiquity):
When the Layman Hóng Qìngshàn of Liàntáng served as the Regional Inspector of Jiāngdōng, he was staying overnight at Chízhōu.

The Master Yú Zōng of Mèishān went out to welcome him, and they conversed throughout the night. Hóng asked, "In which sutra is the practice of feeding monks mentioned? The Master replied, "The *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*."
It is said: Feeding a hundred ordinary people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person;

even feeding ten billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not as good as feeding one who dwells nowhere, acts without action, and realizes nothing—meaning one who has neither cultivation nor realization.
Such a person is one of right mindfulness and solitary liberation, whose merit transcends that of all Buddhas. Hong said: "Many predecessors have known this. Its...
"For whom? Zong replied, "Recently, Qin Shaoyou was demoted to the prefecture of Tengzhou, where he composed his own funeral elegy containing the line:

'Who will provide rice for the yellow-robed monks? When Dongpo learned of Qin's situation, he sent five taels of silver by letter, instructing Fan Yuanzhang to provide alms for Qin’s monastic funeral.
When Dongpo returned north and reached Piling, he passed away due to illness at the Imperial University."

Hesheng collected money and provided a meal for the monks at Huilin Monastery in Dongjing. Su Shi, the Gatekeeper of the Eastern Capital, composed the epitaph for Dongpo’s tomb and recorded this incident at its beginning.
Hong asked, "Is there scriptural authority for such *dakṣiṇā* (monetary offerings)? Zong replied, "Have you not seen the *Mao Shi*, in the *Xiaoya*:

'The Ruru' [The Deer's Call], which describes feasting the ministers and honored guests? Having already provided them with food and drink, one further fills their purses and baskets with silks and fabrics to express one's profound sincerity."
It is because merely providing food and drink is insufficient to fully express reverence; thus, one adds gifts and offerings to manifest earnest devotion.
At such times, one recites the *zhāishū* (vegetarian offering prayers) of Lord Ding Jin; however, these are not recorded here.
The incantation for the dedication of merit (*dhāraṇī-adhiṣṭhāna-dakṣiṇā*): "May all sentient beings be enabled to penetrate the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s scriptures.
[Commentary: This is from the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-sūtra*. Furthermore, a verse states: "The two gifts of material wealth and the Dharma are equal and without distinction;
may the *dāna-pāramitā* be fully perfected. Whenever there is one who bestows a gift, there must be a vow or aspiration; the recipient of the gift should...
Before the Triple Gem, he proclaimed his vow. Regarding the *bhuṣu-mi-lun* (Vasumitra-śāstra), it prescribes the giving of *dāna*—which is translated here as "bestowal of wealth" (*cái-shī*).

The commentary explains that the method of giving in recompense is called *dakṣiṇā*. It guides one toward the ground of merit, and is thus also termed *dakṣiṇā*; the character may also be written with the radical for "hand.
According to the *Xiyùjì* (Records of the Western Regions), *dakṣiṇa* means "right. Alternatively, it is said to be *dakṣiṇī*, referring to the right hand.

When receiving what is bestowed by others, one does so for the sake of generating merit for them. Zao said: "In meeting people according to their circumstances, one cannot expect results in a single breath;
in aiding things with wealth, one cannot encompass them all at once moment. Therefore, those who achieve universal penetration without boundaries weave the whole together without omission;
those whose dharma-beneficence is darkly pervasive provide universal shelter without change. As for the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], they are the Great Wisdom."
The *Dulun* (Vinaya-mātṛkā) states that there are twelve divisions of the Sūtras: 1. **Sūtra**: In the language of China, this is called *qijing* (契經).
