When lying down, one must lie on the right side; this is called "auspicious sleep. One must not lie on the back, lie face down, or lie on the left side.
[Commentary: Lying on the right side is the tradition bequeathed by Śākyamuni Buddha; therefore, it is called "auspicious. As for auspicious sleep:
The right hand is bent so that the elbow serves as a pillow. One does not lie on one’s back, for this is the manner of a corpse.
To lie face down is the supine position. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: "Lying on the back is the posture of the asuras; lying face down is the posture of the pretas;
lying on the left side is the posture of those who indulge in desire; lying on the right side is the posture of the renunciant. The *Huangting Jing* states: "Above is the Yellow Court."
Below lies the *guanyuan* (pass-gate); in front is the *youque* (dark portal), and behind is the *mingmen* (gate of life).
If one lies supine or prone, the qi of the *mingmen* and the *dantian* (cinnabar field) cannot expand; consequently, there arise states of chaotic dreams and disorientation.
The *Lingshu Jing* states: "Heaven does not fill the northwest; therefore, the right ear and eye are not as clear-sighted as the left ear and eye. Earth does not fill the southeast; therefore..."
The left hand and foot are not as strong and healthy as the right hand and foot. Therefore, one who rests with the arm bent uses the left side as a void to fill the right.
One must not sleep having removed one's inner garment.

[Commentary: Those whose will is set upon the Way sleep little and spend much time in walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Even when they reach the height of exhaustion, they rest for only a brief moment.
The ancients used a round log as a pillow to admonish themselves, constantly ensuring they remained alert and tranquil. This was especially so when they lay down after removing their robes.
If one then lets the mind run wild and indulges in sleep, the spirit and will become darkened and degraded; this is like being on the verge of a small death, and one is far removed from the Way.

During the Tang dynasty, Zhang Zhìhé studied the arts of the immortals. Throughout his life, he never took off his clothes while lying down. His sister-in-law, wishing to accommodate his resolve, had a garment sewn with the seams joined all around the body.
When I attended upon the Venerable Mì at Tiāntóng, I would occasionally go to the rear quarters; it was only after passing through more than ten halls and rooms that I [would reach my destination].
Upon arriving, it happened to be a cold season; fearing the chill when rising at night, I consequently lay down without removing my clothes.
This has continued for over thirty years until now, becoming a habitual practice. Living on a boat and sleeping at night while wearing clothes feels particularly comfortable and convenient.
One must not laugh or speak in a loud voice while lying on a bed.
[Commentary: Day is for activity and night is for rest; this is how one physically observes the principles of Yin and Yang within Heaven and Earth. Qian (Heaven) is active and Kun (Earth) is still.
If Yin and Yang lose their proper positions, the underlying principle will inevitably be violated. Therefore, when about to lie down, one should remain silent and without sound. If...
If one laughs or speaks loudly during the quiet night, one will be rebuked by ghosts and spirits. The *Analects* states that one should not speak while lying in bed;
this surely has its own reason. One must not carry a chamber pot past a sacred image or before the Dharma Hall.

[Commentary]: The *Rites of Zhou*, in the "Office of the Heavenly Official" (*Tianguan*), states: "The Grand Marshal (*Taiwei*) presides over the King’s informal attire and all articles of personal use.
Zheng Sannong remarked: "Informal" (*xie*) refers to the chamber pot; it is called the 'Tiger Child' (*huzi*) and is also known as the 'Crouching Tiger.

This passage speaks of the fact that vessels for excrement, urine, filth, and impurity must not be carried past one's elders, let alone before the towering and sacred images [of the Buddha]. How could one dare to treat them with such irreverence?
Section Fifteen: Encircling the Fire [Commentary] When ancient masters opened the hall to preach the Dharma and refined their monastic disciples, it was called "opening the furnace.

I shall remember this forever and never forget it. Few people passed through his door. Consequently, Yuanwu went to his quarters and tested him by citing the story of Qinglin carrying three loads of firewood.

what is there of value in the gold of this world? When the fields of kalpas are emptied, the Buddha-flowers bloom; a fragrant breeze strikes and pierces the nose born of one’s mother.

Second, the lamp is presided over by the Fire Deity (*agni-deva*). In the birth of a person, there is none who does not rely upon this to dispel darkness and bring forth light, thereby maturing and sustaining life.

Sound. Striking objects produces discordant noise, causing others not to sleep and provoking their affliction of anger.

*Brahmajāla Sūtra*. "If a Buddha’s disciple sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them as if they were the Buddha."

Only then will one know the source of the illness and from which meridians (*jīnglù*) it originated. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Once you know where the thief is located, only then do you dispatch the troops."
To eliminate [them]. Once one knows the location of the enemy, then military forces will not be thrown into disorder and the eradication of the enemy will not be difficult.

Once one knows the location of the disease, then the application of medicine will not be erroneous and the removal of the disease will likewise be easy. To know the source of the disease and not err in one's observation is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Having already known the locus where the disease resides, the achievement of the result lies in the application of the medicine. Now, as for disease, it is like an enemy.
Medicine is like the military; medicine is used as the military is used. It is employed only when there is no other alternative.

One must ensure that the military does not become chaotic and turn into bandits, lest the medicine become disordered and cause illness—like the poison of arsenic or aconite, which should not be used. Yet, even such [deadly] things may still have their proper application.

The supplementation provided by *huang shen* (Scutellaria baicalensis) may be employed; yet there are occasions when it must not be used. One must discern whether the disease involves depletion or repletion.
Thus, by selecting a single medicinal ingredient, one adapts its application according to the timing, manifesting transformations as the situation demands—generating life through death.
To kill by means of life—this lies solely within the movement of one’s own grasp. What is called "the finest essence (amṛta) and poison proceeding as one path" is precisely the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
When these six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are practiced in unison while tending to the sick, one becomes equal to the King of Physicians.
Ānanda offered a single response on behalf of Mañjuśrī; how could there be a single stalk [of merit] belonging to Sudhana?

You must be careful not to rashly ordain the novice Śāriputra. The gestures of women are difficult to fathom; their charms last but a moment, yet they give rise to evil intentions.
They are like bubbles on water, arising and then vanishing, possessing no constancy. Only one who can discern the faculties of others [should do so].
Observe their great conduct and see their past transgressions; if they are now ready for deliverance and attain the Way, one must hasten to save them.
Unless one is a Bodhisattva or an Arhat, it is not permissible to ordain a *bhikṣuṇī*.

Master Zili said: "In body, do not discard the outward appearance of a śramaṇa; in mind, do not contravene the regulations of the Tathāgata.
When seated, do not turn your back on the sutras of the Dharma-realm; in nature, do not be stained by the objects of emotional attachment.
Let your feet not tread upon the dust of a nunnery; let your side not touch the couch of a layman. Let your eyes not gaze upon colors that are improper; let your tongue not savor what is excessive."
At noon, he does not let go of his *cintāmaṇi* bead; at night, he does not depart from the side of his robe and bowl.
Yet people today disregard the clear instructions of the Buddhas and patriarchs and do not avoid the suspicions of the world, repeatedly entering the gates of nuns’ monasteries.
Those who are rebuked and cast out by the Dharma of the Buddha, the King of Dharma, have their sense of integrity and shame almost entirely exhausted.
They sit separately from others; even when there is no separate seat, they may not sit together.
[Commentary]: "Sitting separately" means sitting apart. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, both sitting in the open and sitting in a screened place are prohibited.
Although this refers to sitting apart, one must not remain seated for a long time, as it gives rise to suspicion. ◎ If one preaches the Dharma until sunset, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
One must not deliver discourses at an improper time. [Commentary:
"Improper time" refers to speech that is not appropriate for delivery within a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery. It is like knowing the dietary restrictions when taking medicine. Therefore it is said:

"If the preaching of the Dharma does not accord with the proper time, then even that Dharma is non-Dharma. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when entering a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery to preach the Dharma, one must not exceed [the allotted time].
If one speaks more than five or six words, it constitutes an offense. Even for those who deeply love the Dharma, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one should not speak at length;
how much less so should one speak at an improper time?
If one returns [to the source], one cannot speak of its beauty or ugliness.

[Commentary: Within the Great Perfect Mirror, there is fundamentally no beauty or ugliness. It is like the peony flower blooming as the face of a Bodhisattva, or the *tāla* tree growing as the head of a yakṣa.
When their reflections enter the mirror, the mirror never says, "I am a yakṣa," or "I am a Bodhisattva."
"Sa! If it is a path, then this mirror is either a specter or a monster; you should smash it to pieces right now.
Look, where are the beautiful or ugly forms of the Bodhisattvas and Yakṣas?"
One must not engage in the exchange of letters, nor in activities such as borrowing, cutting, or laundering [clothing].
[Commentary: According to the *Neize* (Inner Regulations), there is no mutual solicitation for leave, and men and women do not share clothing.

Therefore, even if young monks and nuns maintain the purity of the precepts and possess a state of dual tranquility in mind and environment, bystanders cannot help but harbor doubts or criticisms regarding matters such as the exchange of letters.
As time passed and months accumulated, his resolve may have faltered, leading to the regret that Yu Tong felt in his later years;
therefore, I resolutely severed [the connection] so that he could not personally perform the rite of tonsure.
[Commentary: As for men and women touching bodies without their minds becoming disturbed, from ancient times until now, there has been only one such person:
Liu Xiaohui. Even Ānanda would have to concede him a step. In this degenerate age, even if Liu Xiaohui were born today, he would undoubtedly emulate the "Man of Lu.
Now, [if one] shaves the head of a nun, even if the mind remains undisturbed, the outward appearance is unseemly; it causes...
When those of the same class have their hair shaved clean, suspicions will be forever dispelled.
Appendix: There must not be two people [acting alone]; one may not enter alone.

[The practitioner] seeks out the recitation of sutras and the performance of repentance rituals. [Commentary: When a monastic community undertakes construction projects, they are not without hope for the alms of lay donors; yet they must wait for conditions to ripen.
Indeed, when one’s moral cultivation is lofty and one’s practice is authentic, then alms will come without seeking them, and conditions will arise without soliciting them.
To what end? Why must one employ such a mind? To an observer from the outside, it appears like the behavior of a rat stealing or a dog pilfering;
when the object of one's pursuit is not achieved, groundless suspicions and slanders arise. Even if a Buddhist temple were built as high as Mount Sumeru, it would be no cause for envy.
How does this compare to cultivating oneself and waiting for conditions to bring success? As the Sūtra says: "If one gives away even a small thing, let alone the seven treasures..."
The construction of a stūpa and its various adornments are not equal to the pure observance of the precepts; this latter is the true offering to the Tathāgata’s precious Dharma-body.
One must not form ties of kinship with *bhikṣuṇīs*, such as by pledging them as parents, sisters, or fellow practitioners.
[Commentary]: Regarding the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*): even a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years’ standing must prostrate before a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera.
Now, for a śrāmaṇera to instead prostrate before nuns is a great violation of the Buddha’s regulations. One does not know how to take leave of one’s kin or sever worldly attachments;

May the "Blow-of-the-Blade" sword sweep across the universe, and may the winds of the *Zheng* Odes clear away all such perversity to reveal the natural order of human relations (*tianlun*). Zhang Meicun’s imitation of Hanshan’s poems: "Parting from One's Kin."

This single robe of the Tathāgata has ultimately been sold by him. To produce such a ruinous son— even the Buddha can do nothing about it.

Chapter Nineteen: Visiting Lay Families [Commentary] In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, it is said that those wicked bhikṣus manifest the appearance of observing the precepts to inspire faith and reverence in the minds of their donors (*dānapati*).
Having done so, they frequently visit the homes of these donors together with their companions. Such bhikṣus act according to their own [selfish] desires.
Having heard a little of the Buddha-dharma, he, together with his companions, explained the teachings he knew to that donor.
By such means, he intended to cause the donor to bestow the gains and offerings obtained by those bhikṣus upon them.
Thus it is with the bhikṣu who is a śramaṇa in appearance only; he is the foremost of great thieves. According to the *Mingxiang ji*:
Senggui of the Song dynasty was invited by Zhang Yu of Jingzhao to receive lay offerings. While free from illness, he suddenly died. After two days, he revived and said:
Bound by five men, he was led away and soon arrived at a city. An official sat with a pen, examining a register.

Another man, dressed in crimson robes and a black cap, approached and said, "This person's name does not appear on the register. The official said, "Why has the Executioner of Ghosts brought this man here indiscriminately?
and he had him whipped. Shortly thereafter, a messenger appeared claiming to be from the Heavenly Emperor, who summoned the practitioner; he arrived immediately. The Emperor—
He said, "You are a śramaṇa; why do you not diligently attend to your practice, that you have been caught crosswise by a minor ghost?
It is simply because your life has not yet ended that you shall now return to life. You ought to be diligent and energetic; do not frequent the houses of laypeople too often.
Ghosts who kill people often commit wrongful excesses, such as those like you. Having finished speaking, he sent a messenger back to escort him home. He returned to the house of Yu.

The layman said, "I remember a saying from when I was in my mother’s womb; let me relate it to you, Master.

The Master said, "How can one not fear such startling words? The Layman said, "A perspective such as this may indeed be called startling.

Xia visited Layman Pang. Seeing his daughter Lingzhao washing vegetables, the Master asked, "Is the Layman at home?
The girl set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands folded. The Master asked again, "Is the Layman at home? The girl picked up the basket and walked away.
The Master then turned back. A short while later, the Layman returned. The girl recounted the previous conversation. The Layman said, "The cinnabar..."
"Is Hsiaya here? The woman replied, "She has gone. The Master said, "It is like applying red earth to milk. On another day, he visited Layman Pang.
Upon meeting at the gate, the Master asked, "Is the Layman at home? The Layman replied, "When hungry, one does not choose one's food.
The Master said, "Is Old Pang at home? The Layman replied, "Heaven! Heaven! and then entered the house. The Master said:
"O Blue Heaven! O Blue Heaven! With these words, he turned back. ◎ Yantou Huo, having been purged from the monastic community, spent the summer retreat at the home of Gānzhì.
While he was mending his robes, Gānzhì passed by. The Master made a gesture with his needle as if piercing something; Gānzhì then straightened his robes and prepared to offer thanks. His wife asked:
"What are you doing? Zhi said, "It cannot be spoken. His wife said, "I want everyone to know it too," and she recounted the previous conversation.
The wife said, "Thirty years from now, you must know that every time one drinks water, one swallows it once.
When the daughter heard this, she said, "Who would have known that the lives of the entire world have been seized by the Venerable Huo?"
Verse on Arriving at a Dwelling: Upon entering another’s door, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the gates of all Buddha-dharmas. [Commentary:

The person of the Great Path of Liberation universally perceives that the myriad doors and ten thousand gates are none other than the single, profound gate of the Flower Treasury (*Kusumagarbha*). One.

The Mysterious Gate of the Flower Treasury accommodates a thousand doors and ten thousand portals; thus, once one recognizes the mind of *nirvāṇa*, one awakens to and enters into differentiated wisdom.
Once differentiated wisdom is fully understood, what need is there to seek the mind of *nirvāṇa*? Do you not see? In butcher shops and wine taverns, every place is a site of practice (*dharma-śālā*);
in willow alleys and flower-lined streets, every point is *prajñā*. Nevertheless, it must be the functioning of the entire body for this to be so.
Attaining mastery and non-obstruction: if there is even a single thread that remains unsevered, it will bind and kill one.
Upon entering their homes, may all beings attain entry into the Buddha Vehicle and realize the equality of the three periods of time.

[Commentary: The sub-commentary states: "Before entering, there are the various distinctions of the different schools; once entered, there is only the One and no plurality. It is like entering the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna), where there are neither two nor three.

Regarding "household": this does not mean that one has not entered [the path]; rather, it means that the conditions for transformation and deliverance have already matured, hence the phrase "one should make a vow.
As for the "Buddha-vehicle," it refers to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the single Buddha-vehicle. Its...

The other vehicles each cling to divergent views, resulting in disparities of high and low; only the Buddha’s Single Vehicle is without high or low, without present or past, without going or coming, and without equality or inequality.
Therefore it is said: "The three periods of time are equal. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is known that all worlds are entirely equal;
there is nothing that is not the mind, speech, or all karma. Sentient beings are illusory transformations and possess no reality.
All karmic retributions arise from this.
There are distinct seats; one should sit accordingly and it is not appropriate to sit in a mixed manner.

[Commentary: The World-Honored One, foreseeing that the Dharma would become turbid and degenerate in the final age and that the Buddha-dharma would be slighted and disparaged, therefore established this chapter to serve as a warning for future generations.
In training, one must not sit in mixed company with worldly people to discuss mundane truths.
When asked about the sutras by others, one should know the proper time; be careful never to give teachings at an inappropriate time.
[Commentary: The Tathāgata observes the capacities of beings and imparts the teaching accordingly; his preaching during the five periods does not transcend knowing the proper time.

The patriarchs of successive generations forged and refined [disciples] with tongs and hammers, yet this too did not transcend knowing the proper time. Thus we know that for one who remains silent through knowing the proper time, their voice is like thunder.
To speak at an inappropriate time is the way of Māra. Nowadays, people in various quarters take sarcasm and verbal abuse as the preaching of the Dharma;
while this may indeed be their practice, it cannot avoid the derision of onlookers.
One must not laugh excessively.
[Commentary: According to the *Neize* (Inner Regulations): "When a man enters the inner quarters, he shall neither laugh nor point.
Even when the host provides food that does not constitute a formal dharma assembly, one must not fail to observe the proper ritual protocols.
[Commentary]: Wherever a practitioner of the Way goes, that place is a Dharma assembly; wherever the host has faith, that is a site of practice (doctrang).

Since the offering is made with sincerity, the recipient should accept it with integrity. For there are those who lack a sense of shame and have no decorum, who not only fail to increase the donor’s faith but instead give rise to doubt and slander. Therefore, this rule was established.
"One must not travel at night. [Commentary:
When a practitioner walks with the great brightness and clarity of the blue sky and the white sun, they may still be subject to scrutiny; how much more so when traveling at night?
Nowadays, royal decrees are somewhat strict, and nighttime travel is not permitted. One must arrive by the break of dawn. Furthermore, tell me, since it is already forbidden...
Traveling by night is permitted; how could one expect to arrive by dawn? Upon hearing this, would those who hear it not be struck with alarm?
One must not sit or converse with a woman in an empty room or a secluded place.

[Commentary: The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Do not engage in sexual intercourse with women, nor converse with them. Those who are able to distance themselves from such things will escape the eight difficulties.
From the *Vinaya-vastu-artha-saṃgraha*: Kālotthiya was infatuated with the wife of a friend, an upāsikā observing the fast.
While on his alms-round, he went to her house and sat upon the same couch as her, speaking improper words.
When Vimalā Mātṛ heard the sound and peered through the opening, she informed the Buddha, who then established this precept in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*:
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman alone in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse and speaks improper words,
and there is a faithful upāsikā who reports one of three matters— whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or..."
*Pāyattika*. This seated bhikṣu himself says, "I have committed this offense. Among the three rules, he should be dealt with one by one:
whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*. As stated by the trustworthy laywoman (*upāsikā*), that bhikṣu should be disciplined according to the Dharma.
This is called the *aniyata-dharma*. [Compiled in] the *Denglu*: Daolin, Yin.
He resided on Mount Taibai. The path was impassable for travel, so he sustained his body with wood and stones, remaining entirely free from worldly concerns.

By imperial decree, he was to reside at Xingguo Monastery, but before long, he fled to Liangshan, where he lived in a cave he had excavated. The Master did not allow women to defile his spiritual environment;

he would not preach the Dharma to them face-to-face, would not accept food from them, and would not permit them to enter his quarters. When he was approaching death, among those close to him, there were some who came to inquire after his illness; they remained hidden behind a screen.
[The master] knew this and immediately stopped her, not allowing them to face one another.
She was not permitted to exchange letters or correspondence (as in the case of the nunnery mentioned previously).

[Commentary]: An ancient saying goes: "If you wish to know a person, observe their pupils. Generally, if the pupils are not upright, the mind is not rectified;
one must not engage in idle conversation."
[Commentary]: These are miscellaneous remarks, plagiarized from common parlance. They are like tangled silk snarled in thorns—utterly without beginning or end.
They are like the hooting of an owl in a desolate mound, filled with many strange sounds; there is no one who would not resent hearing them.
If one speaks with a woman, one must not speak in a low voice or in secret; one must not speak at length. [Commentary:
In the *Dīrgha Āgama*, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should we deal with women who come to receive instruction?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not meet with them. Ānanda spoke again: "Suppose one does meet them..."
“If one encounters such a person, what should one do? The Buddha said, “Do not speak with them. Ānanda asked again, “If one does speak with them, what should one do?
The Buddha said, “One should examine one’s own mind.”
One must not feign the deportment of a practitioner or falsely assume the appearance of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in order to seek the respect of others.

[Commentary: True deportment values one’s natural state; feigned displays lack authenticity. The characteristics of meditation are fundamentally signless (*animitta*); how could that which is signless be contrived?

Even if one were to succeed in such contrivance, it would be difficult to escape the discernment of those with true insight. It is like a monkey learning to sit in meditation: the outward form may be present, but the inner mind remains as it was.
Suddenly, the subtle winds of the sensory realm arise, and one playfully steals and eats the fruit. Behold that noble person: their concentration is profound and silent for long.
They are like refined gold in a red furnace, whose color remains unchanged.
One must not speak deceptively regarding the Buddha-dharma, nor answer others' questions in a confused manner to seek their respect.
[Commentary: In the *Five Lamps*, it is recorded that when Baizhang ascended the hall, an old man followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma.
One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, only the old man remained. The Master asked, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am no ordinary person. In the past..."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he once dwelt on this mountain. Because a student asked him, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within cause and effect or not?
he replied, "He does not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, for five hundred lifetimes, he fell into the body of a wild fox.

Now he requests the Master to provide a turning word on his behalf, so that he may be released from his wild fox body. The Master said, "Ask your question. The old man said, "A great practitioner of the Way..."
“Does a human being still fall under cause and effect? The Master replied, “One is not ignorant of cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.
He prostrated himself and said, “I have already cast off my wild fox body. I reside behind the mountain; I venture to request that you treat me according to the rites for a deceased monk.

The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly: “After the meal, we shall escort a deceased monk. The entire community gathered and deliberated. The whole assembly—
"Everyone is well, and there is no one ill in the Nirvana Hall. Why is this so? After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the back of the mountain.
Beneath a cliff, he used his staff to unearth the carcass of a dead wild fox and performed its cremation according to the Dharma.

That evening, when the Master ascended the hall, he recounted the preceding events. Huangbo then asked, "The ancients were wrong to respond with a single phrase; they fell into five hundred [lifetimes]."
He was reborn in the body of a wild fox; turning and turning, he did not miss his mark. "What should have been done?

The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you. Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. The Master laughed and said, "I thought the beard was red, but there is yet another red-bearded barbarian.
At that time, Guishan was serving as the steward in the assembly. When the itinerant monk Sima raised the story of the wild fox and questioned the steward...
"Master Zu, how about this? Zu shook the door panels three times. Sima said, "That is far too crude. Zu said, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such things.
◎ Regarding the verse on "Hiding the Body within the Northern Dipper," when Wuzu Jie concluded his period of study, he went to visit and converse with Yujian Lin.
Lin inquired about the meaning of the verse; Jie looked up at him and showed it to him. Lin said, "If it is truly like this... Yun.
"One entrance costs one coin; you shall lose two days. He then departed. Lin eventually experienced exactly what had been said. Later in life, Jie also lost an eye.
Now, I take the words of these former virtuous ones to heart, fearing they might mislead future generations; Lin may serve as a warning for others.
One must not send gift boxes or engage in social visits with laypeople as they do.
[Commentary: According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, sending goods to the homes of laypeople is called "defiling their families.
This is because those who receive them are pleased, while those who do not are resentful, leading to slander. Therefore, this rule was established.
One must not manage the household affairs of others.
[Commentary: Though they are one's closest kin by nature, one must have the resolve to sever such affection for the sake of seeking the Way; one ought to eliminate all worldly attachments.

One must study with fierce diligence; only then will there be a ground upon which to repay one's debt of gratitude. There are those who lack understanding: though they have left the household life, they are no different from the laity.

They even shoulder their arms and offer sycophantic smiles, saying today they have come to a certain lord’s house on business, and tomorrow they have gone to a certain official’s house to seek patronage.
They do not raise the matter of their own fundamental duty at all. One day, when old age and sickness arrive—
Urgently: My Lord, my Young Master. I cannot protect you enough.
You must not sit in mixed company at a banquet. [Commentary]:
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that one must not stay in a tavern; sitting in mixed company is especially improper. This refers to the fact that among those who drink wine...
They are reckless and wild. Although one does not drink with them, there is always the danger that they might, through their frivolity, bring disgrace upon the Dharma-gate.

Therefore, it is ordained that one must not prostrate to laypeople as if they were one's parents or siblings (the same applies to nuns prostrating). One must not speak of the faults or transgressions within the Sangha.

[Commentary: When conversing with worldly people, one should inspire their faith with words of truth and sincerity. To speak of the faults of the Sangha is like severing the roots of their faith with a sharp blade.
Nowadays, the path of public righteousness has long been abandoned in all quarters, and the Buddha-dharma is not practiced.

For even the slightest matter, people immediately issue public denunciations; they report matters to government officials, exploiting their power to intimidate and oppress those belonging to the Dharma.
The Dharma-gate of weakening. How painful! If there were still justice remaining in this world, laypeople would preach the Dharma and bhikṣus would listen.
*Shengqin* (Reflecting on One's Kin), No. 20 [Commentary]:
In the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, it is recorded that the Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou was filially pious. He once wove *pú* (rush) sandals to support his mother; therefore, all...
Thus he first acquired the title "Pu-xie (Lotus Shoe) Chen. Later, when the rebels of Chao entered the territory, the Master hung a large straw sandal at the city gate;
the rebels wished to remove it but could not lift it despite their utmost effort. They sighed, saying, "There is a great sage within this," and they departed with it hidden under their arms.
As for Muzhou weaving lotus shoes to support his mother, those who offered provisions did so out of fear that he would not accept them.
This places the mother in a position of unrighteousness. At that time, he hung his straw sandals atop the city wall to ward off the invading enemy;
yet how could straw sandals withstand the valor of ten thousand men? Who would say that straw sandals possess the courage of ten thousand men?
In the end, not even a single blade of grass or a straw sandal could be moved; this was truly the power of his sincere filial piety.

Among those who become monks today, who has not received the grace of being nurtured by their parents and thus come into existence? Yet, once they have "ascended the branch" [entered the monastic order], they claim to have "transcended the world.
Consequently, they disregard their elderly parents, severing the joy of providing them with beans and water, while they themselves suffer the hardships of hunger and cold within their quarters.
Is his mind at peace? Compared to the filial piety of Muzhou, how does he measure up? According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*:

Daopi of Fuxian Temple in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) during the Zhou dynasty was a member of the Tang imperial clan. His father had gone to serve in the military at Mount Huo. Although Daopi would play as a child, he never showed a smile.
At the age of seven, he ceased eating meat and pungent flavors, and petitioned his mother to allow him to take refuge with the Dharma Master Jinen of Baoshou Temple.
The Master was nineteen when he thoroughly mastered the meanings of the scriptures. Later, as the capital was moved to Luoyang and Chang’an was laid waste by fire, Liu Kaidao rose in rebellion.
The Master carried his mother into Mount Hua and settled in a mountain cave. At that time, grain was so scarce and precious that it cost ten thousand coins per bushel.
Bei begged for alms to provide for his mother. His mother asked, "Have you eaten? He replied, "I have been on a fast outside; I feared it might offend your wishes.
When he was twenty years old, his mother said, "After your father passed away at Mount Huo, his bones were exposed to the frost and dew.
Would it not be filial for you to collect them and bring them back for burial? He then took leave of his mother and went to Mount Huo, where he built a thatched hut and gathered the white bones.
Day and night he recited the sutras, saying: "The sincerity of the ancients moved heaven and earth; they recognized their father’s bones by dripping their own blood.
I am now a filial son of the utmost devotion—how could there not be a spiritual response? If, among this mass of bones, there should be one that moves, it must be my father’s remains.
With single-minded concentration, he did not take his eyes off them for even a moment. After several days, a withered skull indeed leaped forth from the heap of bones.
It emerged and swayed for a long while. Sireng Pi immediately leaped up and embraced it. He returned with the bone to Huayin.

That night, his mother dreamed that her husband had returned home; the next morning, the bone arrived. Because of his filial piety, his reputation grew daily, and his practice of the Way expanded further.

During the reigns of the Later Tang emperors Zhuangzong and Mingzong, whenever an incense altar was established within the palace for state-sponsored discussions, Daoxing always occupied the seat of honor.
When he was a novice śrāmaṇera, the world was in great chaos; his mother was abducted by bandits at a distance of sixty *li* from the city.
He pursued them until he reached her, finding her already wounded but not yet dead. Upon seeing him, the bandits said, "This monk is truly most..."
Xiao Zhu followed his mother to this place, whereupon he could not bear to end his life; instead, he turned his back on her and returned to the city.
Shi Datong was a man of supreme filial piety who grieved deeply over the early loss of his parents; on their anniversary dates, he would invariably weep without ceasing.

He nurtured his mother with pure devotion, not merely by being compliant, gentle, and kind, but by ensuring that her heart partook of the flavor of the Way. When she passed away, he performed the ancestral sacrifices without fail. Furthermore—
Qiuming was a renowned scholar whose observance of the precepts was exceptionally strict; he possessed nothing beyond his single alms bowl, save for some five thousand scrolls of books and histories.

◎ Xiadinglin was filially pious, disdained wealth, and delighted in charity. When his mother died and his family was impoverished, the Prefect bestowed upon him five thousand *shí* of rice, which he refused to accept.
He then personally carried earth to plant pine and cypress trees and lived in a thatched hut at her tomb.
He wept blood for three years and subsequently cut off his hair. *Baoxun* records that Huítáng said: "The Master’s deportment was solemn and dignified;
those who saw him felt reverence and awe. When monks requested leave on various matters, he would often sternly refuse them.

Only when he heard of someone visiting their aged parents did his countenance become serene and his expression gracious. He treated them with the utmost courtesy and provided for them generously; his love for others was respectful and filial."
Thus it is. ◎ By Yuan Yungong. A Poem Recalling My Mother. The day-lily has withered in the frost, and my tears drench my robes;
My white-haired mother no longer leans against the thatched gate. Last year in the fifth month, during the plum rains, I sold my *kāṣāya* to buy rice for our return home.

Miscellaneous Records. Gongxingyi was a native of Shangyu. Throughout his life he applied himself to study with great diligence; there were no texts, whether secular or Buddhist, that he did not investigate. He was particularly skilled in poetry.
When his mother grew old and had no one to rely upon, he begged for food to support her. Once, while crossing the Qiantang River with his mother, he wrote a poem:
"The mother is in the sedan chair, the son is on the road; The son walks but cannot keep up, the mother calls out from ahead. The bridge is broken, the river flows slantwise..."
Yang Wai: "Ashamed to see the crows that return to feed their parents in the cold forest. By observing this, one knows what kind of person he was.
In the poem by Shiwu sending Attendant Qing back to his hometown: "Your teacher is old at Zhongshan Temple; morning and evening there is no one to attend him.
If you do not return to sweep the grounds and carry the water pitcher and towel, is the etiquette between teacher and disciple complete? Furthermore, your mother..."
Your years are advanced; apart from you alone, there is no second. With all hope severed by the autumn wind, I have not yet seen your return.
Leaning upon the gate day after day, I shed tears incessantly. Having left your teacher and abandoned your mother to enter the mountains, what purpose have you ultimately achieved?

The ancients said that filial piety is the foremost of all virtues. Whether among the laity or the monastic community, who does not agree? Serving one's teacher and honoring one's mother is called the "field of respect";

why must one necessarily join the assembly or practice Zen meditation? When suddenly longing for stillness, one may resent the clamor; thus, there is no hindrance to wandering back and forth with a short staff.
Verse on Visiting One’s Parents: Filial and obedient toward one’s parents, one should wish that all sentient beings serve the Buddha well and protect and nourish all beings.

[Commentary] *Jian*: According to the *Xiaojing Zhu* (Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety), this refers to the words of the Master addressed to Zengzi: "The former kings possessed the ultimate virtue and the essential Way;

by means of these, the people lived in harmony and there was no resentment between superiors and subordinates. Do you know what they were? The commentary notes that "ultimate virtue" (*zhìdé*) represents filial piety.
Filial piety is the essential Way; it is ritual and music. From the Son of Heaven above to the common people below, all should practice filiality without beginning or end.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "In a world where there is no Buddha, one serves one's parents. To serve one's parents is itself to serve the Buddha.
Because my parents gave birth to me for the sake of the Primordial Enlightenment, I now turn them toward serving [the Dharma], so that they may grow in the Dharmakāya."
Therefore, regarding "protecting and nurturing all": all sentient beings are my children; thus, I protect them. All men and women are my parents; thus, I nurture them.
In every birth, there is none from whom I have not received life; therefore, I revere them with equanimity.
"Because he is the Buddha of the Dharma-body"—this verse is the World-Honored One’s method for filial piety toward one's parents.
This vow is that one should aspire to learn the path of filiality practiced by the World-Honored One. Now, as for the principles of this path of filiality, how should they be described?
The final two lines precisely reveal the essential meaning of filial obedience. One should know that the World-Honored One’s service to his parents was identical to [the way of filiality].

This is serving the Buddha. What is meant by "serving the Buddha in the same way"? It means that whenever a Buddha appears in the world, there is none who does not transmit the Dharma of the supreme path through filial piety and obedience.
Therefore, it is said that being filial and obedient to one's parents is identical to serving the Buddha. To protect and nourish all beings is likewise so.
It is said that parents possess the kindness and love of nurturing, raising, protecting, and mindful of their children; their benevolence is as vast as heaven and has no limit.
As a child, one should likewise reflect upon the grace of being nurtured and protected, repaying it through the way of filial piety and obedience, without ever contravening anything.
If one visits a layperson’s home to see their relatives, one should first enter the central hall to pay homage to the Buddha, or respectfully inquire after the sacred images in the family shrine.
Next, one should inquire after each member of the parents’ kinship circle one by one.

One must not speak to the parents of the strictness of the Teacher’s Dharma, the hardships of leaving the household life, its desolation and lack of flavor, or its toil and submissiveness; rather, one should preach the Buddha-Dharma for them, causing them to give rise to faith.
"Increasing Merit.

[Commentary: Regarding the purpose of visiting one's parents, one should exhort and encourage them with words concerning the advancement of the Way, so that they may find delight in the Way and forget their anxieties.
If one speaks instead of matters such as solitude and desolation, it merely increases the parents' worries; this is not the way to gladden one's kin.
The *Yili* states: "For one who serves as a son, being able to lead his parents toward the Way is the height of filial piety.
One must not sit or stand for long periods with their younger relatives or children, nor engage in miscellaneous talk, jesting, or laughter.
Furthermore, one must not inquire into the right and wrong, or the likes and dislikes, among their kin."
[Commentary]: One who comes specifically to visit their parents should regard all those of the same clan and close kinship as donors (*dānapati*), regardless of whether they are old or young.
One must maintain self-reverence and propriety; for if one sits too long and so forth, feelings of favoritism or aversion will arise. It is for this reason that the rule was established.
If you must stay overnight because it has grown late, you should occupy yourself alone on a single mat, sitting much and sleeping little, recollecting the Buddha with a single mind.
Once your business is finished, you must return immediately; you must not linger.
[Commentary: A śrāmaṇera’s precepts are not yet profound and his power on the Path is not yet firm; he should not stay overnight in a layperson’s house.

However, if he has come specifically to visit his parents and cannot part with them after a single word, he should stay at a nearby temple for a short while to offer consolation. If there is no temple, [he may stay elsewhere].
Prepare a mat for me to stay alone. Guard your sense faculties well. Once you have finished the task of consoling me, do not act like a child or a woman at another time.
(The Five Lamps: Zhaozhou. Having personally received the seal of approval from Nanquan, he returned to Caozhou to visit his preceptor.

His relatives all wished to come and meet him, but the Master said, "The net of worldly passions has no end; I have already taken leave of them to leave the household life, and I do not wish to see them again."
Having seen this, he took up his flask and staff and traveled everywhere throughout the various regions to beg for food. [Commentary]:

According to the *Yijiao sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), when the Buddha was in the world, the robes worn by the assembly of monks consisted solely of pure, dyed-in-death (mṛta-kāṣāya) cloth.
People wore miscellaneous garments of tattered silk. Later, the bhikṣu Rājyavardhana arose; every time he went out for alms, he returned empty-handed and hungry.
The Buddha, knowing his past conduct, commanded the assembly of monks to divide the Vinaya into five sections and to adopt five different types of robe colors.
He commanded that they should each follow one of the schools in their practice and accordingly established the rules of conduct. Each was to exhibit its own strengths:
the Tāmraparṇīya school was to excel in understanding the flavor of principles and opening the Way for the benefit of others; to manifest this superiority, they were to wear red *kāṣāyas*.
The Sarvāstivāda school was to be broad, comprehensive, quick-witted, and skillful in guiding others through the transformation of the Dharma; they were to wear black robes.
The Kāṣāya: The Dharmaguptaka school is diligent, courageous, and swift; they protect and sustain sentient beings and should wear the madder-colored kāṣāya.
The Mahīśāsaka school is subtle in its meditative contemplation and thoroughly elucidates the profound and mysterious; they should wear the blue kāṣāya.
The Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studies the various sūtras and expounds upon their principles and meanings; they should wear the yellow kāṣāya. From that time forth...
Afterwards, he obtained food in great abundance. Why was this? It was because of the lack of merit in Rāhuṇa’s previous lives.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "How did Rāhuṇa, having lacked merit in his previous lives, come to become a śramaṇa?"
The Buddha said, "This Rājyugha was the son of a virtuous man in a previous life. He was prone to jealousy;
whenever he saw a śramaṇa coming for alms, he would immediately shut his door and say, 'The master is not at home.
Later, when the śramaṇa passed by other houses, they all closed their doors and likewise said, 'The master is not at home. Because of this, he is now unable to receive alms."
He attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Upon seeing others giving alms—whether food, drink, or participating in assemblies—he felt joy and thought to himself:
"I too wish to become a śramaṇa; that is why I am currently so impoverished. Thus it is said in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra: "Subhūti, take up your bowl."
He entered the house of Vimalakīrti to beg for alms. Vimalakīrti took his bowl and filled it with food, saying:
"If you can regard food as equal, then all dharmas are also equal; if all dharmas are equal, then food is also equal. It is by practicing in this way that one should beg for alms."
"You may take food [only] when those six heterodox teachers of yours—your masters—have fallen, and you too have followed them in their fall;
only then may you take food. [Otherwise,] you enter into various wrong views, fail to reach the other shore, and remain within the eight difficult conditions."
It is not permissible for you to be without affliction, for that would be identical to the afflictions themselves and a departure from the pure Dharma.

Since all sentient beings can also attain this Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) that you have attained, those who give to you cannot be called a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), nor can those who make offerings to you.
You will fall into the three evil realms. You will be of one hand with the various Māras and act as their companion in toil.
You are no different from the various Māras and all afflictions (*kleśa*). Toward all sentient beings you harbor a heart of enmity; you slander the Buddhas and destroy the Dharma.
You do not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall never attain *nirvāṇa*. If you are thus, only then may you...

Regarding the practice of alms-gathering and the five rules for sequential begging within the city: First, because one has internally realized the principle of equality, one perceives no external distinction between the poor and the wealthy.
Second, the mind is free from greed and pride, and compassion is impartial and without partiality. Third, this manifests one’s majestic virtue;
thus, one does not fear entering the homes of those who keep fierce elephants, liquor vendors, or prostitutes—though the Buddha’s Vinaya for the Śrāvakas prohibits such entry.
Regarding such families as these, the Buddha does not fear that they might cause harm or give rise to defiled thoughts, because his majestic power (*prabhāva*) is supreme.

Fourth, he pacifies the suspicions of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), meaning he fears they might hate him for this while loving them for that. Fifth, he shatters the conceptual discriminations (*vikalpa*) of the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This refers to how Kāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor, while Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kūṭadanta) abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy; this was not because of a great compassion that is impartial.
According to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, regarding the method of begging for alms: one day is limited to seven households so as not to give rise to excessive greed.
The food thus begged is divided into four portions. One portion is offered to fellow practitioners of the holy life. This means that when begging for alms, there must necessarily be...
Those who guard the dwelling, traveling monks, and those who are elderly, ill, or otherwise unable to travel should be given a portion of the food upon returning;
this shall allow them to be fully satisfied and to dwell in peace while practicing the Way. One portion should be given to the destitute beggars;

that is to say, when encountering a poor and suffering beggar during the time of alms-round, one should give rise to a heart of compassion, regard them as if they were one's own hunger, and likewise bestow a portion upon them.
Ensure that they are fully satisfied and encourage them to cultivate virtue. Set aside one portion to give to the various spirits and deities;
when you have obtained food, place it in a clean vessel and, at the time of the meal, burn incense and recite mantras to empower it for universal distribution.
May all ghosts and spirits be fully satisfied, escape the realms of suffering, and attain complete liberation. As for one portion for oneself:
when receiving alms-food, set aside the aforementioned three portions and keep one portion—whether it be more or less—for one's own consumption.
Having eaten, settle the mind and practice the Way, so that the offerings of the faithful are not received in vain. ◎ Accomplishment.

Ten factors constitute the practice of alms-gathering: first, for the sake of gathering in sentient beings; second, for the sake of following the proper sequence; third, for the sake of avoiding weariness;
fourth, for the sake of contentment; fifth, for the sake of distribution; sixth, for the sake of non-attachment to flavors; seventh, for the sake of knowing the proper measure.
Eighth, for the manifestation of wholesome qualities; ninth, for the perfection of the roots of goodness; tenth, for the relinquishing of self-clinging.
Master Sengzhao’s four purposes for begging for alms are: first, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; second, for the subduing of arrogance;

third, for the realization that the body is subject to suffering; fourth, for the removal of attachment and fixation. Regarding etiquette: the alms bowl should always be held at the left side when exiting.

At that time, he was facing outward. When returning with food, he would face inward. At Zhulin Monastery (in present-day Fushangyi, Sui), while staying overnight at Jingde Temple in Yizhou, he tied his large sunshade by the roadside and sat beneath it reading the sutras.
He did not call out to people passing by to solicit alms, nor did he offer prayers of blessing to those who gave. Because the road was quiet, he carried many loads without any [disturbance].
Huobu was told by someone: "To the northwest of this city, the population is dense and alms are plentiful; why remain here? He replied, "One or two coins are sufficient to sustain my life;
what further use would I have for more? Zhao Zhongshu, the Regional Inspector of Lingzhou, was a cruel official who possessed no faith or reverence.
Having heard of Huobu, he went there to test him. Riding his horse past him, he pretended to drop a string of cash. Huobu picked it up and read [the inscription on the coins].

After the scripture had been taken away some distance, Zhongshu ordered someone to retrieve the money, but Fu also did not look back. Zhongshu then asked him, "You earn only one coin a day; when you saw that string of coins being carried away by someone, why did you not stop them? He replied: "I thought it was the Master’s money. Zhongshu said, "It was yours. Fu said, "I am a poor man. If I were to take it, I would surely be suspected of theft. Furthermore, the Master has always taught me to be content with my lot and not to covet what belongs to others. Therefore, I did not dare to take it. Zhongshu sighed and said, "Excellent! You truly possess the Way. He then gave him a thousand coins and sent him on his way. Fu took the money and returned home. His wife asked, "Where did you get this? Fu said, "The Master gave it to me. His wife said, "If you have received it from the Master, you should give it to him. Fu then went back to the Master's gate and returned the money. Zhongshu asked, "Why have you come back? Fu said, "My wife told me that since I received this from the Master, I should return it to you. Zhongshu said, "You are truly a person of integrity. He then gave him another thousand coins and sent him away. Fu again returned the money. Zhongshu asked, "Why have you come back again? He then gave him five thousand coins and sent him away. Fu again returned the money. Zhongshu asked, "Why have you come back again? He then gave him six thousand coins and sent him away. Fu again returned the money. Zhongshu asked, "Why have you come back again? Verse on Begging for Food: Entering a village to beg for food, one should wish that all sentient beings enter the profound Dharma-realm, their minds free from obstruction.

[Commentary]: Regarding "entering the village": it refers to wandering for alms (*piṇḍapāta*) to transform and guide others, without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, the noble and the humble, begging according to one's circumstances.

"One should make this vow" means that the primary purpose of begging for food is to deliver sentient beings; as long as sentient beings are inexhaustible, my vow shall likewise be inexhaustible—hence it is called "profound entry.

It is said that for a practitioner of the Way, begging for food constitutes right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*); apart from this, all is wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*). Since that which is consumed...
How could there be no hindrance? If one wishes to attain non-hindrance, one should know that begging for alms in accordance with the Dharma brings benefit to both oneself and others.
If one attains only self-benefit and does not benefit others, it is called an obstruction. If one benefits only others and does not benefit oneself, [it is likewise an obstruction].
This is also called an "obstruction. To benefit both oneself and others is what is meant by a mind free from obstruction.
Why then is it considered an obstruction to encounter the woman Mātaṅgī while begging for alms? Why is it considered an obstruction to beg only at the homes of the poor and lowly?
And why is it also considered an obstruction to beg only at the homes of the wealthy and noble? There is no distinction whatsoever between the poor and lowly and the wealthy and noble.
Discriminate. This is called having no obstruction in the mind.
One should associate with those who are mature in age; if there is no one to associate with, one should know the places where one ought to practice.
[Commentary] "Venerable Elders" refers to the five types of *ācāryas*. These are those of advanced age who possess the virtue of the precepts.

This means that because the power of the precepts in a beginner is not yet deep, they must rely on teachers and friends as their weapons and support. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that when a *bhikṣu* goes begging for food, he should avoid five places and must not go to them:
first, a household where proclamations are made; this refers to families where songs and melodies are performed solely for the sake of entertainment. They can...
1. One must not go to places where meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is disturbed. 2. One must not go to the houses of courtesans;
their conduct is impure and their reputation is improper, and the conditions of sensual desire are the very root that obstructs the Path. 3. One must not go to taverns;

alcohol is a cause and condition for the arising of transgressions and can produce grave faults. 4. One must not go to royal palaces or the residences of high nobility, which are strictly forbidden places.
5. Caṇḍālas—translated into Chinese as "butchers"—are those whose murderous intent is exceedingly great;
to see them causes injury to one's compassion and destroys the root of goodness. Therefore, one must not go there.
When entering the gates of others' homes, one should carefully examine one's conduct and must not lose one’s dignified demeanor.
[Commentary: In ancient times, begging for alms was done during the first watch of the day; this is therefore the superior time. At such a time, seeking alms is not difficult.
If one begs for alms too early or too late, it is begging at an improper time. If one wishes to give but there is nothing to give, one feels ashamed;
this causes distress to others. If one begs but receives nothing, one suffers from hunger; this causes distress to oneself. Such matters of conduct are inexhaustible if explained in detail.
Therefore, I have spoken briefly. The eight rules below are intended to serve as a warning; the three thousand modes of deportment are likewise contained therein.
Let students not boast of the distant while neglecting the near, nor long for the vast while becoming negligent in the details.
"One should not enter the gate of a household where there are no men.
[Commentary: *Yilin* states: "Zouzi said: 'I do not stay overnight at a sparsely populated door, nor do I sit down when approaching a steamer. This is to avoid suspicion.
Therefore, a gentleman does not enter the inner door of a house where no men are present. Those who transcend the world and are men of high character should especially cherish this principle."
In the Vinaya of the Pi-nai-ye (Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya), in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the son of a brāhmaṇa who, following the instructions of his parents, provided offerings to Kālodāyin.
Later, at another time, he went abroad and entrusted his wife with the task of making offerings. At that time, there were five hundred local bandits.
Among them was one thief with a handsome countenance. When the woman saw him from afar, she had illicit relations with him.
Kāḷodāyin went to her house frequently; fearing that this affair would be revealed, the woman killed him along with the thief.
If one wishes to sit, one should first inspect the seating area. If there are weapons or blades, it is not appropriate to sit. If there are precious objects, it is not appropriate to sit.
If there are women’s garments, bedding, ornaments, and the like, it is not appropriate to sit.
[Commentary: The preceding statement said that if there is no man, one must not enter the gate. This statement says that even if there is a man, one must still examine his seating position;

this refers to "observing conduct to examine auspiciousness. Weapons are instruments of misfortune. According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, one should not keep tools for killing because of a mind of compassion.
Now, if one sees an instrument of killing and cannot bear to sit there, this is the practice of a compassionate mind. Regarding the two types mentioned below, the first is:
First, it is because one fears giving rise to thoughts of greedy attachment. Second, it is to avoid suspicion and scandal.
When wishing to preach the sutra, one must know the appropriate time for preaching and the inappropriate time for preaching.
[Commentary] This is identical in meaning to the second point regarding visiting people's homes. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma in five periods emphasizes the importance of timing.
Regarding the character "time" (時): Confucius said, "Study it and practice it at the proper time. He likewise placed great emphasis on the word "time.

If one speaks of these teachings at an improper time, then even the Classics of the Sages and the Transmissions of the Worthies—though as precious as gold dust—will become like a film over the eye. Therefore, this regulation was established.

If one were to plead piteously, how would it differ from a beggar? The reason why the transformative guidance fails to take effect is because there are such individuals.
[The Buddha] said: "One must not speak extensively of cause and effect in hopes of receiving abundant alms.

When eating, one’s demeanor must be solemn and respectful. One should limit oneself to seven households per day, proceeding from house to house along a fixed path at a distance of three feet from the eaves.

Emptying the mind of all worldly attachments, one should accept whatever is offered according to one's lot, regardless of whether it is much or little. One should remain upright, silent, and composed;

even to speak is considered a perversion, let alone engaging in extensive discourse, which gives rise to greed and affliction. To act like those who frequent rivers and lakes—reciting scriptures for the sake of gain—is to bring disgrace upon our Dharma gate and to incur sin.
Small. The mendicant must strive diligently; do not regard [the offerings] as insignificant.
If you receive much, do not give rise to greed or attachment; if you receive little, do not give rise to distress or vexation.
[Commentary: A single bowl of gruel, a single meal, a copper coin, or a grain of rice—though these are fields of merit in the present life, they are truly planted through conditions from the past.
Therefore, do not covet what you receive in abundance, and do not be distressed by what you receive in small measure. To beg for food according to circumstances is right livelihood;
to deviate from these two paths is wrong livelihood.
One must not exclusively frequent the homes of donors with whom one has a personal intimacy, nor solicit food at monasteries where one has established close ties.
[Commentary: To encounter fragrant rice upon being hungry is indeed a blessing; one should know how to value this and exercise self-restraint within.
Even if others invite you while neglecting the proper etiquette, a man of integrity will never eat food offered with the cry of "Come here! (jialai).
Entering the Village, Chapter Twenty-Two [Commentary]:
After a thousand years, during the three hundred-year period, there will be vast chaos.
Runaway slaves and fugitive servants will cause families to perish and nations to fall; many will not survive. Those who enter my Dharma at such a time are like a band of thieves.
The wicked shall plunder the virtuous. At that time, the twelve divisions of the scriptures shall sink into the earth and no longer be recited.

Even if there are those who practice the dhūta austerities, they will for the most part not be in accordance with the Dharma; they will constantly roam through villages and hamlets rather than dwelling in mountain forests.
Regarding the twelve dhūta practices, bhikṣus shall renounce their bodies, lives, and wealth for the sake of the unsurpassed path, cultivating the three kinds of steadfastness.
One should not harbor attachment to the Dharma. When the time comes to enter [the path] due to the suffering of illness, one should reflect:

"I have now left the household life for the sake of the Dharma. If one practices the Dharma with diligence, that itself constitutes protection. Practitioners originally leave the home because it is full of afflictions.

Having left the household life to practice the Way, if the teacher and disciples, as well as fellow students, again give rise to fetters and attachments, and further cause much disturbance, one should therefore distance oneself from the clamor and bustle.
Even if one is within three *li*, once physical seclusion has been attained, one must also bring about mental seclusion from the five desires and the five hindrances.

As for those who practice protection, if their companions and affairs are both not in accordance with the Dharma, one should not go to them. [If] the companions and affairs are both... [not in accordance with the Dharma, one should not go].
"One should go only when it is appropriate according to the Dharma. In the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home to offer a meal.
While all the bhikṣus departed, the Buddha alone remained at the monastery, sending someone to fetch food instead of going to the invitation himself.
For this reason, he spoke of these five kinds of causes and conditions: first, to remain for the sake of sitting in meditation; second, to invite the devas.
1. To preach the Dharma; 2. To observe the sick; 3. To inspect the bedding and furniture; 4. To establish rules of training (*śikṣāpada*); 5.

At such a time, lacking even a moment of self-mastery, one becomes gradually defiled. The conditions for the hindrance of afflictions are as sharp as a blade.

[Commentary]: "Galloping" refers to letting a horse run at full speed. "Swinging the arms" refers to the manner of unrestrained, flailing movements. *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma), Section Five.

The mind is covered and obscured; the gates of dhyāna are already closed. The six sense objects dwell in one's thoughts, and distracted imaginings constantly race about—like a mad elephant without a hook, or like a playful monkey in a tree. One has not yet seen swift movement or a graceful stride.

Therefore, when lifting the feet, one should be neither slow nor hurried, neither light nor heavy, but proceed with calm composure and slow steps, like clouds entering a deep forest in pursuit of hidden birds.
Do not be startled. When traveling by boat with the current, all the fish will swim along without obstruction. Those of noble resolve should reflect deeply on this;
do not frequently look around at the people and things passing by.

[Commentary: Where a man of the Way travels, he goes straight ahead and comes straight back, without the slightest lingering. He proceeds solely upon the right path with an upright and disciplined mind, keeping his thoughts restrained.
If he were to glance to the left or look backward, it would cause bystanders to be startled; therefore, this was regulated. In the *Lamp Records*, Huanglong Nan said:
"When sitting, one must always sit in the full lotus posture; when walking, one must always gaze straight ahead. To this day, this makes me reminisce; his majestic demeanor remains vividly present.
One must not walk about chatting or laughing with śrāmaṇeras or young children.

[Commentary: Śrāmaṇeras and young children are not to be treated with levity or familiarity. If one were to laugh again and again while walking along a path, it would constitute a great loss of dignified decorum;
therefore, this rule was established.

When walking forward or backward,
one must not follow behind or precede a drunken person or a madman. One must not intentionally gaze at women,
nor look at them with a sidelong glance.

[Commentary]: The entirety of the worlds of the ten directions is but a single eye of pure radiance. It is only because it is obstructed by a single speck of the dust of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) that one falsely distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly.
One fails to realize that the five-colored floating clouds arise within the great void, yet the great void has never distinguished such perceptions as blue, yellow, and so forth.
A person’s possession of a body is likewise like a single [cloud] within the great void of space.
A point. Recognize this one point so that it is not obscured by the point itself. If you cannot see through this point, please consult the *Chanbing jing* (Sutra on the Treatment of Chan Illness).

however, when [the Master] perceived the sound of their voices, he immediately concluded his lecture.
If you encounter venerable elders or close acquaintances, stand to one side and greet them first with a polite inquiry.
If you encounter performers of illusions, strange sights, or the like, it is not appropriate to look at them; simply maintain an upright posture and walk along the correct path.
[Commentary: In the preceding chapter, I previously went to observe and listen in detail regarding the regulations. On this occasion, I happened upon a performance of illusionary arts;

unable to avoid it in time, one must understand that such illusions are not real. They are like drifting clouds and flowing water—passing by without lingering. If one halts for even a moment, one commits an offense; if one halts again, one commits another offense.

Whenever one encounters a water pit or a gap in the water, one must not leap over it; if there is a path, one should walk around it. Only if there is no path and the entire assembly leaps over may it be done.
[Commentary: The account of Vasubandhu leaping across water is found in the seventh fascicle of the aforementioned treatise.
Except in cases of illness or urgent business, one must not ride a horse, nor even gallop it with a whip out of a playful mind.
[Commentary: Riding horses and galloping them are the pursuits of wealthy young masters and brave military officers.
Since such things do not exist within the Dharma-gate, this rule was established.
Whenever one encounters government officials, regardless of their rank or size, it is appropriate to yield the way. [Commentary:
When high-ranking officials pass by, they certainly must not be approached with undue familiarity; yet even those of lower rank must not be treated with irreverent intimacy.
Irreverent intimacy leads to misfortune; it is better to avoid them as a source of blessing. Should one be unable to avoid them in time, and they...

Appendix: When encountering those engaged in quarrels or disputes, one should also avoid them from afar and not go to watch.
[Commentary]: Those engaged in quarrels and disputes do nothing but brandish their fists and bared arms; they often bring harm upon bystanders. Therefore, one must not go.

At that moment, when he suddenly awakens to Linji’s phrase on guest and host, he cannot help but rejoice in his entire life. Nevertheless, one need not apply a bowl to a healthy piece of flesh to form a sore.

Wudeng. Baoshou was the second generation [of the lineage]. Previously, when he served as the master of offerings at Baoshou, Baoshou asked him, "Before your parents were born, show me your original face.
The Master stood there until late at night, but his response did not accord with the truth. The following day, he took his leave. Baoshou said, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "Yesterday I received the Master’s question, but I could not accord with it; I am going [to seek another teacher]."
"Go south to seek out spiritual friends," he said. Baoshou replied, "In the south, they observe the summer retreat but not the winter;
here, we observe the winter but not the summer. You should spend the summer wandering the streets as a lay-preacher (fangjie).

If this is the Buddha-dharma, then even amidst the vast red dust of the marketplace, one constantly preaches the True Dharma. The Master did not dare disobey. One day, on the street, he saw two people quarreling and brandishing—
One punch was given, saying, "You have attained such a faceless state. At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment. He went to see Baoshou;
before he had even spoken, Baoshou said, "You understand; there is no need to say anything. The Master then bowed.

Seeing him strike the punch, Baoshou suddenly attained enlightenment. What did he realize? Try to bring it forth and show me! Thereupon, [the Master] struck a punch once and said, "Do not mistake this!"
Meeting. You must not return to the temple to boast about the magnificent sights you have seen within the city. [Commentary:
There are those who do not value themselves by means of the Way, spending their days idly and aimlessly among the villages; one day they were at a City God Temple.
Previously, you heard and spoke of cause and effect; one day, while at a crossroads watching puppeteers perform, you claimed to be "well-versed in antiquity and conversant with the present.
Yet, when old age and illness press upon you all at once, what will you have to withstand birth and death?
**Section Twenty-Three: Commodities for Trade** [Commentary:

According to the *Lokotpatti-sūtra* (Scripture on the Origin of the World), regarding the commodities used for trade by the people of Jambudvīpa, they may consist of money and precious gems, or grain and silk, or various other treasures.
As for the barter and exchange of the people of Godānīya, it consists of cattle and sheep, or [other such items].
As for the jewel-niṣkas, the inhabitants of Pūrvavideha and Aparagodānīya engage in all manner of trade, whether with wealth and silks, or with the five grains, or with maṇi-jewels.
However, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru have no further need for trade; whatever they desire appears spontaneously.

◎ Among the various heavens of the Desire Realm, such as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is likewise trade for the purpose of pleasure and delighting the mind.

In fact, they differ from ordinary people as previously described. According to the *Xiangfa jueyi jing*, in future ages, all laypeople will treat the Triple Gem with contempt precisely because the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
Clad in the dharma robes, they manage worldly affairs; or they frequent marketplaces, selling goods for their livelihood;
or they travel the roads, engaging in trade to seek profit; or they act as painters, producing images for a living through the craft of craftsmanship;
or they practice physiognomy, divining the various fortunes and misfortunes of men and women, houses, fields, and gardens; or they drink wine until intoxicated, singing, dancing, and making merry.
They engage in board games and dice, or out of greed for wealth and profit, waste months and years, neglecting and forgetting their scriptural studies.
Some practice incantations to treat illnesses, falsely invoking the scriptures; they cultivate meditation to divinate matters, sustaining themselves through such heterodox means.

Others practice medicine, acupuncture, moxibustion, and the compounding of decoctions; they diagnose pulses and prescribe remedies while mixing with men and women, leading to private corruption and the ruin of virtue.
This increases evil and invites the ridicule and slander of the common people; it is for this reason. [The Book of] Yi states:
"Shennong established markets at midday, causing the people of the world to gather the goods of the world to exchange and depart, each obtaining what they required.
The Rites state: "The Superintendent of Markets under the Ministry of Land shall arrange the order, demarcate the sites, and manage the market by laying out the stalls."

To level the market by regulating goods; to prohibit extravagance in goods through administrative decrees and thereby equalize the market; to cause the market to circulate by enriching capital through merchants and peddlers.

As Laozi said: "Beautiful words can be used to trade in the marketplace. In the Five Lamps, it is recorded that when Baizhang Baoji of Youzhou was walking through the marketplace, he saw a man buying pork.

"If you have no heart, then I shall simply let go. Upon hearing this, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
People called him Master Louzhi. Chan Master Baiyunzi Xiang ascended the hall and said: "Do you all understand?
You should seek it at the head of the street and the tail of the market; among butchers and executioners; in the places of the hells, the cauldrons, and the boiling water.
