Furthermore, there is another kind who simply strives to be a "good person" upon their long meditation benches.
You tell me, between these two types of people, which one possesses the superior quality? Be careful, as there is nothing more to it. Adieu!

Do not dispute over the value of things, whether they be expensive or cheap. [Commentary] Proverb: A fine man does not line up in the marketplace. ◎ When a thing is rare, it is precious; therefore, the value of goods is naturally determined by the market price.
If one attempts to suppress or inflate the price, there will inevitably be a dispute. Often, one loses the greater for the sake of the lesser; hence this explanation.
A son should not set up his own stall in the market; he should merely conduct business there according to prevailing market prices.
He must not sit idly at a woman’s stall.
[Commentary: When there are no men in the household, it is improper to sit for long at a place where women trade. If one sits for a long time, even if...

Though as pure as jade and without flaw, one cannot prevent the clamorous mouths of the marketplace from chattering. Therefore it is said: "Guarding the mouths of others is more difficult than damming a river.
If you are offended by someone, you should skillfully avoid them; do not pursue them to seek rectification.
[Commentary] Huisan’s annotation states: When one is provoked or offended by others, one should practice patience (*kṣānti*) rather than engaging in dispute to assert one's own correctness.
Regarding being wronged by another—meaning that the other person incurs offense against me through improper conduct—I should embrace them with a broad measure and listen to them with patience.
If they continue to offend me without ceasing, I should skillfully avoid them; this means simply to accept [the situation].

Once one has already consented to a certain item, even if it becomes more expensive later on, one must not abandon that [original price] and take the new one; otherwise, this will cause the owner resentment.

[Commentary] Huishan’s annotation states: The characters of the ten heavenly stems, such as Jia and Yi, are arranged in a sequence. To refer to "the item of Jia" means it is the property of the first household.
Once its price has been agreed upon, even if it should prove to be of inferior quality, it is improper to rescind the agreement.
Be careful not to act as a guarantor, thereby incurring fault and liability.
[Commentary] Huisan’s annotation states: If you see someone borrowing an object from another, you must not act as a guarantor by speaking on their behalf to assume responsibility.
This refers to taking responsibility for oneself when returning from a mission. "Fault" (*qiān*) means to contravene one's expectations; "breach" (*fù*) means to fail and sink into neglect.

Whenever one assumes the burden of guaranteeing another’s conduct, faults and breaches will inevitably abound; therefore, one must exercise caution from the very beginning. As in a poem by Hanshan: "There is a certain kind of person in this world..."
By nature, he was always busy with many affairs. All day long he frequented the streets and alleys; he never left the wine shops.
He acted as guarantor for others and explained matters on their behalf. One morning, when things went awry, the entire blame fell upon him. (From) *Wudeng Huiyuan*: Jingzhao Mi.
A monk asked the Master, “Since ancient times, have the sages of antiquity attained the true principle or not? The Master said, “They have.
The monk asked, “As for this true principle, how is it attained? The Master said, “It is like when Huo Guang sold a counterfeit silver city to the Xiongnu;
who was the one who drew up the contract? The monk said, “I am truly at a loss for words. The Master said, “Level.”
The precept instructs people to act as guarantors;
in all actions one undertakes, one must not act on one's own authority. [Commentary:
"Not acting on one's own authority" means that since this body has already been dedicated to the teacher, it no longer belongs to oneself. In all matters...

In all matters, one must follow the teacher’s instructions and dare not act independently. Therefore, in ordinary conduct and movements, one should always inform the teacher to fulfill the practice of filial piety, as briefly illustrated by the twelve rules for daily life. Nevertheless, among these there are matters that may be reported and those that may not;
these must be weighed according to the specific circumstances. For further details, consult the *Nanshan Chao*, which extensively expands upon the increase of the Buddha-dharma.

Great success arises from the mutual support of teacher and disciple, who encounter one another with earnestness and provide both material and Dharma sustenance. As days pass and months deepen, their practice endures and their virtue becomes firm;

all of this depends upon these factors. Lately, however, as the True Teaching has declined and the wind of wisdom has been shrouded, the common people harbor contempt and the Way has strayed from the Dharma.
This is entirely because the teacher lacks the heart to lead and inspire, while the disciple lacks the will to practice and uphold it.
Second, they abandon those [virtuous] characteristics and flow into false and vulgar objects; how then can they hope for the Way to shine? Regarding family regulations:
in all matters, whether great or small, juniors must not act on their own authority, but must invariably consult the head of the household.
When entering or leaving, coming or going, one must first inform the teacher.
[Commentary: There are two meanings to informing the teacher upon entering or leaving. First, to comfort the teacher’s mind by letting him know where one is entering or leaving.
Second, to seek the teacher’s decision regarding whether an action may or may not be performed, so as to avoid error. If one acts according to one's own whims, there may be a mistake at any moment.
Only after that should one inform the teacher; then it will be too late for regret. For this reason, one should first inform the teacher when making new Dharma robes;
one should first inform the teacher when wearing new Dharma robes. One should first inform the teacher.

[Commentary] Explanation of the Name: "Clothing" (*yi*) means "reliance. It is that by which one is sheltered from cold and heat. The *Mozi* states: "In antiquity, when clothing did not yet exist, the sages created it.
In winter, silk and fine cloth were light and warm; in summer, *chī* and *qì* (fine linen) were cool and refreshing.
Thus they were suited to the body and harmonized the skin. If one speaks of "Dharma-clothing," it relates to the Dharma-gate and is not made in vain. [The Buddha...]

During his lifetime, only the three robes were transmitted; as for their dimensions—whether broad or narrow, long or short—as well as their colors, whether deep or light, all had a prescribed sequence of distinctions. Therefore, one must inform the teacher.
When shaving one's head, one should first inform the teacher.

[Commentary: This refers to the initial tonsure, which is recorded in detail in the preceding chapter. It states that for ordinary haircuts as well, one should inform the teacher so as to accommodate the teacher’s convenience.
Gāthā for Shaving the Hair: Shaving off the beard and hair, one should wish that all sentient beings distance themselves from afflictions and attain ultimate quiescence.
Oṃ siddhantu mantrāḥ bhadre svāhā. [Commentary] Chengfan:
When shaving the head for a teacher, one should first prepare water, a towel, and a hair-disk. One should then whet and sharpen the razor according to the proper ritual, and spread [a cloth]...
Sit down. First, receive the hair-catcher (*uṣṇīṣa*). Next, perform one prostration to the teacher. Take the razor and wipe it upon your wrist.
You must keep your mouth closed and remain composed. First, shave the crown of the head; do not let any hair fall to the ground.

You must collect the hair according to the proper method; do not snap the hair with your fingernails. When the shaving is finished, take the teacher’s hair-dish from him, offer him fresh water, and then prepare the paste.
The razor. Dry it thoroughly and store it according to the Dharma. When the teacher has taken his seat, you should put on your robes and pay him homage.

The Buddha ordained the shaving of the beard and hair in order to distinguish the appearance of monastics from that of the laity. Since monastics and laypeople are thus distinguished, their conduct must differ from worldly customs;
therefore, one should aspire to share the same vows and the same practice as all those who have shaved their beards and hair.
It is to remain far removed from afflictions and reach ultimate quiescence (*śānti*). This does not merely refer to shaving off the afflictions of a single tuft of beard or hair;

rather, one should vow to bring down the mountain-like and peak-like afflictions of the six sense faculties and six sense objects that have existed since beginningless time, severing them completely through the power of wisdom.
Therefore, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*). [This is] verified in the *Jingxing pin* (Chapter on Pure Conduct) of the *Fajie* (Entering the Dharma Realm).

All these chapters are texts of the *Avataṃsaka*. Regarding the practice of purification through shaving the beard and hair: it is for the purpose of severing afflictions (*kleśa*). This is because the beard and hair are said to be the very root of afflictions.
However, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Ghanavyūha-parivarta*), elders and lay devotees do not remove their beards and hair, nor do they regard the beard and hair as a burden.
Whether afflictions arise or cease does not depend on whether the beard and hair are removed or not. This is the instruction for the practice of purification.

In this chapter, the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s virtues are explained; the contexts in which they are taught differ. In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, the practices of a bodhisattva are explained extensively;

it is not merely the single matter of shaving the head, but rather the dedication [of merit] to all sentient beings within the dharma realm throughout the four modes of deportment, in both movement and stillness.
There is no activity in which one does not wish for sentient beings to attain perfect enlightenment. Therefore, with every movement and pause, one should say:

"May all sentient beings enter [the state of] equality. In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, the elder and the householder are both described as having attained perfect enlightenment, clarifying that defilement and purity share a single source.

The holy and the ordinary are not different. Therefore, lust, anger, and ignorance are in their entirety precept, concentration, and wisdom; how much more so, then, are the beard and hair? Thus, it is said that they merely differ in their location.
One need only look at the passage in the sutras, "One should wish that all sentient beings... to understand its meaning; it does not mean "one should wish for bodhisattvas.
In the *Five Lamps*, it is recorded that Chan Master Tianran of Danxia entered Chang’an to take the imperial examination and stayed overnight at an inn.
He dreamed that white light filled his room. A diviner said, "This is an auspicious omen for the realization of emptiness. Just then, a Chan practitioner asked, "Where are you going, virtuous one?
He replied, "I am going to take the civil service examination. The Chan practitioner said, "What is taking the examination compared to choosing a Buddha?

Now Master Mazu has appeared in Jiangxi; that is the field for choosing a Buddha. You should go there. He then traveled to Jiangxi to see the Patriarch. The Master [Mazu] reached out his hand and patted his head-wrap (*fuhou*).
The Master [Nanyue] looked at him for a long while and said, "Shitou of Nanyue is your teacher. He immediately traveled to Shitou and returned, presenting his previous intention to him.
Shitou said, "Go to the fodder shed. The Master bowed in thanks and entered the quarters of the laborers, where he served as a cook in turn for three years.
One day, Shitou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, we shall clear away the weeds before the Buddha Hall."

"Grass. On the following day, the assembly and the novices each prepared spades and mattocks to clear the weeds. The Master alone took a basin and filled it with water to wash his head; he knelt before the stone and shaved his hair.
When Touzi saw this, he laughed at him, and the Master then proceeded to shave his hair. There was once a monk who built a hut at the foot of the mountain.
For many years he did not shave his head and kept a long-handled ladle with which he drew water from the stream. At that time, another monk asked him:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The stream is deep and the handle of the ladle is long.
Upon hearing this, the Master remarked, "That is quite extraordinary. One day, taking his razor with him, he went to visit the master along with an attendant.

As soon as they met, he raised the previous conversation and asked, "Was that the words of the hut-master? The Master replied, "Yes. The Master said, "If you can speak [to this], I shall not shave your head."
The master shall then wash the disciple’s head, and the disciple shall kneel before the master with palms joined. The master shall immediately shave him.
Regarding the taking of medicine for illness, one must first inform the master.
[Commentary: Observing the master’s illness has already been seen in the preceding section; this states that when one is ill oneself, one must likewise report it to the master.
"Life. Not taking medicine, yet attaining the 'Middle Way'—this is a profound statement. It means that medicine must not be administered haphazardly;
one must first understand the origin of the illness and the roots of its deficiency or repletion, as well as the cold or warm nature of the medicine, before administering it.
This is impossible for anyone who has not extensively studied medical texts and possesses broad insight. Therefore, one must first report the excellence of the medical treatment to one's teacher."
One should not engage in improper deliberation. If one administers medicinal treatments without informing the teacher, it will instead increase the illness caused by the medicine;
therefore, when performing affairs for the Sangha, one must first inform the teacher.
[Commentary: Matters concerning the community of monks are precisely matters pertaining to the permanent property of the monastery (*sāṃghika*).
Those who wish to possess private items such as paper or pens should first inform their teacher.

[Commentary: In the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*), it is said: "Not treating wealth as one's own is the height of filial piety. In our fundamental Vinaya, not grasping gold is likewise the height of filial piety.
It is said: Although the gateways of the Confucian and Buddhist traditions differ, their establishment of the Dharma is the same.
If one gives away material goods as a gift, one should first inform the teacher and only then receive them. When giving away one's own possessions to others, one should first inform the teacher;
once the teacher has granted permission, one may then give them.

[Commentary: When others bestow things upon one, one should know what may be accepted and what may not. If one accepts what may be accepted but does not accept it, one blocks the gateway of giving and severs the path of goodness.
If one accepts what may not be accepted, it may lead to calamity and misfortune; the matter involved is no small one.

As for the giving away of one’s own possessions, there are cases where it cannot be avoided. Because one has a teacher, one must first inform him. When someone requests a loan from oneself, one should first inform the teacher;

only after the teacher grants permission should one give it. When one wishes to borrow an object from another person, one should first inform the teacher; only after the teacher grants permission may one go.
Whether the teacher grants or denies permission upon being informed, one must perform a prostration. If permission is denied, [one must not proceed].
One must not harbor any resentment. [Commentary:

One should act with resolute decisiveness. Merely follow the Master’s instructions; even if one has presented detailed proposals, if they are accepted, one should listen with joy, and if not accepted, there should be no [resentment].
Alas! Yet the way of serving one's teacher reaches its ultimate fulfillment.

This applies even to matters of great importance, whether traveling to other regions, attending lectures, joining the monastic assembly, guarding a mountain retreat, or undertaking projects for the sake of the Dharma.
All matters must be reported to one’s teacher; one must not act on one’s own authority. [Commentary:
It is impossible to enumerate all instances of ancient practitioners traveling to various regions to seek instruction, visiting masters, or dwelling in the mountains.
To mention a few examples: Shitou relied upon Qingyuan; Linji studied under Dayu; Fachang took up residence in the district of Meiwei; and Damei...
In the transmission of the seal of the mind’s essential principle, there are none who do not take the ancients as their model and follow the instructions of their teachers.

How could one imagine that those born in later generations, having only recently undergone tonsure and ordination, would immediately disparage the sages of old, acting recklessly and willfully without relying on the teacher’s guidance?
To study without selecting a teacher—how distant this is from antiquity! How tragic! [Commentary] *Āgama Sūtra*:

It is like three bundles of reeds standing on open ground; they remain upright only by leaning against one another. *Sanfang* (Visiting Teachers), Part 25. [Note] *Āgama Sūtra*: It is as if three bundles of reeds were set up in an empty space, supporting one another so that they may stand erect.
[The two] stand together; if one is removed, the other does not stand, and if the other is removed, the one does not stand.
*Línjiānlù* records that Huánglóng Nán said: "In the past, I traveled through Húnán with Wényuè. We saw a monk carrying his bundle on a pilgrimage.
Yuè was astonished and frowned, then rebuked him, saying: 'This is something from within your own inner chambers, yet you are unwilling to [let it go]...'"
"Put it down! To involve others in the burden of your debt—would that not be too much toil? (The Five Lamps records: A newly arrived monk prostrated before Muzhou;
just as he did so, Muzhou shouted, "Why, Ācārya, have you been stealing the monastery’s fruit to eat? The monk replied:
As soon as the student arrived, why did he say, "You have stolen a plum"? The Master said, "The stolen goods are still here. Gao'an said:

"My late teacher often remarked that when one travels on pilgrimage and crosses the mountain passes, there are many things at the smaller monasteries one visits that do not go according to one's wishes.
It was because I thought of how Fayen visited Dizang and Mingjiao met Shending that I suddenly felt no more affliction."
Also: At Qingliang Monastery in Jinling, Wenyi was frequently traveling on pilgrimage with Master Xiu and Master Wugong.
When they reached the region beyond Lake Huai in Xuzhou, it suddenly began to rain; the mountain streams swelled into torrents, and they were further hindered by snow at Dizang Monastery.
While attending the incense burner, Yaoshan said, "Where is the Senior Monk going? The Master replied, "I am traveling on pilgrimage.
Yaoshan asked, "What is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage? The Master said, "I do not know. Yaoshan said, "Not knowing is most intimate.

At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment, subsequently inheriting his Dharma and later founding the Fayan school. Shishu commented: "Since he said 'I do not know,' and yet [attained] sudden enlightenment..."
"What is it? The verse says: "Not knowing is most intimate; being intimate, one does not know. In the place where there is no knowing, there is neither knowing nor non-knowing.
Changqing ascended the hall and said: "If you bump into a fellow traveler on the path and pass each other shoulder-to-shoulder, the task of a lifetime of study is finished."
"A long journey requires a virtuous companion. [Commentary:
From the *Miaoxi Jingce* (Cautionary Verses of Mount Gui): "A long journey requires a virtuous companion; one's ears and eyes are repeatedly purified thereby.

When dwelling and stopping, one must choose one's associates; from time to time, one hears what was previously unheard. Thus it is said: 'Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who bring me to completion are my friends.'"
Regarding my friend: I have read the biography of Wei Jie throughout. To travel with Jie was like having a bright pearl at one's side; he illuminated those around him with his clarity.
As for a true companion, their character is upright and square, and every word and deed may be taken as a model; thus, we were together from morning until night.
He stands solemnly like a master stone-cutter or a venerable friend leading me forward.
When the minds of people in antiquity had not yet attained penetration, they would travel thousands of miles to seek a teacher.
[Commentary] That "the minds of people in antiquity had not yet attained penetration" is indeed true; by including the word "seek," one already possesses the eye upon one's feet. If one seeks...
If one lacks sincerity, what is the use of traveling even a thousand li?
Attachment: When young, one should be cautioned against superficiality and not permitted to travel far. Should one travel, one must not journey with those of improper character.
[Commentary]: The youth’s blood and qi are at their peak; lacking restraint, he possesses no power of meditative concentration. For this reason, long journeys were not permitted.
Yet, when circumstances leave no choice but to travel, one must select a virtuous friend as a companion. A "non-virtuous" person refers to one who does not cultivate the precepts and conduct.
Fearing that one might gradually be infected by such a person's influence, they should be rejected. As stated in the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*: "For example..."
There was a boar named Mahodara (Great Belly) who led a herd of boars into a deep mountain wilderness. Suddenly they encountered a lion.
Upon seeing the boar, the lion said, "I am the king of beasts; you must quickly clear the way. Mahodara replied, "For me to clear the way is impossible.
If you insist on fighting, wait while I put on my armor; I shall certainly not fail you. The lion asked, "What noble lineage do you belong to?"
He dared to challenge me to a fight. At that time, the Large-Bellied One went to a pit of filth, smeared his entire body with it, and returned before the lion to request a duel.
The lion said, "I am the king among all beasts; I constantly devour animals such as deer and roe for food.
Even those that are weak and inferior I cast aside and do not eat, let alone this impure and defiled body of yours. If I were to fight you, I would be stained."
"It defiles my body. The lion then spoke this verse to Mahodara: "Your body was originally impure; now it is further defiled by stench.
If you seek a fight with your mind, I shall immediately fall upon you. As the king observed, it was like a pig fighting a lion;
I am like the lion, and I shall first fall upon you. In the city of Puṣpapura, King Śatānīka possessed a white elephant.

It was capable of destroying enemies. When a person committed a crime, the king would have the elephant trample them to death. At one time, the elephant stable was consumed by fire, so the elephant was moved near a monastery.
There, it heard the monks reciting the *Dharmapada Sūtra*, which contained the verse: "By doing good, one is born in heaven; by doing evil, one enters the abyss.

Its mind immediately became gentle, and it gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion. Later, when the criminal was brought before it, the elephant merely sniffed him with its trunk and licked him with its tongue before letting him go. When the King saw this...
[The King] summoned his ministers. A minister reported: "This elephant has been hearing the Dharma near the temple, and that is why it is so.
If it were moved closer to the slaughterhouse, its cruelty would increase even further. One should know that the dispositions of all sentient beings are not fixed;

even animals are like this. Therefore, the wise ought to be aware of this: when one sees evil, it must be abandoned. This is the correct principle of the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals): for example, incense is fragrant."
"Grass. *Ryou* (yū) is a foul-smelling herb. If one mixes equal parts of incense and *ryou*, even after they have been stored together for ten years, the foul odor will still persist;
while the fragrance has vanished, the stench remains. This means that good cannot suppress evil, whereas evil can eliminate the good.

One must seek out teachers and inquire after the Way to resolve the matter of birth and death; it is not appropriate to merely gaze at mountains and play with waters, seeking only to travel far and wide to show off to others.
[Commentary] When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, throughout the twelve hours of the day, it is as if one were burdened by a heavy debt to another;

mountains are seen as not being mountains, and waters are seen as not being waters. Suddenly, when the critical barrier is shattered and the single eye is opened wide, mountains are once again mountains, and waters are once again waters.
Ultimately, what was seen before was not [the truth], yet it was perhaps not not [the truth]; as for what follows—
What you see is not necessarily what is. There are those who travel through prefectures and counties, admiring the mountains and waters;

their entire lives are turned by external conditions as they pursue them outwardly, boasting of their travels. Yet when asked about the actual matter of their travels, they have never even dreamed of it.

In the *Five Lamps* (Wudeng Huiyuan), it is recorded that one day Changsha was traveling through the mountains and, upon returning to the gate, the Head Seat asked him, "Where has the Master come from?"
Sha said, "At first he departs following the fragrant grasses; then he returns chasing the falling blossoms. Zuo said, "It is very much like the spirit of spring.
Sha said, "Yet it is even better than autumn dew dripping onto lotuses. Baofu and Changqing were traveling through the mountains. Baofu pointed with his finger and said:
"Right here is the summit of Mount Miaogao. Qingsong said, "It is so, it is so; yet what a pity! Xuedou added a comment:
"Today I am traveling the mountains with this fellow—what is the point? He further said, "In a hundred or a thousand years, it will not be said that there is none, but rather that there is little.
Later, he recounted this to Jingqing, who said, "If it were not for Master Sun, one would see nothing but skulls."
[The mountain] stretches across the fields. ◎ Yangshan asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Lushan. Yangshan said, "Have you ever visited Wulao Peak?
The monk said, "I have not been there. Yangshan said, "Dharma brother, you have never traveled the mountains. Yunmen said:
These words were all spoken out of compassion; they contain colloquial expressions from the countryside. ◎ Fenyang Wude Zhao stayed for only a short time at each place and did not enjoy sightseeing.
Some criticized him for lacking aesthetic refinement, to which he sighed, saying, "How vulgar are such remarks! Previously, when traveling on foot for practice (*xingde*), he had said:
It is precisely because the Sage’s mind has not yet fully penetrated [the truth] that he exerts himself in making decisive choices;
this is not for the sake of mountain scenery or water views. At whatever place one arrives, one must set down one's luggage and must not enter the hall directly.
One person shall look after the luggage while another enters first to inquire after the resident community and ascertain their instructions; only then may the luggage be settled and brought inside.
[Commentary: A Manual on Seeking Lodging. Do not wait until late before seeking lodging; enter the forest and listen for the evening bell. Upon reaching the gate, you must identify the host;

when inquiring after them, be composed and deliberate. You may spread out grass wherever you find it; under which sky is there no *zhuanpeng* (the floating gourd)? This night’s moon rests upon the roof beam.
This is merely to console my own indolence and negligence.
Section Twenty-Six: The Names and Characteristics of the Robe and Alms Bowl.
[Commentary] *Saṃghāṭa*. When the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, he was walking back and forth before the Indra Cave when he saw the furrows of a rice field.
The boundaries were clearly demarcated. He said to Ānanda, "The robes of the Buddhas of the past were of this appearance. From now on, let robes be fashioned according to this model.
[In the *Zenghui ji* (Record of Augmented Splendor): "Just as rice fields hold water to grow fine seedlings, thereby nourishing one's physical life," so too are these robes.
The field of the Dharma robes is moistened by the waters of the four benefits and causes the sprouts of the three virtues to flourish,
thereby nourishing the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.
When donning the kāṣāya robe, one should wish that all sentient beings have minds free from defilement and be endowed with the Way of the Great Sage.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*: "One who wears the *saṃghāṭī* abandons the three poisons. Regarding "the *kāṣāya* is noble because its color is not fixed":
this means it does not abide in [worldly] form (*rūpa*). To abide in form is not to have a "fixed" color; it is also called "dyeing. This signifies that form is dyed by the Dharma.

It is only when there is nothing to be stained that one may truly be said to be "dyed. However, the "dyeing" of the Two Vehicles is not true dyeing; one must have the mind dyed with the Mahāyāna for it to be so named.
True dye! True dye! This is the path of the Great Sage. For the sake of the True Dharma, one eliminates the fetters;
only then does one attain ultimate quiescence. One who dons this robe is called a renunciant; it is the garment of liberation.
The Five-Striped Robe.
[Commentary] Regarding its name and meaning: those who do not possess the marks of a field (i.e., those without the *kṣetra* characteristics) have all three robes as plain (*sama*) cloth.

When the Buddha-dharma reached this point—eighteen hundred years after [the Parinirvāṇa]—those who had left the household life did not yet know the method of cutting and piecing (*khaṇḍa-sīvana*), and thus wore only plain robes. This also applied to the precepts for laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*).

The Buddha prohibited the wearing of the *kṣetra-paṭa* (patchwork robe for the field of merit) and instead required the wearing of the *kṣānti-pūjā-vastra* (robe for prostration and repentance). This refers to the *maṇḍala-vastra* (plain robe) used for prostrations, repentances, and the recitation of sutras.
For the two groups of lay followers, the Buddha instructed them to provide offerings to the Triple Gem according to their own means and prohibited them from receiving the four requisites from others.
Since they are not the field of merit for sentient beings, he did not permit them to wear the patchwork *kṣetra-paṭa*.

Even if one has received the Bodhisattva precepts for leaving the household life, one should maintain the practice of keeping the three robes, the alms bowl, and the mendicant’s staff, and offer them before the Buddha.

Whenever one encounters ordained monks or nuns who lack these requisites, or those who have reached the age of ordination and require robes and bowls, one should give them whatever can be obtained through begging;
furthermore, one should provide new items for offering. As for oneself, one is permitted to wear a single plain robe (*maṇḍala-vāsaka*) while performing prostrations.

Regarding the recitation of mantras: it is not permitted to wear [the robe] while traveling through cities or villages; one should only put it on upon entering a monastery. Therefore, for those living at home, it is appropriate to be separated from the robe;

if they constantly wear it, they violate the regulations. For those who have left the home life, being separated from the robe is not permitted; if they are separated from it, they violate the regulations.
According to the *Ekottarakarmaśataka*, for those among the śrāmaṇeras, the *mantao* (single-layered robe) is their garment; yet some would suddenly don the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
This is a grave instance of unjust over-extension. According to the Vinaya, a śrāmaṇera wears only the five-piece robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*), which the Vinaya does not permit [for others].

Now, upon receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts, one must necessarily possess the three robes (*tricīvara*). If one lacks the means to provide them, the precepts should not be conferred. To do otherwise is to falsely establish a restrictive regulation.

To obstruct others from receiving the precepts is a transgression so grave that nothing surpasses it. Regarding the three robes prescribed in the Vinaya—possessing both their names and their substance, as well as their colors and measurements—even down to subtle matters such as the methods for their construction—I pray that you, who uphold both Chan and the Vinaya, will take these upon yourself.
Examine this carefully and instruct future students so that this Dharma does not perish.

It differs from the worlds of the ten directions. If one is a master of Chan, as soon as this is brought forth, one immediately perceives the functioning of the Dharmakāya, whether it be the Dharmakāya or not. Nevertheless, one must not say that this pure pitcher is itself the Dharmakāya.
Little do they realize that the measure of the Dharmakāya is equal to empty space; how much empty space can this very pitcher contain?
How much is the Dharmakāya? Even if one were to accommodate ten billion Mount Sumerus and ten billion seas of fragrant water, it would ultimately never be fully contained.

As for the Dharmakāya of empty space, even if someone were to say that the seas of fragrance and so forth have already been fully accommodated, what difficulty would there be in fully accommodating the Dharmakāya of empty space?
I admire his audacity! But tell me: when empty space is fully accommodated, what remains outside the Dharmakāya?

The "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom; it does not arise from..."
He attained enlightenment. This was because all phenomena are but mind. From the mountains and rivers to the great earth, every form and color is nothing other than the manifestation of my own mind;
they are all annotations of the mind. The Great Canon of over seven thousand scrolls and the seventeen hundred public cases are nothing other than the elucidation of my own mind;
they too are annotations of the mind. Thus, one is able to awaken to the mind.

As for this, even the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other scriptures would be considered redundant; how much more so the *Śrāmaṇera Vinaya*. Even the various records concerning the transmission of the lamp are merely stale words;
